sec.1.title: Reading the Network — How the Connections Work
sec.1.html:
The defining feature of this ecosystem is that musicians constantly move between bands. There are four kinds of connection:

  • Direct member migration: a musician leaves band A and founds or joins band B (e.g. Greg Lake: King Crimson → ELP).
  • Origin chain: the early bands a musician passed through before reaching prog (e.g. Steve Howe: Syndicats → Tomorrow → Bodast → Yes).
  • Shared sound source: drawing on the same aesthetic roots (Mellotron textures, shifting time signatures, classical form); this ties the later generations (neo-prog, the '90s) back to the old backbone.
  • Supergroup / bridge nodes: projects that join several universes (UK, Asia, GTR, ABWH, World Trade) — the "junctions" of the network.

The central backbone of the network and its reach into later generations:

[ROOTS]                     [PROTO]
Syndicats/Tomorrow/Bodast    The Nice ──► ELP ◄── KING CRIMSON ──► Foreigner / Bad Co / UK
        │                                     │                          │
        ▼                                     ▼                          ▼
       YES ◄───────────── Asia / GTR ──► GENESIS ───► Gabriel / Collins / Hackett
        │                    ▲                │
        ▼                    │                ▼
   ABWH (1989)          (Howe junction)   [NEO-PROG]
        │                                 Marillion / IQ / Pallas / Pendragon
        ▼
   [90s US RENAISSANCE]
   World Trade / Spock's Beard / Echolyn  ◄── (Yes + Genesis + GG synthesis)

A four-generation timeline:

  1. First wave (1967–1976): the genre is founded. King Crimson, Yes, ELP, Genesis, Canterbury.
  2. Transition and commercialisation (1977–1983): supergroups (UK, Asia), pressure from punk, the drift towards AOR.
  3. Second wave / renaissance (1981–1995): neo-prog (UK) and the American symphonic-prog revival — a generation that recreated the old sound with modern production.
  4. Fourth wave (1995–2020): modern prog led by Porcupine Tree and Steven Wilson; supergroups such as Transatlantic and Flying Colors; prog metal with Dream Theater. Members of the classic generation (Fripp, Hackett, Anderson, Levin, Lifeson) reappear as guests on the new generation's albums, and 5.1 remixes of classic albums link the two eras.

The 1995–2020 expansion — new territory

In this version the atlas extends to 2020. The major bands (Yes, King Crimson, Genesis, Pink Floyd, ELP, Jethro Tull, Rush, Camel, Gentle Giant, Van der Graaf Generator, Marillion) now have discographies divided into eras, with line-ups, production credits, key details and listening priorities. The badges on album rows show listening priority: ★ Essential (never skip), Recommended, Optional, Secondary, Skippable. The ★ Essential filter at the top shows only the essential albums.

The Yes discography comes from a dedicated listening-notes module (with critics' notes and context from Edward Macan's Rocking the Classics); that module runs up to 2026.
sec.2.title: Roots: Early Pre-Prog Bands (1963–1969)
sec.2.intro: This section holds the network's "invisible roots". Before reaching prog, the future stars learned their trade in R&B, beat and psychedelia bands. These groups are usually remembered for a single or a shelved album, but they carry the network's DNA.
grp.the-syndicats.kurulus: 1963, North London. An R&B/beat trio recorded by the legendary producer Joe Meek. The first professional band of a 17-year-old Steve Howe.
grp.the-syndicats.dna: Chuck Berry-flavoured R&B; the seed of Howe's love of country and rockabilly tones.
grp.the-syndicats.uyeler: Howe (guitar), Tom Ladd (vocals) and others; Howe left in 1965.
grp.the-syndicats.gecisler: Howe → The In Crowd → Tomorrow → Bodast → Yes.
grp.tomorrow.kurulus: The In Crowd (a soul/covers band) turned psychedelic in 1967 and renamed itself Tomorrow. A brilliant but short-lived band of the London psychedelic scene.
grp.tomorrow.dna: English psychedelia: fuzz guitar, kaleidoscopic production, childlike surrealism. The first laboratory for Howe's experimental guitar language.
grp.tomorrow.uyeler: Keith West (vocals), Steve Howe (guitar), John "Twink" Alder (drums), John Wood (bass). Shared stages with Pink Floyd and jammed with Hendrix.
grp.tomorrow.gecisler: Before → The In Crowd. After → Keith West's solo singles; Howe → Bodast.
alb.tomorrow-1968-tomorrow.an: Their only album. Contains psychedelic classics such as "My White Bicycle" and "Real Life Permanent Dream"; even at this early stage Howe's guitar shows prog's structural curiosity. A commercial failure that became a cult record.
alb.tomorrow-1968-tomorrow.tr: My White Bicycle — psychedelic classic inspired by the Provo movement, with backwards guitar effects
Real Life Permanent Dream — Howe's fuzz guitar and sitar textures
Revolution — the rebellious spirit of the era, sung by Keith West
grp.bodast.kurulus: 1968, the trio Howe formed after Tomorrow (briefly also called "Canto"). Howe's closest early project to prog.
grp.bodast.dna: The core of early British prog — extended forms and melodic guitar figures. Howe's pre-Yes "missing link".
grp.bodast.uyeler: Steve Howe (guitar) with Clive Skinner, Bobby Clarke and Dave Curtiss. The album was shelved when the record label went bankrupt.
grp.bodast.gecisler: After Bodast split, Howe auditioned for The Nice and Jethro Tull (neither worked out), then joined Yes in 1970.
alb.bodast-1981-the-bodast-tapes.an: Session recordings that stayed unreleased for years. Tracks such as "Nether Street" already hint at the chord colours later heard in Yes.
alb.bodast-1981-the-bodast-tapes.tr: Nether Street — carries the chord colours later heard in Yes
grp.the-strawbs-wakeman-koku.name: The Strawbs (Wakeman's roots)
grp.the-strawbs-wakeman-koku.kurulus: Mid-1960s, London; folk-rock origins. Rick Wakeman played here before joining Yes.
grp.the-strawbs-wakeman-koku.hikaye: Founded by Dave Cousins in 1964 as the bluegrass band Strawberry Hill Boys, the group evolved from folk to folk-prog. Sandy Denny briefly sang with them; Rick Wakeman's keyboards in 1970–71 pushed the band towards prog and sent Wakeman on to Yes. 'Part of the Union' (1973) became a hit that turned into a trade-union anthem. Under Cousins' leadership the band began recording again with its classic line-up in the 2000s.
grp.the-strawbs-wakeman-koku.dna: English folk-rock plus increasingly elaborate keyboard ornamentation. A showcase for Wakeman's organ and Mellotron skills.
grp.the-strawbs-wakeman-koku.etki: The station that carried Wakeman to Yes.
alb.the-strawbs-1970-dragonfly.tr: Dragonfly — title track, pastoral English folk
Josephine, For Better or For Worse
alb.the-strawbs-1970-just-a-collection-o: A turning-point record that put Wakeman's keyboard virtuosity in the spotlight — and on Yes's radar.
The Antique Suite — multi-part suite, a showcase for Wakeman's keyboards
Temperament of Mind — Wakeman's instrumental solo showpiece
Where Is This Dream of Your Youth
Wakeman's last Strawbs album; he then moved on to Yes's Fragile.
A Glimpse of Heaven — Cousins' pastoral songwriting
The Hangman and the Papist — dramatic folk narrative
Sheep — one of Wakeman's last Strawbs contributions
alb.the-strawbs-1972-grave-new-world.an: Post-Wakeman, the peak of folk-prog with Blue Weaver's Mellotron; Cousins' religious and existential lyrics.
alb.the-strawbs-1973-bursting-at-the-sea: The band's commercial peak, with the hits 'Part of the Union' and 'Lay Down'.
alb.the-strawbs-1974-hero-and-heroine.an: The most 'prog' Strawbs album, with John Hawken's Mellotron and Dave Lambert's guitar; a concept about the collapse of a relationship.
alb.the-strawbs-2017-the-ferryman-s-curs: A strong late-period album with a line-up close to the classic era, long narrative pieces and Mellotron textures.
sec.3.title: Proto-Prog (1967–1970)
grp.the-nice.kurulus: 1967, London. Formed as P.P. Arnold's backing band, it quickly went its own way. Keith Emerson's aggressive Hammond technique and classical adaptations drew prog's earliest template.
grp.the-nice.dna: Rock adaptations of classical works (Bach, Sibelius, Bernstein); the organ as lead instrument; stage violence (Emerson stabbing knives into the organ).
grp.the-nice.uyeler: Keith Emerson (organ), Lee Jackson (bass/vocals), Brian Davison (drums), David O'List (guitar; left early — an intriguing junction: Howe played one night with The Nice in O'List's place but didn't stay). After O'List left, the trio became organ-centred.
grp.the-nice.gecisler: Before → Gary Farr & The T-Bones, VIP's. After → ELP (Emerson), Jackson & Davison's Refugee.
grp.the-nice.etki: The direct prototype of ELP. The ancestor of the entire "keyboard-centred prog" movement.
alb.the-nice-1968-the-thoughts-of-emerli: The first balance between psychedelia and classical adaptation. The last trace of O'List's guitar; the organ is not yet the only dominant voice. The album where the band asks "what could we become?"
Rondo — organ-rock adaptation of Dave Brubeck's 'Blue Rondo', the band's emblem
The Thoughts of Emerlist Davjack — title track, psychedelia
The title suite is the first serious attempt to fuse rock and orchestration. The section with Davison's drum solo anticipates ELP's future bombast.
Ars Longa Vita Brevis — orchestra-and-rock suite including a Davison drum solo
Daddy, Where Did I Come From?
alb.the-nice-1969-nice.an: Gained both scandal and identity through a provocative adaptation of Bernstein's "America" (with a vocal protest). Their most 'rock' album, bringing live energy into the studio.
alb.the-nice-1969-nice.tr: She Belongs to Me — Dylan adaptation
alb.the-nice-1970-five-bridges.an: The Newcastle symphonic suite: a full-length concert work with orchestra. The "rock + classical form" synthesis Emerson would take into ELP peaks here; the band's farewell recording.
alb.the-nice-1970-five-bridges.tr: Five Bridges Suite — the Newcastle symphonic suite, with orchestra
Intermezzo from the Karelia Suite — Sibelius adaptation
Country Pie / Brandenburg Concerto No. 6 — a Dylan-plus-Bach montage
grp.procol-harum.kurulus: 1967, Southend. Exploded with "A Whiter Shade of Pale"; a fusion of Bach-inspired organ and soul vocals.
grp.procol-harum.hikaye: Born out of the Southend R&B band The Paramounts, Procol Harum brought together Gary Brooker's piano and vocals, Keith Reid's poetic lyrics and Matthew Fisher's Hammond organ. 'A Whiter Shade of Pale' (1967), with its Bach-inspired organ line, became one of the best-selling singles of all time; Fisher's 2009 win in the royalty lawsuit set a precedent in music law. Robin Trower's blues guitar and orchestral experiments (the 1972 live album with the Edmonton Symphony Orchestra) made the band one of prog's pioneers. Brooker died in 2022.
grp.procol-harum.dna: Baroque organ, gospel/soul vocals, literary lyrics. The organ-rock bridge.
grp.procol-harum.uyeler: Gary Brooker (vocals/piano), Matthew Fisher (organ), Robin Trower (guitar; later a solo blues-rock career). Keith Reid wrote the lyrics (a core non-performing member).
grp.procol-harum.gecisler: Before → The Paramounts. After → Robin Trower's solo career.
grp.procol-harum.etki: An early populariser of organ-based prog; a pioneer of orchestra-rock collaboration.
alb.procol-harum-1967-procol-harum.an: A fusion of baroque pop and rock; overshadowed by "A Whiter Shade of Pale" but full of solid songs such as "Conquistador".
alb.procol-harum-1967-procol-harum.tr: A Whiter Shade of Pale — Bach-inspired organ, a proto-monument of the genre
Conquistador — dramatic narrative (its orchestral version later became a hit)
Repent Walpurgis — instrumental, Fisher's organ showcase
"In Held 'Twas in I" is a 17-minute multi-part suite — one of the first side-long concept pieces in British prog.
In Held 'Twas in I — 17-minute multi-part suite, the first great prog form
alb.procol-harum-1969-a-salty-dog.an: Produced by Fisher; orchestral breadth and seafaring melancholy on the title track. The band's best-loved album.
alb.procol-harum-1969-a-salty-dog.tr: A Salty Dog — orchestral seafaring melancholy, the band's best-loved song
alb.procol-harum-1970-home.an: Trower's guitar comes to the fore; darker and bluesier.
alb.procol-harum-1970-home.tr: Whaling Stories — a dark epic with Trower's guitar
Trower's last album; a shift towards hard rock.
Power Failure — includes a drum solo
alb.procol-harum-1972-procol-harum-live-: A live album recorded in Canada with orchestra and choir; with 'Conquistador' it became the band's biggest American success.
Essential — one of the most successful meetings of rock and orchestra.
alb.procol-harum-1973-grand-hotel.an: Orchestral grandeur produced by Chris Thomas; Mick Grabham on guitar.
alb.procol-harum-1991-the-prodigal-stran: The comeback album that reunited Brooker, Fisher, Trower and Reid after fourteen years.
alb.procol-harum-2017-novum.an: Made for the band's 50th anniversary, with lyrics by Pete Brown instead of Keith Reid; Brooker's last studio album.
grp.moody-blues.kurulus: Started in 1964 as an R&B band; became a symbol of prog with Days of Future Passed in 1967. The band that brought the Mellotron into rock.
grp.moody-blues.hikaye: Starting out as a Birmingham R&B band with the 1964 hit 'Go Now', the Moody Blues fused orchestra and rock on Days of Future Passed (1967) after Justin Hayward and John Lodge joined, making the first great symphonic rock album. Mike Pinder's Mellotron defined the texture of the 'Core Seven' albums (1967–72). A hiatus in 1974–77 was followed by an '80s synth-pop period with Patrick Moraz. They were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 2018.
grp.moody-blues.dna: Mellotron textures, orchestral concepts, cosmic/poetic lyrics.
grp.moody-blues.etki: Through its Mellotron aesthetic it anticipated the atmosphere of King Crimson and Genesis.
alb.moody-blues-1967-days-of-future-pass: A concept album about the cycle of a day, recorded with the London Festival Orchestra. With "Nights in White Satin" it is considered the year zero of the orchestral rock concept album.
Nights in White Satin — Mellotron-and-orchestra ballad, the genre's year zero
alb.moody-blues-1968-in-search-of-the-lo: The orchestra is dropped; this time the band builds the layers itself with Mellotron, sitar and wind instruments. A more "hand-made" psychedelic prog.
Legend of a Mind — Timothy Leary theme, flute and Mellotron
alb.moody-blues-1969-on-the-threshold-of: A matured cosmic/inner concept; number one in the UK.
Never Comes the Day — Mellotron ballad
Have You Heard / The Voyage — concept closing suite
alb.moody-blues-1969-to-our-children-s-c: Themed around the space race; their most ambitious studio production.
Higher and Higher — dramatic space-race opener
alb.moody-blues-1970-a-question-of-balan: Simpler, so it could be played on stage; "Question" became a hit.
alb.moody-blues-1971-every-good-boy-dese: Among the closing albums of the classic seven-album period.
The Story in Your Eyes — the band's hardest-rocking song
Procession — opener tracing the evolution of sound
alb.moody-blues-1972-seventh-sojourn.tr: I'm Just a Singer (In a Rock and Roll Band) — Lodge's self-critical hit
Isn't Life Strange — Lodge's orchestral ballad
alb.moody-blues-1978-octave.an: The comeback after the hiatus; Pinder's last album, recorded under difficult circumstances.
alb.moody-blues-1981-long-distance-voyag: The first album with Patrick Moraz; number one in the US. A successful move into the '80s with 'The Voice' and 'Gemini Dream'.
The arrival of Patrick Moraz from Yes joins two universes.
alb.moody-blues-1999-strange-times.an: A warm comeback a decade later, close to the band's root sound.
alb.moody-blues-2003-december.an: The band's last studio album: Christmas and winter themes; the first without Ray Thomas.
grp.the-crazy-world-of-arthur-brown-king: 1967, London. Founded by Arthur Brown (born 1942, Whitby).

With his flaming helmet, face paint and four-octave voice, Brown was a pioneer of rock theatre; 'Fire' (1968) went to number one in the UK. The band's first album was produced by Kit Lambert with Pete Townshend of The Who. Crazy World's drummer Carl Palmer (later Atomic Rooster and ELP) and keyboard player Vincent Crane (founder of Atomic Rooster) make it the hidden root of the ELP universe. In the '70s, with Kingdom Come, he made experimental prog that brought the Bentley Rhythm Ace (one of the first drum machines) onto the stage. His influence on Alice Cooper, Kiss, Peter Gabriel and George Clinton is considerable. He played the priest in Ken Russell's film 'Tommy'.
Theatrical vocals (operatic screams), Hammond-heavy psychedelic soul; later mystical prog with electronic rhythms.
Crazy World (Vincent Crane, Carl Palmer, Drachen Theaker) → Atomic Rooster (Crane, Palmer) → ELP (Palmer); Kingdom Come; guest vocals with Hawkwind and the Alan Parsons Project.
The ancestor of shock rock and prog theatre; the junction leading to Atomic Rooster and ELP.
alb.arthur-brown-1968-the-crazy-world-of: Hellfire-and-apocalypse psychedelic soul dominated by Hammond organ. Side one was conceived as a concept suite.
Essential — one of proto-prog's key records.
Arthur Brown, Vincent Crane, Drachen Theaker (+ Carl Palmer on tour)
I Put a Spell on You
alb.arthur-brown-1971-galactic-zoo-dossi: The first album as Kingdom Come: political satire, science fiction and psychedelic chaos.
alb.arthur-brown-1973-journey.an: Kingdom Come's peak: a pioneer of electronic prog with the Bentley Rhythm Ace drum machine, VCS3 synth and Mellotron.
alb.arthur-brown-1973-journey.oncelik: Recommended — a hidden classic of electronic prog.
alb.arthur-brown-1973-journey.detay: One of the first rock albums on which a drum machine handles all the drumming.
grp.pearls-before-swine.kurulus: 1965, Melbourne, Florida. Tom Rapp's folk-psychedelic project.
grp.pearls-before-swine.hikaye: With Tom Rapp's soft, lisping voice and his anti-war, mystical lyrics, Pearls Before Swine became one of the strangest and most enduring bands of American psychedelic folk through its first two albums for ESP-Disk (a free-jazz label). The Bosch ('The Garden of Earthly Delights') cover of the debut and the Bruegel ('The Triumph of Death') cover of Balaklava became the band's visual identity. The group gradually turned into Rapp's solo project; in the late '70s he left music, became a lawyer and worked on civil-rights cases. He released a comeback album, A Journal of the Plague Year, in 1999 and died in 2018.
grp.pearls-before-swine.dna: Acoustic folk, sitar, organ and sound collages; a dream state somewhere between Leonard Cohen and Syd Barrett.
grp.pearls-before-swine.gecisler: Tom Rapp → solo; influence: Current 93, Damien Jurado and the freak-folk generation of the 2000s.
grp.pearls-before-swine.etki: A key node of American psych-folk; related to English pastoral prog (Trespass, the Incredible String Band).
alb.pearls-before-swine-1967-one-nation-: The debut on ESP-Disk, one of the label's best-selling records; anti-war, mystical folk-psychedelia with a cover detail from Bosch's 'The Garden of Earthly Delights'.
(Oh Dear) Miss Morse — spells F-U-C-K in Morse code
alb.pearls-before-swine-1968-balaklava.a: A concept album on the futility of war, referencing the Charge of the Light Brigade in the Crimean War, built with old recordings and sound collages. Cover: Bruegel's 'The Triumph of Death'.
alb.pearls-before-swine-1968-balaklava.d: Includes a fragment of Florence Nightingale's voice, recorded in 1890.
alb.pearls-before-swine-1969-these-thing: The move to Reprise; a sparer, more acoustic folk album.
grp.aphrodite-s-child.kurulus: 1967, Athens. Vangelis (Evangelos Papathanassiou), Demis Roussos and Loukas Sideras.
grp.aphrodite-s-child.hikaye: Fleeing the pressure of the Greek junta, the trio set off for London but, stuck in Paris because of work-permit problems, scored a huge European pop hit during the events of May 1968 with 'Rain and Tears' (based on Pachelbel's Canon). But Vangelis's real interest was experimental music: the double album 666, built on the Book of Revelation, was recorded while the band was falling apart and became one of prog's cult works. Roussos went on to become a worldwide pop singer, and Vangelis a legendary electronic composer with the scores for Chariots of Fire and Blade Runner.
grp.aphrodite-s-child.dna: Baroque pop, Greek melody, psychedelic rock, then avant-garde sound collages.
grp.aphrodite-s-child.gecisler: The Forminx (Vangelis) / Idols (Roussos) → Aphrodite's Child → Vangelis solo, Jon & Vangelis; Demis Roussos solo; Silver Koulouris (guitar).
grp.aphrodite-s-child.etki: An early classic of continental European prog; 666 is the prototype of the apocalyptic concept album.
alb.aphrodite-s-child-1968-end-of-the-wo: An album of baroque pop and psychedelic ballads; sold millions in Europe on the strength of 'Rain and Tears'.
alb.aphrodite-s-child-1969-it-s-five-o-c: Baroque pop matures, with the hits 'I Want to Live' and 'It's Five O'Clock'.
alb.aphrodite-s-child-1972-666.an: A double concept album based on the Revelation of St John, conceived by Costas Ferris. The label delayed its release because of Irene Papas's screams on 'Infinity', depicting a sexual and spiritual climax; the first great document of Vangelis's experimental genius.
alb.aphrodite-s-child-1972-666.oncelik: Essential — a cult masterpiece of European prog.
alb.aphrodite-s-child-1972-666.detay: The band had already split by the time the album came out.
sec.17.title: The Hard Rock Fringe — Blues and Heavy Rock Neighbours
sec.17.intro: Blues-rock and hard rock bands born in the same clubs as prog and sharing its musicians: Ten Years After, Deep Purple, Uriah Heep (Ken Hensley, John Wetton), Wishbone Ash, Budgie and Rainbow (Cozy Powell, later of Emerson, Lake & Powell).
grp.ten-years-after.kurulus: 1966, Nottingham. Alvin Lee (guitar/vocals), Leo Lyons (bass), Ric Lee (drums), Chick Churchill (keyboards).
grp.ten-years-after.hikaye: Alvin Lee's reputation as 'the fastest guitarist in the world' made the band one of the leading British blues-rock acts; their 1969 Woodstock performance of 'I'm Going Home' and its place in the film turned them into international stars. Although rooted in blues, their jazz, psychedelic and progressive experiments (Ssssh, Cricklewood Green, A Space in Time) place them on the blues wing of proto-prog. They split in 1974 and reunited in 1988. Alvin Lee left in 2003 and died in 2013; the band continued with Joe Gooch and later Marcus Bonfanti.
grp.ten-years-after.dna: Fast blues guitar, jazz swing, psychedelic sound effects and long improvisations.
grp.ten-years-after.gecisler: The Jaybirds → Ten Years After → Alvin Lee solo (Ten Years Later); Leo Lyons → Hundred Seventy Split.
grp.ten-years-after.etki: A bridge from British blues-rock to hard rock and jam-band culture; prog's blues-heavy periphery.
alb.ten-years-after-1968-undead.an: A live album recorded at London's Klooks Kleek club; jazz-heavy improvisations and the first version of 'I'm Going Home'.
alb.ten-years-after-1969-stonedhenge.an: An experimental second studio album full of studio effects, with a short solo piece from each member.
alb.ten-years-after-1969-ssssh.an: The hard, focused blues-rock album of the Woodstock year.
alb.ten-years-after-1970-cricklewood-gre: Considered the band's peak, with psychedelic and progressive touches; 'Love Like a Man' was a UK hit.
alb.ten-years-after-1971-a-space-in-time: Acoustic colours and 'I'd Love to Change the World' made this the band's biggest US success.

1. King Crimson → the node that exported the most members (ELP, Foreigner, Bad Company, UK, Asia; and through Belew/Levin into the '80s and beyond).
2. Yes ⇄ Genesis → the two poles of symphonic prog; their members meet in Asia and GTR.
3. Asia → the classic "super-junction" where the ELP, Yes, King Crimson and Genesis universes meet at a single point; in 2017, through Sherwood, it also connects to the World Trade universe.
4. ABWH → the "inner junction" where Yes temporarily reunited within itself; it dissolved back into the main body with Union.
5. Steve Howe → a junction in his own right: from the Tomorrow/Bodast roots to Yes, and from there through Asia and GTR, a figure who travels across four universes.
6. Billy Sherwood / World Trade → the bridge joining the classic backbone to the '90s American renaissance; connected to Yes and Asia through both sound and membership.
7. Transatlantic (1999) → the network's late mega-junction, gathering the nodes of neo-prog (Trewavas from Marillion), the American renaissance (Morse from Spock's Beard), Scandinavian prog (Stolt from the Flower Kings) and prog metal (Portnoy from Dream Theater) at a single point.

Scope: 1967–2020 (main scale; the Yes module extends to 2026), mainly the Anglo-American ecosystem, with continental European and Scandinavian branches. Axes of connection: origin chain + shared sound + member migration + supergroup junctions. By bringing in the early roots (Tomorrow, Bodast, Syndicats, Strawbs), the inner junctions (ABWH) and the later generations (the neo-prog wave, the American renaissance and the modern era), the atlas offers a network-based map of progressive rock.

sec.13.title: The American & Space-Rock Expansion
sec.13.intro: The network's transatlantic and space-rock wing. These bands connect to the main backbone mostly not through direct member migration but through shared sound (symphonic prog forms, long suites, virtuosity) and a shared era. Kansas represents American symphonic prog, Rush is the giant node that carried prog into the power-trio format, and Hawkwind is the core of British space rock. Alongside them are Happy the Man and Pavlov's Dog from the US and Nektar, an English band formed in Germany.
grp.kansas.kurulus: 1973, Topeka, Kansas. America's most successful symphonic prog band; it blended European prog with American hard rock and country. One of the rare prog bands with a violin.
grp.kansas.hikaye: The band from Topeka, Kansas, combined the boogie-rock energy of the American Midwest with English symphonic prog and Robby Steinhardt's violin. Kerry Livgren's philosophical lyrics reached millions with 'Carry On Wayward Son' and 'Dust in the Wind'. Livgren's and Steve Walsh's turn to Christianity created internal tensions in the '80s; Steve Morse (Dixie Dregs) played guitar from 1986 to 1989. Walsh left in 2014 and was replaced by Ronnie Platt; The Prelude Implicit (2016) was a strong comeback.
grp.kansas.dna: American symphonic prog: European long-form structure + violin + hard guitar + strong vocal harmonies + American radio-rock accessibility. Livgren's philosophical and spiritual lyrics.
grp.kansas.uyeler: Steve Walsh (vocals/keyboards), Kerry Livgren (guitar/keyboards/composer), Robby Steinhardt (violin/vocals — the band's signature), Rich Williams (guitar), Dave Hope (bass), Phil Ehart (drums).
grp.kansas.gecisler: Before → local Topeka bands (White Clover). Livgren later turned to Christian rock (AD). Linked to Yes/ELP through shared sound, and to Curved Air through the violin.
grp.kansas.etki: The band that took prog into American stadiums; 'Carry On Wayward Son' and 'Dust in the Wind' are among the genre's best-known songs. A pioneer of American prog (Spock's Beard included).
alb.kansas-1974-kansas.an: The debut; the first synthesis of European prog and American rock. Steinhardt's violin establishes the identity from the start.
alb.kansas-1975-song-for-america.an: The title track is a 10-minute environmental suite; the band's long-form ambition becomes clear.
alb.kansas-1975-masque.an: Harder and darker; Livgren's compositional ambition approaches its peak.
alb.kansas-1976-leftoverture.an: The band's big breakthrough and masterpiece; 'Carry On Wayward Son' is a huge hit. A perfect balance of symphonic structure and radio accessibility.
alb.kansas-1976-leftoverture.tr: Carry On Wayward Son — one of the genre's best-known anthems
alb.kansas-1977-point-of-know-return.an: The successor to Leftoverture; the acoustic ballad 'Dust in the Wind' is one of America's best-known songs. The commercial and artistic peak.
alb.kansas-1977-point-of-know-return.tr: Dust in the Wind — acoustic/violin ballad, huge hit
Point of Know Return — title track
alb.kansas-1979-monolith.an: One of the classic line-up's last strong albums; Livgren's spiritual search shows in the lyrics.
alb.kansas-1986-power.an: Harder, AOR/hard-rock-oriented album with Steve Morse on guitar; the hit 'All I Wanted'.
alb.kansas-1986-power.detay: Steve Morse later joined Deep Purple — a junction in the network.
alb.kansas-2000-somewhere-to-elsewhere.a: A one-off reunion of the classic line-up, with all songs written by Livgren.
alb.kansas-2000-somewhere-to-elsewhere.d: 'Icarus II' is the sequel to 1975's 'Icarus – Borne on Wings of Steel'.
alb.kansas-2016-the-prelude-implicit.an: The first album by the new line-up with Ronnie Platt and David Manion; a comeback after 16 years, faithful to the symphonic roots.
grp.rush.kurulus: 1968/1974, Toronto, Canada. One of the most influential prog bands in power-trio format; starting from hard rock, they evolved into increasingly complex prog. The identity settled when Neil Peart joined in 1974.
grp.rush.hikaye: Formed in suburban Toronto in 1968 by school friends Alex Lifeson and John Rutsey; Geddy Lee soon took over bass and vocals. After a Led Zeppelin-influenced debut (1974), Rutsey left for health reasons and was replaced by Neil Peart, whose technical mastery and philosophical lyrics would define the band's character. Themes ranging from Ayn Rand to science fiction turned into a commercial breakthrough with 2112 (1976). After Hemispheres they dropped long suites for short but complex songs; Moving Pictures (1981) was the peak. In the '80s they entered a synth-heavy period and in the '90s returned to a guitar-centred sound. In 1997–98 Peart lost his daughter and his wife ten months apart, and the band fell silent for five years; Vapor Trails (2002) came after Peart returned from a long motorcycle journey. Clockwork Angels (2012) was the band's last album and the R40 tour (2015) its last concerts. Peart died of brain cancer in January 2020.
grp.rush.dna: Power-trio prog: Geddy Lee's high vocals and lead bass, Lifeson's textured guitar, Peart's technical drumming and philosophical (Ayn Rand, science fiction) lyrics. The art of drawing an orchestra out of a trio.
grp.rush.uyeler: Geddy Lee (vocals/bass/keyboards), Alex Lifeson (guitar), Neil Peart (drums/lyricist — joined 1974). A rare band in which three virtuosos carry equal weight.
grp.rush.gecisler: The first drummer, John Rutsey, left after the first album → Neil Peart. Linked through shared sound to Yes (long suites), Cream (power trio) and King Crimson (complexity); the direct ancestor of prog metal (Dream Theater).
grp.rush.etki: The bridge that carried prog to the hard-rock audience; a direct inspiration for prog metal (Dream Theater, Tool). The model of a balanced trio of virtuosos.
grp.rush.ipucu: Divide Rush into phases: hard rock (1974–75), long suites (1976–78), short-but-complex songs (1980–84), the synth period (1985–89), and the return to guitar (1991–2012).
Listen to Geddy Lee's bass lines separately; remember he played them while singing and working keyboard pedals at the same time.
Peart's lyrics (individualism, technology, fate) link the albums; Clockwork Angels is a complete novel of these themes.
grp.rush.era.0.note: Zeppelin influence, Peart's arrival and the first conceptual attempts.
grp.rush.era.1.note: 2112 and the Cygnus X-1 cycle: the peak of the long form.
grp.rush.era.2.note: Short but complex songs, reggae and new wave touches.
grp.rush.era.3.note: Bright '80s production with keyboards to the fore.
grp.rush.era.4.t: Return to guitar and the final period
grp.rush.era.4.note: Adapting to the alternative-rock era, Peart's tragedy, Vapor Trails and Clockwork Angels.
alb.rush-1974-rush.an: The only album with John Rutsey; Led Zeppelin-heavy blues-hard rock. Airplay of 'Working Man' on Cleveland radio caught Mercury's attention.
alb.rush-1975-fly-by-night.an: The first album with Peart; the lyrics and complexity deepen. The start of the move from hard rock to prog.
alb.rush-1975-fly-by-night.detay: 'By-Tor and the Snow Dog' is the band's first long narrative piece.
alb.rush-1975-fly-by-night.tr: By-Tor and the Snow Dog — first long-form narrative piece
alb.rush-1975-caress-of-steel.an: The album on which they first moved to long forms with 'The Fountain of Lamneth' and 'The Necromancer', but which flopped commercially; the band themselves refer to the following tour as the 'down the tubes' tour.
alb.rush-1976-2112.an: The band's breakthrough masterpiece; a 20-minute dystopian science-fiction suite filling side one. Made in defiance of label pressure, a symbol of prog courage.
alb.rush-1976-2112.detay: While the label wanted a more commercial album, the band answered with a 20-minute dystopia and saved its career.
Peart dedicated the album to 'the genius of Ayn Rand'.
alb.rush-1976-2112.tr: 2112 — 20-minute, seven-part dystopian suite (dedicated to Ayn Rand)
alb.rush-1977-a-farewell-to-kings.an: More refined and atmospheric; keyboard and acoustic textures broaden. 'Xanadu' is a long epic after Coleridge's poem.
alb.rush-1977-a-farewell-to-kings.detay: Recorded at Rockfield Studios in Wales.
'Closer to the Heart' was the band's first UK hit; 'Cygnus X-1' is a journey into a black hole.
alb.rush-1977-a-farewell-to-kings.tr: Closer to the Heart — the band's emblematic song
alb.rush-1978-hemispheres.an: The band's most complex, most 'prog' album; side one is a single 18-minute suite. The technical peak.
alb.rush-1978-hemispheres.detay: 'La Villa Strangiato' is a 12-part instrumental born of Lifeson's nightmares.
alb.rush-1978-hemispheres.tr: Cygnus X-1 Book II: Hemispheres — 18-minute suite
La Villa Strangiato — instrumental technical showcase
alb.rush-1980-permanent-waves.an: Carrying prog into tighter, radio-friendly forms; 'The Spirit of Radio' is the bridge piece. The sound of the new decade.
alb.rush-1980-permanent-waves.detay: 'The Spirit of Radio' became a radio hit while criticising the commercialisation of radio.
'Natural Science' is their last long piece.
alb.rush-1980-permanent-waves.tr: The Spirit of Radio — prog fused with new wave
alb.rush-1981-moving-pictures.an: The band's best-loved and best-selling album; a perfect balance of prog complexity and song form.
alb.rush-1981-moving-pictures.detay: 'Tom Sawyer', 'Limelight' and 'YYZ' on the same album.
'YYZ' opens with Toronto airport's code in Morse code.
alb.rush-1981-moving-pictures.tr: Tom Sawyer — the band's best-known song
YYZ — instrumental, rhythm in Morse code
alb.rush-1982-signals.an: An album about suburban life and technology, with synths more prominent. 'Subdivisions' is the era's quiet anthem; their last work with Terry Brown.
alb.rush-1984-grace-under-pressure.an: A dark, new wave-influenced (The Police, Ultravox) album about Cold War anxiety, the Holocaust and technology.
alb.rush-1984-grace-under-pressure.oncel: Recommended — the strongest album of the synth period.
alb.rush-1985-power-windows.an: Bright synth rock themed on power, with layers of orchestra and choir.
alb.rush-1987-hold-your-fire.an: The softest album of the synth period; 'Time Stand Still' with guest vocals by Aimee Mann.
alb.rush-1989-presto.an: With the move to Atlantic, the keyboards step back and the sound turns more organic.
alb.rush-1991-roll-the-bones.an: Themed on luck and chance; entering the '90s with the rap section of the title track and the Grammy-nominated 'Where's My Thing?'.
alb.rush-1993-counterparts.an: A hard, full album that put the guitar back at the centre in the alternative-rock era.
alb.rush-1993-counterparts.oncelik: Recommended — the best Rush album of the '90s.
alb.rush-1996-test-for-echo.an: On the media, the internet and herd psychology; the first recording of the drum technique Peart rebuilt with Freddie Gruber. The last album before the personal tragedies.
alb.rush-1996-test-for-echo.detay: Before the album, Peart rebuilt his technique from scratch by studying with jazz drummer Freddie Gruber.
alb.rush-2002-vapor-trails.an: The comeback after Peart's losses: a dense, cramped, angry album without guitar solos or keyboards. Remixed in 2013 (Vapor Trails Remixed) because of its over-loud mastering.
alb.rush-2002-vapor-trails.detay: One of the albums most often cited in the 'loudness war' debate.
alb.rush-2007-snakes-arrows.an: A mature album about faith, war and dogma, with three instrumentals.
alb.rush-2012-clockwork-angels.an: Rush's last studio album and their first full concept album: an individual's journey against the 'Watchmaker' in a fatalistic steampunk world. Turned into a novel with Kevin J. Anderson.
alb.rush-2012-clockwork-angels.oncelik: Essential — both the late peak and the farewell.
alb.rush-2012-clockwork-angels.detay: Canadian author Kevin J. Anderson turned the album's story into a novel of the same name.
Peart died in 2020; 'The Garden' is read as the band's farewell.
alb.rush-2012-clockwork-angels.tr: Headlong Flight — a salute to the band's past
grp.hawkwind.kurulus: 1969, London. The core band of British space rock; between psychedelia, prog and proto-punk, with hypnotic, sci-fi-themed long jams. The longest-lasting band of the underground.
grp.hawkwind.hikaye: Led by Dave Brock, Hawkwind was formed in London's Ladbroke Grove in 1969; with lyrics by science-fiction author Michael Moorcock and poet Robert Calvert, the stage presence of dancer Stacia and otherworldly sound effects, they defined 'space rock'. Bassist Lemmy Kilmister was in the band in 1972–75 (he sang 'Silver Machine'); fired after a drug arrest, he formed Motörhead. With Brock as its only permanent member, the band has kept recording and touring for more than 50 years.
grp.hawkwind.dna: Space rock: hypnotic, repetitive motorik rhythm, layers of electronic noise and synths, science-fiction themes, long jams. An intersection of krautrock and English psychedelia.
grp.hawkwind.uyeler: Dave Brock (guitar/vocals — the only permanent member), Nik Turner (saxophone/flute), Lemmy (bass/vocals — later Motörhead!), DikMik & Del Dettmar (electronics), Robert Calvert (poet/vocals), Simon House (violin).
grp.hawkwind.gecisler: After → Motörhead (Lemmy formed it after being fired from Hawkwind), various space-rock offshoots. Michael Moorcock (science-fiction author) contributed lyrics.
grp.hawkwind.etki: The definer of the space-rock subgenre; through Lemmy a bridge to metal, and through motorik structure to punk and electronics. The underground legend of sci-fi prog.
alb.hawkwind-1971-in-search-of-space.an: The second album, which established the band's identity; the hypnotic space-rock texture falls fully into place. It came with an illustrated 'log book'.
alb.hawkwind-1971-in-search-of-space.tr: You Shouldn't Do That — 15-minute hypnotic opener
Master of the Universe — the band's emblematic riff
We Took the Wrong Step Years Ago
alb.hawkwind-1972-doremi-fasol-latido.an: Lemmy's bass comes to the fore; rawer and heavier. It coincides with the period of the hit single 'Silver Machine'.
alb.hawkwind-1973-space-ritual.an: A double live album from the 1972 Liverpool and London concerts; the sacred text of space rock.
alb.hawkwind-1974-hall-of-the-mountain-g: More melodic and 'prog' with Simon House's violin and keyboards; one of the band's most balanced albums.
Wind of Change — House's orchestral contribution
alb.hawkwind-1975-warrior-on-the-edge-of: A concept album made with the direct contribution of author Michael Moorcock; Lemmy's last Hawkwind record. A sci-fi prog peak.
Assault and Battery / The Golden Void — orchestral epic
alb.hawkwind-1977-quark-strangeness-and-: A more compact album close to new wave, in which Calvert wrote of particle physics and science-fiction humour.
alb.hawkwind-1980-levitation.an: Bright, with Ginger Baker on drums and Tim Blake's synths; one of the first albums recorded digitally.
alb.hawkwind-2017-into-the-woods.an: A calm but solid late album led by Brock, on nature and escape.
grp.happy-the-man.kurulus: 1973, Harrisonburg, Virginia (USA). One of the most virtuosic but least known bands of American symphonic prog; active around Washington, D.C. An American relative of Genesis and Gentle Giant.
grp.happy-the-man.dna: Virtuoso, mostly instrumental symphonic prog; complex unison lines, jazz-fusion influence, Gentle Giant's counterpoint + Genesis's melody. A cool, clean, technical texture.
grp.happy-the-man.uyeler: Stanley Whitaker (guitar), Frank Wyatt (keyboards/saxophone), Kit Watkins (keyboards — later Camel!), Rick Kennell (bass), Mike Beck / Ron Riddle (drums).
grp.happy-the-man.gecisler: After → Camel (Kit Watkins — a bridge linking American prog to the British backbone). Peter Gabriel tried them out as his solo band (it didn't work out) — a moment touching the Genesis universe.
grp.happy-the-man.etki: American symphonic prog's 'musicians' band'; connects to Camel through Kit Watkins. A homegrown pioneer for the '90s American revival (Echolyn).
alb.happy-the-man-1977-happy-the-man.an: The debut; one of the most brilliant instrumental debuts of American symphonic prog. Complex but melodic unison lines.
alb.happy-the-man-1977-happy-the-man.tr: Stumpy Meets the Firecracker in Stencil Forest
alb.happy-the-man-1978-crafty-hands.an: The second album; the technical peak. Kit Watkins's keyboards (before Camel) shine.
alb.happy-the-man-1978-crafty-hands.tr: Ibby It Is — fusion-prog technical showcase
grp.nektar.kurulus: 1969, Hamburg. English musicians living in Germany: Roye Albrighton (guitar/vocals), Allan 'Taff' Freeman (keyboards), Derek 'Mo' Moore (bass), Ron Howden (drums) + lighting artist Mick Brockett.
grp.nektar.hikaye: Founded in Germany, Nektar occupies a unique position between krautrock and English symphonic prog; by counting light-show man Mick Brockett as a full member they brought a 'visual music' approach. With Journey to the Centre of the Eye (1971) they turned to the science-fiction concept album; Remember the Future (1973) reached the US Top 20. They split in 1978 and reunited in the 2000s under Albrighton's leadership; Albrighton died in 2016.
grp.nektar.dna: Space rock, symphonic prog and blues rock; long jams, Hammond and Mellotron, science-fiction themes.
grp.nektar.gecisler: Prophecy (Albrighton) → Nektar; the Hamburg club scene, Bacillus Records; guests in the 2000s: Dave Kilminster, Larry Fast.
grp.nektar.etki: English prog in Germany; a bridge between space rock and symphonic prog.
alb.nektar-1971-journey-to-the-centre-of: A single-piece concept album about the journey of consciousness of an astronaut abducted by aliens.
alb.nektar-1972-a-tab-in-the-ocean.an: The album on which Nektar combined space rock and symphonic prog in a 17-minute title suite.
alb.nektar-1973-sounds-like-this.an: A jam-heavy double album recorded live in the studio.
alb.nektar-1973-remember-the-future.an: A two-sided concept album about the friendship between a blue bird (Bluebird) and a blind boy; the band's greatest success.
alb.nektar-1975-recycled.an: On the environment and consumption; with Larry Fast's Moog synthesis and a more compact suite structure.
alb.nektar-1975-recycled.detay: Larry Fast later became Peter Gabriel's synthesiser specialist — another intersection in the network.
grp.pavlov-s-dog.kurulus: 1972, St. Louis, Missouri. David Surkamp (vocals/guitar), Siegfried Carver (violin), Doug Rayburn (Mellotron/flute), Mike Safron (drums), David Hamilton (keyboards), Steve Scorfina (guitar), Rick Stockton (bass).
grp.pavlov-s-dog.hikaye: With David Surkamp's unusually high, quavering voice (described as somewhere between Geddy Lee and Robert Plant) and its violin-and-Mellotron textures, Pavlov's Dog is a cult band of American prog. The band released its first album after a legendary $600,000 Columbia/ABC deal, but commercial success never came. On the second album Bill Bruford took the drum seat through Sandy Pearlman, Blue Öyster Cult's producer. The third album stayed on the shelf for years. The band was re-formed in the 2000s under Surkamp.
grp.pavlov-s-dog.dna: High falsetto vocals, violin and Mellotron, between hard rock and symphonic prog; romantic and melancholic.
grp.pavlov-s-dog.gecisler: High Cost of Living → Pavlov's Dog; Bill Bruford (guest on At the Sound of the Bell); Sandy Pearlman (Blue Öyster Cult) as producer.
grp.pavlov-s-dog.etki: Cult American prog; often compared with high-voiced singers of a later generation such as The Mars Volta's Cedric Bixler-Zavala.
alb.pavlov-s-dog-1975-pampered-menial.an: A dramatic, romantic and melodic album with Surkamp's voice, violin and Mellotron; a cult classic.
alb.pavlov-s-dog-1975-pampered-menial.de: The album was pressed on both the ABC and Columbia labels — the result of a strange label transfer of the time.
alb.pavlov-s-dog-1976-at-the-sound-of-th: Bill Bruford on drums, Michael Brecker and Andy Mackay (Roxy Music) on horns; more orchestral and polished.
One of Bruford's odd side stops between his Yes, Crimson and Genesis tours.
sec.14.title: Late Bridges and Scandinavian Prog (1990–1995)
sec.14.intro: The network's Scandinavian extension in the 1990s. After neo-prog and the American renaissance, Sweden revived '70s symphonic prog in its purest form: Roine Stolt's Flower Kings, Änglagård, who put the Mellotron back at the centre, and Anekdoten, fed by the darker side of King Crimson. Through Stolt, the Flower Kings connect to Transatlantic and the modern prog generation.
grp.the-flower-kings.kurulus: 1994, Sweden. A band formed around guitarist Roine Stolt's solo album 'The Flower King' (1994). The European locomotive of the '90s symphonic-prog revival; the outfit that revived the classic Yes/Genesis sound most generously.
grp.the-flower-kings.hikaye: Born from former Kaipa guitarist Roine Stolt's 1994 solo album The Flower King, the band is the centre of Sweden's '90s symphonic-prog renaissance. They combined the optimistic, large-scale symphonism of Yes and Genesis with jazz and Beatles melody. In the same period Stolt became a member of Transatlantic. They took a break from 2008 to 2012.
grp.the-flower-kings.dna: Generous, long-form symphonic prog: classic Yes melody + Genesis textures + jazz fusion + positive/spiritual lyrics. Often 'maximalist' double-CD albums.
grp.the-flower-kings.uyeler: Roine Stolt (guitar/vocals/composer — formerly Kaipa), Tomas Bodin (keyboards), Jonas Reingold (bass), Hasse Fröberg (vocals), various drummers. Stolt is the core mastermind.
grp.the-flower-kings.gecisler: Before → Kaipa (Stolt — a '70s Swedish prog band). After → Transatlantic (Stolt, 1999 — the mega-junction with Marillion + Spock's Beard + Dream Theater). The node linking European prog to the American renaissance.
grp.the-flower-kings.etki: The European pillar (with Spock's Beard) of the '90s prog revival; through Stolt it feeds the Transatlantic mega-junction. The template of modern symphonic prog.
alb.the-flower-kings-1995-back-in-the-wo: The band's first official album (following Stolt's 1994 solo record). Fully embraces classic symphonic prog; long suites and generous melodies.
alb.the-flower-kings-1997-stardust-we-ar: A double album; the band's first great work, with a 25-minute title suite.
alb.the-flower-kings-1999-flower-power.a: The band's most enormous album, with the 'Garden of Dreams' suite running over 60 minutes.
alb.the-flower-kings-2002-unfold-the-fut: A double album with increasing jazz and funk colours, opening with 'The Truth Will Set You Free'.
The comeback after the break; with the 25-minute 'Numbers' suite.
grp.anglagard.kurulus: 1991, Stockholm, Sweden. A young band that revived '70s Swedish and English symphonic prog (King Crimson, Genesis, Italian prog) in its purest, most 'retro' form. Devoted to vintage instruments (Mellotron, analogue synths).
grp.anglagard.hikaye: Stockholm's Änglagård became the cult band of the '90s retro-prog wave by reviving the analogue instruments of the '70s (Mellotron, Hammond) and Swedish folk melancholy. They split in 1994 after two albums and returned in 2012 with Viljans öga. Some members later formed All Traps on Earth.
grp.anglagard.dna: Dark, acoustic-heavy, Mellotron-laden retro symphonic prog: sudden dynamic shifts, flute and vintage keyboard textures, almost no English vocals. Fanatical loyalty to the '70s aesthetic.
grp.anglagard.uyeler: Tord Lindman (guitar/vocals), Jonas Engdegård (guitar), Thomas Johnson (keyboards/Mellotron), Johan Brand (bass), Mattias Olsson (drums), Anna Holmgren (flute).
grp.anglagard.gecisler: Circle → the Swedish prog revival (a sister scene with Anekdoten). Mattias Olsson later had a wide-ranging career as a prog session player. Linked through shared sound to Crimson, Genesis and Italian prog.
grp.anglagard.etki: The most respected band of the '90s 'retro-prog' movement; proof of how vintage symphonic prog could be revived. The emblem of the Scandinavian prog scene.
alb.anglagard-1992-hybris.an: The debut and a cult classic of retro-prog. Mellotron-heavy, dark, full of sudden shifts; like a lost album from 1973. Entirely in Swedish or instrumental.
alb.anglagard-1994-epilog.an: An entirely instrumental second album; even darker and more compositional. The close of the band's (first) period and the technical peak of retro-prog.
alb.anglagard-2012-viljans-oga.an: The third album, arriving 18 years later; dark, sprawling and subtle symphonic prog across four long instrumentals.
grp.anekdoten.kurulus: 1991, Borlänge, Sweden. With Änglagård, one of the two pillars of the Swedish retro-prog revival. It began as a King Crimson cover band, focused especially on the dark heaviness of the 'Red' era.
grp.anekdoten.hikaye: Borlänge's Anekdoten combined King Crimson's 1973–74 period (Mellotron, cello, heavy bass) with the dark alternative rock of the '90s. Over time they evolved towards a more psychedelic, song-oriented sound.
grp.anekdoten.dna: Dark, heavy symphonic prog laden with Mellotron and cello; the metallic melancholy of King Crimson's 'Red' era + Swedish coldness. Bass and Mellotron to the fore.
grp.anekdoten.uyeler: Nicklas Berg (guitar/Mellotron/vocals), Jan Erik Liljeström (bass/vocals), Anna Sofi Dahlberg (cello/Mellotron), Peter Nordins (drums).
grp.anekdoten.gecisler: Circle → the Swedish prog revival (sister to Änglagård). Through shared sound most directly linked to King Crimson ('Red', 'Starless'); original in its use of cello.
grp.anekdoten.etki: The Crimson-centred wing of retro-prog; a heavier, more 'rock' alternative to Änglagård's melodic darkness. The other pillar of the Scandinavian prog scene.
alb.anekdoten-1993-vemod.an: The debut; a cult classic rebuilding the heaviness of King Crimson's 'Red' with Mellotron and cello. Dark, melancholic, heavy.
alb.anekdoten-1993-vemod.tr: Karelia — the band's emblem, heavy Mellotron riff
alb.anekdoten-1995-nucleus.an: The second album; more refined but still dark. It deepens their own identity while keeping the Crimson influence.
alb.anekdoten-1999-from-within.an: Plainer, darker songs; the psychedelic texture grows.
alb.anekdoten-2003-gravity.an: An album where the melodic and psychedelic direction comes to the fore.
alb.anekdoten-2007-a-time-of-day.an: Heavy Mellotron and a dreamlike atmosphere.
alb.anekdoten-2015-until-all-the-ghosts-: An album that returns them to the top, with Theo Travis (flute/sax) and Opeth's Per Wiberg as guests.
sec.18.title: Next Generation III — Modern Prog and Prog Metal (1995–2020)
sec.18.intro: The fourth wave: Porcupine Tree and Steven Wilson's remix legacy, the Transatlantic supergroup, Neal Morse and Dream Theater, the definer of prog metal. Musicians of the classic generation reappear as guests on these bands' albums.
grp.porcupine-tree.kurulus: 1987, Hemel Hempstead. Began as Steven Wilson's one-man 'imaginary band' joke; from 1993 with Richard Barbieri (keyboards, formerly Japan), Colin Edwin (bass) and Chris Maitland (drums); from 2002 Gavin Harrison (drums).
grp.porcupine-tree.hikaye: In the late '80s Wilson invented an imaginary '70s psychedelic band and recorded cassettes; he even wrote a fake band biography. The joke became a real band in the '90s: the early period of long, Pink Floyd-influenced space rock peaked with The Sky Moves Sideways (1995). With Stupid Dream and Lightbulb Sun they turned to shorter, melancholic art rock; after Gavin Harrison's arrival and meeting Opeth, they moved towards metal heaviness with In Absentia (2002). Fear of a Blank Planet (2007), about the digital alienation of young people, became a modern classic. In 2010 Wilson focused on his solo career; the band returned in 2022 with Closure/Continuation. Wilson's remixes of King Crimson, Yes, Jethro Tull, ELP, Gentle Giant and XTC albums in the same period made Porcupine Tree the official heir of classic prog.
grp.porcupine-tree.dna: Pink Floyd atmosphere, King Crimson heaviness, '90s alternative-rock melancholy and metal riffs; flawless studio production.
grp.porcupine-tree.gecisler: Steven Wilson (No-Man, Blackfield, Bass Communion, Storm Corrosion) → Porcupine Tree; Richard Barbieri (Japan, Rain Tree Crow); Gavin Harrison → King Crimson (2008–2021); Storm Corrosion with Mikael Åkerfeldt (Opeth).
grp.porcupine-tree.etki: The most influential band of 1995–2020 prog; the ancestor of bands such as Riverside, Anathema and Haken; at the centre of classic prog's remix legacy.
alb.porcupine-tree-1995-the-sky-moves-si: The modern space rock closest to Pink Floyd's 'Shine On': a title suite of over 35 minutes and ambient layers. The album on which the band became a real band.
Recommended — the peak of the psychedelic period.
alb.porcupine-tree-1996-signify.an: The first full band album by the four-piece, with kraut and electronic textures.
alb.porcupine-tree-1999-stupid-dream.an: The move from long jams to short, dense songs; the rise of melancholic art rock, in parallel with Radiohead.
alb.porcupine-tree-2000-lightbulb-sun.an: Personal and hurt; pop subtlety alongside a long, heavy piece like 'Russia on Ice'.
alb.porcupine-tree-2002-in-absentia.an: The first album with Gavin Harrison and a metal-oriented transformation; a dark concept about serial killers and social violence.
alb.porcupine-tree-2002-in-absentia.once: Essential — never skip. A key album of modern prog.
alb.porcupine-tree-2002-in-absentia.deta: 'Trains' is often named as Wilson's best-loved song.
alb.porcupine-tree-2005-deadwing.an: An album born from a ghost-story screenplay written by Wilson, with Adrian Belew and Mikael Åkerfeldt as guests.
alb.porcupine-tree-2005-deadwing.detay: Adrian Belew (King Crimson) and Mikael Åkerfeldt (Opeth) as guests — bringing two generations of prog together.
alb.porcupine-tree-2007-fear-of-a-blank-: A concept album about a teenager lost between screens and pills, inspired by Bret Easton Ellis's 'Lunar Park'. Robert Fripp and Alex Lifeson as guests.
Alex Lifeson (Rush) guests on 'Anesthetize', Robert Fripp on 'Way Out of Here'.
alb.porcupine-tree-2009-the-incident.an: A single 55-minute 'song cycle' and a separate EP; the band's last album before the long break.
grp.steven-wilson-solo.name: Steven Wilson (solo)
grp.steven-wilson-solo.kurulus: Born 1967, Kingston upon Thames. Founder of Porcupine Tree; the No-Man, Blackfield, Bass Communion and Storm Corrosion projects; remix producer.
grp.steven-wilson-solo.hikaye: From 2008, under his own name, Wilson made albums openly leaning on '70s jazz-prog (King Crimson, Canterbury); by taking on King Crimson's 40th-anniversary remixes in 2009 he became classic prog's 'digital curator'. The Raven That Refused to Sing (2013) and Hand. Cannot. Erase. (2015), recorded with his band of Guthrie Govan, Marco Minnemann, Nick Beggs, Adam Holzman and Theo Travis, are considered two peaks of modern prog. On later albums he turned to pop and electronic colours, constantly questioning the prog label.
grp.steven-wilson-solo.dna: '70s jazz-prog and Canterbury harmonies, Crimson's Mellotron, film-score atmosphere, pop melody; a flawless 5.1-mixing aesthetic.
grp.steven-wilson-solo.gecisler: Porcupine Tree → solo; Mikael Åkerfeldt (Storm Corrosion), Aviv Geffen (Blackfield), Tim Bowness (No-Man); remixes: King Crimson, Yes, Jethro Tull, ELP, Gentle Giant, Caravan, XTC, Roxy Music, Tears for Fears.
grp.steven-wilson-solo.etki: The central figure of 1995–2020 prog; the bridge reconnecting the younger generation to classic prog through remixes.
alb.steven-wilson-2008-insurgentes.an: A first solo album recorded partly in Mexico, mixing shoegaze, electronics and prog.
alb.steven-wilson-2011-grace-for-drownin: An open homage to '70s jazz-prog after the Crimson remixes: Mellotron, saxophone and the 23-minute 'Raider II'.
Steve Hackett, Tony Levin and Pat Mastelotto as guests — a direct link to the Genesis and Crimson families.
alb.steven-wilson-2013-the-raven-that-re: An album of supernatural stories, recorded with Alan Parsons as engineer; a canonical work of modern prog.
The Alan Parsons link: The Dark Side of the Moon's engineer recorded a new generation's album 40 years later.
alb.steven-wilson-2015-hand-cannot-erase: A concept album on urban loneliness, inspired by the true story of Joyce Vincent, whose death in London went unnoticed for three years.
alb.steven-wilson-2017-to-the-bone.an: A tribute to '80s art pop (Peter Gabriel's So, Tears for Fears, Talk Talk); a deliberate bridge between prog and pop.
grp.transatlantic.kurulus: 1999. Neal Morse (Spock's Beard), Mike Portnoy (Dream Theater), Roine Stolt (The Flower Kings), Pete Trewavas (Marillion).
grp.transatlantic.hikaye: Born of Mike Portnoy's and Neal Morse's shared love of the Beatles and Yes, Transatlantic is a supergroup uniting one member each from four major bands of the American and European prog renaissance. They brought the optimistic symphonism of Yes, Genesis and the Beatles into modern production with huge suites. With Morse's religious conversion in 2002 the band went on hiatus; they returned in 2009 with The Whirlwind. Each of their albums is 'epic' in scale, with suites of 30 to 70 minutes.
grp.transatlantic.dna: Yes/Genesis-style symphonic prog, Beatles harmonies, long suites and polyphonic harmony with three lead voices.
grp.transatlantic.gecisler: Spock's Beard, Dream Theater, The Flower Kings, Marillion → Transatlantic; Portnoy and Morse → Flying Colors, Neal Morse Band; Daniel Gildenlöw (Pain of Salvation) as touring member.
grp.transatlantic.etki: The flagship supergroup of the '90s prog renaissance; it defined the modern 'epic suite' format.
alb.transatlantic-2000-smpt-e.an: The first album: the 30-minute 'All of the Above' and a cover of Procol Harum's 'In Held (Twas) in I'.
alb.transatlantic-2001-bridge-across-for: The second album, considered the band's peak, with the 26-minute 'Duel with the Devil' and 'Stranger in Your Soul'.
alb.transatlantic-2009-the-whirlwind.an: A comeback album consisting of a single 77-minute suite.
alb.transatlantic-2014-kaleidoscope.an: Two big suites ('Into the Blue', 'Kaleidoscope') and shorter pieces.
grp.neal-morse-solo-ve-neal-morse-band.n: Neal Morse (solo and the Neal Morse Band)
grp.neal-morse-solo-ve-neal-morse-band.k: Born 1960, Van Nuys, California. Founder of Spock's Beard and Transatlantic.
grp.neal-morse-solo-ve-neal-morse-band.h: Morse is the most prolific composer of the '90s American prog renaissance; he wrote huge suites with Spock's Beard and Transatlantic. With his conversion to Christianity in 2002 he left Spock's Beard and devoted his solo career to enormous faith-themed concept albums: Testimony (2003), One (2004), ? (2005), Sola Scriptura (2007). Mike Portnoy played drums on most of them. From 2015 he led a band, The Neal Morse Band, with Eric Gillette and Bill Hubauer; The Similitude of a Dream (2016), a double album based on John Bunyan's 'The Pilgrim's Progress', became one of the great concepts of modern prog.
grp.neal-morse-solo-ve-neal-morse-band.d: Yes and Genesis symphonism, Beatles melody, gospel fervour and Broadway-musical dramaturgy.
grp.neal-morse-solo-ve-neal-morse-band.g: Spock's Beard → Transatlantic → solo → Flying Colors (Steve Morse, Portnoy, Dave LaRue, Casey McPherson) → Neal Morse Band; Morse Portnoy George (cover projects).
grp.neal-morse-solo-ve-neal-morse-band.e: The biggest name in Christian prog; with Transatlantic and Flying Colors, a central node of supergroup culture.
alb.neal-morse-2003-testimony.an: An autobiographical double concept album about Morse's religious conversion.
alb.neal-morse-2007-sola-scriptura.an: A heavy, metal-tinged concept telling the story of Martin Luther and the Reformation, opening with a 29-minute piece.
alb.neal-morse-2007-sola-scriptura.kadro: Neal Morse, Mike Portnoy, Randy George, Paul Gilbert (guest)
alb.neal-morse-2016-the-similitude-of-a-: A double concept album based on John Bunyan's 'The Pilgrim's Progress'; the peak of the Neal Morse Band.
The sequel to Similitude: the journey of the pilgrim's son.
grp.dream-theater.kurulus: 1985, Boston (Berklee College of Music). John Petrucci (guitar), John Myung (bass), Mike Portnoy (drums); Kevin Moore (keyboards), Charlie Dominici (vocals, 1987–89); James LaBrie from 1991.
grp.dream-theater.hikaye: Berklee students Petrucci, Myung and Portnoy turned a synthesis of Rush, Yes, Iron Maiden and Metallica into the genre that would be called 'progressive metal'. They began as Majesty and switched to Dream Theater because another band had the same name. After a difficult debut with Charlie Dominici, they became the genre's pioneers when 'Pull Me Under' from Images and Words (1992), with James LaBrie, went into rotation on MTV. Metropolis Pt. 2: Scenes from a Memory (1999) is considered the reference concept album of modern prog metal. On keyboards Kevin Moore gave way to Derek Sherinian (1994) and Jordan Rudess (1999). Portnoy left in 2010 and was replaced by Mike Mangini (Portnoy returned in 2023). The record executive who signed the band was former Gentle Giant singer Derek Shulman.
grp.dream-theater.dna: The complex structures of Rush and Yes, the metal heaviness of Metallica and Iron Maiden, virtuoso solo sections, concept albums.
grp.dream-theater.gecisler: Majesty → Dream Theater; Portnoy → Transatlantic, Liquid Tension Experiment, Flying Colors, Sons of Apollo; Sherinian → Sons of Apollo; Charlie Dominici → Dominici; Kevin Moore → Chroma Key, OSI; Rudess → Liquid Tension Experiment.
grp.dream-theater.etki: The defining band of prog metal; the model for Symphony X, Haken and countless others.
alb.dream-theater-1989-when-dream-and-da: The only album with Charlie Dominici; despite weak production, the seeds of the band's complex structures.
The first album with James LaBrie; MTV success with 'Pull Me Under'. The founding album of prog metal.
At the label ATCO, the band was backed by Derek Shulman's (Gentle Giant) team.
alb.dream-theater-1994-awake.an: Darker and heavier; Kevin Moore's last album.
alb.dream-theater-1995-a-change-of-seaso: An EP with a 23-minute title track and live medleys of covers of Elton John, Deep Purple, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd, Queen and Kansas.
alb.dream-theater-1999-metropolis-pt-2-s: The sequel to 'Metropolis—Part I' from Images and Words: a man who returns to a past life under hypnosis solves a murder mystery. The first album with Jordan Rudess.
Essential — never skip. Prog metal's reference concept album.
alb.dream-theater-2002-six-degrees-of-in: On the second disc, a single 42-minute suite (six stories about mental health).
alb.dream-theater-2005-octavarium.an: An album built around the idea of an eight-note octave; an open homage to the Yes/Genesis legacy with its 24-minute title track.
alb.dream-theater-2016-the-astonishing.a: The ambitious double concept album of the Mike Mangini era: a rock opera about the power of music in a dystopian future.
alb.dream-theater-2019-distance-over-tim: A more compact, riff-focused comeback; considered by critics the best of the Mangini era.
The Sound Kinship of Three Generations (Influence Map)
alb.pink-floyd-1995-pulse.tr: The Dark Side of the Moon (complete)
sec.4.title: The King Crimson Universe
sec.4.intro: The network's most productive junction. Apart from Robert Fripp there are almost no permanent members, which makes King Crimson the node that has "exported" the most musicians.
grp.king-crimson.kurulus: 1968–69, London. Grew out of the trio Giles, Giles & Fripp and took shape in 1969 when Ian McDonald and Greg Lake joined. In the Court of the Crimson King (1969) is prog rock's symbolic birth certificate.
grp.king-crimson.hikaye: Described by Robert Fripp as 'not a band but a way of doing things', King Crimson was rebuilt with more than eight line-ups over fifty years. The 1969 line-up broke up after a single album (McDonald and Giles left, Lake went to ELP); in 1970–72 Fripp and lyricist Peter Sinfield built a jazz-orchestral Crimson with session players and Mel Collins, Boz Burrell and Ian Wallace. In 1972 Fripp let Sinfield go too and formed an improvisation-based, metal-heavy quartet with John Wetton, Bill Bruford, David Cross and percussionist Jamie Muir; after Red (1974) he disbanded the group, citing an approaching 'end of the world'. The Discipline quartet, formed in 1981 with Adrian Belew and Tony Levin, brought African polyrhythm, gamelan and minimalism into rock. Then came the 1994 'double trio' (two guitars, two basses/Sticks, two drummers), a nu-metal-heavy quartet in the 2000s and, after 2013, a seven- to eight-piece concert orchestra with three drummers lined up at the front, 'reinterpreting the archive'. Fripp never saw the band as a nostalgia vehicle; each line-up was designed as 'the answer to a new question'.
grp.king-crimson.dna: The dark texture of the Mellotron, free improvisation, dissonance, shifting time signatures, jazz-rock weight. It spans both the most lyrical (Crimson King) and the harshest (Red) extremes.
grp.king-crimson.etki: The reference point for all of British prog; the opposite pole to Yes and Genesis; a direct ancestor of prog metal (Tool, Dream Theater) and of the dissonant prog of the '90s.
grp.king-crimson.ipucu: Don't listen to Crimson as one band but as five separate ensembles sharing a common method; each era has its own language.
The way into the 1973–74 line-up is through the live recordings: most of the pieces on the studio albums were edited from stage improvisations (much of Starless and Bible Black is live).
Follow the 'Larks' Tongues in Aspic' series (Parts I–V, 1973–2003) like a thread; every Crimson era wrote its own 'Larks'.
On the '80s trilogy (Discipline–Beat–Three of a Perfect Pair), follow Fripp's and Belew's interlocking ostinato guitars with each ear separately — they are split across the stereo channels.
grp.king-crimson.era.0.note: Mellotron lyricism and jazz-orchestral experiments. The line-up changes with every album; the two constants are Fripp and lyricist Peter Sinfield.
grp.king-crimson.era.1.note: Improvisation turns into composition: the genre's hardest, most 'metal' prog period. It ends with Red; USA (1975) is this line-up's live testament.
grp.king-crimson.era.2.note: The quartet with Adrian Belew and Tony Levin: new wave, minimalism (Reich, Glass) and African polyrhythm. The Mellotron gives way to guitar synthesisers and the Chapman Stick.
grp.king-crimson.era.3.t: The double trio and the ProjeKcts
grp.king-crimson.era.3.note: First the six-piece 'double trio' (THRAK), then a quartet distilled from the ProjeKct laboratories (ConstruKction, Power to Believe). The joint 2001 tour with Tool is the seal of this period.
grp.king-crimson.era.4.t: The seven-headed beast — a concert orchestra
grp.king-crimson.era.4.note: A seven- to eight-piece line-up with three drummers at the front; no studio albums, the 1969–2003 repertoire rearranged and performed on stage. The band fell silent after its December 2021 tour of Japan.
alb.king-crimson-1969-in-the-court-of-th: The genre's manifesto. The ferocity of "21st Century Schizoid Man" meets the Mellotron lyricism of "Epitaph" and "I Talk to the Wind" on the same record. Barry Godber's screaming-face cover also launches prog's visual identity. Perhaps the single most influential album of the genre.
Essential — never skip. The genre's founding document.
Robert Fripp, Greg Lake, Ian McDonald, Michael Giles, Peter Sinfield (lyrics)
King Crimson (self-produced after abandoned sessions with Tony Clarke)
In July 1969, before the album was out, the band played to hundreds of thousands as the opening act for the Rolling Stones in Hyde Park.
Cover artist Barry Godber died aged 24 shortly after the album's release; it is the only record cover he ever made.
Ian McDonald is the album's real orchestrator: the Mellotron, flute, saxophone, clarinet and vibraphone are all his.
21st Century Schizoid Man — distorted vocals, jazz-metal, the genre's hardest opener
I Talk to the Wind — flute and gentle melancholy
The Court of the Crimson King — title track, Mellotron grandeur
alb.king-crimson-1970-in-the-wake-of-pos: Repeats the debut's template almost piece by piece (hard opener / Mellotron lament / jazz piece). A 'safe' successor made by a transitional line-up, and one that stays in the first album's shadow.
Recommended — but hear it as the debut's 'twin'; it offers little that is new.
Fripp, Greg Lake (vocals), Michael Giles, Peter Giles, Mel Collins, Keith Tippett, Gordon Haskell (vocals on 'Cadence and Cascade'), Sinfield
The band had already split before recording; Lake finished his vocals before leaving for ELP.
Keith Tippett's jazz piano heralds the jazz-avant-garde direction of the next two albums.
Pictures of a City — successor to the 'Schizoid Man' formula
Cadence and Cascade — gentle ballad (sung by Haskell)
alb.king-crimson-1970-lizard.an: Jazz-orchestral experimentation; Jon Anderson (Yes) guests on vocals on "Prince Rupert Awakes" — an early contact between two universes. The least understood, most 'chamber-music' Crimson album.
alb.king-crimson-1970-lizard.oncelik: Optional but rewarding — Crimson's most 'chamber-music' album; it takes several listens.
alb.king-crimson-1970-lizard.kadro: Fripp, Gordon Haskell, Mel Collins, Andy McCulloch, Sinfield + Keith Tippett, Jon Anderson (guest), jazz horns (Mark Charig, Nick Evans, Robin Miller)
alb.king-crimson-1970-lizard.detay: Haskell, unhappy with Fripp's direction, left after the album.
The 'Bolero' section of the 'Lizard' suite brings key horn players of the British jazz scene into rock.
Fripp dismissed the album for years; he embraced it again with Steven Wilson's 2009 remix.
alb.king-crimson-1970-lizard.tr: Lizard — 23-minute title suite, Jon Anderson guest vocal
alb.king-crimson-1971-islands.an: Chamber-music-tinged, fragile and melancholic. Sinfield's last album; "Sailor's Tale" is the dissonant climax.
alb.king-crimson-1971-islands.oncelik: Recommended — especially for 'Sailor's Tale' and the title track.
alb.king-crimson-1971-islands.kadro: Fripp, Boz Burrell (bass/vocals), Mel Collins, Ian Wallace, Sinfield + Keith Tippett, Paulina Lucas (soprano)
alb.king-crimson-1971-islands.detay: Fripp taught Boz Burrell to play bass in a few weeks; Burrell later became Bad Company's bassist.
Sinfield's last album with Crimson; he went on to produce Roxy Music's debut.
The cover shows the Trifid Nebula in Sagittarius.
alb.king-crimson-1973-larks-tongues-in-a: An entirely new line-up. With percussionist Jamie Muir's metallic improvised textures and Cross's violin, Crimson invents a formula of 'European avant-garde + hard rock'. The title suite, split into two parts, becomes the band's new emblem.
Essential — never skip. Crimson's second birth.
Fripp, John Wetton, Bill Bruford, David Cross, Jamie Muir; lyrics: Richard Palmer-James
Bruford left Yes at its peak (after Close to the Edge) to join Crimson — the most surprising transfer of the era.
Jamie Muir was a percussionist who used chains, saws, children's toys and fake blood on stage; after the album he withdrew to a Buddhist monastery.
'Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part II' has been a fixture of Crimson concerts for fifty years.
Larks' Tongues in Aspic Part One — Muir's percussion, from silence to explosion
Larks' Tongues in Aspic Part Two — the metallic, rhythmic emblem
alb.king-crimson-1974-starless-and-bible: Half live, half studio. On pieces like "Fracture" Fripp's guitar reaches a mathematical intensity; the dark improvisational aesthetic at its peak.
Recommended — but listen knowing it is essentially a 'live album'.
Fripp, Wetton, Bruford, David Cross; lyrics: Richard Palmer-James
Apart from 'The Great Deceiver' and 'Lament', most tracks come from 1973 concerts in Amsterdam and Glasgow, with the audience noise removed.
The title track and 'Fracture' are entirely improvised; 'Fracture' is considered one of Fripp's most technically demanding compositions.
The title was intended for the song 'Starless', which was held over for the next album.
Fracture — the peak of Fripp's mathematical guitar
The Night Watch — ballad about the Rembrandt painting
Starless and Bible Black — dark improvisation
alb.king-crimson-1974-red.an: The peak of metallic heaviness; the most intense Crimson, in power-trio format (Fripp/Wetton/Bruford). The closing "Starless" combines Mellotron melancholy with a screaming saxophone and ever-rising tension to create one of prog's most powerful finales. The first era's farewell.
alb.king-crimson-1974-red.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The prologue to prog metal.
alb.king-crimson-1974-red.kadro: Fripp, Wetton, Bruford + David Cross, Ian McDonald, Mel Collins, Robin Miller, Mark Charig (guests)
alb.king-crimson-1974-red.detay: Cross left before the sessions; the band recorded as a trio and Fripp disbanded the group before the album came out.
Kurt Cobain often named it among his favourite records; it is an open reference point for Tool and Opeth.
The final section of 'Starless' links two eras through the saxophone of Ian McDonald from the 1969 line-up.
alb.king-crimson-1974-red.tr: Starless — Mellotron melancholy + screaming saxophone, one of prog's most powerful finales
Red — metallic instrumental opener, the ancestor of prog metal
alb.king-crimson-1975-usa.an: A live album compiled from the 1974 American tour (Asbury Park and Providence), released after the band had split. The testament that shows how ferocious the Wetton–Bruford line-up was on stage.
alb.king-crimson-1975-usa.oncelik: Recommended — to understand the live power of the era.
alb.king-crimson-1975-usa.kadro: Fripp, Wetton, Bruford, Cross (+ violin overdubbed later by Eddie Jobson)
alb.king-crimson-1975-usa.detay: Some violin parts on the original release were re-recorded in the studio by Eddie Jobson; the 2013 expanded edition restored Cross's original parts.
alb.king-crimson-1975-usa.tr: 21st Century Schizoid Man — the Wetton-era version
alb.king-crimson-1981-discipline.an: A new-wave/minimalist rebirth. Belew's guitar and Fripp's "Frippertronics" build an interlocking twin-guitar texture; Levin's Chapman Stick and African polyrhythm carry Crimson into the '80s. It sounds like an entirely new band.
alb.king-crimson-1981-discipline.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The bravest prog rebirth of the '80s.
alb.king-crimson-1981-discipline.detay: The band was first formed under the name 'Discipline'; during the tour they decided to take the King Crimson name.
Levin was one of the first to bring the Chapman Stick into a rock line-up.
Bruford combines acoustic drums with Simmons electronic pads in the same kit.
alb.king-crimson-1981-discipline.tr: Discipline — interlocking twin guitars, mathematical polyrhythm
Frame by Frame — the Belew-Fripp guitar weave
alb.king-crimson-1982-beat.an: A Beat Generation (Kerouac) concept; more song-oriented and rougher. The era's most controversial Crimson record.
alb.king-crimson-1982-beat.oncelik: Optional — but hear 'Neal and Jack and Me' and 'Neurotica'.
alb.king-crimson-1982-beat.detay: A concept album referencing the Beat Generation (Kerouac, Cassady, Ginsberg), timed for the 25th anniversary of 'On the Road'.
The sessions coincided with growing tensions within the band; the difference in direction between Fripp and Belew becomes clear on this album.
alb.king-crimson-1982-beat.tr: Heartbeat — one of the most accessible Crimson songs
Neal and Jack and Me — Kerouac/Beat theme
Waiting Man — Levin's Chapman Stick textures
alb.king-crimson-1984-three-of-a-perfect: Built around a 'left side' (accessible songs) / 'right side' (harsh instrumentals) duality; the close of the '80s line-up.
Optional — the experimental instrumental side is the more rewarding one.
The original LP was designed with a 'left side' (accessible) and a 'right side' (experimental).
'Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part III' is on this album.
The band then fell silent for ten years while Fripp focused on his Guitar Craft teaching programme.
Three of a Perfect Pair — melodic 'left side' opener
Larks' Tongues in Aspic Part III — the harsh 'right side' continuation
alb.king-crimson-1995-thrak.an: The only studio album by the 'double trio' line-up: two guitars, two basses/Sticks and two drummers. Material first tested on the VROOOM EP (1994); it brings the grunge and industrial weight of the '90s together with Crimson's mathematics.
alb.king-crimson-1995-thrak.oncelik: Recommended — the bridge between '90s prog metal and Crimson.
alb.king-crimson-1995-thrak.detay: Bruford's last studio album with Crimson.
The 'double trio' concept worked on stage by placing two separate trios apart in the stereo field.
Its direct influence on Tool's later sound is often pointed out.
alb.king-crimson-1995-thrak.tr: VROOOM — opening suite, heavy riff architecture
One Time — the era's most elegant ballad
THRAK — improvised structure with two clashing guitars
alb.king-crimson-2000-the-construkction-: The first album by the band slimmed down to a quartet after the ProjeKct experiments. A cold, metallic and deliberately dry production; with 'Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part IV' and 'FraKctured' it takes its own past apart and reassembles it.
Optional — the era's most controversial record.
The first Crimson album without Levin and Bruford; Mastelotto plays mostly electronic drums.
Critics found the drum sound and mix harsh; later live versions were better received.
Larks' Tongues in Aspic, Part IV
ProzaKc Blues — Belew's 'old man' blues through a voice processor
alb.king-crimson-2003-the-power-to-belie: The peak of 2000s Crimson and the quartet's last studio album. Nu-metal-weight riffs, ambient interludes and Belew's haiku-like title motif frame the album. It remained the band's final studio album.
Essential — the best studio document of modern Crimson.
Producer Machine, coming from hip-hop and metal productions, gave the album a contemporary weight.
The 2001 tour as Tool's opening act helped shape this material.
Level Five — the unofficial fifth part of the 'Larks' series
Eyes Wide Open — Belew's most emotional Crimson song
alb.king-crimson-2016-radical-action-to-: A huge live set compiled from the seven-piece line-up's 2015 concerts in Japan and Canada. Three drummers in the front row; the repertoire from 1969 to 2003 completely re-orchestrated, with the 'Islands' and 'Lizard' eras returning to the stage for the first time.
Recommended — the best representative of late-period Crimson.
Includes sections presented 'like a studio album' with the audience removed — a return to Fripp's 1974 method.
Gavin Harrison comes from Porcupine Tree, Jakko Jakszyk from the 21st Century Schizoid Band.
