alb.king-crimson-2018-meltdown-live-in-m: The eight-piece line-up's 2017 Mexico City concerts. Long sections of the 'Lizard' suite, 'Cirkus' and 'Indiscipline' in the same show; Bill Rieflin now on keyboards, Jeremy Stacey in the drum seat.
Optional — for those who love Radical Action.
Bill Rieflin died in 2020; the recordings of this period document his time in Crimson.
Lizard — the suite performed live at this length for the first time
grp.robert-fripp-solo-ve-ortaklklar.name: Robert Fripp (solo and collaborations)
grp.robert-fripp-solo-ve-ortaklklar.kuru: Born 1946, Wimborne, Dorset. Founder and only permanent member of King Crimson.
grp.robert-fripp-solo-ve-ortaklklar.hika: After disbanding Crimson in 1974, Fripp spent a year at J. G. Bennett's school of thought at Sherborne House; he then developed with Brian Eno the 'Frippertronics' technique of building loops between two tape machines. In New York he worked with Bowie ('Heroes'), Gabriel, Blondie and Talking Heads. In 1985 he launched the Guitar Craft school and a new tuning (New Standard Tuning); his students became The League of Crafty Guitarists. In the '90s he moved on to real-time loop improvisations called 'Soundscapes'. With his label Discipline Global Mobile (DGM) he took a pioneering stance on artists' rights. In the 2010s he reached a new audience through online videos with his wife Toyah Willcox.
grp.robert-fripp-solo-ve-ortaklklar.dna: Tremolo picking, seamless legato soloing, layers of loops; a philosophy of discipline drawn from Gurdjieff.
grp.robert-fripp-solo-ve-ortaklklar.geci: Giles, Giles & Fripp → King Crimson → Fripp & Eno → Bowie/Gabriel sessions → The League of Gentlemen → Guitar Craft → Fripp & Andy Summers → Sylvian/Fripp → ProjeKcts.
grp.robert-fripp-solo-ve-ortaklklar.etki: A pioneer of ambient music (with Eno) and of looping techniques; a teacher of method whose reach extends from prog to post-rock.
alb.robert-fripp-1973-no-pussyfooting.an: The first album with Brian Eno: the birth of 'Frippertronics', built from delayed loops between two Revox tape machines.
alb.robert-fripp-1973-no-pussyfooting.on: Recommended — one of ambient music's founding records.
alb.robert-fripp-1975-evening-star.an: Fripp & Eno's second, more melodic album.
alb.robert-fripp-1979-exposure.an: Fripp's first solo album, part of his 'MOR trilogy' (with Gabriel's second album and Daryl Hall's Sacred Songs); guests include Gabriel, Hall, Eno, Peter Hammill and Terre Roche.
alb.robert-fripp-1979-exposure.oncelik: Essential — Fripp's most comprehensive solo statement.
alb.robert-fripp-1979-exposure.detay: The album brings together punk energy, Frippertronics and recordings of J. G. Bennett, a teacher in the Gurdjieff tradition.
alb.robert-fripp-1982-i-advance-masked.a: An instrumental guitar dialogue with Andy Summers of The Police.
alb.robert-fripp-1993-the-first-day.an: With David Sylvian; heavy rhythms and Fripp's striking guitar. Trey Gunn's path into Crimson runs through here.
grp.john-wetton-solo.name: John Wetton (solo)
grp.john-wetton-solo.kurulus: 1949–2017, Derby. Bassist and singer with Family, King Crimson, Roxy Music (touring), Uriah Heep, U.K. and Asia.
grp.john-wetton-solo.hikaye: Wetton is the network's most mobile 'migrant' musician: from Mogul Thrash and Family to King Crimson (1972–74), then to Roxy Music and Uriah Heep, and on to U.K. and Asia. With his dark, aggressive bass and powerful baritone-tenor voice he was the sound of Crimson's heaviest period and of Asia's stadium melodicism. His struggle with alcoholism and his 2007 heart surgery were turning points in his life. His solo career moved between AOR and prog; with Geoff Downes he ran the Wetton/Downes (Icon) project. He died of colon cancer in 2017.
grp.john-wetton-solo.dna: Distorted, aggressive bass; emotional, powerful vocals; melodic songwriting between prog and AOR.
grp.john-wetton-solo.gecisler: Mogul Thrash → Family → King Crimson → Roxy Music → Uriah Heep → U.K. → Asia → Icon (Downes) → solo.
grp.john-wetton-solo.etki: The only voice shared by Crimson and Asia; the man who joined prog and arena rock.
alb.john-wetton-1980-caught-in-the-cross: His first solo album, after U.K. and before Asia; its AOR leanings sound like a rehearsal for Asia.
alb.john-wetton-1997-arkangel.an: A strong solo album between prog and melodic rock, with Robert Fripp and Steve Hackett as guests.
alb.john-wetton-2005-icon.an: A joint project with Geoff Downes; a return to Asia's classic melodicism that paved the way for the original Asia reunion.
alb.john-wetton-2011-raised-in-captivity: A solo album that reads like a summary of the network, with old companions such as Robert Fripp, Steve Hackett, Eddie Jobson, Geoff Downes and Tony Kaye.
Recommended — the guest list is a map of the network.
grp.21st-century-schizoid-band.kurulus: 2002, London. A tribute/reinterpretation band formed by alumni of the 1969–72 King Crimson.
grp.21st-century-schizoid-band.hikaye: Made up of Ian McDonald, Michael Giles, Peter Giles, Mel Collins and Jakko Jakszyk on vocals and guitar, the band played the early Crimson repertoire that Fripp had never taken on stage (including Poseidon, Lizard and Islands) in the hands of the original musicians. Michael Giles soon handed over to Ian Wallace. The band broke up after a few tours and live albums, but its real significance is that this experience led Jakko Jakszyk to become King Crimson's official singer and guitarist in 2013.
grp.21st-century-schizoid-band.dna: The 1969–72 Crimson repertoire, McDonald's woodwinds and Collins's saxophone; respectful but lively interpretations.
grp.21st-century-schizoid-band.gecisler: King Crimson (1969–72 line-up) → 21CSB → Jakszyk and Collins into King Crimson (2013). Related: Jakszyk, Fripp, Collins (A Scarcity of Miracles, 2011).
grp.21st-century-schizoid-band.etki: The bridge project that encouraged Fripp to bring the early repertoire back to the stage.
alb.21st-century-schizoid-band-2002-offi: Live recordings from the first tour: pieces long absent from the stage, such as 'Cirkus', 'Pictures of a City' and 'Formentera Lady'.
alb.21st-century-schizoid-band-2011-a-sc: Subtitled 'A King Crimson ProjeKct', a joint album by Jakszyk, Fripp and Collins (with Levin and Harrison). The direct precursor of the new Crimson line-up.
Recommended — the doorway to the 2013 Crimson.
grp.projekcts.kurulus: 1997–1999. Projects in which King Crimson's double-trio line-up split into subgroups for improvised 'research and development'.
grp.projekcts.hikaye: Using a method he called 'fraKctalisation', Fripp divided the six-piece Crimson into small, flexible subgroups: ProjeKct One (Fripp, Gunn, Levin, Bruford), Two (Fripp, Gunn, Belew on drums — electronic V-Drums), Three (Fripp, Gunn, Mastelotto) and Four (Fripp, Gunn, Levin, Mastelotto). All were almost entirely improvised; this work produced the material for The ConstruKction of Light and The Power to Believe. Bruford and Levin effectively left Crimson during this period. ProjeKct Six and X also made recordings in the 2000s.
grp.projekcts.dna: Free improvisation, electronic drums, Warr guitar and Soundscapes; a laboratory somewhere between jazz, metal and ambient.
grp.projekcts.gecisler: King Crimson (THRAK line-up) → ProjeKcts → King Crimson (the 2000 quartet); Trey Gunn and Pat Mastelotto → TU; Levin → Stick Men.
grp.projekcts.etki: The umbrella that openly documented Crimson's method (from improvisation to composition) and later inspired the Crimson ProjeKCt and Stick Men.
alb.projekcts-1998-space-groove.an: ProjeKct Two: space-funk improvisations with Belew's electronic drums, Fripp's synth guitar and Gunn's Warr guitar.
alb.projekcts-1999-masque.an: ProjeKct Three: heavy, electronic and dark; the riffs of the ConstruKction era are born here.
alb.projekcts-1999-the-projekcts.an: A four-disc box set collecting live recordings of all four ProjeKcts; the complete document of the period.
alb.projekcts-1999-the-projekcts.oncelik: Secondary priority — for the dedicated listener.
grp.stick-men-the-crimson-projekct.kurul: 2007, Tony Levin's Chapman Stick-focused trio. The Crimson ProjeKCt (2011–2014): Stick Men + the Adrian Belew Power Trio.
grp.stick-men-the-crimson-projekct.hikay: Stick Men grew out of Tony Levin's 2007 solo album devoted to the Stick and became a permanent trio with Pat Mastelotto (drums) and German Stick master Markus Reuter (Touch Guitar). During King Crimson's long silence after 2008, Stick Men and Adrian Belew's Power Trio joined forces as 'The Crimson ProjeKCt', keeping the Crimson repertoire (especially the Discipline–THRAK era) alive on stage. Although Levin and Mastelotto returned to Crimson in 2013, Stick Men continued as an independent creative band and also played joint concerts with Mel Collins and David Cross.
grp.stick-men-the-crimson-projekct.dna: Chapman Stick and Touch Guitar textures, Crimson's polyrhythmic legacy, industrial-electronic colour.
grp.stick-men-the-crimson-projekct.gecis: Tony Levin (Crimson, Gabriel, Bruford Levin Upper Extremities), Pat Mastelotto (Mr. Mister → Crimson), Markus Reuter (Centrozoon, Tuner) → Stick Men; Belew Power Trio → The Crimson ProjeKCt.
grp.stick-men-the-crimson-projekct.etki: The Crimson family's 'side current' in the 2010s; a showcase for instruments like the Stick and Touch Guitar in modern prog.
alb.stick-men-2010-soup.an: The first album with Markus Reuter; an adaptation of Stravinsky's 'Firebird' and hard rhythmic pieces in the Crimson line.
alb.stick-men-2014-live-in-tokyo.an: As The Crimson ProjeKCt: double-drummer versions of Crimson classics with Belew, Levin, Mastelotto, Reuter, Julie Slick and Tobias Ralph.
alb.stick-men-2016-prog-noir.an: A dark direction that Levin called 'prog noir': song-oriented but complex.
sec.5.title: The Yes Universe
grp.yes.kurulus: 1968, London. Formed when Jon Anderson and Chris Squire met. Built on many-layered vocal harmonies and virtuoso instrumentation.
grp.yes.hikaye: Yes was born in 1968 when singer Jon Anderson met bassist Chris Squire at the La Chasse club in London; Peter Banks (guitar), Tony Kaye (organ) and Bill Bruford (drums) joined what was left of Squire's band Mabel Greer's Toyshop. The first two albums featured Beatles, Byrds and West Coast harmonies alongside orchestral experiments. With the arrival of Steve Howe in 1970 and Rick Wakeman in 1971 the band found its own sound; with Roger Dean's covers and logo and Eddie Offord's production, the run from The Yes Album to Close to the Edge became the golden age of symphonic prog. When Bruford left for King Crimson in 1972, Alan White came in; the excess of Tales from Topographic Oceans drove Wakeman away and Swiss keyboardist Patrick Moraz replaced him. After Wakeman's return the band made Going for the One and Tormato, and in 1980, with Anderson and Wakeman gone, took on the Buggles duo Trevor Horn and Geoff Downes (Drama). The band broke up; Cinema, the project Squire and White formed with Trevor Rabin, turned into 90125 and the hit 'Owner of a Lonely Heart' once Anderson joined. By the late '80s there were two Yeses: the Squire-led 'Yes-West' and Anderson Bruford Wakeman Howe; Union (1991) merged them. In the '90s the classic line-up returned with Keys to Ascension. After Anderson's health problems in 2008 the band continued with Benoît David and then Jon Davison; Squire died in 2015 and White in 2022. Under Steve Howe's leadership and production the band kept making new albums. Meanwhile Anderson, Rabin and Wakeman formed a separate branch as 'Yes featuring ARW'.
grp.yes.dna: High-register melodic vocals, the Rickenbacker bass pushed forward like a lead instrument, long multi-part suites, fantastical/spiritual lyrics, Roger Dean's cosmic covers.
grp.yes.etki: The summit of "symphonic prog"; with Genesis, the standard-bearer of the melodic wing. The main reference for the American renaissance of the '90s (World Trade, Spock's Beard).
grp.yes.ipucu: Listen era by era in blocks; don't race through the chronology in one go.
Follow the line-up changes like a chart — especially the keyboard seat's cycle Kaye→Wakeman→Moraz→Wakeman→Kaye→Downes→Wakeman (the son)→Downes; most differences in sound are explained there.
Treat the live albums as 'documentaries' rather than comparing them one-to-one with the studio versions — hear them as a snapshot of that tour.
It makes more sense to hear the post-90125 period (Trevor Rabin's AOR line) as a 'different band' from what came before.
grp.yes.tarih: Macan describes how bands such as Yes, Genesis, ELP, Pink Floyd and Jethro Tull tried in the 1970s to bring the scope and sense of grandeur of classical music into rock, which produced both huge popularity and a critical reaction that found them 'cold and showy'. In his view, the punk/new wave backlash of the late '70s was partly a DIY movement against this 'excess'.
grp.yes.era.0.note: The band has not yet found its own sound; a cover-heavy, folk-to-prog transitional period. Tony Kaye's organ and Peter Banks's guitar are the signature of this era.
grp.yes.era.1.note: With Steve Howe and Rick Wakeman (Patrick Moraz on Relayer) the 'real Yes' takes shape. If possible, listen to this block in LP order, back to back.
grp.yes.era.2.note: Wakeman's return and a 'sunnier' approach to production.
grp.yes.era.3.note: The 90125 era: the AOR transformation brought by Trevor Horn's production and Trevor Rabin's guitar and songwriting. It makes more sense to hear this block as a 'different band' from the previous era.
grp.yes.era.4.note: Union is really an assembly of pieces that were never played together in the studio — keep expectations low.
grp.yes.era.5.note: Documents the reunion of the classic line-up (Anderson-Squire-Howe-Wakeman-White).
grp.yes.era.6.note: Career retrospectives and a new studio era that arrives with Fly from Here.
grp.yes.era.7.note: Attempts to return to the old 'epic' formula begin, produced by Steve Howe.
grp.yes.era.8.note: The current era, produced by Steve Howe, in which Jay Schellen became a full member after Alan White's death in 2022.
alb.yes-1969-yes.an: Cover-heavy (Beatles, Byrds), a search for identity; Peter Banks on guitar, Tony Kaye on organ. The approach to vocal harmony is already distinctive.
alb.yes-1969-yes.dn: The debut. It includes Beatles and Byrds covers; there is no trace yet of the band's later complex structures, but Squire's bass playing is already distinctive.
alb.yes-1969-yes.oncelik: Usually skipped on a first listen — but important for understanding the band's origins.
alb.yes-1969-yes.detay: The first album, before any Roger Dean cover design
Cover songs (e.g. the Beatles) mixed with original material
alb.yes-1969-yes.tr: Beyond and Before — Squire's bass writing
Every Little Thing — Beatles adaptation, extended
alb.yes-1969-yes.crit: Seen as a starting point where the band was still searching for its sound; it carries no clear sign of the complex structures to come.
alb.yes-1970-time-and-a-word.an: An orchestral experiment; it caused tension within the band and led to Banks's departure. Banks's last album.
alb.yes-1970-time-and-a-word.dn: An experiment with orchestral backing; Peter Banks's last album (before the switch to Steve Howe).
alb.yes-1970-time-and-a-word.oncelik: Low priority, but worth hearing to understand the line-up transition.
alb.yes-1970-time-and-a-word.detay: The use of orchestration is the first sign of the epic structure that would become Yes's signature
Peter Banks left after this album and was replaced by Steve Howe
alb.yes-1970-time-and-a-word.tr: Time and a Word — orchestral title track
No Opportunity Necessary, No Experience Needed — Richie Havens adaptation
alb.yes-1970-time-and-a-word.crit: The orchestral writing is read as the first attempt at the epic structure that would become the band's signature; Peter Banks's unhappiness with this choice paved the way for his departure.
alb.yes-1971-the-yes-album.an: With Steve Howe the identity settles. "Yours Is No Disgrace", "Starship Trooper", "I've Seen All Good People" — Howe's acoustic/electric transitions and country-jazz figures define the band's sound. The first great leap.
alb.yes-1971-the-yes-album.dn: Steve Howe's first album. This is where the band finds its own sound.
alb.yes-1971-the-yes-album.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The band's real starting point.
alb.yes-1971-the-yes-album.detay: The origin of concert classics such as "Starship Trooper"
Howe's versatile guitar style (acoustic + electric) is fully on display for the first time
alb.yes-1971-the-yes-album.tr: Starship Trooper — three-part suite, Howe's acoustic-plus-electric finale
Yours Is No Disgrace — the band's first great long-form piece
I've Seen All Good People — acoustic-plus-organ hit
alb.yes-1971-the-yes-album.crit: Considered the turning point where the band found its own sound with Steve Howe's arrival; 'Starship Trooper' and 'Yours Is No Disgrace' laid the foundations of the band's concert repertoire.
alb.yes-1971-fragile.an: Wakeman joins; a format of one solo piece per member plus band pieces. "Roundabout" and "Heart of the Sunrise" become classics, and Roger Dean starts on the covers. The classic line-up is born.
alb.yes-1971-fragile.dn: Rick Wakeman joins and Roger Dean's cover art begins. Each member has a solo piece (a striking concept).
alb.yes-1971-fragile.detay: "Roundabout" is here — listen to the full version, not the radio edit
Each member's short solo piece is part of the album's concept — don't skip them
alb.yes-1971-fragile.tr: Roundabout — Howe's acoustic opening, the band's emblem
Heart of the Sunrise — complex, Crimson-tinged climax
Mood for a Day — Howe solo guitar
alb.yes-1971-fragile.crit: Critics stress how Wakeman's electric and acoustic piano, synthesiser and Mellotron gave the album a new 'hard, swirling' texture.
Fragile is positioned as an album that redefined the 'near-flawless' success of The Yes Album; with Close to the Edge it is counted as part of prog rock's 'holy trinity'.
Chris Squire's bass playing on the album is described as a pioneering approach that moved the instrument from the back of the mix to the front.
alb.yes-1972-close-to-the-edge.an: A single title suite (18 minutes) plus two long pieces. For structural perfection, the balance of voice and instruments and its theme of spiritual ascent, most critics consider it the masterpiece of Yes (and of the genre). Bruford's last studio album before leaving for King Crimson.
alb.yes-1972-close-to-the-edge.dn: Generally regarded as the band's peak. The title track is a single 18-minute suite — listen without interruption.
alb.yes-1972-close-to-the-edge.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The reference album.
alb.yes-1972-close-to-the-edge.detay: Bill Bruford's last album (he then moved to King Crimson)
The title track is a four-part suite; it is best heard unbroken
The starting point of the compositional leap towards Tales from Topographic Oceans
alb.yes-1972-close-to-the-edge.tr: Close to the Edge — 18-minute, four-part suite; one of the genre's masterpieces
And You and I — acoustic-and-orchestral epic
alb.yes-1972-close-to-the-edge.crit: Described as a 'flawless masterpiece' as of 1972; the same review also points to the decline that awaited the band after this peak.
Defined as a key document of how powerful prog rock could be when focused.
On release Rolling Stone was more critical, finding the structure forced and inflated — an example of how prog rock was never unanimously embraced by critics.
alb.yes-1973-yessongs.an: Not just a live album; a document summarising the repertoire of the pre-Relayer era. Also important for Roger Dean's iconic cover art.
alb.yes-1973-yessongs.oncelik: Essential for the dedicated listener; general listeners can prioritise the studio albums.
alb.yes-1973-yessongs.detay: Alan White's first recorded live performances (replacing Bruford)
Roger Dean's cover art is part of the album's identity
alb.yes-1973-tales-from-topographic-ocea: A double LP with four long suites (one per side). Inspired by the Shastric scriptures; the centre of the debate about excess. A polarising peak, the target of both admiration and the charge of being 'bloated'.
Four sides, four long suites — the band's most controversial but most ambitious album. The peak of the shift from short songs to huge suites.
Essential — but challenging for first-time listeners; come prepared.
Rick Wakeman was unhappy with this album and left soon afterwards
The concept was inspired by Shastric texts
It can feel dense at first; listen patiently, one side at a time
In prog history this album is remembered as the symbol of the genre's 'excess' — often cited together with ELP's Works (1977).
The Revealing Science of God — opening suite, the best-loved side
Ritual (Nous Sommes du Soleil) — closer with a percussion climax
On release the album was dismissed as 'psychedelic doodling' and found over-ornamented compared with the earlier records.
Critics noted that some sections were brilliant but that the music often took far longer than necessary to make its point and lacked warmth.

Later assessments reread the album as the 'true destination' of the band's '70s rise, more so than Close to the Edge; Howe's guitar playing is said to set a standard while Wakeman's contribution stayed limited.
Wakeman mocked the album with a nickname in interviews of the time and said he found the record inflated; this dissatisfaction was one of the reasons he left.
alb.yes-1974-relayer.an: With Patrick Moraz's jazz-fusion edge. "The Gates of Delirium" (a war allegory based on Tolstoy's War and Peace) is the band's most aggressive long piece; "Soon" is an island of lyrical calm.
alb.yes-1974-relayer.dn: Patrick Moraz replaced Wakeman; the jazz-fusion influence grew noticeably.
alb.yes-1974-relayer.oncelik: Essential — the close of the classic era.
alb.yes-1974-relayer.detay: Moraz's keyboard style is very different from Wakeman's — more jazz/fusion-oriented
"The Gates of Delirium" is about war and is one of the band's most aggressive compositions
alb.yes-1974-relayer.tr: The Gates of Delirium — 22-minute war allegory (Tolstoy) that ends in the calm of 'Soon'
alb.yes-1974-relayer.crit: Patrick Moraz's jazz-fusion keyboard style is seen as a turning point in its own right, taking the album in a more aggressive and rhythmically complex direction than the Wakeman era.
alb.yes-1975-yesterdays.an: Compiled from the first two albums and stray tracks. Valuable for understanding the band before it found its 'Yes' identity.
alb.yes-1975-yesterdays.oncelik: Secondary priority; those who already know the early period can skip it.
alb.yes-1975-yesterdays.detay: A practical entry point that gathers the early material in one place
alb.yes-1977-going-for-the-one.an: Wakeman returns; in the middle of the punk explosion, a tighter, more 'rock' structure. "Awaken" is a late-period peak.
alb.yes-1977-going-for-the-one.dn: Wakeman's return to the band. Shorter, 'sunnier' and more accessible production.
alb.yes-1977-going-for-the-one.oncelik: Essential — it represents the transitional period well.
alb.yes-1977-going-for-the-one.detay: With Wakeman's return the classic line-up partly reunited
alb.yes-1977-going-for-the-one.tr: Awaken — 15-minute spiritual epic, a late-period peak
Going for the One — Howe's steel guitar, hard-edged opener
alb.yes-1978-tormato.an: The fatigue and scattering of the classic line-up; the start of a critical decline.
alb.yes-1978-tormato.dn: A follow-up to Going for the One that received more mixed reviews.
alb.yes-1978-tormato.detay: The product of a period of growing tension within the band
alb.yes-1978-tormato.tr: Don't Kill the Whale — environmental single
alb.yes-1980-yesshows.an: Live recordings compiled from the 1976–78 tours.
alb.yes-1980-drama.an: No Anderson or Wakeman; the Buggles line-up comes in (Horn on vocals, Downes on keyboards). Unexpectedly hard and modern thanks to "Machine Messiah"; a cult in-between album.
alb.yes-1980-drama.dn: The missing link before Yes's '80s transformation: where classic Yes energy meets new-wave production.
alb.yes-1980-drama.oncelik: Recommended — the only '70s-style album without Anderson; less known than it deserves.
alb.yes-1980-drama.kadro: Trevor Horn (vocals), Steve Howe, Chris Squire, Geoff Downes, Alan White
alb.yes-1980-drama.detay: After Anderson and Wakeman left, the Buggles duo (Horn and Downes) joined; the creators of 'Video Killed the Radio Star' entered the heart of prog.
'Machine Messiah' and 'Tempus Fugit' are among the band's hardest and heaviest pieces.
The band broke up after the album: Howe and Downes formed Asia, and Horn turned to production and made 90125.
This album was missing from the Yes discography notes module; this information is the atlas's own addition.
alb.yes-1980-drama.tr: Machine Messiah — hard, modern 10-minute opener showing the Buggles line-up's power
Into the Lens — the Buggles' 'I Am a Camera'
alb.yes-1981-classic-yes.an: The last compilation before the first hiatus.
alb.yes-1981-classic-yes.oncelik: Skippable — the content is already on other albums.
alb.yes-1983-90125.an: A pop-rock transformation written by Trevor Rabin and produced by Trevor Horn. "Owner of a Lonely Heart" hit number one in the US and the album became the band's best seller. A huge departure from the prog identity — and the commercial peak.
alb.yes-1983-90125.dn: The big transformation brought by Trevor Horn's production. "Owner of a Lonely Heart" is the band's only US #1 — '80s Yes can't be understood without it.
alb.yes-1983-90125.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The commercial peak.
alb.yes-1983-90125.detay: Trevor Rabin's arrival completely changed the guitar and songwriting
"Owner of a Lonely Heart" is the band's only Billboard #1
A production approach cut off from the previous era — hear it as a separate 'era'
alb.yes-1983-90125.tr: Owner of a Lonely Heart — made by Rabin/Horn, a US number one and a huge departure from prog
Changes — rhythmically complex, with traces of prog
alb.yes-1983-90125.crit: Described as a striking reinvention of a band thought dead, and credited with introducing Yes to a new audience.
Critics note that, depending on where you stand, the song can be seen either as the 'ultimate betrayal' of the classic Yes sound or as the band's perfect adaptation to a new age.
alb.yes-1985-9012live-the-solos.an: Live recordings from the 90125 tour, focused on solo performances.
alb.yes-1987-big-generator.an: A more laboured continuation of the 90125 formula; "Rhythm of Love" was a hit.
alb.yes-1987-big-generator.dn: The follow-up to 90125, with a similar AOR direction.
alb.yes-1991-union.an: The merger of ABWH and the Rabin-era Yes; a giant eight-piece line-up. Scattered but historically important — the record on which Billy Sherwood enters the band's history ("The More We Live – Let Go", co-written with Squire).
alb.yes-1991-union.dn: An eight-piece mega line-up, but the parts were never played together in the studio — which is why it is considered inconsistent within the discography.
alb.yes-1991-union.oncelik: Optional — worth hearing out of historical curiosity.
alb.yes-1991-union.kadro: An eight-piece 'merger of two Yeses' (Anderson, Squire, Rabin, Howe, Wakeman, Kaye, White, Bruford)
alb.yes-1991-union.detay: Despite the size of the line-up, the parts were recorded separately and combined later
alb.yes-1991-union.tr: The More We Live - Let Go — written by Sherwood/Squire, the World Trade connection
I Would Have Waited Forever — the ABWH side
alb.yes-1991-union.crit: Although the eight-piece 'reunion' concept looked very appealing, the result is described as feeling less like a family reunion than a stitched-together 'Frankenstein's monster'.
Years later Bruford described it as the most embarrassing record of his career and said he joined the tour only for financial reasons.
alb.yes-1991-yesyears.an: An overview of the whole career.
alb.yes-1991-yesyears.oncelik: Skippable — the content is available elsewhere.
alb.yes-1993-symphonic-music-of-yes.an: Shouldn't be compared one-to-one with the studio versions; hear it as a separate interpretation, a 'snapshot of that tour'.
alb.yes-1994-talk.an: Written by Rabin with digital production, the album that closes his era; Sherwood joins on tour.
alb.yes-1994-talk.dn: The last studio album of the 90125/Big Generator line.
alb.yes-1994-talk.tr: Endless Dream — 15-minute epic, Rabin's farewell to prog
alb.yes-1994-an-evening-of-yes-music-plu: A small-scale, mostly acoustic live recording.
alb.yes-1996-keys-to-ascension.an: Not just a live album — it hides several new studio tracks, so don't dismiss it as 'just a live album'.
alb.yes-1996-keys-to-ascension.detay: The reunion of the classic line-up (Anderson, Squire, Howe, Wakeman, White)
alb.yes-1997-keys-to-ascension-2.an: The sequel to the first Keys album, again with new tracks.
alb.yes-1997-open-your-eyes.an: The period that began with Billy Sherwood joining.
alb.yes-1998-beyond-and-before.an: A compilation focused on the early period.
alb.yes-1999-the-ladder.an: Produced by Bruce Fairbairn, an album with growing world-music influences.
alb.yes-2000-house-of-yes-live-from-hous: Live recordings from The Ladder tour.
alb.yes-2001-keystudio.an: A compilation gathering the new studio tracks from Keys to Ascension 1 and 2.
alb.yes-2001-keystudio.oncelik: Optional — a repeat for those who already know the Keys albums.
alb.yes-2001-keystudio.tip: compilation (studio recordings from the Keys sessions)
alb.yes-2001-keystudio.detay: Collects the Keys studio tracks in one place — handy for those who only want the new songs without the live material
alb.yes-2001-magnification.an: An album recorded without a keyboard player, with an orchestra instead.
alb.yes-2001-magnification.oncelik: Optional, but an interesting period in line-up terms.
alb.yes-2001-magnification.detay: No Tony Kaye or Rick Wakeman — the orchestra takes on the keyboard role
alb.yes-2002-in-a-word-yes-1969.an: Contains rare B-sides and demo material — the real treasure for collectors.
alb.yes-2002-in-a-word-yes-1969.oncelik: Important for serious collectors, optional for general listeners.
alb.yes-2003-the-ultimate-yes-35th-anniv: A compilation summarising the whole career.
alb.yes-2005-the-word-is-live.an: A box set bringing together live recordings from different eras.
alb.yes-2011-fly-from-here.an: Produced by Trevor Horn, a kind of return to the 90125 era. Linked to the 2018 Return Trip version and to From a Page (2019/2026).
alb.yes-2011-fly-from-here.oncelik: Essential — the start of the modern era.
alb.yes-2011-fly-from-here.kadro: Benoît David (vocals) instead of Anderson, Geoff Downes (keyboards)
alb.yes-2011-fly-from-here.detay: Benoît David is the singer in this period
Material left over from the 2010 Phoenix sessions was released separately as From a Page
alb.yes-2013-like-it-is-yes-at-the-brist: Complete performances of the classic albums Close to the Edge and Fragile.
Classic albums performed live from start to finish
alb.yes-2014-heaven-earth.detay: Jon Davison became the singer with this album
alb.yes-2015-like-it-is-yes-at-the-mesa-: Includes a complete performance of Going for the One.
alb.yes-2017-topographic-drama-live-acro: Live performances of selections from Tales from Topographic Oceans and Close to the Edge.
alb.yes-2018-fly-from-here-return-trip.a: The 2011 album re-recorded with Trevor Horn's own vocals (instead of Benoît David's) — hear it as two different 'identities' of the same album.
alb.yes-2018-fly-from-here-return-trip.o: Essential — very rewarding to compare with the original.
alb.yes-2018-fly-from-here-return-trip.d: A side-by-side listen with the original Fly from Here is recommended
alb.yes-2019-from-a-page.an: The 'lost' side of the 2010 Fly from Here sessions, with Oliver Wakeman's keyboard parts.
alb.yes-2019-from-a-page.oncelik: Optional — best heard together with the 2026 expanded version.
alb.yes-2019-from-a-page.detay: A version expanded to 15 tracks was released in 2026 (see below)
alb.yes-2021-the-quest.an: The 22nd studio album. One of Alan White's last albums.
alb.yes-2021-the-quest.oncelik: Essential — a turning point of the modern era.
alb.yes-2021-the-quest.detay: Orchestral arrangements on some tracks with the FAMES Orchestra (North Macedonia)
alb.yes-2021-the-quest.crit: Summed up as a middling but clearly better effort than Heaven & Earth from the prog-rock icons; generally found lacking in fire and too soft.
alb.yes-2023-mirror-to-the-sky.an: Alan White died in 2022; Jay Schellen became a full member in 2023. This is the first album Schellen recorded as a full member.
alb.yes-2023-mirror-to-the-sky.kadro: Jay Schellen (drums, first album as a full member)
alb.yes-2023-mirror-to-the-sky.detay: The first album after Alan White's death
The orchestral collaboration with the FAMES Orchestra continues
alb.yes-2023-mirror-to-the-sky.crit: Described as the best Yes album in more than twenty years.
Said to have unexpectedly and easily surpassed The Quest, signalling momentum for the future.
While some critics found The Quest 'fireless and too sweet', the same publication framed Mirror to the Sky more positively.
alb.yes-2023-yessingles.an: Brings together rare single versions from 1970–1983.
alb.yes-2023-yessingles.detay: The first digital release of the promo radio edit of "And You and I"
alb.yes-2026-from-a-page-expanded-remast: The 2019 four-song mini-album expanded to 15 tracks. It can be heard as an 'alternative universe' of Fly from Here with Oliver Wakeman on keyboards — comparing the two versions is an interesting exercise.
Optional, but important for fans of Fly from Here — listen comparatively.
Oliver Wakeman's original keyboard parts replace Geoff Downes's parts from the studio version
The studio version of Chris Squire's song "Aliens" appears for the first time
The second disc contains demo versions
Reviewers stress that the expanded edition presents, for the first time and all together, the pieces from the Fly from Here sessions that went unused at the time.
alb.yes-2026-aurora.an: The 24th studio album, released 12 June 2026. Led by the 'creative axis' of Howe and Geoff Downes; recorded piecemeal in home studios and assembled afterwards (a production model similar to 2011's Fly from Here).
alb.yes-2026-aurora.oncelik: Essential — the most recent studio album.
alb.yes-2026-aurora.kadro: The second album Jay Schellen recorded as a full member
alb.yes-2026-aurora.detay: Recorded separately in home studios and combined later
An important reference point as the matured form of the post-Alan White era
grp.anderson-bruford-wakeman-howe-abwh.k: 1989. Because Chris Squire owned the rights to the name "Yes", the four classic members who had broken away (Jon Anderson, Bill Bruford, Rick Wakeman, Steve Howe) formed an "almost-Yes" under their surnames. A rare node in the network that "reunites a universe from within".
grp.anderson-bruford-wakeman-howe-abwh.d: The classic Yes sound (Howe's guitar + Anderson's voice + Wakeman's keyboards + Bruford's drums) recreated with late-'80s production.
grp.anderson-bruford-wakeman-howe-abwh.u: The four-man core + Tony Levin (bass — another King Crimson link).
grp.anderson-bruford-wakeman-howe-abwh.g: Before → Yes. After → officially dissolved back into Yes with Union (1991).
alb.anderson-bruford-wakeman-howe-1989-a: Revives the long-form approach of classic Yes with pieces like "Brother of Mine" and "Order of the Universe". Commercially successful; it really plays like a 'true Yes' album. Without the legal obstacle over the name it would have counted as a Yes album.
Brother of Mine — multi-part, a revival of classic Yes long form
Order of the Universe — energetic epic
grp.flash.kurulus: 1971–72. Formed by Yes's first guitarist Peter Banks after he left the band (after Time and a Word), with singer Colin Carter. Tony Kaye (Yes keyboards) guests on the first album.
grp.flash.dna: A guitar-centred continuation of the early Yes sound: Banks's angular, melodic guitar and vocal harmonies. An alternative history of what Yes 'might have been'.
grp.flash.uyeler: Peter Banks (guitar), Colin Carter (vocals), Ray Bennett (bass), Mike Hough (drums). Tony Kaye guests on keyboards on the first album — two former Yes members side by side.
grp.flash.gecisler: Before → Yes (Banks), Yes (Kaye as guest). Banks later formed Empire. The 'first member to leave' branch of Yes.
grp.flash.etki: The earliest offshoot of the Yes universe; Banks carrying Yes's characteristic guitar language into his own band. Cult status.
alb.flash-1972-flash.an: The debut; Tony Kaye guests on keyboards. 'Small Beginnings' became a hit in the US — melodic prog carrying the texture of early Yes.
alb.flash-1972-flash.tr: Small Beginnings — the band's best-known piece, a hit
alb.flash-1972-in-the-can.an: The second album; longer-form and more complex. Banks's guitar comes to the fore.
alb.flash-1973-out-of-our-hands.an: The third and final album; the band's most mature but lowest-selling record. They split afterwards.
grp.rick-wakeman-solo.name: Rick Wakeman (solo)
grp.rick-wakeman-solo.kurulus: Born 1949, London. A session keyboardist who left the Royal College of Music; he played Mellotron and piano on Bowie's 'Space Oddity' and 'Life on Mars?'. Keyboardist with the Strawbs (1970–71) and Yes.
grp.rick-wakeman-solo.hikaye: With his caped stage image and the castles of keyboards surrounding him, he became the most iconic keyboardist of the '70s. In the solo career he began while still in Yes, he turned historical and literary concepts into huge works with orchestra and choir; he staged King Arthur as an ice show at Wembley and ran up large debts. He left and returned to Yes four times. In the '80s he made his living from film scores and new age piano albums; from the '90s on he made sequels to his classic works (Journey part 2, Six Wives live at Hampton Court in 2009). His sons Adam and Oliver Wakeman are also keyboardists (Oliver played in Yes; Adam toured with Ozzy Osbourne and Black Sabbath). He is also known on British television for his witty storytelling.
grp.rick-wakeman-solo.dna: Classical piano technique, Minimoog solos, Mellotron and church organ; narrative programme music with orchestra and choir.
grp.rick-wakeman-solo.gecisler: Strawbs → Yes → solo; ABWH (1989), Anderson Rabin Wakeman (2016–18). His son Oliver Wakeman: Yes (2008–11), From a Page.
grp.rick-wakeman-solo.etki: The most popular face of keyboard-centred symphonic rock; with Keith Emerson, the archetype of the 'keyboard virtuoso'.
alb.rick-wakeman-1973-the-six-wives-of-h: An instrumental portrait of each of Henry VIII's six wives. A solo masterpiece featuring members of Yes and the Strawbs, showing Wakeman's technique in its purest form.
Essential — the peak of his solo career.
Wakeman + members of Yes and the Strawbs (Steve Howe, Chris Squire, Bill Bruford, Alan White, Dave Lambert, Chas Cronk and others)
Entirely instrumental; each 'wife' is entrusted to a different keyboard colour.
Anne Boleyn — with the hymn 'The Day Thou Gavest Lord Hath Ended'
alb.rick-wakeman-1974-journey-to-the-cen: A rock cantata on Jules Verne's novel, recorded live at the Royal Festival Hall with the London Symphony Orchestra and the English Chamber Choir. Number one in the UK; Wakeman's commercial peak.
A&M initially rejected the project as too expensive; Wakeman recorded it with his own means.
alb.rick-wakeman-1975-the-myths-and-lege: The Arthurian legend told with orchestra and choir; staged on ice at Wembley.
alb.rick-wakeman-1976-no-earthly-connect: An ambitious allegorical concept about the soul of music and the human universe, recorded in a band format.
alb.rick-wakeman-1977-criminal-record.an: An instrumental album with Squire and White, recorded during the Going for the One sessions with Yes in Switzerland; dominated by church organ.
alb.rick-wakeman-1999-return-to-the-cent: The sequel to the 1974 work: with the London Symphony Orchestra, narrator Patrick Stewart and guests such as Ozzy Osbourne, Bonnie Tyler, Trevor Rabin and Justin Hayward.
grp.steve-howe-solo.name: Steve Howe (solo)
grp.steve-howe-solo.kurulus: Born 1947, London. From the Syndicats, Tomorrow and Bodast to Yes (1970); founder of Asia and GTR.
grp.steve-howe-solo.hikaye: Howe's guitar language is a unique synthesis of jazz (Wes Montgomery), country picking (Chet Atkins), classical guitar and rock; he is known as a vintage-instrument master who plays prog on a Gibson ES-175 jazz guitar. He was one of the architects of Yes's 1971–80 peak; he formed Asia in 1981 and GTR with Steve Hackett in 1986, returning to Yes via ABWH in 1989. Throughout his solo career he made instrumental albums exploring every colour of acoustic and electric guitar; his son Dylan Howe, a jazz drummer, played on some of them. After 2008 he became Yes's de facto leader and producer.
grp.steve-howe-solo.dna: Jazz chords, country fingerpicking, Portuguese guitar and lap steel; a narrative style that travels through several genres within a single solo.
grp.steve-howe-solo.gecisler: Syndicats → Tomorrow → Bodast → Yes → Asia → GTR → ABWH → Yes; Steve Howe Trio (jazz).
grp.steve-howe-solo.etki: Prog guitar's 'poet of tone'; with his eclectic approach he set an example for the next generation (Roine Stolt, Steve Morse).
alb.steve-howe-1975-beginnings.an: Part of the wave of Yes solo albums; a plain first solo album with Howe's own vocals but rich in guitar.
alb.steve-howe-1975-beginnings.oncelik: Optional — listen to it like a set of guitar lessons.
alb.steve-howe-1975-beginnings.tr: Beginnings — classical guitar and chamber orchestra
alb.steve-howe-1979-the-steve-howe-album: His most eclectic solo album, mostly instrumental, with a Vivaldi adaptation and lap-steel pieces.
Concerto in D (Vivaldi) — acoustic guitar and orchestra
alb.steve-howe-1991-turbulence.an: An electric-guitar-centred instrumental album with Bill Bruford on drums; Howe's rock side in a '90s sound.
alb.steve-howe-2003-elements.an: A mix of world music and rock with his band Remedy (including his sons Dylan and Virgil Howe).
alb.steve-howe-2011-time.an: An elegant instrumental album orchestrated by Paul K. Joyce, highlighting Howe's classical and acoustic side.
grp.jon-anderson-solo.name: Jon Anderson (solo)
grp.jon-anderson-solo.kurulus: Born 1944, Accrington, Lancashire. Founding singer and main lyricist of Yes.
grp.jon-anderson-solo.hikaye: Anderson's alto-tenor voice and mystical, nature-centred lyrics defined the soul of Yes. On Olias of Sunhillow (1976) he played every instrument himself. With Vangelis, as Jon & Vangelis, he made electronic/new age classics in the '80s ('I'll Find My Way Home'). He left Yes in 1980 and 1988 and formed ABWH. In 2008 a Yes tour was cancelled because of his respiratory failure, and when the band replaced him with Benoît David he never returned. He formed ARW with Rabin and Wakeman and made joint albums with Jean-Luc Ponty and Roine Stolt.
grp.jon-anderson-solo.dna: Spiritual lyrics, a near-falsetto high tenor, an approach of 'sound rather than words' through vocal colour; world music and electronics.
grp.jon-anderson-solo.gecisler: The Warriors → Yes → Jon & Vangelis → ABWH → Yes → ARW; Anderson Ponty Band, Anderson/Stolt.
grp.jon-anderson-solo.etki: The archetype of the prog vocalist; his 'cosmic optimism' influenced the generation of Neal Morse and the Flower Kings.
alb.jon-anderson-1976-olias-of-sunhillow: A fantasy concept album on which Anderson plays every instrument, telling how Olias builds a spaceship, the Moorglade, to save his people from their dying planet. The sonic counterpart of the Roger Dean aesthetic.
Recommended — the mystical face of Yes.
The album was designed like a book called 'Olias', with illustrations by David Fairbairn.
alb.jon-anderson-1980-short-stories.an: The first album as Jon & Vangelis: songs over synth improvisations. The hit 'I Hear You Now'.
alb.jon-anderson-1981-the-friends-of-mr-: The peak of Jon & Vangelis: the film-noir-themed title track and 'I'll Find My Way Home'.
'State of Independence' was later turned into a hit by Donna Summer with Quincy Jones producing.
alb.jon-anderson-2011-survival-other-sto: A mature solo album recorded through online collaborations with musicians around the world.
alb.jon-anderson-2016-invention-of-knowl: A joint album with Roine Stolt of the Flower Kings; the late-period Anderson record closest to the '70s Yes aesthetic.
Essential — where Yes meets Swedish prog.
alb.jon-anderson-2019-1000-hands-chapter: An album begun in 1990 and left unfinished, completed with guests such as Chick Corea, Ian Anderson, Steve Howe, Chris Squire, Alan White and Jean-Luc Ponty.
Optional — the guest list reads like a map of the network.
grp.chris-squire-solo.name: Chris Squire (solo)
grp.chris-squire-solo.kurulus: 1948–2015, London. Founding bassist of Yes; the only member to play on all of the band's studio albums.
grp.chris-squire-solo.hikaye: Playing his Rickenbacker 4001 with a pick and a trebly, distorted tone, Squire turned the bass into a melodic instrument; with a voice trained in a church choir he carried Yes's three-part vocal harmonies. The nickname 'The Fish' came from his long baths. He was the one who kept the band going even when it fell apart, who held the rights to the Yes name and who launched the 90125 era (the Cinema project). He died of leukaemia in 2015; Billy Sherwood took his place at his request.
grp.chris-squire-solo.dna: Lead bass: pick, Rickenbacker treble, contrapuntal melodies; vocal harmony from the choir tradition.
grp.chris-squire-solo.gecisler: The Syn → Mabel Greer's Toyshop → Yes; Cinema (1982, with Rabin/White, became 90125); XYZ (1981 demos with Page); Squackett (with Hackett).
grp.chris-squire-solo.etki: One of the most influential figures in bringing the bass guitar to the fore in rock; a model for bassists such as Geddy Lee, Steve Harris and Billy Sheehan.
His only 'true' solo album, with Bill Bruford and Patrick Moraz and orchestral arrangements by Andrew Pryce Jackman. Church organ, orchestra and bass melodies; considered the best Yes solo album.
Mel Collins (King Crimson) and Jimmy Hastings (Caravan) on woodwinds — three universes meeting.
alb.chris-squire-2007-chris-squire-s-swi: An album of Christmas carols; Squire returning to his church-choir roots.
alb.chris-squire-2012-a-life-within-a-da: A joint album with Steve Hackett as Squackett; the common ground of Yes and Genesis.
'Aliens' is a Squire composition that also appears on the expanded edition of Yes's From a Page.
alb.rick-wakeman-1999-return-to-the-cent: Never Is a Long Long Time — Justin Hayward
sec.6.title: The ELP Universe
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.kurulus: 1970, London. Keith Emerson from The Nice, Greg Lake from King Crimson and Carl Palmer from Atomic Rooster — the network's first true "supergroup".
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.hikaye: Formed in 1970 by Keith Emerson (The Nice), Greg Lake (King Crimson) and Carl Palmer (Atomic Rooster, the Crazy World of Arthur Brown), ELP is regarded as prog's first 'supergroup'. Their big breakthrough came at the Isle of Wight festival in August 1970, with cannons firing on stage. Emerson wedging his Hammond keys with knives and toppling it, and being one of the first musicians to take the Moog modular synthesiser on stage, became the band's signature. Rock adaptations of classical works (Mussorgsky, Copland, Ginastera, Bartók) and Lake's acoustic ballads were the band's two poles. Touring with a full symphony orchestra in 1977 turned into a financial disaster; Love Beach (1978) was recorded to fulfil contractual obligations and the band split. The '80s brought Emerson, Lake & Powell (with Cozy Powell) and 3 (Emerson–Palmer–Robert Berry); the classic trio reunited in 1991 and made two albums. Emerson died in March 2016 and Lake in December of the same year.
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.dna: Organ/Moog virtuosity, adaptations of classical works (Mussorgsky, Ginastera, Copland, Bartók), bombastic stage show, maximum sound from a trio.
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.uyeler: The core trio stayed fixed. In 1986 Cozy Powell stood in for Palmer (Emerson, Lake & Powell); short-lived.
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.etki: The far extreme of keyboard-centred prog; the direct continuation of The Nice and the bridge to Asia.
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.ipucu: Listen to ELP as two separate veins: Emerson's classical adaptations and suites (Tarkus, Karn Evil 9) and Lake's acoustic ballads (Lucky Man, From the Beginning, C'est la Vie).
Listen to the classical sources (Pictures at an Exhibition, Fanfare for the Common Man, Toccata) in their original form first; only then can you appreciate the audacity of the adaptations.
The live albums (Pictures at an Exhibition, Welcome Back My Friends) are the band's true habitat.
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.era.0.note: The peak across five studio and live albums: Moog, Hammond, classical adaptations and the Manticore legend.
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.era.1.note: Orchestral ambition, financial crisis and Love Beach.
grp.emerson-lake-palmer-elp.era.2.note: The Victory Records years: two studio albums, a brief renaissance.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1970-emerson-lak: The introduction. With Lake's acoustic "Lucky Man" (whose closing Moog solo becomes Emerson's signature) and the Bartók adaptation "The Barbarian" it presents both faces of the band (lyrical / aggressive).
The Moog solo on 'Lucky Man' was an Emerson improvisation captured in a single take and became one of the Moog's first big moments in pop music.
'The Barbarian' is an adaptation of Bartók's 'Allegro Barbaro'; Bartók's name was missing from the first pressings.
Lucky Man — Lake's acoustic ballad; the closing Moog solo became Emerson's signature
The Barbarian — adaptation of Bartók's 'Allegro Barbaro'
Take a Pebble — piano-centred long form
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1971-tarkus.an: A 20-minute title suite filling one side of the LP; an allegory of war and evolution around a mechanical armadillo-tank. Emerson's Moog becomes a fully fledged weapon. The band's first great concept triumph.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1971-tarkus.once: Essential — never skip. For the 20-minute title suite.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1971-tarkus.deta: Tarkus is a war story about a creature that is half armoured vehicle, half armadillo; the cover is by William Neal.
The band almost split because Lake initially disliked the suite's concept.
It went to number one in the UK.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1971-tarkus.tr: Tarkus — 20-minute, seven-part suite of war and evolution, the Moog in full battle mode
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1971-pictures-at: A live rock adaptation of Mussorgsky's piano suite, recorded at Newcastle City Hall. With interludes composed by Lake ('The Sage') and Emerson's Moog/Hammond showmanship, one of the most daring bridges ever built between classical music and rock.
Essential — the purest statement of the ELP philosophy.
The label didn't want to release it at first; after bootlegs spread it came out at a budget price and was a big success.
The Sage — Lake's acoustic guitar interlude
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1972-trilogy.an: More melodic and more layered in the studio. "Hoedown" (a Copland adaptation) becomes a stage classic; "From the Beginning" is one of Lake's finest ballads. Layers hard to reproduce on stage start the band's studio-versus-live tension.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1972-trilogy.onc: Recommended — for Lake's 'From the Beginning' and the Copland adaptation 'Hoedown'.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1972-trilogy.det: The record Emerson named as his favourite ELP album.
The cover is a Hipgnosis design merging the faces of the three members.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1972-trilogy.tr: From the Beginning — one of Lake's finest ballads
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1973-brain-salad: H. R. Giger's biomechanical cover. "Karn Evil 9" (a huge suite divided into three "Impressions"; the line "Welcome back my friends to the show that never ends..." becomes ELP's anthem) and Ginastera's "Toccata". The band's artistic and technical peak.
The cover is by H. R. Giger, years before his 'Alien' designs.
'Karn Evil 9' runs to about 30 minutes and is famous for the line 'Welcome back my friends to the show that never ends'.
The first album on which Peter Sinfield joined ELP as lyricist — the Crimson connection.
Karn Evil 9 — huge suite in three 'Impressions', the 'Welcome back my friends...' anthem
Toccata — adaptation of Ginastera's Piano Concerto
Jerusalem — rock adaptation of the Blake/Parry hymn
Still... You Turn Me On — Lake ballad
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1974-welcome-bac: A triple live album from the 1974 Anaheim concert, with long versions of Karn Evil 9, Tarkus and 'Take a Pebble'. The peak of ELP's stage grandeur.
Secondary priority — for the dedicated listener.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1977-works-volum: A double LP; one side for each of the three members, the fourth for the band. Emerson's Piano Concerto and "Fanfare for the Common Man" (Copland) come from this album. The weight and cost of the orchestra strain the band.
Optional — but the band pieces on side four ('Fanfare for the Common Man', 'Pirates') are a must.
Each member got one LP side; the fourth side was reserved for the band.
Emerson's Piano Concerto No. 1 fills the album's first side.
Piano Concerto No. 1 — Emerson's classical composition (side one)
Fanfare for the Common Man — Copland adaptation, hit
Leftovers from earlier sessions; an inconsistent collection.
Skippable — a scattered collection of short pieces.
Honky Tonk Train Blues — Emerson's boogie piano
Made to pay off a contractual debt, an album even the band never embraced; the symbol of the collapse.
Skippable — apart from 'Memoirs of an Officer and a Gentleman' on side two.
Recorded in the Bahamas to fulfil a contractual obligation.
Palmer and Emerson always complained about the disco-style cover.
Canario — Rodrigo adaptation, the album's only prog moment
Memoirs of an Officer and a Gentleman — a last attempt at a long suite
The reunion; an attempt to return to the classic formula with '90s production. The "Romeo and Juliet" (Prokofiev) adaptation stands out.
Optional — a document of the reunion.
Nerve damage in Emerson's right hand began to affect his playing in this period.
The Prokofiev adaptation 'Romeo and Juliet' was played often in concert.
alb.emerson-lake-palmer-1994-in-the-hot-: In the shadow of Emerson's hand problems, one of the weakest endings to any career.
Skippable — the trio's last and weakest studio album.
grp.atomic-rooster-yan-dugum.name: Atomic Rooster (side node)
grp.atomic-rooster-yan-dugum.kurulus: 1969; formed by Vincent Crane (organ) and Carl Palmer (drums) from Arthur Brown's band. Palmer soon moved on to ELP.
grp.atomic-rooster-yan-dugum.dna: Heavy organ rock, dark atmosphere; a bridge between proto-prog and hard rock.
grp.atomic-rooster-yan-dugum.etki: The way station that carried Carl Palmer to ELP; Steve Howe also briefly auditioned here ("it didn't quite fit").
alb.atomic-rooster-1970-atomic-rooster.a: The first line-up with Palmer; heavy organ rock.
alb.atomic-rooster-1970-death-walks-behi: Their strongest, darkest album; the title track has a proto-doom feel.
Death Walks Behind You — proto-doom title track, dark organ riff
alb.atomic-rooster-1971-in-hearing-of-at: Organ-rock maturity (Palmer is already in ELP by this point).
grp.refugee.kurulus: 1974. After Emerson left for ELP, The Nice's rhythm section (Lee Jackson + Brian Davison) formed this band with Swiss keyboardist Patrick Moraz. Short-lived but a crucial bridge.
grp.refugee.dna: Keyboard-centred symphonic prog; Moraz's virtuoso, jazz-influenced keyboards expand The Nice's organ rock to ELP-like proportions.
grp.refugee.uyeler: Lee Jackson (bass/vocals), Brian Davison (drums) — both from The Nice; Patrick Moraz (keyboards). When the band split, Moraz joined Yes (Relayer).
grp.refugee.gecisler: Before → The Nice (Jackson, Davison). After → Yes (Moraz), Moody Blues (Moraz). The direct member-bridge linking The Nice to Yes.
grp.refugee.etki: The band that put Moraz on Yes's radar; a hidden junction between the ELP and Yes universes. A single album, but important for the network.
alb.refugee-1974-refugee.an: Their only studio album. Symphonic prog that showcases Moraz's keyboard virtuosity and carries on The Nice's legacy. The 'Grand Canyon' suite shows the band's ambition.
grp.emerson-lake-powell-3.kurulus: 1985. Keith Emerson and Greg Lake with drummer Cozy Powell (Rainbow, Jeff Beck), because of Carl Palmer's commitments to Asia.
grp.emerson-lake-powell-3.hikaye: With Palmer tied up in Asia, Emerson and Lake made a one-album project with hard-rock drummer Cozy Powell, keeping ELP's 'P'; the sound moved towards a harder, brighter '80s production. In 1988 Emerson and Palmer made another one-off project, '3', with American multi-instrumentalist Robert Berry. Both projects paved the way for the reunion of the classic ELP.
grp.emerson-lake-powell-3.dna: ELP's tradition of classical adaptation, '80s synth production and the weight of hard-rock drumming.
grp.emerson-lake-powell-3.gecisler: ELP → ELPowell (Powell: Rainbow, Whitesnake, Black Sabbath) → 3 (Emerson, Palmer, Robert Berry) → ELP reunion (1991).
grp.emerson-lake-powell-3.etki: Examples of adapting prog to the radio age in the '80s; through Powell, a bridge to the hard-rock universe.
alb.emerson-lake-powell-1986-emerson-lak: The hard, bright '80s version of ELP, with an adaptation of Holst's 'Mars' and 'The Score'.
alb.emerson-lake-powell-1988-to-the-powe: The only album by the trio '3': AOR-oriented, with Emerson's keyboards to the fore.
sec.7.title: The Genesis Universe
grp.genesis.kurulus: 1967, Charterhouse School (Surrey). Founded by Peter Gabriel, Tony Banks, Mike Rutherford and Anthony Phillips while they were pupils. Set apart by pastoral English lyricism and a theatrical stage identity.
grp.genesis.hikaye: Genesis was born when two pupil bands at Charterhouse boarding school in Surrey merged: Gabriel and Banks's Garden Wall and Rutherford and Anthony Phillips's Anon. A pop-oriented debut produced by old boy Jonathan King flopped; the band shut itself away in a country cottage and rehearsed for months until it found the pastoral-dramatic sound of Trespass. Steve Hackett and Phil Collins, who replaced Anthony Phillips (who left because of stage fright) and drummer John Mayhew, completed the 'classic five'. Gabriel's masked, costumed stage characters made the band the emblem of theatrical prog, but he left in 1975 after the Lamb tour. While searching for a new singer, Collins took over the microphone; when Hackett also left in 1977, the Banks–Rutherford–Collins trio first carried on with symphonic prog and then became one of the biggest pop-rock bands of the '80s. After Collins left in 1996 came a single album with Ray Wilson; the trio reunited for farewell tours in 2007 and 2021–22.
grp.genesis.dna: Pastoral Mellotron textures, layers of 12-string acoustic guitar, theatrical narrative (Gabriel's masked costumes), English humour and mythology; later an evolution towards radio-friendly pop.
grp.genesis.etki: The direct ancestor of Marillion and neo-prog; the narrative wing of symphonic prog. Also a basic reference for '90s bands such as Spock's Beard.
grp.genesis.ipucu: Listen to Genesis as three separate bands: theatrical prog with Gabriel (1970–75), the symphonic transition with Collins (1976–80) and the Banks–Rutherford–Collins pop-rock trio (1981–92).
Tony Banks's keyboard textures are the one constant thread linking the eras — you can follow the same harmonic mind from 'The Cinema Show' to 'Home by the Sea'.
The Gabriel-era lyrics are full of English mythology, Victorian fairy tales and satire; reading them while you listen doubles the experience.
The live album Seconds Out (1977), Hackett's last recording, is a bridge between the two eras: hearing Gabriel-era pieces sung by Collins makes a good comparison.
grp.genesis.era.0.note: A school band under the wing of pop producer Jonathan King. With Trespass it finds its own sound.
grp.genesis.era.1.t: The Gabriel era — the classic five
grp.genesis.era.1.note: The classic line-up with the arrival of Hackett and Collins. Theatrical staging, long suites, English folklore and satire.
grp.genesis.era.2.note: Collins moves to vocals; Hackett leaves in 1977. A balance between symphonic prog and shorter songwriting.
grp.genesis.era.3.note: Banks–Rutherford–Collins. Stadium-scale success; drum machines, gated-reverb drums and radio hits.
grp.genesis.era.4.note: The one-album Ray Wilson era, followed by the 2007 'Turn It On Again' reunion tour.
alb.genesis-1969-from-genesis-to-revelat: A pop-orchestral attempt dominated by producer Jonathan King's vision. No 'Genesis sound' yet.
Kitschy orchestral layers were added without the band's permission.
It sold almost nothing, partly because record shops filed it under 'religious music'.
The Silent Sun — deliberately Bee Gees-like early single
alb.genesis-1970-trespass.an: "The Knife" gives them their first real prog identity; the tension between pastoral acoustic textures and dramatic outbursts is born. Anthony Phillips's last album.
alb.genesis-1970-trespass.oncelik: Recommended — the birthplace of the Genesis sound.
alb.genesis-1970-trespass.detay: The layers of 12-string acoustic guitar (Phillips–Rutherford) became the band's signature texture.
Phillips's last album; according to Banks, his departure nearly broke up the band.
'The Knife' remained the closing number of their concerts until the late 1970s.
alb.genesis-1970-trespass.tr: The Knife — the band's first real prog piece, dramatic outbursts
alb.genesis-1971-nursery-cryme.an: Hackett and Collins join. With "The Musical Box" (a chilling Victorian tale) the theatrical, narrative Genesis sound falls fully into place. Hackett's tapping and sustain techniques begin here.
alb.genesis-1971-nursery-cryme.oncelik: Recommended — a must for 'The Musical Box' and 'The Return of the Giant Hogweed'.
alb.genesis-1971-nursery-cryme.detay: Collins's and Hackett's first album; Collins sings lead for the first time on 'For Absent Friends'.
Paul Whitehead's cover of a Victorian girl playing croquet illustrates the story of 'The Musical Box'.
The album charted in Italy and Belgium before Britain — Genesis's early audience in continental Europe.
alb.genesis-1971-nursery-cryme.tr: The Musical Box — chilling Victorian tale, Hackett's sustain technique
The Return of the Giant Hogweed — humorous-dramatic epic
The Fountain of Salmacis — mythological, Mellotron-textured
alb.genesis-1972-foxtrot.an: "Supper's Ready" (23 minutes, a seven-part apocalyptic suite) is the band's monumental work. Mellotron, acoustic guitar and Gabriel's character-shifting vocals at their peak.
alb.genesis-1972-foxtrot.oncelik: Essential — never skip. Worth it for 'Supper's Ready' alone.
alb.genesis-1972-foxtrot.detay: The 23-minute 'Supper's Ready' is a seven-part apocalyptic allegory; Gabriel's appearances on stage in a red dress and fox's head began on this tour.
'Horizons' is Hackett's Bach-inspired acoustic guitar miniature.
With its Mellotron intro, 'Watcher of the Skies' was the fixed opening number of their concerts.
alb.genesis-1972-foxtrot.tr: Supper's Ready — 23-minute, seven-part apocalyptic suite, the band's monument
Watcher of the Skies — Mellotron opening
alb.genesis-1973-selling-england-by-the-: For many fans the most balanced masterpiece. "Firth of Fifth" (Banks's piano intro + Hackett's lyrical guitar solo) and "The Cinema Show" are among the high points of elegance in English prog; "I Know What I Like" is the first hit.
Essential — never skip. For most listeners, the peak of Genesis.
John Lennon saying he liked the album boosted the band's critical standing.
'I Know What I Like (In Your Wardrobe)' is the band's first UK chart single.
The album was conceived as a satire on English identity in the face of Americanisation and commercialism.
Firth of Fifth — Banks's piano intro + Hackett's lyrical solo, a peak of elegance
The Cinema Show — 11 minutes, a keyboard climax in 7/8
I Know What I Like (In Your Wardrobe) — first hit
alb.genesis-1974-the-lamb-lies-down-on-b: A double-LP concept: the surreal journey of a young Puerto Rican named Rael through the streets of New York. Gabriel wrote the lyrics on his own, and the increasingly abstract narrative foreshadows his departure. Gabriel's farewell.
Essential — but listen to the double album in one sitting, following the story.
Gabriel, Banks, Rutherford, Hackett, Collins + Brian Eno ('Enossification' sound treatments)
The story is the surreal underground journey of a young Puerto Rican, Rael, in New York; almost all the lyrics are Gabriel's.
During recording, Gabriel's family problems and a film project strained the band; he left when the tour ended.
On tour the whole album was played in sequence at all 102 concerts.
The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway — title track, Rael's story begins
The Carpet Crawlers — atmospheric, one of the best-loved moments
In the Cage — dramatic keyboard climax
alb.genesis-1976-a-trick-of-the-tail.an: Collins on vocals; proof of a smooth, even brilliant transition just when everyone said 'Genesis is finished'. "Squonk" and "Ripples" carry on the classic form.
alb.genesis-1976-a-trick-of-the-tail.det: After hearing more than 400 singers, the band decided Collins should sing himself.
On tour Bill Bruford took the drum seat temporarily (1976), followed by Chester Thompson.
'Los Endos' was the concert finale for many years.
alb.genesis-1976-a-trick-of-the-tail.tr: Squonk — heavy, the proof of Collins's vocal transition
A Trick of the Tail — playful title track
alb.genesis-1976-wind-wuthering.an: Hackett's last album; a romantic peak with "One for the Vine" and melodic instrumentals. The shrinking of Hackett's creative space leads to his departure.
alb.genesis-1976-wind-wuthering.oncelik: Recommended — the last great album of symphonic Genesis.
alb.genesis-1976-wind-wuthering.detay: The title refers to Emily Brontë's 'Wuthering Heights'; the names of the last two pieces come from the novel's final sentence.
Hackett left after the album, feeling his pieces were not getting enough room.
In concert 'Afterglow' was played joined to 'In the Cage'.
alb.genesis-1976-wind-wuthering.tr: One for the Vine — 10 minutes, Banks's peak as a composer
Blood on the Rooftops — Hackett's classical guitar intro
alb.genesis-1977-seconds-out.an: A double live album from the 1976–77 tours; Hackett's last Genesis recording. The Gabriel-era repertoire sung by Collins, with the energy of two drummers (Collins + Chester Thompson; Bruford on one track).
alb.genesis-1977-seconds-out.oncelik: Recommended — considered the best Genesis live album.
alb.genesis-1977-seconds-out.detay: Hackett's departure became final during the mixing.
The album draws mainly on the concerts at the Palais des Sports in Paris.
alb.genesis-1977-seconds-out.tr: Supper's Ready — full version with Collins on vocals
The Cinema Show — Bruford on drums
Firth of Fifth — Hackett's legendary solo
alb.genesis-1978-and-then-there-were-thr: A trio, as the title announces. Shorter forms; "Follow You Follow Me" is the first big pop hit — the sign of a change of direction.
The title is an ironic reference to the line-up shrinking to three after Hackett left.
'Follow You Follow Me' is the band's first big success on American radio.
Follow You Follow Me — first big pop hit, a change of direction
Burning Rope — the last traces of long form
alb.genesis-1980-duke.an: The last good balance point between pop and prog; "Turn It On Again" is a hit, but the album still has connected long-form pieces.
alb.genesis-1980-duke.oncelik: Recommended — the Genesis album where prog and pop meet in the best balance.
alb.genesis-1980-duke.detay: The album was designed as a suite spread across the record, closing with 'Duke's Travels / Duke's End'.
Some of the songs Collins wrote during his divorce were kept for his first solo album, Face Value.
alb.genesis-1980-duke.tr: Turn It On Again — hit in 13/8
Duke's Travels / Duke's End — connected instrumental suite, traces of prog
alb.genesis-1981-abacab.an: A full turn to pop-rock; punchy, stripped-down production.
alb.genesis-1981-abacab.oncelik: Optional — the manifesto of the new sound.
alb.genesis-1981-abacab.detay: The band deliberately threw out every idea that 'sounded like Genesis'; the Earth, Wind & Fire horns appear on 'No Reply at All'.
The first album recorded at the band's own studio, The Farm.
alb.genesis-1981-abacab.tr: No Reply at All — Earth, Wind & Fire horn section
Man on the Corner — Collins's drum-machine ballad
alb.genesis-1983-genesis.an: "Mama" (a dark drum-machine atmosphere) and "That's All"; an arena-pop identity.
alb.genesis-1983-genesis.oncelik: Optional — listen for 'Home by the Sea / Second Home by the Sea'.
alb.genesis-1983-genesis.detay: Almost all the pieces were developed from group improvisations in the studio — the trio's most 'band-made' album.
The drum-machine pattern and Collins's laugh in 'Mama' are emblems of '80s Genesis.
alb.genesis-1983-genesis.tr: Mama — dark drum-machine atmosphere, Collins's laugh
Home by the Sea / Second Home by the Sea — the last long-form suite
alb.genesis-1986-invisible-touch.an: The commercial peak, with many hit singles. Almost completely removed from the prog identity.
alb.genesis-1986-invisible-touch.oncelik: Optional — the commercial peak; 'Domino' carries a trace of prog.
alb.genesis-1986-invisible-touch.detay: Five singles from the album reached the US Top 5.
The title track is the band's only US #1.
'Domino', a ten-minute suite in two parts, salutes the old Genesis.
alb.genesis-1986-invisible-touch.tr: Invisible Touch — US number one pop
Land of Confusion — political hit (the famous puppet video)
Tonight, Tonight, Tonight — long and atmospheric
Domino — two parts, traces of prog
alb.genesis-1991-we-can-t-dance.an: The album that closes the Collins era; "No Son of Mine", "I Can't Dance". Collins left shortly afterwards.
alb.genesis-1991-we-can-t-dance.oncelik: Optional — for 'Driving the Last Spike' and 'Fading Lights'.
alb.genesis-1991-we-can-t-dance.detay: The last studio album with Collins.
'Fading Lights' is the band's long, farewell-like piece.
alb.genesis-1991-we-can-t-dance.tr: No Son of Mine — dark single
Fading Lights — the Collins era's long-form farewell
alb.genesis-1997-calling-all-stations.an: The only album recorded with Scottish singer Ray Wilson (Stiltskin) after Collins left. Dark, slow and atmospheric; close to the melancholic alternative-rock sound of the '90s. It did reasonably in Europe but poorly in the US, and the North American tour was cancelled.
alb.genesis-1997-calling-all-stations.on: Optional — but a better album than its bad reputation suggests.
alb.genesis-1997-calling-all-stations.ka: Tony Banks, Mike Rutherford, Ray Wilson + Nir Zidkyahu, Nick D'Virgilio (drums)
alb.genesis-1997-calling-all-stations.de: Spock's Beard's Nick D'Virgilio also plays drums — the point where the network intersects American prog.
Afterwards Banks and Rutherford effectively put the band on hold.
In later years Ray Wilson performed this period's songs and Gabriel/Collins pieces at his solo concerts.
alb.genesis-1997-calling-all-stations.tr: Calling All Stations — heavy, tense opener
The Dividing Line — Nick D'Virgilio's drumming
alb.genesis-2007-live-over-europe-2007.a: A double live album from the European leg of the 'Turn It On Again' reunion tour. The Banks–Rutherford–Collins trio with Daryl Stuermer (guitar/bass) and Chester Thompson (drums); prog-era medleys and '80s hits side by side.
alb.genesis-2007-live-over-europe-2007.d: The Circo Massimo concert in Rome, with around 500,000 people, was one of the band's biggest shows.
grp.peter-gabriel-solo-dugum.name: Peter Gabriel (solo node)
grp.peter-gabriel-solo-dugum.hikaye: After leaving Genesis in 1975, Gabriel began his solo career with four untitled albums, which fans named after their covers (Car, Scratch, Melt, Security). Working with producers such as Bob Ezrin, Robert Fripp and Steve Lillywhite, he shaped '80s production — notably by banning cymbals on the third album and adopting the Fairlight sampler early. By founding the WOMAD festival in 1980 and Real World Records and studios in 1989, he played a pioneering role in spreading world music in the West. With So (1986) he became a global pop star; human-rights work (the Amnesty tours, the Witness organisation) became an inseparable part of his art. His output slowed in the 2000s; through orchestral reinterpretation projects (Scratch My Back, New Blood) he returned to songwriting from a different angle.
grp.peter-gabriel-solo-dugum.dna: World music, experimental production, socio-political themes, rhythm-centred structures.
grp.peter-gabriel-solo-dugum.ipucu: Listen to the first four albums as a series: each is darker and more rhythmic than the last.
Tony Levin's bass is the permanent bridge between Gabriel and the Crimson universe; he plays on almost every album.
The film scores (Birdy, Passion) are Gabriel's world-music laboratory — they feed the song albums.
grp.peter-gabriel-solo-dugum.era.0.note: Art rock and early digital production with Fripp, Lillywhite and Hugh Padgham.
grp.peter-gabriel-solo-dugum.era.1.note: Global pop success and a world-music synthesis through WOMAD and Real World Records.
grp.peter-gabriel-solo-dugum.era.2.note: Sparse but ambitious work: a concept album (OVO), dark art rock (Up), orchestral reinterpretations.
alb.peter-gabriel-1977-peter-gabriel-car: "Solsbury Hill" (the anthem of his departure from Genesis). Art rock plus accessibility.
Recommended — for 'Solsbury Hill' and 'Here Comes the Flood'.
'Solsbury Hill' is an autobiographical song about his decision to leave Genesis.
On stage Fripp played offstage under the pseudonym 'Dusty Rhodes'.
Solsbury Hill — the anthem of leaving Genesis, in 7/4
Here Comes the Flood — dramatic ballad
alb.peter-gabriel-1978-peter-gabriel-scr: Produced by Robert Fripp; more angular and experimental.
Conceived as a twin project alongside Fripp's own solo album Exposure.
On the Air — Fripp production, angular
alb.peter-gabriel-1980-peter-gabriel-mel: "Games Without Frontiers", "Biko". The invention of the gated-reverb drum sound (with Collins's contribution); political weight.
Essential — never skip. One of the founding records of '80s production.
Gabriel asked the drummers not to play cymbals; Collins and Padgham discovered the gated-reverb drum sound here, on 'Intruder'.
Atlantic Records rejected the album as 'not commercial'; Mercury released it.
'Biko', dedicated to South African activist Steve Biko, became an anti-apartheid anthem.
Games Without Frontiers — hit with Kate Bush on vocals
Biko — political lament for Steve Biko
Intruder — the birth of the gated-reverb drum sound
alb.peter-gabriel-1982-peter-gabriel-sec: The full fusion of world music and electronics; "Shock the Monkey".
Recommended — the first great synthesis of the Fairlight and ethnic percussion.
One of the first rock albums to make extensive use of the Fairlight CMI sampler.
In the US it was labelled 'Security'; 'Shock the Monkey' was an MTV hit.
Shock the Monkey — first big US hit, electronic
The Rhythm of the Heat — African percussion
alb.peter-gabriel-1986-so.an: "Sledgehammer", "In Your Eyes". The commercial peak; a balance of pop and art.
alb.peter-gabriel-1986-so.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The commercial peak.
alb.peter-gabriel-1986-so.detay: The 'Sledgehammer' video is one of the most awarded in MTV history.
'Don't Give Up' is a duet with Kate Bush; 'In Your Eyes' became iconic through the film 'Say Anything'.
alb.peter-gabriel-1986-so.tr: In Your Eyes — world-music peak (Youssou N'Dour)
Don't Give Up — duet with Kate Bush
alb.peter-gabriel-1989-passion.an: Music written for Martin Scorsese's film 'The Last Temptation of Christ'. Working with musicians from the Middle East, North Africa and South Asia, Gabriel laid the foundations of the Real World aesthetic; it won a Grammy.
alb.peter-gabriel-1989-passion.oncelik: Recommended — the reference record where world music meets ambient.
alb.peter-gabriel-1989-passion.kadro: Gabriel + Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan, L. Shankar, Youssou N'Dour, Hossam Ramzy, David Rhodes and others
alb.peter-gabriel-1989-passion.detay: Real World Records' first major release.
It played a decisive role in introducing Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan to the West.
alb.peter-gabriel-1989-passion.tr: The Feeling Begins — opening with Armenian duduk
alb.peter-gabriel-1992-us.an: Personal and relationship themes; the world-music texture deepens.
alb.peter-gabriel-1992-us.detay: An album about relationships, drawn from his divorce and time in therapy.
alb.peter-gabriel-1992-us.tr: Digging in the Dirt — therapeutic, dark single
Blood of Eden — duet with Sinéad O'Connor
alb.peter-gabriel-2000-ovo.an: A concept album written for the show at London's Millennium Dome, telling the story of industrialisation through three generations of a family. Dominated by guest singers; Gabriel's own voice is heard little.
alb.peter-gabriel-2002-up.an: A dark, slow, layered art-rock album after a decade of silence, on death, the media and addiction. Long structures and industrial textures make it the late-period album closest to Gabriel's prog roots.
alb.peter-gabriel-2002-up.oncelik: Recommended — the strongest album of his late period.
alb.peter-gabriel-2002-up.detay: 'Signal to Noise' uses a vocal Nusrat recorded before his death in 1997.
'I Grieve' featured in the film 'City of Angels'.
alb.peter-gabriel-2002-up.tr: Signal to Noise — Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan's vocal
alb.peter-gabriel-2010-scratch-my-back.a: An album interpreting other artists' songs (Bowie, Radiohead, Talking Heads, Arcade Fire, Lou Reed) with only orchestra and piano, no drums or guitars. In return, those artists were meant to cover Gabriel songs ('I'll Scratch Yours', 2013).
alb.peter-gabriel-2010-scratch-my-back.o: Optional — to get to know Gabriel the interpreter.
alb.peter-gabriel-2010-scratch-my-back.d: Arranger John Metcalfe; Ezrin had also produced Gabriel's first solo album.
alb.peter-gabriel-2011-new-blood.an: Orchestral reinterpretations of his own songs: 'Rhythm of the Heat', 'Solsbury Hill', 'Don't Give Up' (with Ane Brun). The logic of Scratch My Back applied to Gabriel's own repertoire.
alb.peter-gabriel-2011-new-blood.oncelik: Optional — the dramatic new versions of Security-era pieces are intriguing.
grp.steve-hackett-solo-dugum.name: Steve Hackett (solo node)
grp.steve-hackett-solo-dugum.hikaye: Hackett joined Genesis in 1971 through an advert he placed in Melody Maker ('guitarist determined to strive beyond existing stagnant music forms'). He was one of the guitarists using tapping and sweep-picking before Eddie Van Halen. Leaving Genesis in 1977, he built a prolific solo career moving between electric prog, classical guitar and blues; in 1986 he formed GTR with Steve Howe. From the '90s on, through his Genesis Revisited projects, he became the main figure keeping the Gabriel era alive on stage; in the 2010s, with orchestral, world-music-coloured symphonic rock albums, he enjoyed the second peak of his career.
grp.steve-hackett-solo-dugum.dna: Lyrical/classical guitar, atmospheric instrumentals, the Genesis aesthetic continued from a guitarist's point of view.
alb.steve-hackett-1975-voyage-of-the-aco: Made while he was still in Genesis, with Collins and Rutherford as guests. Brings the classic Genesis texture into a solo format.
Shadow of the Hierophant — Collins on drums/vocals, classic Genesis texture
Hands of the Priestess — lyrical guitar
alb.steve-hackett-1978-please-don-t-touc: A stylistic expansion with various guest singers.
Please Don't Touch — instrumental title track
