alb.steve-hackett-1979-spectral-mornings: A fan favourite; regarded as one of the bedside records of the neo-prog generation.
Spectral Mornings — lyrical guitar title track, fan favourite
Clocks - The Angel of Mons — rhythmic instrumental
alb.steve-hackett-1981-cured.tr: A Cradle of Swans — classical guitar
alb.steve-hackett-1983-bay-of-kings.an: Entirely acoustic/classical guitar; Hackett's other face.
alb.steve-hackett-1983-bay-of-kings.tr: Bay of Kings — classical guitar title track
alb.steve-hackett-1984-till-we-have-face: Experimental, with Brazilian percussion. He then turned to GTR.
A Doll That's Made in Japan
Matilda Smith-Williams Home for the Aged
alb.steve-hackett-1993-guitar-noir.an: A dark, urban-themed 'jazz-noir' rock album with sparer production; the start of his '90s reinvention.
alb.steve-hackett-1996-genesis-revisited: Gabriel-era Genesis pieces re-recorded with orchestra and guests (John Wetton, Chester Thompson, Bill Bruford, Tony Levin, Colin Blunstone, Paul Carrack); plus a new piece and 'Déjà Vu', which never made it onto a Genesis album.
Recommended — Hackett's take on the Genesis legacy.
Déjà Vu — an unfinished piece co-written with Gabriel
alb.steve-hackett-1999-darktown.an: Hackett's darkest and most personal album: memories of childhood, boarding school and violence. An experimental work with electronic textures and harsh cuts.
alb.steve-hackett-2003-to-watch-the-stor: An eclectic but balanced album on his own label, Camino Records; the first major recording of his long-lasting band with Roger King (keyboards) and Gary O'Toole (drums).
alb.steve-hackett-2011-beyond-the-shroud: The album where his orchestral, symphonic direction crystallised; 'Catwalk', with Chris Squire, paved the way for the Squackett project.
Around the same time he recorded the album 'A Life Within a Day' with Chris Squire (Squackett, 2012).
alb.steve-hackett-2012-genesis-revisited: A double album: Genesis-era pieces re-recorded with guests such as Steven Wilson, Mikael Åkerfeldt, Neal Morse, Roine Stolt, John Wetton and Nik Kershaw. A junction album bringing together old and new generations of prog.
The tour that followed made Hackett the living ambassador of the Genesis repertoire; singer Nad Sylvan became a fixture of this period.
The Musical Box — Nad Sylvan on vocals
Shadow of the Hierophant — Amanda Lehmann
alb.steve-hackett-2015-wolflight.an: Symphonic rock themed on wolves, migrations and ancient history, enriched with world-music instruments (tar, duduk, didgeridoo).
alb.steve-hackett-2017-the-night-siren.a: A peaceful world album on the theme of 'migrants and borders', with musicians from many countries (including Israeli and Palestinian singers).
alb.steve-hackett-2019-at-the-edge-of-li: A mature late-period album blending symphonic, world-music and blues colours.
grp.brand-x.kurulus: 1975–76, London. The side project through which Phil Collins (Genesis) expressed his passion for jazz fusion. Even as Genesis moved towards pop, Collins kept up his virtuoso drumming here.
grp.brand-x.hikaye: Born in London in 1975 as a jazz-rock studio band, Brand X became famous as Phil Collins's 'workshop' outside Genesis. Guitarist John Goodsall, bassist Percy Jones (a fretless virtuoso) and keyboardist Robin Lumley formed the core. Because of Collins's Genesis commitments, the drum seat was shared with players such as Kenwood Dennard and Chuck Burgi. The band split in the early '80s, re-formed in the '90s around the Goodsall–Jones duo and toured again after 2016.
grp.brand-x.dna: Pure British jazz fusion: Percy Jones's fluid fretless bass, Goodsall's searing guitar, complex time signatures. A blend of humour and virtuosity.
grp.brand-x.uyeler: Phil Collins (drums), Percy Jones (fretless bass — the band's signature), John Goodsall (guitar), Robin Lumley (keyboards). As Collins got busier, Kenwood Dennard and Chuck Burgi stepped in on drums.
grp.brand-x.gecisler: Before/in parallel → Genesis (Collins). Goodsall also played on Bruford's 'Feels Good to Me' — the fusion nodes are intertwined.
grp.brand-x.etki: Collins's 'other face'; a parallel node carrying the prog/fusion banner while Genesis moved to pop. A pillar (with Bruford) of the British fusion scene.
alb.brand-x-1976-unorthodox-behaviour.an: The debut; entirely instrumental. Percy Jones's fretless bass and Collins's drumming establish the band's identity from the very first record.
alb.brand-x-1976-unorthodox-behaviour.tr: Nuclear Burn — Collins's explosive opening drums
alb.brand-x-1977-moroccan-roll.an: The band's best-loved album; more melodic and textured. Jones's bass to the fore.
alb.brand-x-1977-moroccan-roll.tr: Sun in the Night — Indian/world influence
Why Should I Lend You Mine...
Malaga Virgen — Percy Jones's bass showcase
alb.brand-x-1978-masques.an: An album on which Collins, busy with Genesis, plays less drums, but the band keeps its fusion identity.
alb.brand-x-1979-product.an: More song-oriented, with some vocal tracks; a commercial attempt. Collins partly on drums.
alb.brand-x-1980-do-they-hurt.an: An album compiled from material left over from the Product sessions; among Collins's last contributions.
alb.brand-x-1997-manifest-destiny.an: The Goodsall–Jones duo's '90s reunion album; harder, more modern jazz-rock.
grp.anthony-phillips.kurulus: Born 1951, Chiswick, London. Founding guitarist of Genesis (1967–70).
grp.anthony-phillips.hikaye: Phillips was one of the Charterhouse pupils who founded Genesis and the person who shaped the band's musical direction up to Trespass; his 12-string guitar textures are the root of the Genesis sound. He left in 1970 because of severe stage fright and bronchitis; according to Banks, his departure nearly finished the band. He then studied classical guitar, piano and orchestration and built a solo career of pastoral, English, delicate instrumentals as well as a career in television and documentary music. Mike Rutherford and Phil Collins appeared on his first solo album; the 'Private Parts & Pieces' series is like a personal sketchbook. He never returned to the stage.
grp.anthony-phillips.dna: 12-string acoustic guitar, pastoral English lyricism, chamber music and orchestra; melodies as delicate and fragile as a music box.
grp.anthony-phillips.gecisler: Anon → Genesis (1967–70) → solo; Rutherford, Collins, Camel (guest on The Single Factor), Andrew Latimer.
grp.anthony-phillips.etki: The 'lost ancestor' of Genesis; the quiet master of pastoral prog and the English acoustic guitar tradition.
alb.anthony-phillips-1977-the-geese-the-: Co-produced by Rutherford, with Collins singing on two songs; like a continuation of the pastoral world of Trespass. Phillips's best-loved album.
Essential — a must for Genesis fans.
Phillips + Mike Rutherford, Phil Collins, orchestra
Recording began in 1974; finding a label took three years.
Which Way the Wind Blows — Collins
alb.anthony-phillips-1978-wise-after-the: Produced by Rupert Hine, with Phillips's own vocals to the fore; more song-oriented.
alb.anthony-phillips-1978-private-parts-: The first in a long-running series: personal acoustic guitar and piano sketches.
alb.anthony-phillips-1979-sides.an: A balance between more rock-oriented songs and pastoral instrumentals; with Crimson alumni such as Mel Collins and Michael Giles.
alb.anthony-phillips-1990-slow-dance.an: A single orchestral and electronic work in two long parts; the peak of the mature Phillips.
sec.16.title: The Pink Floyd Universe
sec.16.intro: Pink Floyd and its members' solo work: from Barrett to The Endless River, Gilmour's guitar, Waters's concept albums, Wright's solo albums and Mason's jazz/Canterbury connections. Alongside them, the Alan Parsons Project of Alan Parsons, engineer of The Dark Side of the Moon.
grp.pink-floyd.kurulus: 1965, London. Psychedelia centred on Syd Barrett; after Barrett's breakdown (1968) David Gilmour joined and Roger Waters became the conceptual leader.
grp.pink-floyd.hikaye: Pink Floyd was born when the childhood friendship of Syd Barrett and Roger Waters from Cambridge joined up with London architecture students Nick Mason and Richard Wright (the name came from two blues musicians, Pink Anderson and Floyd Council). With their light shows at the UFO Club they became the soundtrack of the London underground. When Barrett, through LSD and mental collapse, could no longer function on stage, David Gilmour joined in 1968, first as support and then as permanent guitarist. Searching for a direction without Barrett through film scores and long improvisations, the band found its own sound with 'Echoes' on Meddle. The Dark Side of the Moon (1973) became one of the best-selling albums in history; four albums followed with Waters as spokesman: alienation, loss (Barrett), a critique of capitalism and, on The Wall, personal collapse. Wright was fired during The Wall; The Final Cut was effectively a Waters solo album. Waters left in 1985 and declared the band finished; Gilmour and Mason kept the name in court, brought Wright back and made two albums and huge tours. The four reunited on stage one last time at Live 8 in 2005; Wright died in 2008, and The Endless River (2014) was a farewell in his memory.
grp.pink-floyd.dna: Space rock, atmospheric breadth, mastery of the concept album, minimal but deep textures; 'mood' and production rather than technical virtuosity. It feeds the atmospheric approach of neo-prog (Twelfth Night, Pendragon).
grp.pink-floyd.ipucu: Read the four albums from The Dark Side of the Moon to The Wall as a tetralogy: all of them treat Waters's theme of absence and alienation from different angles.
Hear the Barrett era as 'a different band' — but Barrett's ghost haunts every album that follows (especially Wish You Were Here).
'Echoes' (1971) is the DNA of the band's next twenty years — Gilmour's guitar tone and Wright's atmosphere come together here.
On the post-Waters albums, listen to Gilmour's guitar and Wright's quiet return; The Division Bell is largely their album.
grp.pink-floyd.era.0.note: Psychedelic pop and space improvisations. Syd Barrett's songwriting and collapse.
grp.pink-floyd.era.1.note: Film scores, avant-garde experiments, orchestral collaborations; the band's identity is found with 'Echoes'.
grp.pink-floyd.era.2.note: From Dark Side to The Final Cut: Waters's conceptual leadership, studio perfectionism and internal conflict.
grp.pink-floyd.era.3.note: Floyd without Waters: stadium production, the Gilmour–Wright atmosphere and the farewell of The Endless River.
alb.pink-floyd-1967-the-piper-at-the-gat: Barrett's childlike, eerie psychedelia; the masterpiece of the English underground.
Essential — the peak of English psychedelia.
Recorded in the same Abbey Road building while the Beatles were making Sgt. Pepper.
The title comes from a chapter of Kenneth Grahame's 'The Wind in the Willows'.
The only Floyd album with Barrett's full contribution.
alb.pink-floyd-1968-a-saucerful-of-secre: Transition: Gilmour comes in, Barrett goes out. The space-rock texture is born in the title suite.
Recommended — the only record by the five-piece line-up.
Waters, Wright, Mason, David Gilmour, Syd Barrett (partial)
The only album featuring all five members; Barrett is prominent only on 'Jugband Blues'.
With its 'battle–lament' structure, the title track is the prototype of the later long suites.
A Saucerful of Secrets — birth of the space-rock texture, title suite
Set the Controls for the Heart of the Sun — Waters's hypnotic piece
Jugband Blues — Barrett's last contribution, his farewell
alb.pink-floyd-1969-more.an: Music written for Barbet Schroeder's film 'More'; the first album on which Gilmour comes forward as a singer.
alb.pink-floyd-1969-more.oncelik: Optional — the birth of Gilmour the singer.
alb.pink-floyd-1969-more.detay: Recorded in a few weeks for Barbet Schroeder's film.
'The Nile Song' is the band's hardest piece; 'Cymbaline' stayed in the live set for a long time.
alb.pink-floyd-1969-more.tr: The Nile Song — one of the band's hardest pieces
alb.pink-floyd-1969-ummagumma.oncelik: Optional — the live disc is valuable, the studio disc experimental.
alb.pink-floyd-1969-ummagumma.detay: The first disc comes from 1969 concerts in Birmingham and Manchester; on the second, each member produced half a side of solo material.
The live 'Careful with That Axe, Eugene' is considered the strongest recording of the period.
alb.pink-floyd-1969-ummagumma.tr: Careful with That Axe, Eugene (live) — a peak of tension
Several Species of Small Furry Animals... — Waters's sound experiment
alb.pink-floyd-1970-atom-heart-mother.on: Optional — the 23-minute title suite is historically important.
alb.pink-floyd-1970-atom-heart-mother.de: The cow on the cover (Lulubelle III) makes it the first major prog cover without the band's name or album title.
The first Floyd album to reach number one in the UK.
alb.pink-floyd-1970-atom-heart-mother.tr: Atom Heart Mother — 23-minute suite with orchestra and choir
Fat Old Sun — Gilmour's pastoral piece
alb.pink-floyd-1971-meddle.detay: 'Echoes' opens with a 'ping' made by sending a single piano note of Wright's through a Leslie speaker.
'One of These Days' contains Mason's only vocal line.
The concert film shot in the Pompeii amphitheatre (1972) documents this material.
alb.pink-floyd-1971-meddle.tr: Echoes — 23-minute suite that defines the future Floyd
One of These Days — bass-driven instrumental
alb.pink-floyd-1973-the-dark-side-of-the: A seamlessly flowing concept about life, death, money and madness. With its studio production (cash registers, heartbeats, spoken fragments) and the 7/4 of "Money" it is both experimental and universal. One of the best-selling albums in history.
Essential — never skip. One of the best-selling albums in rock history.
Pink Floyd; recording engineer Alan Parsons
It spent more than 900 weeks in total on the Billboard 200.
Alan Parsons's engineering opened the door to his later Alan Parsons Project career.
Clare Torry improvised the wordless vocal on 'The Great Gig in the Sky'.
The prism cover is by Storm Thorgerson and Hipgnosis.
The Great Gig in the Sky — Clare Torry's vocal peak
alb.pink-floyd-1975-wish-you-were-here.a: A lament for Barrett ("Shine On You Crazy Diamond") and a critique of the music industry. A melancholic masterpiece.
alb.pink-floyd-1975-wish-you-were-here.d: During the sessions an unrecognisable Syd Barrett — overweight, head shaved — turned up at the studio unannounced; at first the band didn't recognise him.
'Shine On You Crazy Diamond', dedicated to Barrett, is a nine-part suite framing the album.
Both Waters and Gilmour name it as their favourite Floyd album.
alb.pink-floyd-1975-wish-you-were-here.t: Shine On You Crazy Diamond — 26-minute lament for Barrett (in two parts)
Wish You Were Here — acoustic title track
Welcome to the Machine — critique of the industry
alb.pink-floyd-1977-animals.an: An Orwell-inspired satire of society (pigs/dogs/sheep); long, harsh pieces.
alb.pink-floyd-1977-animals.oncelik: Essential — Floyd's hardest and most political album.
alb.pink-floyd-1977-animals.detay: A dog–pig–sheep allegory inspired by Orwell's 'Animal Farm'.
During the cover shoot, the inflatable pig over Battersea Power Station broke loose and drifted into Heathrow's airspace.
Released at the height of punk, this is Floyd's angriest reply to the 'dinosaur' criticism.
alb.pink-floyd-1979-the-wall.an: Waters's concept of isolation and collapse; a double-LP rock opera. "Another Brick in the Wall" is a giant hit.
alb.pink-floyd-1979-the-wall.oncelik: Essential — never skip. But hear it start to finish as a rock opera.
alb.pink-floyd-1979-the-wall.kadro: Waters, Gilmour, Mason, Wright (as a session musician)
alb.pink-floyd-1979-the-wall.detay: It grew out of Waters's idea of 'building a wall between me and the audience' after he spat at a fan during a 1977 concert.
Wright was fired during the sessions but played on the tour as a paid musician.
With Alan Parker's 1982 film and Gerald Scarfe's animations it became a cultural phenomenon.
alb.pink-floyd-1979-the-wall.tr: Comfortably Numb — Gilmour's legendary guitar solo
Another Brick in the Wall Part 2 — huge hit with children's choir
alb.pink-floyd-1983-the-final-cut.an: Essentially a Waters solo album; anti-war anger. The end of the Waters era.
alb.pink-floyd-1983-the-final-cut.onceli: Optional — effectively Waters's first solo album.
alb.pink-floyd-1983-the-final-cut.detay: Its subtitle is 'A requiem for the post-war dream by Roger Waters'.
The only Floyd album without Wright; the Waters–Gilmour conflict reached its peak.
alb.pink-floyd-1983-the-final-cut.tr: The Final Cut — Waters's anti-war peak
Not Now John — the only Gilmour vocal
alb.pink-floyd-1987-a-momentary-lapse-of: Floyd without Waters, led by Gilmour; atmospheric but controversial.
Gilmour, Mason + Richard Wright (partial), Tony Levin, Jim Keltner, Carmine Appice
After Waters left, the right to use the band's name went to court.
Mason's and Wright's contributions are limited; the album grew out of a Gilmour solo project.
alb.pink-floyd-1994-the-division-bell.an: The maturity of the Gilmour era; a melancholic close with "High Hopes".
alb.pink-floyd-1994-the-division-bell.on: Recommended — the best Floyd album after Waters.
alb.pink-floyd-1994-the-division-bell.de: Wright took part as a full member for the first time since 1979; 'Wearing the Inside Out' is his vocal.
Most of the lyrics were written by Gilmour's wife Polly Samson; the theme of (failed) communication unifies the album.
'Marooned' is the only Floyd track to win a Grammy.
alb.pink-floyd-1994-the-division-bell.tr: High Hopes — melancholic closer, bell textures
alb.pink-floyd-1995-pulse.an: A double live album from The Division Bell tour; the recording on which The Dark Side of the Moon is played in full on stage. The sound document of a spectacular light and laser show.
alb.pink-floyd-1995-pulse.oncelik: Secondary priority — the best summary of the Gilmour-era stage sound.
alb.pink-floyd-1995-pulse.detay: The flashing red LED on the spine of the CD box is one of the era's famous packaging designs.
alb.pink-floyd-2014-the-endless-river.an: An almost entirely instrumental ambient album, mostly drawn from The Division Bell sessions (1993) and built around Richard Wright's keyboard parts. The one song, the finale 'Louder than Words', is the band's farewell.
alb.pink-floyd-2014-the-endless-river.on: Optional — hear it as an epilogue dedicated to Wright.
alb.pink-floyd-2014-the-endless-river.de: Wright died in 2008; the album was made in his memory.
Roxy Music's Phil Manzanera was among the producers — another intersection in the network.
Gilmour declared it the last Pink Floyd album.
alb.pink-floyd-2014-the-endless-river.tr: Louder than Words — the only vocal track, a farewell
grp.david-gilmour-solo.name: David Gilmour (solo)
grp.david-gilmour-solo.kurulus: Born 1946, Cambridge. Syd Barrett's childhood friend; Pink Floyd's guitarist and singer from 1968.
grp.david-gilmour-solo.hikaye: Gilmour grew up in Cambridge practising guitar with Barrett and first joined Floyd as Barrett's stand-in. His blues-rooted guitar style — few notes, each one 'singing' — became Floyd's emotional centre. He discovered Kate Bush and paid for her first demos. After Waters left, as Floyd's de facto leader he took the band into the '90s. His solo albums are rare but carefully made; his wife, the writer Polly Samson, has been his main lyricist since 1994. In 2016 he played in Pompeii, in the amphitheatre where the 1971 Floyd film was shot — the first rock concert there with an audience.
grp.david-gilmour-solo.dna: Blues bends, long sustain, delay and Leslie effects; lap steel; melancholic, broad-tempo songs.
grp.david-gilmour-solo.gecisler: Jokers Wild → Pink Floyd → solo; a long partnership with Roxy Music's Phil Manzanera (On an Island, Rattle That Lock, The Endless River).
grp.david-gilmour-solo.etki: The leading representative of the 'feeling, not speed' school of rock guitar; a reference for post-rock and modern prog guitarists (Steven Wilson, Mariusz Duda).
alb.david-gilmour-1978-david-gilmour.an: Between Animals and The Wall, a loose, blues-heavy first solo album from a Gilmour who felt he lacked room in the band; recorded with friends from his Jokers Wild days.
alb.david-gilmour-1984-about-face.an: An album with '80s production and lyrics by Pete Townshend on two songs, made in the shadow of the fight with Waters.
alb.david-gilmour-1984-about-face.tr: Murder — anger at John Lennon's killer
alb.david-gilmour-2006-on-an-island.an: Co-produced by Phil Manzanera and Chris Thomas, with vocals by David Crosby and Graham Nash and Richard Wright on keyboards: Floyd's calmest 'sibling'. Number one in the UK.
alb.david-gilmour-2006-on-an-island.once: Essential — the peak of Gilmour's solo work.
alb.david-gilmour-2006-on-an-island.deta: Robert Wyatt playing cornet brings Floyd and Canterbury together.
Wright's last big tour was made with this album (2006).
alb.david-gilmour-2008-live-in-gdansk.an: The last concert of the On an Island tour: at the Gdańsk shipyards, marking the 26th anniversary of the Solidarity movement, with the Polish Baltic Philharmonic.
alb.david-gilmour-2008-live-in-gdansk.tr: Echoes — the last great performance with Wright
A loose concept album following the cycle of a day, inspired by Milton's 'Paradise Lost'.
grp.roger-waters-solo.name: Roger Waters (solo)
grp.roger-waters-solo.kurulus: Born 1943, Great Bookham. Founding bassist of Pink Floyd; the band's conceptual leader and main lyricist from 1973 to 1983.
grp.roger-waters-solo.hikaye: Waters's father was killed in the Second World War at the Anzio landings in Italy when Roger was five months old; that loss seeped into all his work through themes of war, authority and alienation. From Dark Side to The Final Cut he wrote Floyd's lyrics on his own. In 1985 he left and declared the band finished; he lost the lawsuit over the name. His solo albums are conceptual, political and theatrical. In 1990 he staged 'The Wall – Live in Berlin' on the site of the fallen Berlin Wall, one of the biggest concerts in history; The Wall Live tour of 2010–13 was one of the highest-grossing tours of all time. His outspoken political positions often stir controversy.
grp.roger-waters-solo.dna: Conceptual narrative, political and personal anger, sound effects and radio collages; cinematic rock opera.
grp.roger-waters-solo.gecisler: Sigma 6 → Pink Floyd → solo; Eric Clapton (Pros and Cons tour), Jeff Beck (Amused to Death), Nick Mason (Live 8 in 2005, guest in 2019).
grp.roger-waters-solo.etki: One of the greatest authors of the concept album and the rock opera; he turned the stadium show into political art.
alb.roger-waters-1984-the-pros-and-cons-: The second concept originally offered to Floyd alongside The Wall: a man's dreams over the course of a night, told in real time (4:30–5:11). Eric Clapton on guitar.
Gerald Scarfe's cover of a naked hitchhiker caused controversy at the time.
alb.roger-waters-1987-radio-k-a-o-s.an: An '80s synth-rock concept about a disabled young man who can hear radio waves and tries to prevent a nuclear war.
alb.roger-waters-1992-amused-to-death.an: Inspired by Neil Postman's 'Amusing Ourselves to Death', about the media and war turning into spectacle; Waters's solo masterpiece. Jeff Beck's guitar stands out.
alb.roger-waters-1992-amused-to-death.de: Recorded in Q Sound; reissued in 2015 with a new mix by James Guthrie.
With its cover image of a monkey watching television, the album is close to Floyd's visual language.
alb.roger-waters-2017-is-this-the-life-w: The studio album that came 25 years later, with Radiohead producer Nigel Godrich; about refugees, the Trump era and digital surveillance.
grp.nick-mason-solo-ve-saucerful-of-secr: Nick Mason (solo and Saucerful of Secrets)
Born 1944, Birmingham. Pink Floyd's founding drummer and the only member to play on every Floyd album.

Mason is the band's diplomat and historian; his book 'Inside Out: A Personal History of Pink Floyd' (2004) is one of the most balanced sources on the band. He is a racing-car collector and has driven at Le Mans. As a producer he made Robert Wyatt's Rock Bottom and The Damned's Music for Pleasure. His solo work consists of jazz-rock partnerships with Carla Bley and with Rick Fenn of 10cc. In 2018 he formed Nick Mason's Saucerful of Secrets (Guy Pratt, Gary Kemp, Lee Harris, Dom Beken) to play the Barrett-era and early Floyd repertoire.
Tom-tom-heavy, atmospheric, textured drumming; a curiosity for jazz and the experimental recording studio.
Sigma 6 → Pink Floyd → production (Wyatt, The Damned, Gong's Shamal) → Carla Bley → Mason + Fenn → Saucerful of Secrets.
The architect of Floyd's rhythmic atmosphere; a quiet junction in the network through production links reaching Canterbury and punk.
alb.nick-mason-1981-nick-mason-s-fictiti: A jazz-rock album actually composed entirely by Carla Bley, with Robert Wyatt on vocals; Mason on drums and production.
alb.nick-mason-1985-profiles.an: A synth-heavy instrumental album with Rick Fenn of 10cc; David Gilmour sings on 'Lie for a Lie'.
alb.nick-mason-2020-live-at-the-roundhou: Saucerful of Secrets' 2019 concerts: 'Interstellar Overdrive', 'Lucifer Sam', sections of 'Atom Heart Mother' and 'Echoes'. An energetic live recording that revives the Barrett era.
Recommended — to hear early Floyd on stage.
sec.8.title: The Canterbury Scene
sec.8.intro: A sub-network where jazz-rock, humour and English eccentricity intersect. Soft Machine is at the centre; members constantly circulate between Caravan, Hatfield and the North, National Health, Egg and Matching Mole. The Wilde Flowers are the root; around them are the solo work of Robert Wyatt, Kevin Ayers and Hugh Hopper, Khan, Gilgamesh and Dave Stewart's pop songs with Barbara Gaskin.
grp.soft-machine.kurulus: 1966, Canterbury. Formed by Robert Wyatt, Kevin Ayers, Mike Ratledge and Daevid Allen. Evolved from psychedelia to jazz fusion.
grp.soft-machine.hikaye: The central node of the Canterbury scene. Formed in 1966 by Daevid Allen, Robert Wyatt, Kevin Ayers and Mike Ratledge from what was left of the Wilde Flowers; the name came from William Burroughs's novel. First a psychedelic band of the London underground alongside Pink Floyd, then a pioneer of British jazz-rock. When Allen stayed in France he formed Gong; Ayers went solo, and Wyatt left in 1971 to form Matching Mole. In the '70s, with Karl Jenkins and John Marshall (from Nucleus), it became an all-out fusion band; when Ratledge left in 1976 no founding member remained. In the 2000s it returned to the stage as Soft Machine Legacy with Elton Dean, Hugh Hopper, John Marshall and Theo Travis, taking back the Soft Machine name after 2015.
grp.soft-machine.dna: Fuzz-organ textures, asymmetric time signatures, jazz improvisation, deadpan English humour.
grp.soft-machine.uyeler: Daevid Allen (→ Gong), Kevin Ayers (→ solo), Robert Wyatt (→ Matching Mole, solo), Hugh Hopper (bass), Karl Jenkins (later, from Nucleus).
grp.soft-machine.gecisler: After → Gong (Allen), Matching Mole (Wyatt), the Nucleus bridge (Jenkins).
alb.soft-machine-1968-the-soft-machine.a: Psychedelic prog; Wyatt's high, fragile voice and fuzz-organ textures.
alb.soft-machine-1968-the-soft-machine.t: Why Are We Sleeping? — Wyatt's fragile vocal
alb.soft-machine-1969-volume-two.an: Wyatt's absurd humour (the alphabet song) and a growing turn towards jazz.
alb.soft-machine-1969-volume-two.tr: A Concise British Alphabet — Wyatt's absurd humour
As Long as He Lies Perfectly Still
Pataphysical Introduction — the turn towards jazz
alb.soft-machine-1970-third.an: A double LP with one long piece per side. Wyatt's "Moon in June" is the band's last great 'song' moment; the rest slides towards fusion. A turning point.
alb.soft-machine-1970-third.tr: Moon in June — Wyatt's last great 'song' moment, 19 minutes
alb.soft-machine-1971-fourth.an: The move to entirely instrumental jazz fusion; Wyatt is about to leave.
alb.soft-machine-1972-fifth.an: Increasingly pure fusion; Canterbury loses its 'song' face and turns to its 'jazz' face.
alb.soft-machine-1975-bundles.tr: Hazard Profile — Allan Holdsworth's guitar showcase
The Man Who Waved at Trains
alb.soft-machine-1976-softs.an: Ratledge's last album; John Etheridge on guitar, replacing Allan Holdsworth. Karl Jenkins's minimalist, rhythmic compositions come to the fore.
alb.soft-machine-1976-softs.kadro: Karl Jenkins, John Etheridge, Roy Babbington, John Marshall, Mike Ratledge (partial), Alan Wakeman
alb.soft-machine-1976-softs.detay: Alan Wakeman is Rick Wakeman's cousin.
alb.soft-machine-2007-steam.an: As Soft Machine Legacy: the last recording with Hugh Hopper. After Elton Dean's death in 2006, Theo Travis took over the horns.
alb.soft-machine-2018-hidden-details.an: A studio album under the Soft Machine name 37 years after the last one; modern Canterbury jazz-rock that also reinterprets old pieces such as 'The Man Who Waved at Trains'.
alb.soft-machine-2018-hidden-details.onc: Recommended — the best recording of their late period.
grp.caravan.kurulus: 1968, Canterbury. Formed by Wilde Flowers members (the root shared with Soft Machine) Pye Hastings, Richard Sinclair, Dave Sinclair and Richard Coughlan.
grp.caravan.hikaye: Born out of the 'melodic' branch of the Wilde Flowers, Caravan (Pye Hastings, Richard and David Sinclair, Richard Coughlan) is Canterbury's most pop-friendly, most English and warmest band. Hastings's soft vocals and Dave Sinclair's fuzz organ became the band's signature. Cousins Richard and Dave Sinclair left in 1972 to lay the foundations of Hatfield and the North; the band then took an orchestral direction with viola master Geoffrey Richardson. Scattered in the '80s, it has recorded and toured regularly under Hastings's leadership since the '90s; Coughlan died in 2013.
grp.caravan.dna: Melodic Canterbury; long fusion suites, but more pastoral, humorous and English.
alb.caravan-1968-caravan.an: The transition from psychedelic pop to Canterbury.
alb.caravan-1968-caravan.tr: Place of My Own — from psychedelic pop to Canterbury
Where but for Caravan Would I?
alb.caravan-1970-if-i-could-do-it-all-ov: A humorous title and maturing organ-jazz textures.
If I Could Do It All Over Again... — humorous title, organ jazz
And I Wish I Were Stoned / Don't Worry
alb.caravan-1971-in-the-land-of-grey-and: The masterpiece. "Nine Feet Underground" (an organ-centred suite filling an LP side) is the peak of Canterbury melodicism.
Nine Feet Underground — organ-centred suite filling an LP side, the Canterbury peak
In the Land of Grey and Pink — pastoral title track
alb.caravan-1972-waterloo-lily.an: More jazz-heavy; Steve Miller (keyboards) replaces Dave Sinclair.
alb.caravan-1972-waterloo-lily.tr: The Love in Your Eye — long suite
alb.caravan-1973-for-girls-who-grow-plum: Enriched by orchestration, the most balanced of their later albums.
The Dog, the Dog, He's at It Again — orchestral, the best-loved later piece
alb.caravan-1975-cunning-stunts.tr: Stuck in a Hole — commercial single
alb.caravan-1976-blind-dog-at-st-dunstan: The Arista years; a jazzy, entertaining album named after a Canterbury street.
The first major studio album of the band as reshaped in the '90s under Pye Hastings; the title is a pun on his name.
alb.caravan-2003-the-unauthorised-breakf: A mature, acoustic-tinged album by the line-up with Jim Leverton and Doug Boyle; considered by critics one of the best late-period Caravan albums.
alb.caravan-2013-paradise-filter.an: Released shortly before Richard Coughlan's death; Hastings's pop-prog melodicism carries on.
grp.gong.kurulus: 1967–70, Paris/Canterbury. Formed by Daevid Allen (Soft Machine) and Gilli Smyth. The 'Planet Gong' / 'Pot Head Pixie' mythology.
grp.gong.hikaye: When Australian Daevid Allen couldn't return to Britain after Soft Machine's 1967 French tour because of visa problems, he stayed in Paris and formed Gong with Gilli Smyth. In the 'Radio Gnome Invisible' trilogy (Flying Teapot, Angel's Egg, You) he told the mythology of Planet Gong's flying teapots, the 'pot head pixies' and Zero the Hero. With Steve Hillage (guitar), Tim Blake (synths), Didier Malherbe (woodwinds) and Pierre Moerlen (percussion) the band reached its 1973–74 peak. When Allen left in 1975 the jazz-fusion period of 'Pierre Moerlen's Gong' began. Allen ran countless side projects over the years (Mother Gong, Planet Gong, New York Gong); before his death in 2015 he handed the band over to a younger line-up led by Kavus Torabi, and Gong lives on.
grp.gong.dna: Psychedelic fusion, space humour, Steve Hillage's glissando guitar, Tim Blake's synths.
alb.gong-1971-camembert-electrique.an: The mythology and humour settle in.
alb.gong-1971-camembert-electrique.tr: You Can't Kill Me — the Pot Head Pixie mythology
alb.gong-1973-flying-teapot.an: The 'Radio Gnome Invisible' trilogy; the peak of space fusion, with Hillage's guitar shining.
alb.gong-1973-flying-teapot.tr: Flying Teapot — opening of the Radio Gnome trilogy, space fusion
Witch's Song / I Am Your Pussy
alb.gong-1973-angel-s-egg.tr: I Never Glid Before — Hillage's glissando guitar
alb.gong-1974-you.tr: A Sprinkling of Clouds — Tim Blake's synth textures
You Never Blow Yr Trip Forever
alb.gong-1976-shamal.an: After Allen's departure, a turn to purer jazz fusion.
alb.gong-1976-shamal.tr: Wingful of Eyes — post-Allen, pure fusion
alb.gong-1976-gazeuse.an: Vibraphone- and marimba-heavy jazz fusion led by Pierre Moerlen, with Allan Holdsworth on guitar. Released in the US as 'Expresso'.
alb.gong-2000-zero-to-infinity.an: An album reuniting Allen, Smyth, Malherbe and Mike Howlett, returning to the 'Radio Gnome' mythology.
alb.gong-2009-2032.an: A mythological 'sequel' about the year Planet Gong will make contact with Earth; with the return of Steve Hillage and Miquette Giraudy.
alb.gong-2016-rejoice-i-m-dead.an: Recorded after Allen's death under Kavus Torabi's leadership; a strong new beginning honouring his legacy.
alb.gong-2016-rejoice-i-m-dead.detay: Torabi comes from Cardiacs and Knifeworld — an intersection of Canterbury and English eccentric rock.
alb.gong-2019-the-universe-also-collapse: The Torabi line-up's second album: a long psychedelic journey built around the 20-minute 'Forever Reoccurring'.
grp.hatfield-and-the-north-national-heal: Hatfield and the North / National Health (sub-nodes)

Hatfield and the North (1972–75) is a Canterbury supergroup formed by Richard Sinclair from Caravan, Dave Stewart from Egg, and Phil Miller and Pip Pyle from Delivery; it took its name from the motorway sign heading north out of London. The Northettes vocal trio (Amanda Parsons, Barbara Gaskin, Ann Rosenthal) completed the band's light, ironic spirit. After it split, Stewart and Alan Gowen (Gilgamesh) formed National Health: broader, more composed Canterbury jazz-rock. After Gowen's death in 1981 the band closed with D.S. al Coda, made up of his compositions.
alb.hatfield-and-the-north-national-heal: A fluid blend of short fragments and long suites; the female vocal textures of "The Northettes".
Son of 'There's No Place Like Homerton' — long suite with the Northettes on vocals
With the "Mumps" suite, one of Canterbury's most sophisticated moments.
Mumps — multi-part suite, one of Canterbury's most sophisticated moments
The peak of Canterbury's chamber-music wing.
Tenemos Roads — Dave Stewart's peak as a composer
National Health's farewell album, recording Alan Gowen's compositions after his death from leukaemia in 1981.
grp.egg.kurulus: 1968, London. The first important band of Dave Stewart (later of Hatfield and National Health). The organ-centred trio form of Uriel (with Steve Hillage) after Hillage left.
grp.egg.dna: Organ-centred, classically influenced (Stravinsky, broken time signatures) cerebral prog; humour, asymmetric rhythms, composer-driven structures. The exact opposite of ELP: unflashy but intellectual.
grp.egg.uyeler: Dave Stewart (organ/keyboards), Mont Campbell (bass/vocals/composer), Clive Brooks (drums). An organ-rock trio format — but with a more 'cerebral' sound nothing like ELP.
grp.egg.gecisler: Before → Uriel (Stewart + Steve Hillage). After → Hatfield and the North & National Health (Stewart), Khan (Stewart as guest). The starting point of Canterbury's keyboard-composer wing.
grp.egg.etki: Where Dave Stewart's identity as a composer was born; the root of Canterbury's organ-centred 'chamber music' wing. The herald of Hatfield and National Health.
alb.egg-1970-egg.an: The debut; classically influenced prog in broken time signatures, in an organ-trio format. Stravinsky adaptations and original compositions side by side.
alb.egg-1970-egg.tr: While Growing My Hair — melodic opener
Symphony No. 2 — an attempt at classical form
Fugue in D Minor — Bach adaptation
alb.egg-1971-the-polite-force.an: The band's masterpiece; darker and more ambitious. 'Long Piece No. 3' is a suite woven from asymmetric metres that fills an LP side. Organ prog nothing like ELP.
alb.egg-1971-the-polite-force.tr: A Visit to Newport Hospital — Campbell's semi-autobiographical piece
Long Piece No. 3 (Parts 1-4) — the album's centrepiece, a suite in broken metres
alb.egg-1974-the-civil-surface.an: An album of 'unreleased material' recorded after the band split, with backing from the Hatfield circle and Virgin. The last collaboration between Stewart and Campbell.
grp.khan.kurulus: 1971, London. A guitar-centred Canterbury band formed by Steve Hillage (later of Gong) before he joined Gong. From the circle around the University of Kent (Canterbury).
grp.khan.dna: Guitar-centred Canterbury prog: Hillage's fluid, pre-glissando guitar, Stewart's organ textures, an intersection of prog and hard rock. A herald of the sound Kansas would develop a few years later.
grp.khan.uyeler: Steve Hillage (guitar/vocals), Dave Stewart (organ — guesting from Egg), Nick Greenwood (bass), Eric Peachey (drums). Stewart's organ adds Canterbury texture to Hillage's guitar.
grp.khan.gecisler: Before → the Uriel/Egg circle (Hillage, Stewart). After → Gong & solo (Hillage), Hatfield (Stewart). The link connecting Canterbury to Gong's space fusion.
grp.khan.etki: Where Steve Hillage's identity as a composer-guitarist was born; the bridge carrying the Canterbury scene into the Gong universe. A single album, but a cult gem.
alb.khan-1972-space-shanty.an: Their only studio album and one of Canterbury's hidden masterpieces. Hillage's guitar and Stewart's organ hold a dialogue across long-form pieces; prog meets hard rock.
alb.khan-1972-space-shanty.tr: Space Shanty — title track, the band's emblem
Driving to Amsterdam — long-form Canterbury jam
grp.matching-mole.kurulus: 1971, London. The band Robert Wyatt (Soft Machine's drummer and singer) formed after Soft Machine slid into pure fusion. The name is a pun on the French 'Machine Molle' (Soft Machine).
grp.matching-mole.dna: Song-based Canterbury: Wyatt's fragile, melancholic voice and melodic writing; jazz-rock improvisation combined with pop sensibility. A continuation of Soft Machine's 'song' face.
grp.matching-mole.uyeler: Robert Wyatt (drums/vocals), Phil Miller (guitar; later Hatfield), Dave MacRae / Dave Sinclair (keyboards), Bill MacCormick (bass). Later Dave Sinclair of Caravan on keyboards.
grp.matching-mole.gecisler: Before → Soft Machine (Wyatt). After → Hatfield and the North (Phil Miller), Wyatt's solo career (after his 1973 accident). The bridge linking Soft Machine's 'Third' to Hatfield.
grp.matching-mole.etki: The bridge to Wyatt's post-Soft Machine sound; it carried Phil Miller to Hatfield. The last band recording just before Wyatt's tragic accident (1973).
alb.matching-mole-1972-matching-mole.an: The debut; Wyatt's ballad 'O Caroline' is the band's best-loved moment. A balance between song form and improvisation.
alb.matching-mole-1972-matching-mole.tr: O Caroline — Wyatt's fragile love ballad, a Canterbury classic
Signed Curtain — a meta-song (describing its own structure)
Part of the Dance — long jam
alb.matching-mole-1972-matching-mole-s-l: Produced by Robert Fripp; more political and experimental (a Mao-inspired cover). The missing link between Soft Machine's 'Third' and Hatfield.
Starting in the Middle of the Day...
Gloria Gloom — experimental piece with Eno contributing
grp.kevin-ayers.kurulus: Solo from 1969. Kevin Ayers, Soft Machine's founding bassist and singer, left after the first album and built a solo career of his own, lazy and elegant.
grp.kevin-ayers.hikaye: Exhausted by the 1968 US tour, Soft Machine's founding bassist Ayers left the band, withdrew to Ibiza and began a solo career as a bohemian, ironic songwriter with a deep baritone. The young Mike Oldfield (bass and guitar) and David Bedford (keyboards) learned their trade in his band, The Whole World. At the famous 'June 1, 1974' concert he shared the stage with Brian Eno, John Cale and Nico. He died in 2013; his last album, The Unfairground (2007), was widely admired.
grp.kevin-ayers.dna: Canterbury's singer-songwriter wing: a deep, lazy baritone, surreal and humorous lyrics, a relaxed blend of psychedelic pop and the avant-garde. A more sophisticated relative of Syd Barrett.
grp.kevin-ayers.uyeler: Solo (Kevin Ayers, vocals/bass/guitar). His backing band The Whole World included Mike Oldfield (bass/guitar, very young!), David Bedford (keyboards) and Lol Coxhill (saxophone).
grp.kevin-ayers.gecisler: Before → Soft Machine (Ayers). Circle → Mike Oldfield (who grew up in Ayers's band before Tubular Bells), Brian Eno, Nico, John Cale (the 1974 live album 'June 1, 1974' brought the four together).
grp.kevin-ayers.etki: He carried Canterbury's 'song' spirit into a solo format and trained Mike Oldfield. One of the underground masters of English art-pop.
alb.kevin-ayers-1969-joy-of-a-toy.an: His first solo album after Soft Machine, with former bandmates still contributing. An elegant blend of Canterbury humour and pop melody.
alb.kevin-ayers-1970-shooting-at-the-moo: Recorded with The Whole World (including a young Mike Oldfield); his most experimental solo album. Pop and the avant-garde side by side.
alb.kevin-ayers-1971-whatevershebringswe: One of Ayers's best-loved albums: a gentle but strange masterpiece with Mike Oldfield, David Bedford and Robert Wyatt.
alb.kevin-ayers-1973-bananamour.an: More accessible and song-oriented; 'Caribbean Moon' is one of the era's favourites. Includes a tribute to Syd Barrett.
alb.kevin-ayers-1973-bananamour.tr: Don't Let It Get You Down
Oh! Wot a Dream — a tribute to Barrett
alb.kevin-ayers-1974-the-confessions-of-: The Island years; Ayers's most ambitious album, with a title suite featuring Mike Oldfield and Nico.
alb.kevin-ayers-2007-the-unfairground.an: A late comeback album after fifteen years of silence, with admirers such as Teenage Fanclub, Neutral Milk Hotel and Robert Wyatt taking part. Ayers's last recording.
grp.robert-wyatt.kurulus: Solo from the 1970s. After Soft Machine and Matching Mole, and following his 1973 accident (paralysis below the waist), he gave up the drums and turned entirely to composing and singing.
grp.robert-wyatt.hikaye: Soft Machine's drummer-singer and then founder of Matching Mole, Wyatt fell from a fourth-floor window at a party on 1 June 1973 and was paralysed from the waist down. Reborn as a musician in a wheelchair, he gave up drums for keyboards and percussion and built a shared artistic life with his wife, the painter Alfreda Benge. Rock Bottom (1974) became one of the most respected albums in British music. In the '80s, as a Communist Party member, he made political cover singles ('Shipbuilding', 'At Last I Am Free'). Having worked with Björk, Paul Weller, Brian Eno and Phil Manzanera, Wyatt announced in 2014 that he had stopped making music.
grp.robert-wyatt.dna: Utterly original: a fragile, high, deeply emotional voice; jazz-influenced minimalist compositions; political and personal themes. Canterbury's most personal, most moving voice.
grp.robert-wyatt.uyeler: Solo (Robert Wyatt, vocals/keyboards/percussion). On 'Rock Bottom' and after, guests from the Canterbury circle (Mike Oldfield, Fred Frith, Hugh Hopper).
grp.robert-wyatt.gecisler: Before → Soft Machine, Matching Mole (Wyatt). Circle → Henry Cow (a left-political link), Pink Floyd (Nick Mason produced 'Rock Bottom'). He links Canterbury with RIO and the avant-garde.
grp.robert-wyatt.etki: After his accident he became one of prog's most respected 'solo' figures; 'Rock Bottom' is one of the genre's best-loved solo albums. A bridge to the RIO/left-political wing.
An experimental first solo album released while he was still in Soft Machine; dominated by jazz improvisation and sound manipulation.
alb.robert-wyatt-1974-rock-bottom.an: Wyatt's masterpiece and one of prog's best-loved solo albums. Written and completed after his accident; produced by Nick Mason (Pink Floyd). A deep, underwater-like melancholy.
alb.robert-wyatt-1974-rock-bottom.tr: Sea Song — the emblematic ballad, a fragile love song
Little Red Riding Hood Hit the Road — with Fred Frith and Mike Oldfield
Alifib / Alife — a double piece dedicated to his wife Alfreda
alb.robert-wyatt-1975-ruth-is-stranger-t: The successor to Rock Bottom; more jazz-oriented and guest-heavy. Wyatt's identity as singer and composer has matured.
alb.robert-wyatt-1985-old-rottenhat.an: A political, minimalist album played entirely by Wyatt himself; about colonialism and the Cold War.
alb.robert-wyatt-1991-dondestan.an: Built on Alfreda Benge's poems and Wyatt's political lyrics, with a plain home-recording aesthetic.
alb.robert-wyatt-1997-shleep.an: A brilliant late album on sleep and dreams, with Paul Weller, Brian Eno, Phil Manzanera and Evan Parker.
alb.robert-wyatt-1997-shleep.oncelik: Essential — the masterpiece of his late period.
alb.robert-wyatt-2003-cuckooland.an: Nominated for the Mercury Prize; an elegant mixture of jazz, Latin music and chamber music.
alb.robert-wyatt-2007-comicopera.an: An 'opera' in three acts: love, war and exile. The final act is sung in Italian and Spanish.
grp.the-wilde-flowers.kurulus: 1964, Canterbury. Brian Hopper, Hugh Hopper, Robert Wyatt, Kevin Ayers, Richard Sinclair; later Pye Hastings and Richard Coughlan.
grp.the-wilde-flowers.hikaye: The 'mother band' of the Canterbury scene. The young musicians who gathered at Wellington House in Canterbury — the Wyatt family home, where Daevid Allen was a lodger — played songs influenced by jazz, R&B and the Beatles. The band never released an official album, but when it split it produced two main branches: Soft Machine with Wyatt, Ayers and Hugh Hopper, and Caravan with Hastings, the Sinclair cousins and Coughlan. Its demo recordings were compiled and released in 1994.
grp.the-wilde-flowers.dna: R&B, beat, jazz chords, English songwriting; all the seeds of the later Canterbury sound.
grp.the-wilde-flowers.gecisler: Wilde Flowers → Soft Machine (Wyatt, Ayers, H. Hopper) and Caravan (Hastings, R. & D. Sinclair, Coughlan).
grp.the-wilde-flowers.etki: The root of Canterbury; the purest example of a single local band giving birth to two major ones.
alb.the-wilde-flowers-1994-the-wilde-flo: A compilation of demo and rehearsal recordings from 1965–69; early pieces sung by Wyatt and the first versions of Caravan and Soft Machine songs.
Optional — for those curious about the roots.
Memories — a Hugh Hopper composition (later also covered by Wyatt and Daevid Allen)
grp.steve-hillage-solo-ve-system-7.name: Steve Hillage (solo and System 7)
grp.steve-hillage-solo-ve-system-7.kurul: Born 1951, London. Guitarist with Uriel/Arzachel, Khan, Kevin Ayers and Gong.
grp.steve-hillage-solo-ve-system-7.hikay: At 16 Hillage formed Uriel with Dave Stewart (its only album appeared under the name Arzachel); while studying at the University of Kent in Canterbury he moved in Caravan's circle, formed Khan and in 1973–75 became Gong's 'glissando guitar' specialist. In his solo career, with his partner Miquette Giraudy (synths), he made the brightest albums of mystical, optimistic, 'hippie' space rock. During punk he remained one of the few prog names people liked; in the '80s he produced Simple Minds and Robyn Hitchcock. In the '90s, encouraged by Alex Paterson (The Orb), he formed System 7 with Giraudy and moved into ambient house and trance — one of the most successful bridges from prog to electronic dance music.
grp.steve-hillage-solo-ve-system-7.dna: Glissando and delay guitar, spiritual lyrics, synth textures; later ambient techno.
grp.steve-hillage-solo-ve-system-7.gecis: Uriel/Arzachel (Dave Stewart) → Khan → Kevin Ayers → Gong → solo → System 7; collaborations with The Orb and Derrick May; back on stage with Gong after 2014.
grp.steve-hillage-solo-ve-system-7.etki: A bridge between space rock and rave culture; a keeper of the tradition of 'psychedelic optimism'.
alb.steve-hillage-1975-fish-rising.an: His first solo album, recorded with Gong members (Dave Stewart, Pierre Moerlen, Didier Malherbe, Mike Howlett); themed around fish and a mystical journey.
alb.steve-hillage-1976-l.an: Produced by Todd Rundgren and recorded with members of Utopia; with versions of Donovan's 'Hurdy Gurdy Man' and the Beatles' 'It's All Too Much'.
alb.steve-hillage-1976-l.detay: Utopia's Roger Powell and Kasim Sulton played on it — an intersection with the Rundgren universe.
Electronic, funk-tinged space rock produced by Malcolm Cecil (Tonto's Expanding Head Band).
alb.steve-hillage-1979-rainbow-dome-musi: A meditative album of two long ambient pieces, heralding System 7.
alb.steve-hillage-1991-system-7.an: The first System 7 album, recorded with The Orb and the Detroit techno circle, bringing prog guitar together with house rhythms.
grp.phil-manzanera-quiet-sun-801.kurulus: Born 1951, London. Roxy Music's guitarist; founder of the Quiet Sun (1970–72, 1975) and 801 (1976–77) projects.
grp.phil-manzanera-quiet-sun-801.hikaye: Raised in Havana and Caracas by his Colombian mother, Manzanera formed the Canterbury-style jazz-rock band Quiet Sun at Dulwich College (Bill MacCormick, Charles Hayward, Dave Jarrett). When he joined Roxy Music in 1972 Quiet Sun was shelved; in 1975 Quiet Sun's only album, Mainstream, was recorded at the same time as his solo album Diamond Head. In 1976 801, formed with Brian Eno, Bill MacCormick and Simon Phillips, left a legendary live album combining glam, Canterbury and art rock. In later years he turned to Latin American music and became David Gilmour's close producer and partner.
grp.phil-manzanera-quiet-sun-801.dna: Clipped, effects-laden art-rock guitar; Canterbury jazz harmonies and Latin colours.
grp.phil-manzanera-quiet-sun-801.gecisle: Quiet Sun → Roxy Music → 801 (Eno, MacCormick, Simon Phillips, Francis Monkman) → solo → David Gilmour (On an Island, Rattle That Lock, The Endless River). Charles Hayward → This Heat. MacCormick → Matching Mole.
grp.phil-manzanera-quiet-sun-801.etki: A three-way junction between the Roxy/Eno universe, Canterbury and Pink Floyd.
alb.phil-manzanera-1975-mainstream.an: Quiet Sun's only album, recorded in spare hours during Manzanera's solo sessions. A lost classic of Canterbury jazz-rock, with changing metres and fuzz organ.
alb.phil-manzanera-1975-mainstream.detay: Charles Hayward went on to form This Heat — a RIO/post-punk connection.
alb.phil-manzanera-1975-diamond-head.an: His first solo album, with friends from Roxy and Canterbury: Eno, Wyatt (singing in Spanish), John Wetton and Eddie Jobson.
alb.phil-manzanera-1975-diamond-head.det: John Wetton and Robert Wyatt on the same album shows how wide the network's connections reach.
alb.phil-manzanera-1976-801-live.an: From the Queen Elizabeth Hall concert: Eno's songs and versions of the Beatles' 'Tomorrow Never Knows' and the Kinks' 'You Really Got Me'. Simon Phillips's drumming and the best live sound of the era.
alb.phil-manzanera-1976-801-live.oncelik: Essential — one of the best live albums of the '70s.
alb.phil-manzanera-1976-801-live.detay: Francis Monkman is Curved Air's founding keyboardist.
sec.9.title: UK, Supergroups and Bridge Projects
sec.9.intro: The network's inter-universe junctions. These projects connect the King Crimson, Yes, ELP and Genesis universes directly.
grp.uk.kurulus: 1977. John Wetton (King Crimson) + Bill Bruford (Yes/King Crimson) + Allan Holdsworth (guitar) + Eddie Jobson (violin/keyboards, Roxy Music/Zappa). A pure supergroup.
grp.uk.dna: Technical fusion-prog; Crimson's hardness + melodic structure + Jobson's symphonic keyboard and violin textures.
grp.uk.uyeler: Holdsworth & Bruford left → Terry Bozzio (Zappa) took over the drums and the band became a trio.
alb.uk-1978-u-k.an: The four-piece line-up. With the "In the Dead of Night" suite, a late peak of technical prog; Holdsworth's fluid guitar races Jobson's keyboards.
alb.uk-1978-u-k.tr: In the Dead of Night — technical prog suite, a Holdsworth-vs-Jobson race
Alaska / Time to Kill — Jobson's keyboard and violin textures
alb.uk-1979-danger-money.an: As a trio; more melodic and song-oriented. "Nothing to Lose" is a stab at radio. It anticipates Asia's future AOR direction.
alb.uk-1979-danger-money.tr: Nothing to Lose — a stab at radio, the herald of Asia
grp.asia.kurulus: 1981. John Wetton (UK/King Crimson, vocals/bass) + Steve Howe (Yes, guitar) + Geoff Downes (Yes/Buggles, keyboards) + Carl Palmer (ELP, drums). The super-junction where four major universes meet at a single point.
grp.asia.hikaye: Asia was formed in 1981 by John Wetton (King Crimson/UK), Steve Howe (Yes), Carl Palmer (ELP) and Geoff Downes (Buggles/Yes); its first album was the best-selling album of 1982 in the US. It was soon shaken by clashing egos and by Wetton leaving and returning. In the '90s a new Asia led by John Payne carried on with Downes; in 2006 the original four reunited and made three studio albums. After Wetton's death in 2017 the band continued touring with Billy Sherwood.
grp.asia.dna: Prog virtuosity turned into radio-friendly AOR; short song forms, huge choruses, glossy production.
grp.asia.uyeler: Howe left (1985) → Mandy Meyer; then various line-ups. After Wetton's death in 2017 Billy Sherwood took over bass and vocals — a late merger of the World Trade and Asia universes.
grp.asia.etki: The symbol of prog's commercialisation in the '80s; the network's "transformation" node.
alb.asia-1982-asia.an: "Heat of the Moment", "Only Time Will Tell". Nine weeks at number one in the US; squeezing four virtuosos' talent into the three-minute hit mould brought both huge success and a debate about prog purity.
alb.asia-1982-asia.tr: Heat of the Moment — huge hit
Only Time Will Tell — melodic single
alb.asia-1983-alpha.an: More of the formula; "Don't Cry". Sales fall and internal tension grows.
alb.asia-1983-alpha.tr: The Smile Has Left Your Eyes — Wetton ballad
alb.asia-1985-astra.an: Howe has left (replaced by Mandy Meyer); the band's identity weakens and sales decline.
alb.asia-1992-aqua.an: An attempt to regroup around the Wetton/Downes axis.
alb.asia-1994-aria.an: Continuing with '90s production; aimed at the core fan base.
alb.asia-1996-arena.an: The John Payne era: world-music colours and melodic AOR.
alb.asia-2008-phoenix.an: The original four's first studio album in 25 years; 'An Extraordinary Life' is a song about life that Wetton wrote after his heart surgery.
alb.asia-2008-phoenix.oncelik: Recommended — a document of the reunion.
alb.asia-2010-omega.an: The original line-up's second reunion album; more compact and melodic.
alb.asia-2012-xxx.an: The band's 30th anniversary; Steve Howe's last album with the original line-up.
alb.asia-2014-gravitas.an: An album with young guitarist Sam Coulson replacing Howe; Wetton's last studio recording.
grp.gtr.kurulus: 1985–86. Steve Howe (Yes/Asia) + Steve Hackett (Genesis) — two great prog guitarists meet. A rare node directly joining the Yes and Genesis universes.
grp.gtr.dna: Guitar-centred melodic prog-pop; the two guitarists' 'guitar as orchestra' approach, packaged with '80s AOR production.
grp.gtr.uyeler: Max Bacon (vocals), Phil Spalding (bass), Jonathan Mover (drums). Tension between Howe and Hackett quickly ended the band.
alb.gtr-1986-gtr.an: "When the Heart Rules the Mind" (a US Top 20 hit). Their only studio album. Hackett's lyrical textures and Howe's angular figures meet under '80s gloss; an interesting but short-lived synthesis of two schools.
alb.gtr-1986-gtr.tr: When the Heart Rules the Mind — US Top 20 hit, the Howe+Hackett guitar weave
Sketches in the Sun — Howe solo guitar
Hackett to Bits — Hackett solo guitar
grp.buggles-kopru-dugum.name: Buggles (bridge node)
grp.buggles-kopru-dugum.kurulus: 1979. Trevor Horn + Geoff Downes. With "Video Killed the Radio Star" they opened the MTV era. In 1980 both joined Yes (Drama); Downes later moved on to Asia.
grp.buggles-kopru-dugum.dna: Synth-pop, but a crucial bridge connecting to prog through Yes; Horn would later become a major producer (90125 included).
alb.buggles-1980-the-age-of-plastic.an: A synth-pop classic; themes of anxiety about technology.
alb.buggles-1980-the-age-of-plastic.tr: Video Killed the Radio Star — the hit that opened the MTV era, the first video MTV played
alb.buggles-1981-adventures-in-modern-re: More complex and experimental after the Yes experience.
Adventures in Modern Recording — more complex, after the Yes experience
I Am a Camera — the pop version of 'Into the Lens' from Yes's 'Drama'
grp.bad-company-foreigner-uye-gocu-uclar: Bad Company / Foreigner (ends of member migration)
grp.bruford.kurulus: 1977, London. Formed by Bill Bruford (Yes/King Crimson) to express his own identity as a composer, after King Crimson split in 1974. Signed to EG Records (Crimson's label).
grp.bruford.dna: Complex jazz-rock fusion: asymmetric metres, Holdsworth's fluid legato guitar, Berlin's melodic bass, Stewart's soaring keyboard textures. One of the most elegant bridges between prog and fusion.
grp.bruford.uyeler: Bill Bruford (drums), Allan Holdsworth (guitar; later UK and solo), Jeff Berlin (bass — a fusion virtuoso), Dave Stewart (keyboards, from Hatfield/National Health).
grp.bruford.gecisler: Before → Yes, King Crimson (Bruford); Hatfield (Stewart). After → UK (Holdsworth), Earthworks (Bruford), National Health (Stewart). UK's sister node: both share Holdsworth and Crimson's hardness.
grp.bruford.etki: With UK, the peak of late-'70s British technical fusion; a reference for later prog musicians (especially drummers). The first stop on Bruford's journey from rock to jazz.
alb.bruford-1978-feels-good-to-me.an: Under Bruford's solo name but effectively a band album. Atmospheric jazz-rock with Annette Peacock's vocals and Kenny Wheeler's flugelhorn. Holdsworth's guitar and Berlin's bass already hold a dialogue on this first record.
alb.bruford-1978-feels-good-to-me.tr: Beelzebub — the band's emblem, with Berlin's bass theme and a Holdsworth solo
Sample and Hold — Peacock's vocal, a cool-warm texture
Feels Good to Me — John Goodsall (Brand X) guests on rhythm guitar on the title track
alb.bruford-1979-one-of-a-kind.an: The band's masterpiece and its most 'prog' album; entirely instrumental. For most critics one of the high points of '70s fusion-prog. Holdsworth's guitar and Stewart's keyboards are constantly in competition.
alb.bruford-1979-one-of-a-kind.tr: Hell's Bells — Bruford's signature rhythmic theme
One of a Kind (Part 1 & 2) — multi-part suite, the band's most ambitious composition
Forever Until Sunday — Stewart's melodic keyboard writing
alb.bruford-1980-gradually-going-tornado: Holdsworth has left; Jeff Berlin comes forward and sings on a few tracks. More 'song'-oriented, a compromise of fusion purity according to some fans. The band's last studio album.
Age of Information — sung by Berlin, the era's anxiety about technology
grp.bill-bruford-s-earthworks.kurulus: 1986. The band Bruford formed after King Crimson's 1981–84 period, turning to his real passion, jazz. He gathered young talent from the British jazz orchestra Loose Tubes.
grp.bill-bruford-s-earthworks.hikaye: Representing Bruford's move from rock to acoustic jazz, Earthworks (1986–2009) introduced young British jazz musicians such as Django Bates and Iain Ballamy; here Bruford played chords and melodies on Simmons electronic drum pads. In 2009 Bruford retired from active performing and completed a doctorate at the University of Surrey on drummers' creativity.
grp.bill-bruford-s-earthworks.dna: Acoustic/electronic jazz fusion: Bruford's melodic and chordal use of Simmons drums, Bates's strange synth solos, Ballamy's lyrical saxophone. More jazz than rock, but with a prog sensibility.
grp.bill-bruford-s-earthworks.uyeler: Bill Bruford (acoustic + electronic Simmons drums), Django Bates (keyboards/tenor horn/trumpet), Iain Ballamy (saxophones), Mick Hutton (double bass; later Tim Harries). Dave Stewart produced the debut and played bass synth.
grp.bill-bruford-s-earthworks.gecisler: Before → Bruford, King Crimson, ABWH (Bruford). In 1988 Bruford put Earthworks on hold for ABWH — the two nodes intersect directly. After → King Crimson's 'double trio' in the '90s.
grp.bill-bruford-s-earthworks.etki: The band that began the 'jazz' half of Bruford's career; a bridge connecting prog listeners to contemporary British jazz. Bates and Ballamy went on from here to major jazz careers.
alb.bill-bruford-s-earthworks-1987-earth: The most 'prog' Earthworks album; thanks to Dave Stewart's production and guest role it carries the fusion feel of the Bruford band. A unique texture of Simmons drums playing melodies.
Bridge of Inhibition — the Middle Eastern-tinged emblem, with Bruford playing melody on drum synth
Making a Song and Dance — Ballamy's dreamy soprano saxophone
Emotional Shirt — Bates's bizarre synth solo, reminiscent of the Fragile era
alb.bill-bruford-s-earthworks-1989-dig.a: The band's second album; the jazz direction strengthens and the prog texture thins out. Bates's identity as a composer becomes clear.
alb.bill-bruford-s-earthworks-1991-all-h: The last studio album of the first period; social themes (the Gulf War, Pigalle). The last recording before Bates left.
alb.bill-bruford-s-earthworks-1999-a-par: The second Earthworks line-up: fully acoustic drums and modern jazz.
alb.bill-bruford-s-earthworks-2001-the-s: With Tim Garland's horns, the most consistent jazz album by Earthworks.
sec.10.title: The Outer Ring — Independent Nodes Fed by the Same Sound
grp.jethro-tull.kurulus: 1967, Blackpool/Luton. Evolved from blues to folk-prog around Ian Anderson (flute/vocals).
grp.jethro-tull.hikaye: Born out of the mid-'60s blues bands of Blackpool's Ian Anderson, Jethro Tull took its name from an 18th-century agricultural reformer (suggested by a history buff at their booking agency). Playing flute on one leg in a beggar's overcoat, Anderson soon became the band's sole driving force; blues guitarist Mick Abrahams left after the first album to form Blodwyn Pig and was replaced by Martin Barre, who would remain Anderson's right-hand man from 1969 to 2011. Having produced one of rock's great conceptual albums with Aqualung, the band wrote Thick as a Brick as a mocking reply to critics who called Aqualung a 'concept album': the single-piece 'poem' of a fictional child poet. The late '70s brought the folk-rock trilogy (Songs from the Wood, Heavy Horses, Stormwatch); the '80s brought electronic experiments and, with Crest of a Knave, a controversial Grammy (1989) won ahead of Metallica. After 2012 Anderson worked under his own name; in 2017 he began using the Jethro Tull name again.
grp.jethro-tull.dna: Rock flute (a unique signature), English folk + hard rock + classical form, literary/satirical lyrics, Anderson's one-legged flute stance.
grp.jethro-tull.uyeler: Mick Abrahams (guitar, → Blodwyn Pig) → Martin Barre (permanent guitarist). Many keyboard players and bassists came and went. (Note: Howe also briefly auditioned for Tull.)
grp.jethro-tull.ipucu: Focus on Anderson's acoustic guitar as much as his flute; that's where Tull's folk face shows most.
Listen to Aqualung and Thick as a Brick together: one is the concept album he said wasn't one, the other a parody of that misunderstanding.
The folk-rock trilogy (1977–79) is a love letter to the English countryside and pagan tradition.
grp.jethro-tull.era.0.note: From Mick Abrahams's blues to Aqualung with Martin Barre.
grp.jethro-tull.era.1.note: Single-piece albums, theatrical staging, orchestral arrangements.
grp.jethro-tull.era.2.note: English folklore, rural life, layers of David Palmer's portative organ.
grp.jethro-tull.era.3.note: Synth experiments, the Dire Straits-like hard rock of Crest of a Knave, the Grammy controversy.
grp.jethro-tull.era.4.note: World-music colours, a Christmas album and a final period intertwined with Anderson's solo line.
alb.jethro-tull-1968-this-was.an: Blues rock; the only album with Abrahams. The 'Tull sound' has not formed yet.
alb.jethro-tull-1968-this-was.detay: Abrahams's only Tull album; he then formed Blodwyn Pig.
'Serenade to a Cuckoo' is a Rahsaan Roland Kirk cover — Anderson's flute model.
alb.jethro-tull-1968-this-was.tr: Serenade to a Cuckoo — Roland Kirk cover, Anderson's flute
alb.jethro-tull-1969-stand-up.an: With Barre the identity settles; folk and hard rock fuse, and the Bach adaptation ("Bourée") is a hit.
alb.jethro-tull-1969-stand-up.oncelik: Recommended — the birth of Tull's identity.
alb.jethro-tull-1969-stand-up.detay: It went to number one in the UK.
On the original LP, opening the gatefold makes cardboard figures of the band stand up like a pop-up book.
'Bourée' is a jazz-flute adaptation of Bach's lute suite.
alb.jethro-tull-1969-stand-up.tr: A New Day Yesterday — blues rock
alb.jethro-tull-1970-benefit.oncelik: Optional — a dark, hard-edged transitional album.
alb.jethro-tull-1970-benefit.detay: Keyboard player John Evan's first album (partial contribution).
alb.jethro-tull-1970-benefit.tr: With You There to Help Me — dark opener
alb.jethro-tull-1971-aqualung.an: The masterpiece; a semi-concept on religion and society. "Aqualung" and "Locomotive Breath" become classics.
alb.jethro-tull-1971-aqualung.detay: Side one was conceived as 'Aqualung' (people on the margins of society), side two as 'My God' (a critique of organised religion).
The title character grew out of a photo of a homeless man taken by Anderson's wife Jennie.
alb.jethro-tull-1971-aqualung.tr: Aqualung — riff-driven title track, portrait of a homeless man
Locomotive Breath — rock classic with piano intro
My God — critique of religion, flute peak
alb.jethro-tull-1972-thick-as-a-brick.an: The whole album is one piece (a single song across two LP sides); a brilliant, satirical answer to prog's taste for 'side-long' works. Packaged in a spoof newspaper cover. One of the genre's touchstones.
alb.jethro-tull-1972-thick-as-a-brick.on: Essential — never skip. Listen to it as a single piece.
alb.jethro-tull-1972-thick-as-a-brick.de: The album was presented as the disqualified prize poem of a fictional eight-year-old, 'Gerald Bostock'; the cover is a 12-page spoof local newspaper.
It went to number one in the US.
In 2012 Anderson told the story of Gerald's adulthood on 'Thick as a Brick 2'.
alb.jethro-tull-1972-thick-as-a-brick.tr: Thick as a Brick — one piece covering the whole album (two LP sides), a prog touchstone
Thick as a Brick Part II — the second half, thematic returns
alb.jethro-tull-1973-a-passion-play.an: Another single-piece concept (a journey through the afterlife); the darker, less accessible sibling of Thick as a Brick.
alb.jethro-tull-1973-a-passion-play.deta: An allegory of life after death; the fable in the middle, 'The Story of the Hare Who Lost His Spectacles', is famous.
Despite harsh reviews it went to number one in the US.
alb.jethro-tull-1973-a-passion-play.tr: A Passion Play — journey to the afterlife, a single-piece concept
The Story of the Hare Who Lost His Spectacles — humorous interlude
alb.jethro-tull-1974-war-child.oncelik: Optional — for 'Bungle in the Jungle' and 'Skating Away'.
alb.jethro-tull-1974-war-child.tr: Skating Away on the Thin Ice of the New Day
alb.jethro-tull-1975-minstrel-in-the-gal: Recommended — Anderson's most personal album of the '70s.
Recorded in Monte Carlo on a mobile studio.
'Baker St. Muse' is a 17-minute portrait of London.
Minstrel in the Gallery — acoustic-electric title track
alb.jethro-tull-1977-songs-from-the-wood: The rural/pagan peak of English folk-prog.
Essential — one of the peaks of folk-prog.
Written after Anderson moved from London to the countryside.
The madrigal-like polyphonic vocals recall Gentle Giant.
Songs from the Wood — folk-prog, pagan/rural theme
alb.jethro-tull-1978-heavy-horses.detay: Darryl Way of Curved Air guests on violin — an intersection in the network.
The title track is a lament for the working horses displaced by the tractor.
alb.jethro-tull-1978-heavy-horses.tr: Heavy Horses — title track, rural lament, violin peak
alb.jethro-tull-1979-stormwatch.an: The last and darkest link of the folk trilogy: a maritime album about the environment, climate and the end of the oil age. Bassist John Glascock could play on only a few tracks because of heart disease (Anderson played the remaining bass) and died shortly after the album's release, in November 1979.
alb.jethro-tull-1979-stormwatch.kadro: Anderson, Barre, Evan, Barlow, Palmer, John Glascock (partial)
alb.jethro-tull-1979-stormwatch.detay: After the album Evan, Palmer and Barlow left the band; an era ended.
alb.jethro-tull-1980-a.an: Planned as an Anderson solo album and released under the Tull name; a synth-heavy, new wave-oriented album with Eddie Jobson (keyboards/violin) of Roxy Music and Curved Air and Mark Craney (drums).
alb.jethro-tull-1980-a.detay: Dave Pegg (Fairport Convention) stayed on bass until 1995.
The Eddie Jobson link: Curved Air → Roxy Music → U.K. → Jethro Tull.
alb.jethro-tull-1982-the-broadsword-and-: An album themed on medieval fantasy and seafaring that reconciles synths with folk. The best-loved Tull album of the '80s; especially successful in Germany.
Recommended — the best Tull album of the '80s.
alb.jethro-tull-1987-crest-of-a-knave.an: A comeback album dominated by hard guitar recalling Dire Straits, with Anderson singing in a lower register after vocal problems. Winning the first 'Hard Rock/Metal' Grammy in 1989 ahead of Metallica became one of the most famous award controversies in music history.
alb.jethro-tull-1987-crest-of-a-knave.on: Recommended — 'Budapest' and 'Farm on the Freeway' are musts.
alb.jethro-tull-1987-crest-of-a-knave.de: After the Grammy, Chrysalis ran ads in magazines joking that 'the flute is a heavy, metal instrument'.
alb.jethro-tull-1995-roots-to-branches.a: A mature, jazzy album coloured by 'world music', drawing on Anderson's travels in India and the Middle East. Considered Tull's strongest work of the '90s.
alb.jethro-tull-1995-roots-to-branches.o: Recommended — the best album of their late period.
alb.jethro-tull-1999-j-tull-dot-com.an: An ironic salute to the internet age; continues the world-music direction of Roots to Branches in a more rock frame. Jonathan Noyce on bass.
alb.jethro-tull-1999-j-tull-dot-com.deta: The last Tull studio album of new material until The Zealot Gene in 2022.
alb.jethro-tull-2003-the-jethro-tull-chr: A mostly acoustic album of winter-themed re-recordings of classic Tull pieces, English carols and new compositions.
grp.gentle-giant.kurulus: 1970. The Shulman brothers (Derek, Ray, Phil) — formerly Simon Dupree and the Big Sound. The most 'contrapuntal' prog band.
grp.gentle-giant.hikaye: In the '60s the Shulman brothers (Derek, Ray, Phil) from Portsmouth had psychedelic pop hits such as 'Kites' as Simon Dupree and the Big Sound; but they tired of pop and in 1970 formed Gentle Giant with Kerry Minnear (a classically trained keyboardist) and Gary Green (a blues guitarist). They became a band that wove together medieval madrigals, Renaissance counterpoint, jazz and hard rock, with the members playing more than 30 instruments between them; recorder, cello, vibraphone, trumpet and violin changed hands even on stage. The eldest brother, Phil, left in 1972 for family reasons and fatigue; the drum seat settled with John Weathers. Commercial success always remained limited; an attempt at a radio-friendly sound in the late '70s alienated old listeners and the band split in 1980. Derek Shulman moved into the record industry and became an executive at PolyGram and Atco who signed bands such as Bon Jovi, Dream Theater and Cinderella — an unexpected junction in the network. The band never reunited in full; Gary Green and Malcolm Mortimore, briefly their drummer in 1972, took the repertoire on stage with Three Friends, formed in 2008.
grp.gentle-giant.dna: Madrigal/Renaissance polyphony, constant instrument-swapping (every member a multi-instrumentalist), extremely complex arrangements, vocal counterpoint. A direct inspiration for the next generation (Spock's Beard).
grp.gentle-giant.ipucu: Follow how two, three or four separate melodies are woven together at once; the vocal counterpoint in 'Knots' and 'On Reflection' is the best example.
The four albums from Octopus to The Power and the Glory are the band's core.
Derek Shulman's later career (the A&R executive who signed Dream Theater) is the hidden thread linking the '70s to '90s prog metal.
grp.gentle-giant.era.0.note: The first line-up with Phil Shulman: experimental, sprawling, bold.
grp.gentle-giant.era.1.note: The line-up with John Weathers: counterpoint, concept albums and live mastery.
grp.gentle-giant.era.2.note: Shorter songs, AOR experiments; farewell in 1980.
alb.gentle-giant-1970-gentle-giant.an: Announces their programme of complex arrangements.
alb.gentle-giant-1970-gentle-giant.tr: Giant — the opener announcing their programme of complex arrangements
Nothing at All — long form, drum solo
alb.gentle-giant-1971-acquiring-the-tast: A manifesto: 'to expand the frontiers of music, regardless of commercial expectations'. Studio experimentation.
The House, the Street, the Room
alb.gentle-giant-1972-three-friends.an: The first concept album (the life paths of three friends).
alb.gentle-giant-1972-three-friends.tr: Peel the Paint — hard guitar vs vocal contrast
alb.gentle-giant-1972-octopus.an: The masterpiece; eight pieces ('octo-opus'), each a different structural experiment. The balance between complexity and listenability is best here.
alb.gentle-giant-1972-octopus.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The best way in.
alb.gentle-giant-1972-octopus.detay: The title comes from a pun by Phil's wife Roberta: 'octo-opus' (eight works).
Phil Shulman's last album; Weathers's first.
'Knots' uses lyrics from R. D. Laing's book of the same name.
alb.gentle-giant-1972-octopus.tr: Knots — a vocal-counterpoint masterpiece based on R. D. Laing
alb.gentle-giant-1973-in-a-glass-house.a: Opening with the sound of breaking glass, their most texturally daring album (not released in the US for a long time).
alb.gentle-giant-1973-in-a-glass-house.d: In the US the label refused to release it as 'uncommercial'; imported copies became one of the best-selling imports.
It opens and closes with the sound of breaking glass.
alb.gentle-giant-1973-in-a-glass-house.t: The Runaway — opens with breaking glass
An Inmate's Lullaby — vibraphone and percussion textures
alb.gentle-giant-1974-the-power-and-the-: A concept about power and corruption; the peak of rhythmic complexity.
Essential — a concept album about power and corruption.
Proclamation — opening of the power/corruption concept
Cogs in Cogs — peak of rhythmic complexity
alb.gentle-giant-1975-free-hand.an: The best point of balance between the commercial and the artistic; the band's best seller.
alb.gentle-giant-1975-free-hand.oncelik: Essential — their most successful album in the US.
alb.gentle-giant-1975-free-hand.detay: 'On Reflection', which opens with a four-voice vocal fugue, is the band's signature piece.
alb.gentle-giant-1975-free-hand.tr: Just the Same — opener, one of the best-loved pieces
alb.gentle-giant-1976-interview.an: A concept (a fictional interview); the start of a slight decline.
The final phase, moving towards accessibility and eventually dissolution.
Two Weeks in Spain — an attempt at accessible pop
Betcha Thought We Couldn't Do It
alb.gentle-giant-1980-civilian.detay: The band played its last concert at the Roxy in Los Angeles in June 1980.
alb.gentle-giant-1980-civilian.tr: I Am a Camera — (same title as the Buggles song, but a different song)
grp.van-der-graaf-generator.kurulus: 1967, Manchester. Centred on Peter Hammill; King Crimson's dark relative.
grp.van-der-graaf-generator.hikaye: Formed in 1967 at Manchester University by Peter Hammill, Chris Judge Smith and Nick Pearne; the name came (misspelled) from the Van de Graaff generator, which produces static electricity. Hammill's existential, dark lyrics — earning him comparisons to 'rock's Nietzsche' — and his dramatic voice; David Jackson's twisted horns, often two saxophones at once; Hugh Banton's self-modified church-organ sounds; and Guy Evans's drums defined the band's identity. Pawn Hearts (1971) went to number one in Italy but didn't sell in Britain; the band split in 1972. They reunited in 1975–78 and made three studio albums, then turned into a raw line-up with violin under the name 'Van der Graaf' and broke up. The admiration for Hammill among the punk generation (John Lydon, Mark E. Smith) made VdGG that rare prog band punk loved. The classic four returned with Present in 2005; when Jackson left in 2006, the Hammill–Banton–Evans trio made albums until 2016.
grp.van-der-graaf-generator.dna: Organ and saxophone-heavy (for a long time without guitar), apocalyptic/existential lyrics, Hammill's theatrical, tense voice, dissonant intensity. The prog band even punk respected (Lydon was a fan).
grp.van-der-graaf-generator.ipucu: Hear VdGG not as 'rock theatre' but as 'rock's existential poetry'; following the lyrics is essential.
Notice that it is a rock band without guitar: the organ and saxophones take on the guitar's role.
The line between Hammill's solo albums and VdGG is blurred; Nadir's Big Chance (1975) is a bridge between the two worlds.
grp.van-der-graaf-generator.era.0.note: The classic quartet takes shape and peaks with Pawn Hearts.
grp.van-der-graaf-generator.era.1.note: From Godbluff to Vital: harder, more compact.
grp.van-der-graaf-generator.era.2.note: The return with Present; the trio years and the farewell of Do Not Disturb.
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1969-the-aer: Almost a Hammill solo album; early and light.
Optional — originally planned as a Hammill solo album.
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1970-the-lea: The band's identity settles; the apocalyptic texture of "After the Flood".
After the Flood — apocalyptic epic, organ + saxophone
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1970-h-to-he: The saxophone (David Jackson) and organ textures grow stronger.
Robert Fripp guests on guitar on 'The Emperor in His War-Room' — the first intersection with Crimson.
Killer — the band's best-known piece, saxophone riff
House with No Door — fragile ballad
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1971-pawn-he: The masterpiece. "A Plague of Lighthouse Keepers" (a suite about mental collapse filling an LP side) is the band's monument; Fripp guests on guitar. The peak of dark prog.
The 23-minute 'A Plague of Lighthouse Keepers' is the monologue of a lighthouse keeper on the brink of madness.
It went to number one in Italy and strongly influenced Italian prog (Banco, Le Orme).
A Plague of Lighthouse Keepers — side-long suite of mental collapse, Fripp guesting on guitar
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1975-godbluf: The second period; tighter and more aggressive.
Essential — a flawless document of the comeback.
Four pieces, four compact and intense narratives.
