alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1976-still-l: On the theme of immortality; existential intensity.
'Childlike Faith in Childhood's End' is inspired by Arthur C. Clarke.
The title track is about the curse of immortality.
Still Life — on immortality, an existential peak
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1976-world-r: The close of the second period; long jams.
'Meurglys III' ends with a long guitar improvisation that slides into reggae.
Banton's and Jackson's last album of this period.
Meurglys III, the Songwriter's Guild — 20-minute jam
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1978-vital.a: A live album released under the name 'Van der Graaf', recorded at London's Marquee. A raw, near-punk sound with Graham Smith's violin and Charles Dickie's cello.
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-1978-vital.k: Hammill, Evans, Nic Potter, Graham Smith, Charles Dickie + David Jackson (guest)
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-2005-present: The classic quartet's reunion album after 27 years. One disc of new songs, the other of studio improvisations.
The same year they played a comeback concert at the Royal Festival Hall; Jackson left afterwards.
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-2008-trisect: The first album by the trio without saxophone: Hammill takes on more guitar and the sound is sparer and sharper.
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-2011-a-groun: A trio album of short, dense pieces on themes of mathematics and numbers.
alb.van-der-graaf-generator-2016-do-not-: The trio's last album; a warm, mature close on themes of ageing, memory and farewell.
grp.camel.kurulus: 1971. Centred on Andrew Latimer (guitar/flute); melodic, mostly instrumental prog.
grp.camel.hikaye: Born out of Brew, the Surrey blues band of guitarist Andrew Latimer, bassist Doug Ferguson and drummer Andy Ward, Camel took shape in 1972 when keyboardist Peter Bardens joined. They became the standard-bearers of mostly instrumental, melodic, lyrical symphonic prog; the entirely instrumental The Snow Goose (1975), inspired by Paul Gallico's novella, was performed with the London Symphony Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall. In 1977 Ferguson left, replaced by Richard Sinclair from Caravan, and Mel Collins's horns added Canterbury colour. When Bardens left in 1978 and Ward in 1981, Camel effectively became Latimer's project. After legal trouble with Decca, Latimer moved to California and founded his own label, Camel Productions; in the '90s he returned with concept albums on personal and historical themes (Irish emigration, Steinbeck). In 2007 Latimer had a serious blood disorder and a bone-marrow transplant; from 2013 the band toured again.
grp.camel.dna: Lyrical, singing guitar, warm melody, suites with few words; a texture somewhere between Pink Floyd and Genesis. A main reference for neo-prog (especially Pendragon).
grp.camel.ipucu: Listen to Camel by following Latimer's guitar tone — it sits somewhere between David Gilmour and Peter Green.
Listen to The Snow Goose while reading the story; Gallico's text is short and moving.
For the Canterbury connection, play Rain Dances and Breathless alongside Caravan.
grp.camel.era.0.note: Latimer, Bardens, Ferguson, Ward: the peak of melodic symphonic prog.
grp.camel.era.1.note: Jazz and pop touches with Richard Sinclair and Mel Collins.
grp.camel.era.3.note: The independent era: personal and historical concept albums.
alb.camel-1973-camel.an: The seed of their melodic instrumental identity.
alb.camel-1973-camel.tr: Never Let Go — the band's emblem
alb.camel-1974-mirage.detay: 'Lady Fantasy' became a mainstay of Camel concerts.
'Nimrodel/The Procession/The White Rider' is inspired by Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings.
The original cover parodies a cigarette brand's camel logo; after legal trouble the US edition was changed.
alb.camel-1974-mirage.tr: Lady Fantasy — multi-part suite, the best-loved Camel piece
Nimrodel / The Procession / The White Rider — Tolkien-inspired
alb.camel-1975-the-snow-goose.an: An almost entirely instrumental concept album inspired by Paul Gallico's story; Camel's signature work. The peak of the lyrical guitar-keyboard dialogue.
alb.camel-1975-the-snow-goose.oncelik: Essential — never skip. Hear it start to finish as a single piece.
alb.camel-1975-the-snow-goose.detay: Because Paul Gallico didn't endorse the work, 'Music Inspired by' was added to the album title.
Performed with the London Symphony Orchestra at the Royal Albert Hall in October 1975.
alb.camel-1975-the-snow-goose.tr: Rhayader / Rhayader Goes to Town — opening of the instrumental concept
alb.camel-1976-moonmadness.an: The classic line-up's final peak; each piece a 'musical portrait' of a member.
alb.camel-1976-moonmadness.oncelik: Essential — the classic quartet's last album.
alb.camel-1976-moonmadness.detay: Some pieces were written to reflect the characters of the band's four members.
'Lunar Sea' is one of Ward's best drum performances.
alb.camel-1977-rain-dances.an: Jazz and pop touches, line-up changes.
alb.camel-1977-rain-dances.kadro: Latimer, Bardens, Richard Sinclair, Ward, Mel Collins + Brian Eno (guest)
alb.camel-1977-rain-dances.detay: Brian Eno guests on Minimoog and piano on 'Elke'.
Richard Sinclair's vocals give the album a distinct Canterbury warmth.
alb.camel-1977-rain-dances.tr: First Light — opener with jazz touches
One of These Days I'll Get an Early Night
alb.camel-1978-breathless.detay: Bardens's last album; he left before the tour.
alb.camel-1979-i-can-see-your-house-from: The increasingly atmospheric period that continues around Latimer.
Kit Watkins comes from Happy the Man — a bridge to American prog.
'Ice' is one of Latimer's best-loved guitar instrumentals.
Ice — a 10-minute lyrical guitar peak, Latimer's most beautiful solo
Your Love Is Stranger Than Mine
alb.camel-1981-nude.oncelik: Recommended — one of the best concepts of their later period.
alb.camel-1981-nude.detay: The story of Hiroo Onoda, the Japanese soldier who kept fighting in the jungle for 29 years after the Second World War ended.
alb.camel-1982-the-single-factor.oncelik: Skippable — a pop-oriented album made under label pressure.
alb.camel-1982-the-single-factor.detay: Anthony Phillips (Genesis) contributed as a guest.
alb.camel-1984-stationary-traveller.once: Recommended — a concept album about the Berlin Wall.
alb.camel-1984-stationary-traveller.deta: About the East–West German division and stories of escape.
Latimer's pan-flute and guitar sounds are the album's signature.
alb.camel-1984-stationary-traveller.tr: Stationary Traveller — instrumental on the Berlin Wall theme
alb.camel-1991-dust-and-dreams.an: A concept album inspired by Steinbeck's 'The Grapes of Wrath', about a family migrating from Oklahoma to California during the Great Depression. The first release on Latimer's own label; atmospheric and largely instrumental.
alb.camel-1991-dust-and-dreams.kadro: Andrew Latimer + Colin Bass, Ton Scherpenzeel, Paul Burgess and guests
alb.camel-1991-dust-and-dreams.detay: The first Camel Productions album; recorded after Latimer moved to California.
alb.camel-1996-harbour-of-tears.an: A concept album drawing on the death of Latimer's father and his family's Irish roots, telling the story of 19th-century Irish emigration from the port of Cobh. With Celtic melodies and Latimer's emotional guitar, the peak of late Camel.
alb.camel-1996-harbour-of-tears.oncelik: Essential — the best Camel album of the late period.
alb.camel-1999-rajaz.an: A guitar-centred album with Middle Eastern colours, named after the Arabic poetic metre said to follow the rhythm of camels' steps in desert caravans. Latimer's longest and freest solo excursions are here.
alb.camel-1999-rajaz.kadro: Andrew Latimer, Colin Bass, Ton Scherpenzeel, Dave Stewart (drums)
alb.camel-1999-rajaz.detay: This Dave Stewart is not the keyboardist of Egg/Hatfield but Camel's drummer in the '90s.
alb.camel-1999-rajaz.tr: Lawrence — a portrait of T. E. Lawrence
alb.camel-2002-a-nod-and-a-wink.an: A light, nostalgic album of flute and acoustic textures, dedicated to Peter Bardens after his death in 2002. Camel's last studio album (apart from the 2013 re-recording of The Snow Goose).
grp.renaissance.kurulus: 1969, Surrey. Formed by Keith Relf and Jim McCarty after the Yardbirds split; the line-up then changed completely, and the band's classic period was shaped by Annie Haslam's five-octave voice.
grp.renaissance.hikaye: Formed in 1969 by the Yardbirds' Keith Relf and Jim McCarty, Renaissance was reborn in 1971 with an entirely new line-up around Annie Haslam's five-octave voice, Michael Dunford's composing and Betty Thatcher's lyrics. They produced some of the most elegant symphonic prog, where classical music (Rachmaninoff, Rimsky-Korsakov) meets folk. Their 1976 Carnegie Hall concert is famous. Dunford died in 2012; the band continued under Haslam's leadership.
grp.renaissance.dna: Orchestral, classically based symphonic prog; piano-centred compositions, real orchestral backing, Haslam's soprano with operatic clarity. More 'chamber orchestra + folk' than rock.
grp.renaissance.uyeler: Classic line-up: Annie Haslam (vocals), Michael Dunford (acoustic guitar/composer), John Tout (keyboards), Jon Camp (bass), Terence Sullivan (drums). Lyricist Betty Thatcher as a core outside contributor.
grp.renaissance.gecisler: Before → The Yardbirds (the Relf/McCarty founding core). Indirect links with Eric Burdon and the folk-rock scene.
grp.renaissance.etki: The wing of symphonic prog closest to 'classical music'; a rare major prog band led by a female voice. An inspiration for later bands such as Mostly Autumn.
alb.renaissance-1972-prologue.an: The first album by the classic Haslam–Dunford line-up; the band's piano-centred orchestral identity settles.
alb.renaissance-1972-prologue.tr: Prologue — title track with a piano opening
alb.renaissance-1973-ashes-are-burning.a: The band's first big breakthrough; Andy Powell (Wishbone Ash) plays a guest guitar solo on the title track. Haslam's voice shines in full.
alb.renaissance-1973-ashes-are-burning.t: Ashes Are Burning — 11-minute epic with a guest guitar solo
Carpet of the Sun — pastoral hit
alb.renaissance-1974-turn-of-the-cards.a: Darker and more orchestral; literary themes such as 'Mother Russia' (Solzhenitsyn).
alb.renaissance-1975-scheherazade-and-ot: The band's masterpiece; 'Song of Scheherazade', filling side two, is a multi-part suite with full orchestra. One of the high points of rock-orchestra fusion.
Song of Scheherazade — 24-minute, nine-part orchestral suite
alb.renaissance-1976-live-at-carnegie-ha: A double live album with members of the New York Philharmonic; long versions of 'Scheherazade' and 'Mother Russia'.
alb.renaissance-1977-novella.an: An album dominated by long forms, with the orchestral grandeur continuing.
alb.renaissance-1978-a-song-for-all-seas: A UK Top 10 hit with 'Northern Lights'; more accessible but still orchestral.
Northern Lights — the band's biggest hit single
A Song for All Seasons — title epic
alb.renaissance-2013-grandine-il-vento-s: The last album, completed before Dunford's death; Ian Anderson and John Wetton as guests.
grp.curved-air.kurulus: 1970, London. One of the early female-fronted British prog bands, combining classical music (Darryl Way's violin), folk (Sonja Kristina's vocals) and electronics.
grp.curved-air.dna: Violin-centred symphonic/art prog; a combination of classical form, folk melody and early synth/VCS3 textures. Kristina's theatrical vocals.
grp.curved-air.uyeler: Sonja Kristina (vocals), Darryl Way (violin/keyboards), Francis Monkman (keyboards/guitar), Florian Pilkington-Miksa (drums). Later Stewart Copeland (later of The Police) took over the drums; Eddie Jobson also briefly played violin.
grp.curved-air.gecisler: After → The Police (Stewart Copeland), UK and Roxy Music (Eddie Jobson — another junction passing through Curved Air), Sky (Francis Monkman).
grp.curved-air.etki: One of the pioneers of female-fronted prog; it fed figures such as Eddie Jobson and Stewart Copeland into the network. A pre-punk art-rock bridge.
alb.curved-air-1970-air-conditioning.an: The debut; one of the first picture-disc LPs. Establishes their classical-folk-electronic identity.
alb.curved-air-1970-air-conditioning.tr: Vivaldi — Way's violin showcase, baroque rock
alb.curved-air-1971-second-album.an: The band's best-known album; 'Back Street Luv' was a UK Top 5 hit. The compositional tension between Monkman and Way brings a creative peak.
alb.curved-air-1972-phantasmagoria.an: More song-oriented; Kristina's vocals come to the fore.
alb.curved-air-1973-air-cut.an: The line-up with Eddie Jobson; Way and Monkman have left. Traces of Jobson before UK.
grp.greenslade.kurulus: 1972, London. Dave Greenslade's (formerly of Colosseum) guitarless, keyboard-centred band with two keyboard players. Visually connected to the Yes ecosystem through Roger Dean covers.
grp.greenslade.dna: Twin-keyboard, guitarless symphonic prog; a dialogue between organ and synth textures, jazz-influenced arrangements. A relative of Gentle Giant.
grp.greenslade.uyeler: Dave Greenslade (keyboards), Dave Lawson (keyboards/vocals) — the twin-keyboard set-up is the signature; Tony Reeves (bass, formerly Colosseum), Andrew McCulloch (drums, formerly King Crimson — 'Lizard').
grp.greenslade.gecisler: Before → Colosseum (Greenslade, Reeves), King Crimson (McCulloch). Connected to the visual universe of Yes/Gentle Giant through Roger Dean's covers.
grp.greenslade.etki: A more chamber-music-oriented branch of keyboard-centred prog (the ELP/Nice line); linked to King Crimson through McCulloch.
alb.greenslade-1973-greenslade.an: The debut; introduces the twin-keyboard concept and a Roger Dean cover.
alb.greenslade-1973-bedside-manners-are-: The second album, released the same year; the band's best-loved record, with the twin-keyboard interplay at its peak.
Bedside Manners Are Extra — title track
alb.greenslade-1974-spyglass-guest.an: More polished and varied; the texture widens with guest musicians.
alb.greenslade-1975-time-and-tide.an: With a Patrick Woodroffe cover; the band's last album (of its first period), more song-oriented.
grp.gryphon.kurulus: 1971, London. Founded by students of the Royal College of Music; a unique band combining medieval/Renaissance music (period instruments such as crumhorn and bassoon) with rock.
grp.gryphon.dna: Medieval folk + prog: period instruments (crumhorn, recorder, bassoon), contrapuntal arrangements, English folk melody. Related to Gentle Giant and the folk wing of Jethro Tull.
grp.gryphon.uyeler: Richard Harvey (keyboards/woodwinds), Brian Gulland (bassoon/crumhorn/vocals), Graeme Taylor (guitar), David Oberlé (drums/vocals). Classically trained multi-instrumentalists.
grp.gryphon.gecisler: They toured with Yes (Yes invited them on the Tales from Topographic Oceans tour) — a direct stage link to the main backbone. Harvey later became a film composer.
grp.gryphon.etki: The purest example of prog's 'early music' wing; with Gentle Giant and Tull, it feeds English folk-prog. Touched the mainstream through the Yes tour.
alb.gryphon-1973-gryphon.an: The debut; almost entirely medieval/folk instrumentals. Announces the band's unique identity.
alb.gryphon-1974-midnight-mushrumps.an: More 'prog'; the title track is a 19-minute multi-part suite. Long-form rock on medieval instruments.
alb.gryphon-1974-red-queen-to-gryphon-th: The band's masterpiece; four long, entirely instrumental pieces on a chess theme. The technical peak of folk-prog and the sound of the Yes tour.
alb.gryphon-1975-raindance.an: More accessible, electric and song-oriented; a move away from the pure medieval texture.
alb.gryphon-1977-treason.an: The last album; entirely rock-oriented, with the period instruments in the background. The band's loss of identity and break-up.
grp.family.kurulus: 1966, Leicester. Known for Roger Chapman's quavering, unique voice; an uncategorisable English band moving between psychedelia, prog, folk and R&B.
grp.family.dna: Eclectic art rock: Chapman's vibrato-laden vocals, a mix of psychedelia and folk-prog, experimental arrangements. English eccentricity that fits no single mould.
grp.family.uyeler: Roger Chapman (vocals) and Charlie Whitney (guitar) at the core; the bass seat passed through Ric Grech (later Blind Faith), John Weider, John Wetton (before King Crimson!) and Jim Cregan.
grp.family.gecisler: After → Blind Faith (Ric Grech), King Crimson & UK (John Wetton — Family was Wetton's stop before Crimson!), Streetwalkers (Chapman/Whitney). The Wetton link is a crucial junction.
grp.family.etki: The band that developed John Wetton (the root of the Crimson/UK/Asia line passes through here); an important, uncategorisable node of English art rock.
The debut; produced by Dave Mason (Traffic). A fusion of psychedelia and orchestral experimentation.
alb.family-1969-family-entertainment.an: The band's best-loved early album; Chapman's vocals and the eclectic arrangements reach a peak.
alb.family-1969-family-entertainment.tr: The Weaver's Answer — the band's emblem
alb.family-1970-a-song-for-me.an: The John Weider line-up; more rock-oriented, self-produced by the band.
alb.family-1970-anyway.an: Half live, half studio; an experimental structure. John Wetton is about to join.
alb.family-1971-fearless.an: John Wetton on bass and vocals — before Crimson! One of the band's most balanced, mature albums.
alb.family-1972-bandstand.an: Wetton's last album (he then joined King Crimson); 'Burlesque' was a hit. Tighter and melodic.
grp.focus.kurulus: 1969, Amsterdam. Dutch, but fully part of the British prog scene. Built around the duo of Thijs van Leer (keyboards/flute/vocals) and Jan Akkerman (guitar).
grp.focus.hikaye: Led by flautist-keyboardist Thijs van Leer and guitarist Jan Akkerman in Amsterdam, Focus became world-famous with the yodelling and guitar frenzy of 'Hocus Pocus'. A virtuoso instrumental band between classical, jazz and rock; Akkerman left in 1976. From the 2000s van Leer re-formed the band and continued its series of numbered albums.
grp.focus.dna: Classically influenced instrumental prog: Akkerman's lute-tinged virtuoso guitar, van Leer's baroque organ and flute, yodelled vocals. Instrumental texture rather than words.
grp.focus.uyeler: Thijs van Leer (organ/flute/yodelling vocals), Jan Akkerman (guitar — one of the most respected prog guitarists of his time), Pierre van der Linden (drums, from Brainbox), Bert Ruiter (bass).
grp.focus.gecisler: Before → Brainbox (Akkerman and van der Linden both left Brainbox for Focus). Akkerman later had an influential solo guitar career.
grp.focus.etki: The continental European prog band that mixed most with the British mainstream; with 'Hocus Pocus' and 'Sylvia' it took prog onto the radio. A reference for Akkerman's guitar virtuosity.
alb.focus-1970-in-and-out-of-focus.an: The debut; the seed of the band's classical-rock-flute identity. 'House of the King' became a hit.
alb.focus-1970-in-and-out-of-focus.tr: House of the King — folk-prog hit
alb.focus-1971-moving-waves.an: The band's masterpiece; 'Hocus Pocus' (a yodelling instrumental) was an international hit. Side two, 'Eruption', is a 23-minute multi-part suite.
alb.focus-1971-moving-waves.tr: Hocus Pocus — yodelling rock instrumental, international hit
alb.focus-1972-focus-3.an: A double LP; 'Sylvia' became a hit. Akkerman's guitar and van Leer's flute hold a dialogue in long jams.
alb.focus-1974-hamburger-concerto.an: The band's most ambitious, most 'classical' album; the title track is a large suite based on a theme by Brahms.
alb.focus-1974-hamburger-concerto.tr: Hamburger Concerto — multi-part suite based on Brahms
alb.focus-1975-mother-focus.an: One of Akkerman's last albums; shorter, funky pieces.
alb.focus-2002-focus-8.an: The first album by the new line-up van Leer formed 25 years later.
alb.focus-2012-focus-x.an: A late album with a Roger Dean cover, faithful to the classic Focus sound.
grp.barclay-james-harvest.kurulus: 1966, Oldham. Orchestral, melodic symphonic prog; in their early years they recorded with a real orchestra (a costly ambition). Nicknamed 'the poor man's Moody Blues' (they even mocked it in their own songs).
grp.barclay-james-harvest.hikaye: Barclay James Harvest from Oldham (John Lees, Les Holroyd, Stuart 'Woolly' Wolstenholme, Mel Pritchard) made melancholic symphonic rock with orchestral backing, dubbed 'the poor man's Moody Blues'. Their 1980 free concert in front of the Berlin Wall (to hundreds of thousands) became legendary in East Germany. In 1998 they split in two: John Lees' BJH and Les Holroyd's BJH.
grp.barclay-james-harvest.dna: Mellotron-heavy, orchestral, melodic symphonic prog; pastoral English melancholy, social and emotional lyrics. A soft texture between the Moody Blues and Pink Floyd.
grp.barclay-james-harvest.uyeler: John Lees (guitar/vocals), Les Holroyd (bass/vocals), Stuart 'Woolly' Wolstenholme (keyboards/Mellotron), Mel Pritchard (drums). Wolstenholme's Mellotron is the band's atmospheric signature.
grp.barclay-james-harvest.gecisler: Shares the same orchestral-Mellotron aesthetic as the Moody Blues (a shared-sound link). They became hugely popular in Germany.
grp.barclay-james-harvest.etki: The melodic wing of Mellotron-orchestral prog; an example of prog becoming a mass phenomenon, especially in Germany. An indirect contribution to neo-prog's atmospheric vein.
alb.barclay-james-harvest-1970-barclay-j: The debut; establishes their Mellotron-heavy symphonic prog identity with orchestral backing.
alb.barclay-james-harvest-1971-once-agai: The band's best-loved early album; 'Mockingbird' becomes their signature ballad.
Mockingbird — the band's emblem, an orchestral ballad
alb.barclay-james-harvest-1972-baby-jame: The last album of the orchestral period; 'Summer Soldier' is a long anti-war piece.
alb.barclay-james-harvest-1974-everyone-: They dropped the orchestra and returned to their own Mellotron-heavy sound; considered one of their strongest albums.
Child of the Universe — socio-political epic
alb.barclay-james-harvest-1975-time-hono: Recorded in the US; a more polished, melodic period.
Titles — woven from Beatles song titles
alb.barclay-james-harvest-1976-octoberon: The band's most refined album with orchestra.
alb.barclay-james-harvest-1977-gone-to-e: The band's most popular album, with 'Hymn' and 'Poor Man's Moody Blues'; a big success in Germany.
alb.barclay-james-harvest-2013-north.an: A strong late album as John Lees' Barclay James Harvest, following Woolly Wolstenholme's death in 2010.
grp.henry-cow.kurulus: 1968, Cambridge. Founded at the university by Fred Frith and Tim Hodgkinson. The founding band of the 'Rock in Opposition' (RIO) movement in Europe; the most political and most experimental British prog band.
grp.henry-cow.dna: Composed avant-garde + free improvisation + Marxist politics: dissonance, atonal passages, a Brecht-Weill influence, a rejection of metre and genre. The far end of King Crimson's 'Larks' Tongues' experimentalism.
grp.henry-cow.uyeler: Fred Frith (guitar/violin), Tim Hodgkinson (organ/saxophone), Chris Cutler (drums), John Greaves (bass; later National Health), Lindsay Cooper (bassoon/oboe), Dagmar Krause (vocals, later).
grp.henry-cow.gecisler: Before → the Cambridge university circle. After → Art Bears (Frith/Cutler/Krause), National Health (John Greaves), a merger with Slapp Happy. Linked through RIO to the European avant-garde (Univers Zero, Stormy Six).
grp.henry-cow.etki: The theoretical and musical founder of the RIO movement; with its stance against the commercial industry it defined an entire subgenre. The ancestor of avant-prog (Univers Zero, Thinking Plague).
alb.henry-cow-1973-legend-leg-end.an: The debut, famous for its sock cover. The first great synthesis of composed complexity and free improvisation. One of Virgin's most daring early signings.
alb.henry-cow-1973-legend-leg-end.tr: Nirvana for Mice — the band's emblematic instrumental
Nine Funerals of the Citizen King
alb.henry-cow-1974-unrest.an: Even more experimental; dominated by studio manipulation and free improvisation. One of the band's most 'difficult' albums.
alb.henry-cow-1975-in-praise-of-learning: The product of the merger with Slapp Happy; Dagmar Krause's Brecht-like vocals come to the fore. Their most political album.
Living in the Heart of the Beast — 15-minute political epic
alb.henry-cow-1979-western-culture.an: The last studio album; entirely instrumental, two composer-suites (Hodgkinson and Cooper). A mature close to the RIO aesthetic.
grp.art-bears.kurulus: 1978, a trio born during Henry Cow's break-up. Recorded alongside the 'Western Culture' sessions; the less improvised, more 'song'-oriented core of Henry Cow.
grp.art-bears.dna: Song-based avant-garde: Krause's harsh, Brecht-Weill-influenced vocals; Frith's multi-layered instrumentation; Cutler's literary and political lyrics. Henry Cow with 'less improvisation, more composition'.
grp.art-bears.uyeler: Fred Frith (guitar/keyboards/everything), Chris Cutler (drums/lyrics), Dagmar Krause (vocals). Three core members of Henry Cow.
grp.art-bears.gecisler: Before → Henry Cow (all three). After → Frith's wide-ranging solo/avant-garde career, Cutler's ReR Megacorp label (the publishing centre of RIO). A node of the avant-prog network.
grp.art-bears.etki: Continued Henry Cow's legacy in song form; the most accessible (yet still demanding) face of RIO/avant-prog.
alb.art-bears-1978-hopes-and-fears.an: The debut, born from the 'Western Culture' sessions. Krause's vocals and Frith's textures meet in song form.
alb.art-bears-1979-winter-songs.an: The band's masterpiece; a concept of short, dense pieces inspired by the carvings of Amiens Cathedral. The elegant peak of avant-prog.
alb.art-bears-1981-the-world-as-it-is-to: Their most political and harsh album; a Marxist critique of society. The band's last recording.
grp.this-heat.kurulus: 1976, London. An uncategorisable band at the intersection of punk and prog/avant-garde. A pioneer combining prog's technical legacy with the raw energy of post-punk.
grp.this-heat.dna: Tape-loop manipulation, musique concrète, motorik rhythm, dissonance and improvisation combined with post-punk energy. The intersection of King Crimson's experimentalism and krautrock.
grp.this-heat.uyeler: Charles Bullen (guitar/clarinet/vocals), Charles Hayward (drums/vocals/keyboards), Gareth Williams (keyboards/bass — a member with no musical training, chosen for his experimental approach).
grp.this-heat.gecisler: Circle → the Canterbury/RIO scene (an experimental kinship), post-punk (the generation they influenced). A bridge node between prog and post-punk.
grp.this-heat.etki: A herald of post-rock and industrial music; a crucial link passing prog's technical legacy to a post-punk generation. Rediscovered much later (Radiohead, post-rock).
alb.this-heat-1979-this-heat.an: The debut (also known as 'Blue and Yellow'), woven from tape loops and improvisation. A montage of two years of recordings. A fusion of prog, punk and avant-garde.
alb.this-heat-1981-deceit.an: The band's masterpiece; themed on Cold War and nuclear anxiety, more 'song'-based but still radical. The strongest synthesis of post-punk and prog.
alb.this-heat-1981-deceit.tr: Independence — on the text of the US Declaration of Independence
grp.ian-anderson-solo.name: Ian Anderson (solo)
grp.ian-anderson-solo.kurulus: Born 1947, Dunfermline, Scotland. Founder, flautist, singer and main lyricist of Jethro Tull.
grp.ian-anderson-solo.hikaye: Because Anderson is Tull's core, his solo albums are intertwined with the band; A (1980) actually began as a solo record. He is also known as the owner of a salmon farm. In the 1980s he had vocal problems, which affected his later songwriting. When he parted ways with Martin Barre in 2011, he worked under his own name from 2012 to 2017, continuing the conceptual Tull tradition with Thick as a Brick 2 and Homo Erraticus. In 2017 he began using the Jethro Tull name again.
grp.ian-anderson-solo.dna: Flute (overblown, hummed while playing), acoustic guitar, English folk and classical music; witty, literary lyrics.
grp.ian-anderson-solo.gecisler: The Blades → John Evan Band → Jethro Tull → solo → Jethro Tull; orchestral projects (Divinities, 1995).
grp.ian-anderson-solo.etki: The icon of rock flute; the main architect of folk-prog.
alb.ian-anderson-1983-walk-into-light.an: His first solo album, synth-heavy and oriented towards electronic pop, with Peter-John Vettese.
alb.ian-anderson-1995-divinities-twelve-: An instrumental suite for flute and orchestra for EMI Classics, inspired by the world's religions.
alb.ian-anderson-2000-the-secret-languag: Acoustic, warm and bird-themed; a mature continuation of Tull's folk face.
alb.ian-anderson-2012-thick-as-a-brick-2: The sequel telling the possible lives at 50 (banker, homeless man, soldier, preacher, ordinary shopkeeper) of the child poet Gerald Bostock from 1972; the cover is again a spoof newspaper, now in web form.
Essential — the late peak of the Tull legacy.
Mixed by Steven Wilson, who was remixing the Tull catalogue at the time.
alb.ian-anderson-2014-homo-erraticus.an: A concept album starting from a manuscript found by Gerald Bostock, telling the history of England (from prehistory to the future).
grp.peter-hammill-solo.name: Peter Hammill (solo)
grp.peter-hammill-solo.kurulus: Born 1948, London. Founder, singer and lyricist of Van der Graaf Generator.
grp.peter-hammill-solo.hikaye: In the solo career he has run in parallel with VdGG since 1971, Hammill has made more than 40 albums; he is one of the few musicians to bridge prog and punk. Rikki Nadir, his alter ego on Nadir's Big Chance (1975), heralded punk before punk; John Lydon named him among his favourite singers. Since the '80s he has been fully independent with his own label, Fie! Records. After a heart attack in 2003, themes of death and time deepened his work further. David Bowie also openly praised Hammill.
grp.peter-hammill-solo.dna: Expressionist vocals (from whisper to scream), piano and acoustic guitar, existential and scientific lyrics, lo-fi experimentation.
grp.peter-hammill-solo.gecisler: VdGG → solo (frequent collaboration with VdGG members) → K Group → Robert Fripp (vocals on Exposure) → a joint album with Gary Lucas.
grp.peter-hammill-solo.etki: The prog singer the punk generation loved; an influence reaching Nick Cave, Julian Cope and Mikael Åkerfeldt (Opeth).
alb.peter-hammill-1971-fool-s-mate.an: A warm first solo album of short songs left over from the late '60s, recorded with VdGG members and Fripp.
alb.peter-hammill-1971-fool-s-mate.kadro: Hammill + Robert Fripp, VdGG members, Ray Jackson (Lindisfarne)
alb.peter-hammill-1974-the-silent-corner: A dark solo album on which VdGG effectively reunited; with the 12-minute 'A Louse Is Not a Home'.
alb.peter-hammill-1975-nadir-s-big-chanc: Raw, noisy proto-punk in the voice of his alter ego Rikki Nadir. The album Johnny Rotten loved.
Essential — the missing link between prog and punk.
alb.peter-hammill-1980-a-black-box.an: Hammill's most ambitious solo album, with the sounds of digital clocks, loops and the 20-minute 'Flight' suite; with David Ferguson (Random Hold) and David Jackson.
alb.peter-hammill-2004-incoherence.an: His first major work after the heart attack: a single 40-minute song cycle about language and communication.
sec.11.title: Next Generation I — The Neo-Prog Wave (1981–1990)
sec.11.intro: The first great 'renaissance'. After punk and new wave, a British generation that recreated the symphonic prog template of the 1970s — especially Gabriel-era Genesis, Camel, Pink Floyd and VdGG. London's Marquee Club was the heart of the movement. They connect to the old backbone through shared sound; member migration circulates within the scene itself (figures like Clive Nolan link several bands).
grp.marillion.kurulus: 1979, Aylesbury. Began as 'Silmarillion' (after Tolkien) with Mick Pointer (drums) and Doug Irvine. The core settled with Scottish singer Fish (Derek Dick) and guitarist Steve Rothery. By far the most successful neo-prog band.
grp.marillion.hikaye: Formed in Aylesbury in 1979, the band took its name by shortening Tolkien's Silmarillion. Scottish poet-singer Fish (Derek Dick) joined in 1981 and, with face paint and a theatrical stage act recalling Gabriel, became the face of neo-prog. The four albums beginning with Script for a Jester's Tear peaked with the hits 'Kayleigh' and 'Lavender' from Misplaced Childhood. Fish left in 1988 over management and creative disagreements; Steve Hogarth of The Europeans replaced him, and the band evolved towards a more atmospheric sound close to Radiohead and Talk Talk. Having lost label support, Marillion financed its 1997 US tour with money raised online by fans and in 2001 recorded Anoraknophobia through pre-orders, becoming a pioneer of crowdfunding. Marbles (2004) and F.E.A.R. (2016) are the critics' favourites of the Hogarth era.
grp.marillion.dna: The theatrical narrative of Gabriel-era Genesis + Fish's vocals recalling Peter Hammill; Rothery's lyrical, Gilmour-inspired guitar solos; a post-punk 'heat' and social bitterness. Described as 'a bridge between punk and classic prog'.
grp.marillion.uyeler: Fish (vocals) → left for a solo career in 1988; replaced by Steve Hogarth (1989). Permanent core: Steve Rothery (guitar), Pete Trewavas (bass), Mark Kelly (keyboards), Ian Mosley (drums, replacing Pointer in 1984).
grp.marillion.gecisler: After → Fish solo; Trewavas later in Transatlantic (with Neal Morse of Spock's Beard) — a bridge joining neo-prog and the American renaissance.
grp.marillion.etki: The locomotive of the whole neo-prog movement; the only neo-prog band to reach arena status.
grp.marillion.ipucu: Read the Fish era and the Hogarth era not as two separate bands but as two novels by the same band.
Steve Rothery's guitar tone (delay and chorus) is the signature that unites the eras.
In the Hogarth era, the four albums Brave, Afraid of Sunlight, Marbles and F.E.A.R. are the core.
grp.marillion.era.0.note: The founding of neo-prog: the Genesis legacy, poetic and personal lyrics.
grp.marillion.era.1.note: A new singer and a conceptual peak (Brave).
grp.marillion.era.2.note: Pioneers of the fan-funded model; atmospheric art rock.
alb.marillion-1983-script-for-a-jester-s: The manifesto. Long, multi-part pieces on personal collapse and betrayal. Number 7 in the UK; it popularised the movement. (The 'Genesis clone' criticism also starts here.)
Mick Pointer's last album; he went on to form Arena.
Mark Wilkinson's Jester cover marks the start of Marillion's visual identity.
Script for a Jester's Tear — title epic on personal collapse
He Knows You Know — single, about addiction
Garden Party — satire on the English class system
alb.marillion-1984-fugazi.an: More angular and harder; the pseudo-funk intro of "Assassing". Ian Mosley's fluid drumming raises the bar. On social alienation.
alb.marillion-1984-fugazi.detay: Ian Mosley's first album; he had previously worked with Steve Hackett and Gordon Giltrap.
alb.marillion-1985-misplaced-childhood.a: The masterpiece and turning point. An almost seamlessly flowing concept album; Fish's semi-autobiography of childhood, fame and substances. "Kayleigh" (UK #2) and "Lavender" become hits, and the album reaches number one in the UK. Neo-prog's 'cornerstone'.
alb.marillion-1985-misplaced-childhood.o: Essential — never skip. Listen straight through.
alb.marillion-1985-misplaced-childhood.d: A concept album born from the image of a child soldier Fish saw during an LSD trip.
Number one in the UK; 'Kayleigh' reached number 2.
alb.marillion-1985-misplaced-childhood.t: Kayleigh — UK #2, the band's best-known song
Pseudo Silk Kimono — opener (the album flows without breaks)
alb.marillion-1987-clutching-at-straws.a: Fish's dark farewell album about alcohol and exhaustion; "Incommunicado" was a hit. Fish's last record with the band.
alb.marillion-1987-clutching-at-straws.o: Essential — Fish's darkest and best lyrics.
alb.marillion-1987-clutching-at-straws.d: About alcoholism and the burnout of life on the road; Fish's last Marillion album.
alb.marillion-1987-clutching-at-straws.t: Sugar Mice — Fish's ballad of exhaustion
alb.marillion-1989-seasons-end.an: The Steve Hogarth era begins; a smooth transition, Top 10.
alb.marillion-1989-seasons-end.detay: Some of the music comes from writing sessions begun with Fish.
alb.marillion-1989-seasons-end.tr: Seasons End — title track of the Hogarth era
Easter — about Northern Ireland, Rothery's guitar peak
alb.marillion-1991-holidays-in-eden.an: A more pop-oriented phase of the Hogarth era.
alb.marillion-1991-holidays-in-eden.once: Optional — the most pop-focused Hogarth album.
alb.marillion-1991-holidays-in-eden.tr: Cover My Eyes (Pain and Heaven) — pop-oriented single
alb.marillion-1994-brave.an: A concept album inspired by a radio news item; critical respect, commercially more niche. One of the artistic peaks of the Hogarth era.
alb.marillion-1994-brave.oncelik: Essential — the first masterpiece of the Hogarth era.
alb.marillion-1994-brave.detay: Inspired by a radio report about a young girl found on the Severn Bridge having lost her memory.
Recorded over months in a French château with producer Dave Meegan; EMI was not pleased by the budget overrun.
alb.marillion-1994-brave.tr: The Great Escape — the concept's climax
alb.marillion-1995-afraid-of-sunlight.an: A concept about the price of fame, referencing Muhammad Ali, Mike Tyson, Elvis, John Lennon and Kurt Cobain. Their last album on EMI; considered by critics one of the peaks of the Hogarth era.
alb.marillion-1997-this-strange-engine.a: An acoustic, folk-tinged album that came with the move to Castle Records; the title track is a 15-minute life story dedicated to Hogarth's father.
alb.marillion-1997-this-strange-engine.d: The same year fans raised about $60,000 online for a US tour — one of the pioneering examples of crowdfunding.
alb.marillion-1998-radiation.an: The band's alternative-rock and psychedelic experiments; a raw, deliberately 'dirty' production.
alb.marillion-2001-anoraknophobia.an: The first major album whose recording was financed by fans' pre-orders; trip-hop and electronic touches.
alb.marillion-2001-anoraknophobia.detay: Around 12,000 fans bought the album a year before it came out; that's how the recording was paid for.
alb.marillion-2004-marbles.an: Again fan-funded, released as a double album (deluxe); the best-loved album of the Hogarth era, about memory, childhood and loss.
alb.marillion-2004-marbles.oncelik: Essential — never skip. The peak of the Hogarth era.
alb.marillion-2004-marbles.tr: Ocean Cloud — 17-minute story of an ocean rower
alb.marillion-2007-somewhere-else.an: Shorter, plainer songs; an album that stayed in Marbles' shadow.
alb.marillion-2008-happiness-is-the-road: A double album: 'Essence' (meditative, conceptual) and 'The Hard Shoulder' (a collection of songs).
alb.marillion-2012-sounds-that-can-t-be-: An album opening with the 17-minute 'Gaza', treating political and personal themes in broad structures.
alb.marillion-2016-f-e-a-r.an: Built around three long suites and named for 'Fuck Everyone and Run', an album about the anxiety and inequality of pre-Brexit Britain. Number 4 in the UK — their highest position since 1987.
alb.marillion-2016-f-e-a-r.oncelik: Essential — the masterpiece of the late period.
grp.iq.kurulus: 1981, Southampton. Came out of the same Marquee scene as Marillion but chose to stay 'purer prog'. The movement's longest-lasting, least compromising band.
grp.iq.hikaye: Founded by Mike Holmes and Martin Orford in 1981, IQ became one of neo-prog's most consistent bands with Peter Nicholls's theatrical vocals. Nicholls left in 1985–89 (replaced by Paul Menel) and then returned. They went independent in the '90s with their own label, Giant Electric Pea; Subterranea (1997) and The Road of Bones (2014) became critics' favourites.
grp.iq.dna: Richly textured, dark and introspective symphonic neo-prog; long conceptual pieces, atmospheric layers of keyboards.
grp.iq.uyeler: Peter Nicholls (vocals) and Mike Holmes (guitar) at the core; Martin Orford (keyboards, later also in Jadis). Nicholls left for a while and returned.
alb.iq-1983-tales-from-the-lush-attic.an: An independent debut; a complex, dark sound.
alb.iq-1985-the-wake.an: A neo-prog classic; refines the concept-album approach and deepens the symphonic elements.
alb.iq-1987-nomzamo.an: More accessible during the major-label (Vertigo) period; a record that divided fans.
alb.iq-1987-nomzamo.tr: Promises (As the Years Go By) — major-label single
The second major-label album; it failed to gain commercial momentum and the band returned to independence.
alb.iq-1993-ever.an: A return to the 'classic IQ' sound with Nicholls back; a fan favourite.
alb.iq-1993-ever.tr: The Darkest Hour — return to the classic IQ sound
alb.iq-1997-subterranea.an: A double concept album about an imprisoned man encountering the outside world; considered IQ's masterpiece.
alb.iq-2000-the-seventh-house.an: On war, memory and loss; with the 14-minute title track.
alb.iq-2004-dark-matter.an: With the 24-minute 'Harvest of Souls', the peak of neo-prog in the 2000s.
alb.iq-2009-frequency.an: After Martin Orford, with Mark Westworth on keyboards.
alb.iq-2014-the-road-of-bones.an: Dark and heavy, about a serial killer and conscience; Neil Durant on keyboards, Paul Cook back on drums.
alb.iq-2019-resistance.an: A double album: a main disc and a second disc of long pieces; themes of resistance and collapse.
grp.pendragon.kurulus: 1978 (first as 'Zeus Pendragon'), Stroud. Rose with support from Marillion's management and joint tours.
grp.pendragon.hikaye: Led by Nick Barrett, Pendragon (1978, Stroud) represents the romantic wing of neo-prog with melodic guitar and atmospheric keyboards influenced by Camel and Pink Floyd. They stayed independent with their own label, Toff Records. In the 2000s they turned to a darker, heavier sound; Pure (2008) symbolises this change.
grp.pendragon.dna: 'Pendragon = the neo-prog version of Camel', as the saying goes; melodic, Gilmour-inspired guitar solos, accessible, romantic symphonic prog.
grp.pendragon.uyeler: Nick Barrett (guitar/vocals) at the centre; Clive Nolan (keyboards) — also the figure linking the network through Arena and other projects.
alb.pendragon-1985-the-jewel.an: The debut; echoes Marillion's melodic grandeur.
alb.pendragon-1991-the-world.an: On their own label (Toff); the start of the band's maturing, cinematic period.
alb.pendragon-1993-the-window-of-life.an: A fan favourite; an elegant example of melodic neo-prog.
alb.pendragon-1996-the-masquerade-overtu: The peak of the classic Pendragon sound: symphonic, romantic and long pieces.
alb.pendragon-2001-not-of-this-world.an: A personal, emotional three-part title suite drawn from Barrett's divorce.
alb.pendragon-2008-pure.an: A rebirth with heavy riffs and modern prog-metal touches.
alb.pendragon-2020-love-over-fear.an: A return to classic Pendragon romanticism, inspired by the Cornish coast.
grp.pallas.kurulus: 1974 (first as 'Rainbow'; they dropped the name when Blackmore took it), Aberdeen, Scotland. Murray meeting Fish led to joint Pallas–Marillion tours; each opened the other's market.
grp.pallas.dna: 'Pallas = the neo-prog version of Yes', as the saying goes; harder, more epic, with Cold War and dystopian themes.
grp.pallas.uyeler: Graeme Murray (bass) and Derek Forman (drums) at the core; changes on vocals. They worked with Eddy Offord (Yes/ELP engineer) — a technical link to the old backbone.
alb.pallas-1984-the-sentinel.an: With EMI and Eddy Offord. A dystopian concept based on the 'Atlantis Suite', reordered into a more commercial running order for the major label. One of the emblems of neo-prog's epic wing.
alb.pallas-1986-the-wedge.an: Their last album for EMI; after it they were dropped.
grp.twelfth-night-ksa-not.name: Twelfth Night (short note)
grp.twelfth-night-ksa-not.kurulus: 1978, Reading. Remembered for Geoff Mann's theatrical vocals (he later left). The label 'Twelfth Night = the neo-prog version of Pink Floyd' stuck.
Their best-loved album; political pieces such as "We Are Sane".
A major-label (Virgin) attempt; loss of direction and a break-up in 1987.
grp.fish-solo.name: Fish (solo)
grp.fish-solo.kurulus: Born 1958, Dalkeith, Scotland. Derek William Dick; Marillion's singer and lyricist from 1981 to 1988.
grp.fish-solo.hikaye: Fish, who joined Marillion while working as a forestry labourer, got his nickname from his long baths (like Chris Squire). He left Marillion in 1988 over management and creative disagreements and continued his poetic, personal and political writing in a solo career. After leaving EMI he went independent with his own label, Chocolate Frog. He also had an acting career. He announced Weltschmerz (2020) as his last studio album and began retiring from music.
grp.fish-solo.dna: Poetic storytelling, Scottish folk colours, dramatic vocals; more personal and rock-heavy than Marillion's neo-prog.
grp.fish-solo.gecisler: Not Quite Red Fish → Marillion → solo; long-term partners such as Mickey Simmonds, Frank Usher and Steve Vantsis.
grp.fish-solo.etki: Neo-prog's poet; through his post-Marillion solo career, an example of the independent prog artist model.
alb.fish-1990-vigil-in-a-wilderness-of-m: His first solo album after Marillion, with Hal Lindes and Mickey Simmonds; a strong start gathering Fish's anger and hope.
alb.fish-1997-sunsets-on-empire.an: A modern, hard-edged Fish album produced and co-written by Steven Wilson — where neo-prog meets the Porcupine Tree generation.
alb.fish-1997-sunsets-on-empire.detay: One of the rare projects through which Wilson came into contact with neo-prog in the '90s.
alb.fish-2007-13th-star.an: A dark, mature album written after a divorce and a painful separation.
alb.fish-2013-a-feast-of-consequences.an: The late peak, with the 'High Wood' suite drawing on his grandfather's experiences in the First World War.
alb.fish-2020-weltschmerz.an: A double album planned as Fish's farewell: ageing, dementia, politics and world-weariness. Critics considered it the peak of his career.
sec.12.title: Next Generation II — The American Renaissance (1985–1995)
sec.12.intro: The second great 'renaissance', and the network crossing the Atlantic. In a period dominated by grunge, American musicians deliberately revived the symphonic prog of the 1970s (especially Yes, Genesis and Gentle Giant). This generation connects to the old backbone not through member migration but through shared sound and direct personal links (such as Billy Sherwood working with Squire).
grp.world-trade.kurulus: 1989, Los Angeles. Formed after Billy Sherwood's previous band Lodgic (Nomadic Sands, 1985, under the wing of Toto's Paich and Porcaro) split. Sherwood (bass/vocals) + Bruce Gowdy (guitar) + Guy Allison (keyboards, from Lodgic) + Mark T. Williams (drums).
grp.world-trade.dna: In Sherwood's own words, 'a link between the virtuoso bands of the past like King Crimson / Genesis / Yes / Pink Floyd and the future of prog'. Very close to the melodic, polished sound of post-90125 Yes; strong vocal harmonies, AOR melody + prog structure.
grp.world-trade.uyeler: On the second album Jay Schellen replaced Williams on drums. When the band split, Gowdy & Allison → Unruly Child (AOR).
grp.world-trade.etki: The springboard for Sherwood's Yes/Asia career; the missing link between late-'80s melodic prog and the '90s renaissance. That two Yes members (during Anderson's and Rabin's temporary absence) considered working with Sherwood and Gowdy shows how close the sound was to Yes.
alb.world-trade-1989-world-trade.an: Co-produced by Keith Olsen. Lush, ambitious arrangements + sharp melodies; compared with 90125 and It Bites. The pieces are mostly 4–5 minutes, 'light progressive pop-rock' — but Sherwood's signature vocal harmonies and Gowdy's guitar stand out. A product of its time; polished and melodic.
alb.world-trade-1995-euphoria.an: Schellen on drums. It coincides with prog's '90s revival and is a clear step forward from the debut. It includes two 'Chris Squire Experiment' pieces; Squire sings uncredited backing vocals — a concrete trace of the Yes connection. The closing 'One by One by One / Wheels of Life' is one of the strongest moments and points to Sherwood's future solo direction.
alb.world-trade-1995-euphoria.tr: One by One by One / Wheels of Life — the strongest moment, a herald of Sherwood's solo direction
grp.spock-s-beard.kurulus: 1992, Los Angeles. Formed by Neal Morse (vocals/keyboards/guitar) with his brother Alan Morse (guitar) and Nick D'Virgilio (drums); Dave Meros replaced bassist John Ballard before the debut, and Ryo Okumoto (keyboards) joined right after. An 'alternative to the alternative' in the grunge era.
grp.spock-s-beard.hikaye: Formed in Los Angeles in 1992 by brothers Neal and Alan Morse, the band combined a Yes–Genesis–Gentle Giant synthesis with American pop energy and became the flagship of the '90s prog renaissance. When Neal Morse turned to Christianity and left in 2002, drummer Nick D'Virgilio took over vocals; Ted Leonard (Enchant) arrived in 2011. Neal Morse has occasionally returned to the band's albums as a writer and guest.
grp.spock-s-beard.dna: A Yes + Genesis + Gentle Giant synthesis; multi-part vocal harmonies and counterpoint (the Gentle Giant legacy), long suites, melodic and accessible compositions. The most faithful '90s follower of classic symphonic prog.
grp.spock-s-beard.etki: One of the pioneers of the American prog renaissance (along with the Flower Kings and Transatlantic wave); part of the '90s movement that 'made prog cool again'.
alb.spock-s-beard-1995-the-light.an: A self-financed debut of four long pieces. The 15-minute title track and the 23-minute suite 'The Water' fully embrace classic long-form prog. Great praise in the prog community, silence among the wider public. The opening statement of '90s American symphonic prog.
alb.spock-s-beard-1995-the-light.tr: The Light — 15-minute title epic, classic long-form prog
alb.spock-s-beard-1996-beware-of-darknes: The album on which Ryo Okumoto joined, with a George Harrison cover as the title track.
'Thoughts' is a modern example of Gentle Giant-style vocal counterpoint.
alb.spock-s-beard-1998-the-kindness-of-s: Compact, energetic and melodic; one of the band's most accessible classics.
alb.spock-s-beard-2000-v.an: The band's long-form peak with 'At the End of the Day' and 'The Great Nothing'.
alb.spock-s-beard-2002-snow.an: A double concept album about the spiritual journey of an albino young man; Neal Morse's farewell album.
alb.spock-s-beard-2002-snow.detay: Read in parallel with Morse's own conversion story; he left after the tour.
alb.spock-s-beard-2003-feel-euphoria.an: The first album with Nick D'Virgilio on vocals.
alb.spock-s-beard-2013-brief-nocturnes-a: The first album by the new line-up with Ted Leonard and Jimmy Keegan; Neal Morse as a guest writer.
grp.echolyn-ksa-not.name: Echolyn (short note)
grp.echolyn-ksa-not.kurulus: 1989, Pennsylvania. The other pioneer of the '90s American prog revival, mentioned alongside Spock's Beard.
grp.echolyn-ksa-not.hikaye: Pennsylvania's Echolyn combined Gentle Giant's counterpoint with the energy of '90s alternative rock. One of the rare prog bands to sign with Sony; after the commercial failure of As the World they split in 1996 and returned in 2000. Mei (2002) is a single 50-minute composition.
grp.echolyn-ksa-not.dna: Gentle Giant's contrapuntal complexity + Yes/Genesis textures + an American rock vein; dense vocal harmonies.
alb.echolyn-1992-suffocating-the-bloom.a: The peak of their Gentle Giant-inspired counterpoint.
alb.echolyn-1992-suffocating-the-bloom.t: Suffocating the Bloom — a Gentle Giant-inspired counterpoint peak
alb.echolyn-1995-as-the-world.an: A major-label (Sony/Epic) attempt — a rare moment when an American prog band signed to a major; the label and band then parted ways.
alb.echolyn-1995-as-the-world.tr: As the World — major-label concept piece
alb.echolyn-2002-mei.an: A single piece of about 50 minutes, a sprawling narrative on life and memory. Echolyn's most ambitious work.
alb.echolyn-2012-echolyn-window.an: A double album also known as 'Window'; a mature, deep and subtle comeback.
alb.echolyn-2015-i-heard-you-listening.a: More compact and rock-heavy; about relationships and losses.

grp.deep-purple.name: Deep Purple
grp.deep-purple.kurulus: 1968, Hertford (England). Jon Lord (organ), Ritchie Blackmore (guitar) and Ian Paice (drums) formed the core of the classic line-ups.
grp.deep-purple.hikaye: Assembled in 1968 around Jon Lord and Ritchie Blackmore, the first line-up (Mark I, with Rod Evans on vocals and Nick Simper on bass) mixed psychedelic covers with Lord's classical arrangements; 'Hush' was a US hit. In 1969 Ian Gillan and Roger Glover arrived from Episode Six (Mark II), and within weeks the band performed Lord's Concerto for Group and Orchestra with the Royal Philharmonic at the Royal Albert Hall. Blackmore then pushed toward loud, riff-based hard rock: In Rock, Fireball, Machine Head ('Smoke on the Water') and the live Made in Japan made them, with Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath, the defining British heavy band. Gillan and Glover left in 1973; David Coverdale and Glenn Hughes (Mark III) brought soul and funk, Blackmore left in 1975 to form Rainbow, and the Tommy Bolin line-up (Mark IV) split in 1976. Mark II reunited in 1984 with Perfect Strangers. After Blackmore's final exit in 1993, Steve Morse (Dixie Dregs, Kansas) joined, and Don Airey replaced Jon Lord when he retired in 2002; Lord died in 2012.
grp.deep-purple.dna: Lord's distorted Hammond, run through Marshall amplifiers, against Blackmore's classical-scale Stratocaster; call-and-response organ–guitar duels, Paice's swing, Gillan's screams. Baroque and blues meet at full volume.
grp.deep-purple.uyeler: Jon Lord (keyboards, 1968–76, 1984–2002), Ritchie Blackmore (guitar, 1968–75, 1984–93), Ian Paice (drums, every line-up), Rod Evans (vocals) and Nick Simper (bass) in Mark I, Ian Gillan (vocals), Roger Glover (bass), David Coverdale (vocals, 1973–76), Glenn Hughes (bass/vocals, 1973–76), Tommy Bolin (guitar, 1975–76), Steve Morse (guitar, 1994–2022), Don Airey (keyboards, 2002–).
grp.deep-purple.gecisler: Episode Six → Gillan and Glover; Trapeze → Glenn Hughes. Blackmore → Rainbow (where Glover later joined as bassist and producer); Coverdale → Whitesnake. Steve Morse came from Dixie Dregs and Kansas (Power); Don Airey from Rainbow and Colosseum II. Via Rainbow's Cozy Powell the line runs on to Emerson, Lake & Powell.
grp.deep-purple.etki: With Led Zeppelin and Black Sabbath, the founding triangle of British hard rock and heavy metal. Lord's Concerto was one of the first full rock–orchestra collaborations, alongside the Moody Blues and The Nice; the organ–guitar duel became a template for prog metal (Dream Theater covered 'Perfect Strangers' on A Change of Seasons).
grp.deep-purple.ipucu: Start Mark I with the 'April' suite on the third album and the Concerto to hear Lord's classical side — the prog link.
In Rock and Machine Head show the switch to hard rock; Made in Japan shows how much they improvised on stage.
Compare the Lord–Blackmore duels with Keith Emerson in The Nice: the same Hammond school heading in two directions.
grp.deep-purple.era.0.note: Psychedelic covers, Lord's classical arrangements, the first orchestral ideas.
grp.deep-purple.era.1.note: Gillan and Glover: the Concerto, then the hard-rock classics.
grp.deep-purple.era.2.note: Coverdale and Hughes bring soul and funk; Blackmore leaves.
grp.deep-purple.era.3.note: Mark II returns; Steve Morse arrives.

alb.deep-purple-1968-the-book-of-taliesy: Longer arrangements with Lord's classical quotations, alongside covers such as 'Kentucky Woman' and 'River Deep – Mountain High'.
alb.deep-purple-1969-deep-purple.an: Mark I's most ambitious album; the 12-minute 'April' joins band and chamber orchestra — the most prog moment of early Purple.
alb.deep-purple-1969-concerto-for-group-: Jon Lord's three-movement concerto, performed at the Royal Albert Hall on 24 September 1969; an early landmark of rock meeting the orchestra.
Recommended — the prog link of the Purple story.

alb.deep-purple-1971-fireball.an: A more varied, experimental follow-up: odd metres in the title track, the country parody 'Anyone's Daughter', the slow-building 'Fools'.
alb.deep-purple-1972-machine-head.an: Recorded in Montreux with the Rolling Stones Mobile after the casino fire immortalised in 'Smoke on the Water'. The definitive Purple album.
alb.deep-purple-1972-machine-head.detay: The Montreux Casino burned down during a Frank Zappa concert on 4 December 1971, the night before the sessions were due to start there.
alb.deep-purple-1972-made-in-japan.an: Recorded in Osaka and Tokyo in August 1972; long improvisations and the definitive versions of the classics. One of rock's great live albums.
alb.deep-purple-1973-who-do-we-think-we-: Mark II's tired farewell, made amid internal tensions; 'Woman from Tokyo' is the highlight.
alb.deep-purple-1974-burn.an: A powerful restart with two lead singers; the title track and 'Mistreated' became classics.
alb.deep-purple-1974-stormbringer.an: Funk and soul take over; Blackmore's last album before Rainbow, closing with the ballad 'Soldier of Fortune'.

grp.uriah-heep.name: Uriah Heep
grp.uriah-heep.kurulus: 1969/1970, London. Mick Box (guitar), David Byron (vocals), Ken Hensley (keyboards/guitar, main songwriter) and Paul Newton (bass); drummers changed until Lee Kerslake settled in 1971.
grp.uriah-heep.hikaye: Guitarist Mick Box and singer David Byron led the London band Spice; at Christmas 1969 bassist Paul Newton brought in Ken Hensley, his former bandmate in The Gods — a group that had also included Greg Lake (later King Crimson and ELP), Lee Kerslake and John Glascock (later Jethro Tull). Renamed after the Dickens character in early 1970, and produced by Gerry Bron, they combined Hensley's church-like Hammond with Byron's operatic tenor and stacked 'aah' harmonies. After a heavy debut, Salisbury added a 16-minute orchestral title piece, and the classic line-up — with Kerslake and bassist Gary Thain — peaked in 1972 with Demons and Wizards and The Magician's Birthday, both with Roger Dean covers. John Wetton came from King Crimson for 1975–76. Byron was fired in 1976 (John Lawton of Lucifer's Friend replaced him), Hensley left in 1980, and Peter Goalby fronted the hard-rock reboot Abominog (1982). From 1986 Bernie Shaw and Phil Lanzon joined Box, Trevor Bolder and Kerslake in the band's longest-lasting line-up; in 1987 they were among the first Western rock bands to play Moscow. Mick Box is the only constant member.
grp.uriah-heep.dna: Church-organ Hammond, Byron's operatic high voice and stacked 'aah' choirs, wah-wah guitar; heavy rock with fantasy lyrics and long multi-part pieces. The meeting point of Deep Purple's riffs and Yes-style harmony vocals.
grp.uriah-heep.uyeler: Mick Box (guitar, the only constant member), David Byron (vocals, 1969–76), Ken Hensley (keyboards/guitar, 1970–80), Lee Kerslake (drums, 1971–79, 1981–2007), Gary Thain (bass, 1972–75), John Wetton (bass/vocals, 1975–76), John Lawton (vocals, 1976–79), Trevor Bolder (bass, 1976–81, 1983–2013), Peter Goalby (vocals, 1981–85), Bernie Shaw (vocals, 1986–), Phil Lanzon (keyboards, 1986–).
grp.uriah-heep.gecisler: Spice → Uriah Heep. Hensley, Kerslake and Newton came from The Gods (with Greg Lake → King Crimson/ELP and John Glascock → Jethro Tull) and Toe Fat. John Wetton: King Crimson → Uriah Heep → Roxy Music (live) → UK → Wishbone Ash → Asia. Kerslake later drummed for Ozzy Osbourne; Trevor Bolder came from David Bowie's Spiders from Mars; John Lawton from Lucifer's Friend.
grp.uriah-heep.etki: With Deep Purple and Black Sabbath one of the 'big three' of early British heavy rock; the harmony vocals and keyboard drama fed into the NWOBHM, power metal and AOR. Hugely popular in Germany, Scandinavia and, later, Eastern Europe and Russia.
grp.uriah-heep.ipucu: Start with Demons and Wizards and The Magician's Birthday — both with Roger Dean covers, the closest Heep came to prog.
Hear the title tracks of Salisbury and The Magician's Birthday for the band's long-form ambitions.
For the network, play Return to Fantasy: John Wetton between King Crimson's Red and UK.

grp.uriah-heep.era.2.note: The most stable line-up in the band's history; well-received late albums.
alb.uriah-heep-1970-very-eavy-very-umble: A rough, heavy debut of Hammond and wah-wah guitar; 'Gypsy' became the band's first signature song. Released in the US simply as Uriah Heep.

alb.uriah-heep-2008-wake-the-sleeper.kad: Shaw, Box, Lanzon, Bolder, Russell Gilbrook
grp.wishbone-ash.name: Wishbone Ash
grp.wishbone-ash.kurulus: 1969, Torquay (Devon), soon based in London. Martin Turner (bass/vocals), Steve Upton (drums), Andy Powell and Ted Turner (guitars).
grp.wishbone-ash.hikaye: Wishbone Ash grew out of the trio The Empty Vessels; their sound came about almost by accident when Martin Turner and Steve Upton, unable to choose between two guitarists, kept both Andy Powell and Ted Turner. Ritchie Blackmore, impressed at a shared gig, recommended them to Deep Purple's producer Derek Lawrence, who produced their first three albums for MCA. The harmony twin-lead guitar became their trademark, and Argus (1972), with its medieval imagery and interlocking guitar lines, reached No. 3 in the UK and was voted best rock album of the year by Sounds readers. Ted Turner left in 1974 (replaced by Laurie Wisefield of Home) and the band moved to the US; Martin Turner left in 1980 and was briefly replaced by John Wetton on Number the Brave (1981), just before Wetton co-founded Asia. The original four reunited for Nouveau Calls (1987); since the 1990s Andy Powell has led the band, and a 2013 court ruling left the name with him.
grp.wishbone-ash.dna: Twin harmony lead guitars, melodic blues and folk, long instrumental passages, gentle singing; medieval and pastoral imagery. The folk-prog end of British hard rock.
grp.wishbone-ash.uyeler: Andy Powell (guitar, 1969–), Ted Turner (guitar, 1969–74, 1987–93), Martin Turner (bass/vocals, 1969–80, 1987–91), Steve Upton (drums, 1969–90), Laurie Wisefield (guitar, 1974–85), John Wetton (bass/vocals, 1980–81).
grp.wishbone-ash.gecisler: The Empty Vessels → Wishbone Ash. Laurie Wisefield came from Home; John Wetton (King Crimson, Uriah Heep) passed through on his way to Asia. Andy Powell plays the guitar solo on the title track of Renaissance's Ashes Are Burning (1973).
grp.wishbone-ash.etki: The twin-lead harmony guitar shaped Thin Lizzy, Iron Maiden, the NWOBHM and the guitar pairs of Southern rock; a melodic bridge between hard rock, folk and prog.
grp.wishbone-ash.ipucu: Argus is the gateway; hear 'The King Will Come', 'Throw Down the Sword' and 'Warrior' as one medieval suite.
Then play Renaissance's 'Ashes Are Burning' for Andy Powell's guest solo.
alb.wishbone-ash-1970-wishbone-ash.an: A confident debut built on long jams; the 10-minute 'Phoenix' became the live centrepiece.
alb.wishbone-ash-1970-wishbone-ash.kadro: Powell, T. Turner, M. Turner, Upton
alb.wishbone-ash-1971-pilgrimage.an: More varied, with jazz and folk colours; largely instrumental, the twin guitars to the fore.
alb.wishbone-ash-1971-pilgrimage.kadro: Powell, T. Turner, M. Turner, Upton
alb.wishbone-ash-1972-argus.an: The band's masterpiece: medieval themes, interlocking twin guitars and a Hipgnosis cover; voted best rock album of 1972 by Sounds readers.
alb.wishbone-ash-1972-argus.kadro: Powell, T. Turner, M. Turner, Upton
alb.wishbone-ash-1973-live-dates.an: One of the era's great live albums: the classic line-up at its peak.
alb.wishbone-ash-1973-live-dates.kadro: Powell, T. Turner, M. Turner, Upton
alb.wishbone-ash-1973-wishbone-four.an: Self-produced, more acoustic and song-based; less celebrated than Argus but with fine moments.
alb.wishbone-ash-1973-wishbone-four.kadr: Powell, T. Turner, M. Turner, Upton
alb.wishbone-ash-1974-there-s-the-rub.an: Laurie Wisefield's debut, recorded in Miami with Eagles producer Bill Szymczyk; the instrumental 'F.U.B.B.' is a highlight.
alb.wishbone-ash-1974-there-s-the-rub.ka: Powell, Laurie Wisefield, M. Turner, Upton
alb.wishbone-ash-1976-new-england.an: A return to the twin-guitar sound after the US-oriented Locked In.
alb.wishbone-ash-1981-number-the-brave.a: The only album with John Wetton on bass, recorded just before he co-founded Asia.
alb.wishbone-ash-1981-number-the-brave.k: Powell, Wisefield, Upton, John Wetton, Claire Hamill
alb.wishbone-ash-1987-nouveau-calls.an: The original four reunited for an all-instrumental album with a gentle, jazz-tinged sound.
alb.wishbone-ash-1987-nouveau-calls.kadr: Powell, T. Turner, M. Turner, Upton
grp.budgie.name: Budgie
grp.budgie.kurulus: 1967, Cardiff (Wales), first as Hills Contemporary Grass, Budgie from 1969. Burke Shelley (bass/vocals), Tony Bourge (guitar) and Ray Phillips (drums).
grp.budgie.hikaye: A power trio built around Burke Shelley's high voice and bass. Their debut (1971) was produced by Rodger Bain, fresh from Black Sabbath's first records, and the band combined crushing riffs with absurd humour (the bird-themed titles), acoustic interludes and long, multi-part tracks. Never Turn Your Back on a Friend (1973), recorded at Rockfield with a Roger Dean cover, contains 'Breadfan' and the ten-minute 'Parents'; drummer Ray Phillips left after it, followed by Pete Boot and then Steve Williams. Tony Bourge left in 1978; with guitarist John Thomas the band found a second audience in the New Wave of British Heavy Metal. Budgie split in 1988, reunited at intervals, and ended when Shelley fell seriously ill in 2010; he died in 2022.
grp.budgie.dna: Heavy riffs and a high, melodic voice; sudden turns into acoustic, folky passages; long tracks in several sections; absurd bird humour. Cousins of Black Sabbath with a prog sense of form.
grp.budgie.uyeler: Burke Shelley (bass/vocals, 1967–2010), Tony Bourge (guitar, 1967–78), Ray Phillips (drums, 1967–73), Pete Boot (drums, 1973–74), Steve Williams (drums, 1974–88, 1995–2010), John Thomas (guitar, 1978–88).
grp.budgie.gecisler: Producer Rodger Bain ties Budgie to Black Sabbath; Roger Dean's cover art ties them visually to Yes and Uriah Heep. Tony Bourge and Ray Phillips later played together in Tredegar.
grp.budgie.etki: A cult influence on heavy metal: Metallica covered 'Breadfan' and 'Crash Course in Brain Surgery', and Iron Maiden, Megadeth, Van Halen and Soundgarden all covered Budgie songs. The riff-plus-acoustic-section structure foreshadows progressive metal.
grp.budgie.ipucu: Start with 'Breadfan' and 'Parents' on Never Turn Your Back on a Friend: riff power and a ten-minute ballad-epic on one record.
Play 'Breadfan' next to Metallica's cover to hear the line to thrash metal.
alb.budgie-1971-budgie.an: A raw, heavy debut produced by Black Sabbath's Rodger Bain; long riff tracks next to short acoustic pieces.
alb.budgie-1972-squawk.an: A more varied second album, with stronger songs and acoustic interludes.
alb.budgie-1973-never-turn-your-back-on-: The classic: 'Breadfan', the ten-minute ballad-epic 'Parents' and a Roger Dean cover; recorded at Rockfield.
In the Grip of a Tyrefitter's Hand
alb.budgie-1974-in-for-the-kill.an: Heavier and tighter: the title track, 'Zoom Club' and a new recording of 'Crash Course in Brain Surgery'.
alb.budgie-1975-bandolier.an: Steve Williams arrives; 'Breaking All the House Rules' and the long 'Napoleon Bona-Part One & Two'.
alb.budgie-1976-if-i-were-brittania-i-d-: A funkier, more polished A&M debut; mixed reception.
alb.budgie-1980-power-supply.an: With John Thomas: a fast, metallic record that won them a NWOBHM audience.
grp.rainbow.name: Rainbow
grp.rainbow.kurulus: 1975, formed by Ritchie Blackmore after leaving Deep Purple; first with Ronnie James Dio and his American band Elf.
grp.rainbow.hikaye: Blackmore recorded the debut with Dio's band Elf, then replaced everyone except Dio. With Cozy Powell (drums), Tony Carey (keyboards) and Jimmy Bain (bass) came Rising (1976), whose eight-minute 'Stargazer', recorded in Munich with the Munich Philharmonic, is the band's epic. After Long Live Rock 'n' Roll Dio left for Black Sabbath; Roger Glover joined as bassist and producer, Graham Bonnet sang on Down to Earth ('Since You Been Gone') and Don Airey played keyboards. With Joe Lynn Turner Rainbow turned to radio-friendly AOR until Blackmore re-formed Deep Purple in 1984. Later revivals (1994–97, 2015–) were occasional.
grp.rainbow.dna: Blackmore's neoclassical Stratocaster, Dio's medieval-fantasy lyrics and powerful voice, Powell's thunderous drums; minor-key epics with orchestra. Later melodic hard rock.
grp.rainbow.uyeler: Ritchie Blackmore (guitar), Ronnie James Dio (vocals, 1975–79), Cozy Powell (drums, 1975–80), Tony Carey (keyboards, 1975–77), Jimmy Bain (bass, 1975–77), Roger Glover (bass/producer, 1979–84), Graham Bonnet (vocals, 1979–80), Don Airey (keyboards, 1979–81), Joe Lynn Turner (vocals, 1980–84).
grp.rainbow.gecisler: Deep Purple → Rainbow → Deep Purple (1984). Elf → Rainbow; Dio → Black Sabbath, then Dio. Cozy Powell → Michael Schenker Group, Whitesnake, Emerson, Lake & Powell (1986), Black Sabbath. Don Airey (also Colosseum II) → Ozzy Osbourne → Deep Purple (2002). Roger Glover links the two bands as bassist and producer.
grp.rainbow.etki: The bridge from Deep Purple to power metal: Rising's fantasy epics shaped Iron Maiden, Helloween and the European power-metal school, and Blackmore's neoclassical style inspired Yngwie Malmsteen.
grp.rainbow.ipucu: Play 'Stargazer' and 'A Light in the Black' back to back: the second side of Rising is Rainbow's prog moment.
Follow Cozy Powell from Rising to Emerson, Lake & Powell to hear how the network ties hard rock to ELP.
alb.rainbow-1975-ritchie-blackmore-s-rai: Blackmore's escape from Purple, recorded with Dio's band Elf; medieval atmosphere and 'Man on the Silver Mountain'.
Blackmore, Dio, Micky Lee Soule, Craig Gruber, Gary Driscoll
Martin Birch, Ritchie Blackmore, Ronnie James Dio
alb.rainbow-1976-rising.an: Six songs in 33 minutes and one of heavy rock's peaks; 'Stargazer', with the Munich Philharmonic, is the band's epic.
alb.rainbow-1976-rising.kadro: Blackmore, Dio, Cozy Powell, Tony Carey, Jimmy Bain
alb.rainbow-1976-rising.detay: Recorded at Musicland Studios in Munich in February 1976.
Ken Kelly's cover painting became one of hard rock's iconic images.
alb.rainbow-1977-on-stage.an: Live from the 1976 tour: extended versions with long keyboard and guitar solos.
alb.rainbow-1978-long-live-rock-n-roll.a: Dio's last Rainbow album: the orchestral epic 'Gates of Babylon' and the speed of 'Kill the King'.
alb.rainbow-1978-long-live-rock-n-roll.k: Blackmore, Dio, Powell, David Stone, Bob Daisley
alb.rainbow-1978-long-live-rock-n-roll.p: Martin Birch, Ritchie Blackmore, Ronnie James Dio
alb.rainbow-1979-down-to-earth.an: A turn toward radio-friendly hard rock; 'Since You Been Gone' (by Russ Ballard) and 'All Night Long' were UK hits.
alb.rainbow-1979-down-to-earth.kadro: Blackmore, Graham Bonnet, Powell, Roger Glover, Don Airey
alb.rainbow-1981-difficult-to-cure.an: Joe Lynn Turner's debut: AOR songs plus the title track, Blackmore's arrangement of Beethoven's Ninth.
alb.rainbow-1981-difficult-to-cure.kadro: Blackmore, Joe Lynn Turner, Glover, Airey, Bobby Rondinelli
alb.rainbow-1983-bent-out-of-shape.an: A polished, melodic farewell before the Purple reunion; 'Street of Dreams' and the instrumental 'Anybody There'.
alb.rainbow-1983-bent-out-of-shape.kadro: Blackmore, Turner, Glover, David Rosenthal, Chuck Burgi
grp.syd-barrett-solo.name: Syd Barrett (solo)
grp.syd-barrett-solo.kurulus: Syd Barrett (Roger Keith Barrett, 1946–2006), Cambridge. Pink Floyd's founding guitarist, singer and main songwriter (1965–68); two solo albums in 1970.
grp.syd-barrett-solo.hikaye: Barrett named Pink Floyd and wrote most of The Piper at the Gates of Dawn (1967) as well as the singles 'Arnold Layne' and 'See Emily Play'. As his behaviour became increasingly erratic, aggravated by heavy LSD use, he was eased out in early 1968 and replaced by his Cambridge friend David Gilmour. His solo recordings, begun in 1968 with Peter Jenner, were finished in 1969–70 with Malcolm Jones of Harvest and then with Gilmour and Roger Waters; members of Soft Machine played on some tracks. The Madcap Laughs and Barrett (produced by Gilmour and Richard Wright) both appeared in 1970. After the short-lived trio Stars (1972) he withdrew from music and lived quietly in Cambridge, painting and gardening, until his death in 2006. Pink Floyd's 'Shine On You Crazy Diamond' and much of Wish You Were Here are about him.
grp.syd-barrett-solo.dna: Childlike, surreal lyrics (nursery rhymes, Edward Lear, Hilaire Belloc), loose acoustic guitar, sudden tempo changes and unpredictable timing; fragile, unpolished takes left as they were.
grp.syd-barrett-solo.uyeler: Syd Barrett (vocals/guitar). With David Gilmour, Roger Waters, Richard Wright, Jerry Shirley (drums, Humble Pie), and Mike Ratledge, Hugh Hopper and Robert Wyatt of Soft Machine.
grp.syd-barrett-solo.gecisler: Pink Floyd (1965–68) → solo → Stars (1972, with Twink of the Pretty Things and Pink Fairies). Soft Machine's Ratledge, Hopper and Wyatt played on The Madcap Laughs; Gilmour, Waters and Wright produced the albums.
grp.syd-barrett-solo.etki: The archetype of the English psychedelic songwriter, admired by David Bowie, Robyn Hitchcock, Julian Cope and Blur. As an absent figure he shaped Pink Floyd's later themes of absence and madness.
grp.syd-barrett-solo.ipucu: Hear the solo albums after Piper and A Saucerful of Secrets — 'Jugband Blues' is his farewell to the band.
Then listen to Wish You Were Here, the band's album about him.
alb.syd-barrett-1970-the-madcap-laughs.a: Barrett's first solo album: fragile, unvarnished takes — false starts included — of strange and beautiful songs.
alb.syd-barrett-1970-the-madcap-laughs.o: Essential — the other face of the Pink Floyd story.
alb.syd-barrett-1970-the-madcap-laughs.k: Barrett + David Gilmour, Roger Waters, Mike Ratledge, Hugh Hopper, Robert Wyatt
alb.syd-barrett-1970-the-madcap-laughs.p: Peter Jenner, Malcolm Jones, David Gilmour, Roger Waters
alb.syd-barrett-1970-the-madcap-laughs.d: 'Golden Hair' sets a poem by James Joyce.
Soft Machine's Mike Ratledge, Hugh Hopper and Robert Wyatt play on 'No Good Trying' and 'Love You'.
alb.syd-barrett-1970-barrett.an: More arranged than Madcap, with Gilmour and Wright as producers and band; whimsical songs such as 'Baby Lemonade' and 'Gigolo Aunt'.
alb.syd-barrett-1970-barrett.kadro: Barrett, Gilmour, Richard Wright, Jerry Shirley
alb.syd-barrett-1988-opel.an: Previously unreleased outtakes and alternate versions from the 1968–70 sessions; for those who want more.
alb.syd-barrett-1988-opel.kadro: Barrett and the session musicians of 1968–70
grp.roxy-music.name: Roxy Music
grp.roxy-music.kurulus: 1970–71, London. Bryan Ferry (vocals/keyboards), Andy Mackay (saxophone/oboe), Brian Eno (synthesizer/tapes), Phil Manzanera (guitar) and Paul Thompson (drums).
grp.roxy-music.hikaye: Founded by art-school graduate Bryan Ferry with Andy Mackay and the self-declared non-musician Brian Eno, Roxy Music mixed 1950s rock 'n' roll nostalgia, glam fashion and avant-garde electronics. Their first album (1972), produced by King Crimson lyricist Peter Sinfield, and the single 'Virginia Plain' made them stars; Phil Manzanera came from the Canterbury-linked Quiet Sun. After For Your Pleasure (1973) Eno left after clashing with Ferry; Eddie Jobson (from Curved Air, later UK) took over keyboards and violin for Stranded, Country Life and Siren, and John Wetton toured with them on bass in 1974–75. After a break (1976–78) the band returned as a sleeker unit with session players, ending with the luxurious Avalon (1982).
grp.roxy-music.dna: Art-school glam: Ferry's ironic crooning, Mackay's oboe and saxophone, Eno's treated synths and tapes, Manzanera's angular guitar; a collage of pastiche and avant-garde. Later polished, atmospheric soft rock.
grp.roxy-music.uyeler: Bryan Ferry (vocals/keyboards), Andy Mackay (sax/oboe), Phil Manzanera (guitar, 1972–), Paul Thompson (drums), Brian Eno (synthesizer, 1971–73), Eddie Jobson (keyboards/violin, 1973–76); the bass chair rotated (Graham Simpson, Rik Kenton, John Porter, John Gustafson, John Wetton on tour, Gary Tibbs).
grp.roxy-music.gecisler: Brian Eno → solo, Fripp & Eno, producer (Bowie, Talking Heads, U2). Phil Manzanera came from Quiet Sun (with Charles Hayward, later of This Heat) → 801 with Eno → co-producer of Pink Floyd's The Endless River. Eddie Jobson: Curved Air → Roxy Music → Frank Zappa → UK. John Wetton toured with them between King Crimson and Uriah Heep. King Crimson's Peter Sinfield produced the debut.
grp.roxy-music.etki: The art-rock blueprint for punk, new wave, synth-pop and the New Romantics (Talking Heads, Japan, Duran Duran). In the prog network they are the glam side door through which Eno, Jobson, Wetton and Manzanera passed.
grp.roxy-music.ipucu: Hear the first two albums for Eno, then Stranded and Country Life for Eddie Jobson's violin and keyboards — the line to UK.
Phil Manzanera's guitar links Roxy to Quiet Sun, 801 and Pink Floyd's The Endless River.
grp.roxy-music.era.1.note: Violin and keyboards; the most rock-oriented, ambitious period.
alb.roxy-music-1972-roxy-music.an: An astonishing debut produced by King Crimson's Peter Sinfield: rock 'n' roll pastiche meets synthesizer noise.
alb.roxy-music-1972-roxy-music.kadro: Ferry, Mackay, Eno, Manzanera, Thompson, Graham Simpson
alb.roxy-music-1973-for-your-pleasure.an: Darker and more adventurous; Eno's last album with the band. 'In Every Dream Home a Heartache' and 'The Bogus Man' stretch the form.
alb.roxy-music-1973-for-your-pleasure.pr: Chris Thomas, John Anthony, Roxy Music
alb.roxy-music-1973-for-your-pleasure.tr: In Every Dream Home a Heartache
alb.roxy-music-1973-stranded.an: Eddie Jobson's first album; Ferry's ballads deepen, with 'Mother of Pearl' and 'A Song for Europe' as highlights.
alb.roxy-music-1973-stranded.kadro: Ferry, Mackay, Manzanera, Eddie Jobson, Thompson
alb.roxy-music-1974-country-life.an: Hard-edged and witty: 'The Thrill of It All' and 'Out of the Blue' with Jobson's violin solo.
alb.roxy-music-1975-siren.an: More streamlined; 'Love Is the Drug' was their US breakthrough.
alb.roxy-music-1976-viva.an: Live recordings from 1973–75; a raw document of the Jobson line-up.
alb.roxy-music-1979-manifesto.an: The comeback after a three-year break; disco-tinged 'Dance Away' and 'Angel Eyes'.
alb.roxy-music-1979-manifesto.kadro: Ferry, Mackay, Manzanera, Thompson + session players
alb.roxy-music-1980-flesh-and-blood.an: Smooth and commercial: 'Over You', 'Oh Yeah' and 'Same Old Scene'.
alb.roxy-music-1982-avalon.an: The final studio album: a luxurious, atmospheric sound that defined sophisticated 1980s pop.
grp.brian-eno.name: Brian Eno
grp.brian-eno.kurulus: Brian Eno (b. 1948, Woodbridge, Suffolk). A self-described 'non-musician' working with synthesizers, tape and studio treatments; solo career from 1973.
grp.brian-eno.hikaye: After art school Eno joined Roxy Music as its 'technical adviser', processing the band through a VCS3 synthesizer. Leaving in 1973, he made (No Pussyfooting) with Robert Fripp using two Revox tape recorders, then four albums of oblique, playful art-rock songs (1974–77) with guests from Roxy Music, King Crimson, Brand X and Genesis. Bedridden after being hit by a taxi in 1975, he began to think of music as an environment: Discreet Music (1975) and Music for Airports (1978) founded 'ambient music'.
