He also treated Peter Gabriel's voice on Genesis's The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, created the Oblique Strategies cards with painter Peter Schmidt, and became one of the most influential producers of his time (David Bowie's Berlin trilogy, Talking Heads, Devo, U2, Coldplay).
grp.brian-eno.dna: The studio as an instrument: tape loops, treatments and chance procedures (Oblique Strategies). In the songs, absurd wordplay over angular art-rock; in ambient, slow, self-generating textures.
grp.brian-eno.uyeler: Solo. Recurring collaborators: Robert Fripp, Phil Manzanera, Andy Mackay, Phil Collins, Percy Jones, John Cale, Fred Frith, Robert Wyatt, Daniel Lanois, Roger Eno, Jon Hassell, David Byrne.
grp.brian-eno.gecisler: Roxy Music → solo; Fripp & Eno ((No Pussyfooting), Evening Star); 801 with Phil Manzanera. Guest on Genesis's The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, Robert Wyatt's Ruth Is Stranger Than Richard and Kevin Ayers's June 1, 1974. Phil Collins and Percy Jones of Brand X play on Another Green World; Fred Frith (Henry Cow) on Before and After Science. Producer of David Bowie, Talking Heads and U2.
grp.brian-eno.etki: The founder of ambient music and one of rock's key producers; the bridge from prog's studio experiments to post-punk, electronic and ambient music. Through Fripp and the Lamb sessions he is tied directly to the King Crimson and Genesis universes.
grp.brian-eno.ipucu: Start with Another Green World: half songs, half instrumental miniatures — the hinge between his two worlds.
Play Music for Airports quietly, in the background, as he intended.
For the network, hear (No Pussyfooting) under Robert Fripp and look for the 'Enossification' credit on The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway.
grp.brian-eno.era.0.note: Oblique, witty songs with Roxy and Crimson guests.
grp.brian-eno.era.1.note: From Discreet Music to Apollo: music as an environment.
grp.brian-eno.era.2.note: Sampling with David Byrne; a late return to singing.
alb.brian-eno-1974-here-come-the-warm-je: A glam art-rock debut full of treated guitars; Fripp's solo on 'Baby's on Fire' is famous.
Eno + Robert Fripp, Phil Manzanera, Andy Mackay, Paul Thompson, Chris Spedding and others
alb.brian-eno-1974-taking-tiger-mountain: A loose concept album inspired by postcards of a Chinese revolutionary opera; catchy, strange and inventive.
Eno + Phil Manzanera, Robert Wyatt and others
Burning Airlines Give You So Much More
alb.brian-eno-1975-another-green-world.a: The masterpiece: instrumental miniatures and a handful of songs, with Fripp and Brand X's Phil Collins and Percy Jones; the hinge between art rock and ambient.
alb.brian-eno-1975-another-green-world.k: Eno + Robert Fripp, Phil Collins, Percy Jones, John Cale, Rod Melvin, Paul Rudolph
alb.brian-eno-1977-before-and-after-scie: His last song album of the 1970s: a busy, rhythmic first side and a calm, ambient second side.
Eno + Phil Collins, Percy Jones, Robert Fripp, Fred Frith, Phil Manzanera and others
alb.brian-eno-1975-discreet-music.an: A half-hour piece built from two delayed synthesizer lines, plus variations on Pachelbel's Canon; the birth of ambient.
alb.brian-eno-1975-discreet-music.kadro: Eno; side two with the Cockpit Ensemble
alb.brian-eno-1978-ambient-1-music-for-a: The album that named ambient music: four slow, looping pieces meant to calm an airport terminal.
alb.brian-eno-1983-apollo-atmospheres-an: Music for a documentary about the Apollo moon missions; 'An Ending (Ascent)' became widely used.
alb.brian-eno-1981-my-life-in-the-bush-o: With David Byrne: found voices and radio recordings over funk and world rhythms; a landmark of sampling.
A late return to singing after decades of instrumentals; warm, melancholy electronic songs.
grp.mike-oldfield.name: Mike Oldfield
grp.mike-oldfield.kurulus: Mike Oldfield (b. 1953, Reading). Multi-instrumentalist; his debut, recorded at 19, was the first release of Virgin Records (1973).
grp.mike-oldfield.hikaye: Oldfield began in the folk duo Sallyangie with his sister Sally, then played bass and guitar in Kevin Ayers's band The Whole World, alongside David Bedford and Lol Coxhill. With Ayers's encouragement he developed a long instrumental piece; Richard Branson's new Virgin label released it as Tubular Bells on 25 May 1973, after Oldfield had overdubbed almost every instrument himself at The Manor studio. Boosted by its use in The Exorcist, it sold millions and financed the label. Hergest Ridge (1974) and Ommadawn (1975) refined the side-long, folk-tinged form. After a personal turning point in 1978 he became more outgoing: the double Incantations, a large touring ensemble (Exposed) and, from 1979, shorter songs — 'Moonlight Shadow' (1983, sung by Maggie Reilly) was a European hit. In the 1990s he returned to long form with Amarok and the Tubular Bells sequels, the second produced by Trevor Horn.
grp.mike-oldfield.dna: Side-long instrumental suites built from overdubbed guitars, bass, piano, bells and folk melodies; Celtic and African touches; slow layering, then release. Later, crystalline pop songs.
grp.mike-oldfield.uyeler: Solo, playing most instruments himself. Collaborators: David Bedford (arranger), Sally Oldfield, Pierre Moerlen (Gong), Maddy Prior, Maggie Reilly, Tom Newman (producer).
grp.mike-oldfield.gecisler: Sallyangie → Kevin Ayers and the Whole World (bass/guitar on Shooting at the Moon and Whatevershebringswesing) → solo. Guitar on Robert Wyatt's Rock Bottom ('Little Red Robin Hood Hit the Road'). David Bedford orchestrated The Orchestral Tubular Bells; Pierre Moerlen of Gong drums on Incantations and Exposed; Jon Anderson sings 'In High Places' and Family's Roger Chapman 'Shadow on the Wall' on Crises; Trevor Horn (Buggles, Yes) produced Tubular Bells II.
grp.mike-oldfield.etki: Tubular Bells proved that a long instrumental by an unknown teenager could become a mass hit, and it launched Virgin Records — the label that went on to release Henry Cow, Gong, Hatfield and the North and Tangerine Dream. A forerunner of new age and minimalist rock.
grp.mike-oldfield.ipucu: Hear Tubular Bells, Hergest Ridge and Ommadawn as one trilogy; Ommadawn is often considered his finest.
Go back to Kevin Ayers's Shooting at the Moon to hear the teenage Oldfield on bass.
Amarok (1990), a single hour-long track, is a return to the early method.
grp.mike-oldfield.era.0.note: Side-long instrumental pieces: the Tubular Bells trilogy and Incantations.
grp.mike-oldfield.era.2.note: Amarok and the Tubular Bells sequels.
alb.mike-oldfield-1973-tubular-bells.an: The 49-minute instrumental that launched Virgin Records, with almost every instrument played by the 19-year-old Oldfield; its opening became famous through The Exorcist.
alb.mike-oldfield-1973-tubular-bells.kad: Oldfield (almost all instruments) + Viv Stanshall (master of ceremonies), Sally Oldfield, Steve Broughton
alb.mike-oldfield-1973-tubular-bells.pro: Tom Newman, Simon Heyworth, Mike Oldfield
alb.mike-oldfield-1973-tubular-bells.det: Viv Stanshall of the Bonzo Dog Doo-Dah Band announces the instruments in the finale of Part One.
alb.mike-oldfield-1974-hergest-ridge.an: A calmer, pastoral follow-up named after a hill near his Herefordshire retreat; it replaced Tubular Bells at No. 1 in the UK.
alb.mike-oldfield-1975-ommadawn.an: Celtic folk and African drums in two long parts; for many listeners his finest work.
alb.mike-oldfield-1975-ommadawn.kadro: Oldfield + Paddy Moloney (uilleann pipes), Jabula (African drums), Pierre Moerlen, Sally Oldfield
alb.mike-oldfield-1978-incantations.an: A 72-minute double album of hypnotic, minimalist-influenced movements with choir and orchestra; Maddy Prior sings lines from Longfellow's Hiawatha.
alb.mike-oldfield-1978-incantations.kadr: Oldfield + Pierre Moerlen, Maddy Prior, choir and orchestra
alb.mike-oldfield-1979-exposed.an: Live from the 1979 European tour with a large ensemble: Incantations and Tubular Bells in full.
alb.mike-oldfield-1979-exposed.kadro: Oldfield + a large ensemble incl. Pierre Moerlen
alb.mike-oldfield-1979-platinum.an: Side one a disco-tinged suite ending with Philip Glass's 'North Star', side two shorter pieces.
alb.mike-oldfield-1979-platinum.kadro: Oldfield + Pierre Moerlen, Morris Pert and others
alb.mike-oldfield-1982-five-miles-out.an: Side one is the 24-minute 'Taurus II'; the title song recalls a near-disastrous flight through a storm.
alb.mike-oldfield-1982-five-miles-out.ka: Oldfield + Maggie Reilly, Morris Pert, Tim Cross, Rick Fenn, Mike Frye
alb.mike-oldfield-1983-crises.an: A 20-minute title piece plus songs: 'Moonlight Shadow' with Maggie Reilly, 'In High Places' with Jon Anderson and 'Shadow on the Wall' with Family's Roger Chapman.
alb.mike-oldfield-1983-crises.kadro: Oldfield + Maggie Reilly, Jon Anderson, Roger Chapman, Simon Phillips
alb.mike-oldfield-1990-amarok.an: A single hour-long piece, a deliberately anti-commercial statement in his dispute with Virgin; dense, playful and unpredictable.
A re-imagining of the original produced by Trevor Horn; his first album for WEA.
Trevor Horn, Tom Newman, Mike Oldfield
alb.mike-oldfield-1994-the-songs-of-dist: Inspired by Arthur C. Clarke's novel; ambient and new-age textures.
grp.vangelis.name: Vangelis
grp.vangelis.kurulus: Vangelis (Evangelos Odysseas Papathanassiou, 1943–2022), born in Agria near Volos, Greece. Keyboardist and composer; Aphrodite's Child, then solo.
grp.vangelis.hikaye: Largely self-taught, Vangelis led the Athens beat group The Forminx, then in 1968 moved to Paris with Demis Roussos and Loukas Sideras as Aphrodite's Child, whose 'Rain and Tears' was a European hit and whose double album 666 (1972) is a psychedelic-prog cult classic. After film work and the album Earth (1973) he settled in London in 1975 and built Nemo Studios. Around that time he rehearsed with Yes as a possible replacement for Rick Wakeman but declined; his friendship with Jon Anderson led to Anderson singing on Heaven and Hell (1975) and to the Jon & Vangelis albums. Heaven and Hell, Albedo 0.39 and China mixed synthesizers, choir and orchestral sweep. His score for Chariots of Fire won the 1982 Academy Award, and Blade Runner (1982) became the archetype of electronic film music. Later works included 1492: Conquest of Paradise and Mythodea, linked to NASA's Mars Odyssey mission. He died in Paris in 2022.
grp.vangelis.dna: A huge, orchestral synthesizer sound (above all the Yamaha CS-80), improvised and recorded live in the studio; Greek and Eastern melodic colour, choirs, crashing percussion and cinematic sweep.
grp.vangelis.uyeler: Solo. Collaborators: Jon Anderson, Demis Roussos, Irene Papas, Vana Veroutis, the English Chamber Choir.
grp.vangelis.gecisler: The Forminx → Aphrodite's Child (666) → solo. Rehearsed with Yes in 1974 after Wakeman's departure (Patrick Moraz got the job); Jon Anderson sings on Heaven and Hell; Jon & Vangelis (1980–91).
grp.vangelis.etki: Shaped the sound of synthesizers in film and television (Carl Sagan's Cosmos used his music); a bridge between symphonic prog, electronic music and new age. Blade Runner's sound inspired generations of electronic and synthwave musicians.
grp.vangelis.ipucu: Start with Heaven and Hell: a symphonic suite with Jon Anderson's 'So Long Ago, So Clear' at its centre.
Hear Aphrodite's Child's 666 for the prog roots, then the Jon & Vangelis albums under Jon Anderson.
grp.vangelis.era.0.note: Synthesizer symphonies and electronic experiments from his London studio.
grp.vangelis.era.1.note: Chariots of Fire, Blade Runner and grand commissions.
alb.vangelis-1975-heaven-and-hell.an: His first album from Nemo Studios: a symphonic suite with choir in which Jon Anderson sings 'So Long Ago, So Clear'. Parts were used in Carl Sagan's Cosmos.
alb.vangelis-1975-heaven-and-hell.onceli: Essential — the closest Vangelis came to symphonic prog.
alb.vangelis-1975-heaven-and-hell.kadro: Vangelis + Jon Anderson (vocals), English Chamber Choir, Vana Veroutis
alb.vangelis-1976-albedo-0-39.an: A space-themed album: 'Pulstar', the jazz-rock of 'Nucleogenesis', and the Earth's physical data read aloud in the title track.
alb.vangelis-1977-spiral.an: Sequencer-driven pieces on cosmic and Taoist themes, including 'To the Unknown Man'.
alb.vangelis-1979-china.an: Chinese melodies and instruments evoked with synthesizers; atmospheric and lyrical.
alb.vangelis-1981-chariots-of-fire.an: The Oscar-winning score; the title theme became one of the best-known instrumentals of all time.
alb.vangelis-1994-blade-runner.an: The score to Ridley Scott's 1982 film, officially released only in 1994; the archetype of noir electronic film music.
alb.vangelis-1983-antarctica.an: Music for Koreyoshi Kurahara's film; glacial, meditative themes.
alb.vangelis-1992-1492-conquest-of-parad: The score for Ridley Scott's Columbus film; the choral title theme became a stadium favourite.
alb.vangelis-2001-mythodea.an: A choral symphony written in 1993 and released in connection with NASA's 2001 Mars Odyssey mission.
alb.vangelis-2001-mythodea.kadro: Vangelis + Kathleen Battle, Jessye Norman, London Metropolitan Orchestra
grp.kate-bush.name: Kate Bush
grp.kate-bush.kurulus: Kate Bush (b. 1958, Bexleyheath, Kent). Singer, songwriter, pianist and producer; signed to EMI as a teenager with David Gilmour's help.
grp.kate-bush.hikaye: Bush wrote songs from early adolescence; a family friend passed her tape to David Gilmour, who financed professional demos in 1975 and took them to EMI. 'Wuthering Heights' (1978), written at 18, made her the first woman to top the UK singles chart with a self-written song. Her only full tour (1979) was a theatrical, dance-based show. From The Dreaming (1982) she produced herself, building dense, Fairlight-driven soundscapes; Hounds of Love (1985), with the 'Ninth Wave' suite on its second side, is widely regarded as her masterpiece. She sang with Peter Gabriel on 'Games Without Frontiers' and 'Don't Give Up', and Gilmour played guitar on two songs of The Sensual World. After a twelve-year silence came Aerial (2005), then Director's Cut and 50 Words for Snow (2011) and the 22-night London residency Before the Dawn (2014). In 2022 'Running Up That Hill' returned to No. 1 in the UK after appearing in Stranger Things.
grp.kate-bush.dna: A wide-ranging, theatrical voice; literary and cinematic subjects (Emily Brontë, James Joyce, Houdini); piano songs grown into layered studio worlds with Fairlight, folk instruments and orchestra; concept suites.
grp.kate-bush.uyeler: Solo. Musicians: Ian Bairnson, David Paton and Stuart Elliott (Pilot / Alan Parsons Project), Del Palmer, Preston Heyman, Charlie Morgan, John Giblin; guests David Gilmour, Peter Gabriel, Eberhard Weber, Jeff Beck, Prince, Eric Clapton.
grp.kate-bush.gecisler: Discovered by David Gilmour (Pink Floyd). The Kick Inside was produced by Andrew Powell, arranger for the Alan Parsons Project, with Pilot / APP musicians Ian Bairnson, David Paton and Stuart Elliott. Duets and backing vocals with Peter Gabriel ('Games Without Frontiers' on Melt, 'Don't Give Up' on So); Gilmour plays on 'Love and Anger' and 'Rocket's Tail'.
grp.kate-bush.etki: The model of the self-producing art-pop auteur, admired by Björk, Tori Amos, Florence Welch and St. Vincent; 'The Ninth Wave' brought prog's concept-suite thinking into 1980s pop.
grp.kate-bush.ipucu: Hear side two of Hounds of Love, 'The Ninth Wave', as a prog suite without the genre label.
Pair 'Don't Give Up' with Peter Gabriel's So, and 'Rocket's Tail' with David Gilmour's guitar.
Aerial's second disc, 'A Sky of Honey', is a song cycle tracing a single summer day.
grp.kate-bush.era.0.note: Piano songs and literary subjects, with Andrew Powell's production.
grp.kate-bush.era.1.note: Fairlight soundscapes, concept suites, the peak years.
grp.kate-bush.era.2.note: After twelve years of silence: long song cycles in quieter colours.
alb.kate-bush-1978-the-kick-inside.an: A remarkable debut written largely in her teens: 'Wuthering Heights' and 'The Man with the Child in His Eyes'.
alb.kate-bush-1978-the-kick-inside.kadro: Bush + Ian Bairnson, David Paton, Stuart Elliott, Andrew Powell
alb.kate-bush-1978-the-kick-inside.tr: The Man with the Child in His Eyes
alb.kate-bush-1978-lionheart.an: A hurried follow-up recorded within months; 'Wow' and 'Hammer Horror' stand out.
alb.kate-bush-1980-never-for-ever.an: Her first co-production and the first UK No. 1 album by a British female solo artist; first steps with the Fairlight.
alb.kate-bush-1980-never-for-ever.kadro: Bush + Bairnson, Elliott, Del Palmer and others
alb.kate-bush-1982-the-dreaming.an: Her first self-produced album: radical, percussive and densely layered — an art-rock record in all but name.
alb.kate-bush-1982-the-dreaming.oncelik: Essential — Kate Bush at her most experimental.
alb.kate-bush-1982-the-dreaming.kadro: Bush + Del Palmer, Preston Heyman, Stuart Elliott and others
alb.kate-bush-1985-hounds-of-love.an: Her masterpiece: side one five singles-calibre songs ('Running Up That Hill', 'Cloudbusting'), side two the seven-part suite 'The Ninth Wave'.
alb.kate-bush-1985-hounds-of-love.kadro: Bush + Del Palmer, Charlie Morgan, Stuart Elliott, Eberhard Weber and others
alb.kate-bush-1985-hounds-of-love.detay: 'The Ninth Wave' follows a woman adrift in the sea at night, between sleep and drowning.
'Running Up That Hill' returned to No. 1 in the UK in 2022 after appearing in Stranger Things.
alb.kate-bush-1985-hounds-of-love.tr: Running Up That Hill (A Deal with God)
alb.kate-bush-1989-the-sensual-world.an: Warmer and more personal: the Joyce-inspired title track, the voices of Trio Bulgarka and Gilmour's guitar on 'Love and Anger' and 'Rocket's Tail'.
alb.kate-bush-1989-the-sensual-world.kad: Bush + Trio Bulgarka, David Gilmour, Nigel Kennedy, Del Palmer and others
alb.kate-bush-1993-the-red-shoes.an: Long and uneven, with guests Prince, Eric Clapton and Jeff Beck.
alb.kate-bush-1993-the-red-shoes.kadro: Bush + Prince, Eric Clapton, Jeff Beck and others
alb.kate-bush-2005-aerial.an: The comeback after twelve years; the second disc, 'A Sky of Honey', is a song cycle following a summer day from dawn to dawn.
alb.kate-bush-2005-aerial.kadro: Bush + Del Palmer, Dan McIntosh, John Giblin, Peter Erskine and others
alb.kate-bush-2011-director-s-cut.an: New recordings of songs from The Sensual World and The Red Shoes.
alb.kate-bush-2011-director-s-cut.kadro: Bush + Del Palmer, Steve Gadd and others
alb.kate-bush-2011-50-words-for-snow.an: Seven long, slow, piano-led pieces on a winter theme; quiet and hypnotic.
alb.kate-bush-2011-50-words-for-snow.kad: Bush + Steve Gadd, Elton John, Stephen Fry and others
sec.19.title: The Art-Rock Neighbourhood — Glam, Ambient and Electronic Kin
sec.19.intro: Artists outside prog proper whose paths run straight through the network: Roxy Music and Brian Eno (Fripp, Jobson, Wetton), Phil Manzanera's Quiet Sun and 801 projects, Mike Oldfield and David Bedford (Kevin Ayers, Robert Wyatt, Virgin Records), Vangelis and Jon & Vangelis (Aphrodite's Child, Jon Anderson) and Kate Bush (David Gilmour, Peter Gabriel).
alb.moody-blues-1972-seventh-sojourn.an: The seventh and last album of the classic era; the Mellotron gives way to the Chamberlin and the mood turns weary and inward. A US No. 1.
alb.steve-hackett-1981-cured.an: Hackett sings all the lead vocals himself for the first time; the songs get shorter and the sound moves towards early-'80s pop.
alb.steve-hackett-1983-highly-strung.an: Continues Cured's pop direction; 'Cell 151' aims at radio, yet the guitar still takes centre stage.
alb.pink-floyd-1969-ummagumma.an: A double album: 1969 concert recordings on one disc, half a side of solo experiment from each member on the other. The best document of the early live Floyd.
alb.pink-floyd-1970-atom-heart-mother.an: A side-long title suite with brass and choir, arranged with Ron Geesin. The band's first UK No. 1 album.
alb.pink-floyd-1971-meddle.an: The album where the band finds its own voice: it opens with 'One of These Days' and closes with the 23-minute 'Echoes'. The road to Dark Side starts here.
alb.soft-machine-1973-six.an: A double album, half live, half studio; Karl Jenkins joins and Hugh Hopper leaves. Minimalist repetition meets jazz-rock.
alb.soft-machine-1973-seven.an: Roy Babbington on bass; Jenkins's compositions take over and the sound turns into a tighter, more ordered jazz-rock.
alb.soft-machine-1975-bundles.an: With Allan Holdsworth on guitar the band plays guitar-led fusion for the first time; 'Hazard Profile' is his showcase.
alb.gong-1973-angel-s-egg.an: The second part of the Radio Gnome trilogy. With Hillage, Malherbe, Tim Blake and Pierre Moerlen the classic line-up settles and the sound opens out into space music.
alb.gong-1974-you.an: The peak of the Radio Gnome trilogy: long, hypnotic jams and 'Master Builder'. Daevid Allen's last album of the classic period.
alb.hatfield-and-the-north-national-heal: National Health's second and most mature album, with John Greaves on bass. Intricate chamber jazz meets Canterbury humour.
alb.jethro-tull-1975-minstrel-in-the-gal: Anderson's most personal album, moving between acoustic guitar and strings and hard rock; 'Baker St. Muse' is its centre.
alb.jethro-tull-1978-heavy-horses.an: The middle of the folk trilogy: a lament for rural England, the vanishing working horses and an older way of life.
alb.gentle-giant-1978-giant-for-a-day.an: An attempt at commercial success with short, radio-friendly songs; the band's intricate counterpoint is largely left behind.
alb.gentle-giant-1980-civilian.an: The farewell album: direct, short rock songs. The band's progressive identity is barely audible here.
alb.camel-1978-breathless.an: A transitional album split between pop songs and long instrumentals; Peter Bardens's last Camel record.
alb.camel-1981-nude.an: The story of Hiroo Onoda, the Japanese soldier who kept fighting in the jungle for decades; Camel's strong return to the concept album.
alb.camel-1982-the-single-factor.an: A pop-leaning album made under label pressure; a stopgap Latimer recorded almost alone with guests.
alb.camel-1984-stationary-traveller.an: A concept album about the Berlin Wall and the East–West divide; melancholic and atmospheric in an '80s keyboard sound.
alb.twelfth-night-1986-twelfth-night-xii: A more commercial, streamlined final album made for a major label, with Andy Sears on vocals. The band split soon after.
grp.frank-zappa.name: Frank Zappa & The Mothers of Invention
grp.frank-zappa.kurulus: 1964–65, Los Angeles. Frank Zappa (guitar, composition, 1940–1993) took over the R&B bar band the Soul Giants and renamed it The Mothers (of Invention, at the record company's insistence).
grp.frank-zappa.hikaye: Zappa grew up in Lancaster, California, a teenage fan of both Edgard Varèse and doo-wop. The Mothers' debut Freak Out! (1966) was one of rock's first double albums and one of its first concept albums; Absolutely Free and We're Only in It for the Money (a parody of Sgt. Pepper aimed at both the establishment and the hippies) followed, along with the orchestral collage Lumpy Gravy. Zappa disbanded the original Mothers in 1969 and released Hot Rats, a largely instrumental jazz-rock album built around Ian Underwood's reeds and keyboards. The early-seventies bands (with Flo & Eddie, then the big-band records Waka/Jawaka and The Grand Wazoo) led to the 1973–75 group many fans consider his best: George Duke, Ruth Underwood, Napoleon Murphy Brock, Tom and Bruce Fowler, Chester Thompson and, briefly, Jean-Luc Ponty — heard on Over-Nite Sensation, Apostrophe ('), Roxy & Elsewhere and One Size Fits All. Later bands brought in Terry Bozzio, Adrian Belew, Patrick O'Hearn, Vinnie Colaiuta, Warren Cuccurullo and Steve Vai. He produced Captain Beefheart's Trout Mask Replica on his own label, fought record companies and, in 1985, testified before the US Senate against record censorship. In the eighties he composed on the Synclavier (Jazz from Hell won a Grammy) and for orchestras; The Yellow Shark, played by Ensemble Modern, appeared a month before his death from prostate cancer in December 1993.
grp.frank-zappa.dna: Composed chaos: odd meters and polyrhythms, abrupt cuts between doo-wop, big band, modern classical and hard rock, long guitar solos over vamps, mallet percussion doubling impossible unison lines, and satirical lyrics. Under the jokes, strict through-composition and relentless rehearsal.
grp.frank-zappa.uyeler: Frank Zappa (guitar, vocals, composition). Original Mothers: Ray Collins, Roy Estrada, Jimmy Carl Black, Don Preston, Bunk Gardner, Motorhead Sherwood, Art Tripp, Ian Underwood. Later: Flo & Eddie (Mark Volman, Howard Kaylan), Aynsley Dunbar, George Duke, Ruth Underwood, Napoleon Murphy Brock, Tom and Bruce Fowler, Chester Thompson, Ralph Humphrey, Jean-Luc Ponty, Terry Bozzio, Eddie Jobson, Patrick O'Hearn, Adrian Belew, Tommy Mars, Peter Wolf, Ed Mann, Ike Willis, Vinnie Colaiuta, Warren Cuccurullo, Arthur Barrow, Steve Vai, Scott Thunes, Chad Wackerman.
grp.frank-zappa.gecisler: Out of the Zappa school: Adrian Belew → David Bowie, Talking Heads, King Crimson; Terry Bozzio and Eddie Jobson → UK (and Bozzio, with Cuccurullo and Patrick O'Hearn, → Missing Persons); Chester Thompson → Weather Report, then Genesis on stage; Jean-Luc Ponty → Mahavishnu Orchestra; Aynsley Dunbar → Journey; Steve Vai → Whitesnake, solo; Flo & Eddie (ex-Turtles) → T. Rex backing vocals. Art Tripp left the Mothers for Captain Beefheart's Magic Band.
grp.frank-zappa.etki: Zappa proved that a rock musician could be a composer in the full sense — writing for orchestra, chamber ensemble and computer as well as band. His mixture of complexity and humour runs through Henry Cow, Gentle Giant's angular counterpoint, Phish, Mr. Bungle and the prog-metal guitar school via Steve Vai; Varèse and Stravinsky reached many rock listeners through him.
grp.frank-zappa.ipucu: Start with Hot Rats ('Peaches en Regalia') and One Size Fits All ('Inca Roads') — the most prog-friendly doors into Zappa.
Roxy & Elsewhere shows the 1973–74 band live; listen for Ruth Underwood's marimba doubling the guitar and Chester Thompson's drumming.
For the composer, compare 'G-Spot Tornado' on Jazz from Hell (Synclavier) with the Ensemble Modern version on The Yellow Shark.
grp.frank-zappa.era.0.note: Satire, doo-wop, Varèse and studio collage.
grp.frank-zappa.era.1.t: Hot Rats and the big bands
grp.frank-zappa.era.1.note: Instrumental jazz-rock, Flo & Eddie, the Grand Wazoo orchestra.
grp.frank-zappa.era.2.note: Duke, Underwood, Brock, Thompson; then Bozzio, Belew, the rock operas.
grp.frank-zappa.era.3.note: Guitar albums, computer music and the Ensemble Modern.
alb.frank-zappa-1966-freak-out.an: The Mothers' debut: one of rock's first double albums, moving from satirical doo-wop to the 12-minute freak-out collage 'The Return of the Son of Monster Magnet'.
alb.frank-zappa-1966-freak-out.kadro: Zappa, Ray Collins, Roy Estrada, Jimmy Carl Black, Elliot Ingber
alb.frank-zappa-1966-freak-out.detay: Paul McCartney is often quoted as saying that Sgt. Pepper was the Beatles' answer to Freak Out!
alb.frank-zappa-1967-absolutely-free.an: Two side-long suites of satire, studded with quotations from Stravinsky; the band is now a seven-piece.
alb.frank-zappa-1967-absolutely-free.kad: Zappa, Ray Collins, Roy Estrada, Jimmy Carl Black, Billy Mundi, Don Preston, Bunk Gardner, Jim Fielder
alb.frank-zappa-1968-we-re-only-in-it-fo: A Sgt. Pepper parody that attacks the establishment and the flower-power scene in equal measure; short songs, tape edits and musique concrète.
Zappa, Ray Collins, Roy Estrada, Jimmy Carl Black, Billy Mundi, Don Preston, Bunk Gardner, Ian Underwood, Motorhead Sherwood
The Chrome Plated Megaphone of Destiny
alb.frank-zappa-1968-lumpy-gravy.an: Zappa's first 'solo' album: orchestral music, surf guitar and mumbled conversations recorded inside a piano, cut together into two long collages.
alb.frank-zappa-1968-lumpy-gravy.kadro: Zappa with the Abnuceals Emuukha Electric Symphony Orchestra & Chorus
alb.frank-zappa-1969-uncle-meat.an: Soundtrack to an unfinished film and the Mothers' most musically ambitious record: chamber pieces for mallets and woodwinds, and the first 'King Kong'.
alb.frank-zappa-1969-uncle-meat.kadro: Zappa, Ian Underwood, Roy Estrada, Don Preston, Bunk Gardner, Jimmy Carl Black, Art Tripp, Motorhead Sherwood, Ray Collins
alb.frank-zappa-1969-uncle-meat.tr: Dog Breath, in the Year of the Plague
alb.frank-zappa-1969-hot-rats.an: Zappa's first album after breaking up the Mothers: almost entirely instrumental jazz-rock built from multitracked reeds and keyboards; Captain Beefheart sings 'Willie the Pimp'.
alb.frank-zappa-1969-hot-rats.oncelik: Essential — the gateway album for prog listeners.
alb.frank-zappa-1969-hot-rats.kadro: Zappa, Ian Underwood, Max Bennett, John Guerin, Paul Humphrey, Ron Selico, Shuggie Otis; guests Captain Beefheart (vocals), Don 'Sugarcane' Harris and Jean-Luc Ponty (violin)
alb.frank-zappa-1972-waka-jawaka.an: Recorded while Zappa was recovering from being pushed off a London stage in 1971; the first of two big-band jazz-rock albums, opening with the 17-minute 'Big Swifty'.
alb.frank-zappa-1972-waka-jawaka.kadro: Zappa, George Duke, Sal Marquez, Aynsley Dunbar, Alex Dmochowski, Tony Duran, Don Preston, Jeff Simmons
alb.frank-zappa-1972-the-grand-wazoo.an: The second big-band album, more orchestral and fully composed; the closing 'Blessed Relief' is one of Zappa's most lyrical pieces.
alb.frank-zappa-1972-the-grand-wazoo.kad: Zappa, George Duke, Aynsley Dunbar, Alex Dmochowski, Ernie Watts, Sal Marquez, Tony Duran and a large horn section
alb.frank-zappa-1973-over-nite-sensation: Shorter, funkier songs with dense arrangements; the first record of the 1973–75 band, with Tina Turner and the Ikettes uncredited on backing vocals.
Zappa, George Duke, Ian Underwood, Ruth Underwood, Jean-Luc Ponty, Tom Fowler, Bruce Fowler, Ralph Humphrey, Sal Marquez
alb.frank-zappa-1974-apostrophe.an: His highest-charting album in the US: the 'Yellow Snow' suite on side one, and the title instrumental, a jam with Cream's Jack Bruce.
alb.frank-zappa-1974-apostrophe.kadro: Zappa, George Duke, Ruth Underwood, Napoleon Murphy Brock, Tom Fowler, Ralph Humphrey, Jim Gordon, Jack Bruce (bass on 'Apostrophe'')
alb.frank-zappa-1974-roxy-elsewhere.an: Recorded mostly at the Roxy in Hollywood in December 1973 by the two-drummer line-up; 'Echidna's Arf (Of You)' and 'Be-Bop Tango' show how tightly the band played Zappa's hardest writing.
alb.frank-zappa-1974-roxy-elsewhere.kadr: Zappa, George Duke, Napoleon Murphy Brock, Bruce Fowler, Tom Fowler, Ruth Underwood, Ralph Humphrey, Chester Thompson, Jeff Simmons, Don Preston, Walt Fowler
alb.frank-zappa-1974-roxy-elsewhere.tr: Don't You Ever Wash That Thing?
Be-Bop Tango (Of the Old Jazzmen's Church)
alb.frank-zappa-1975-one-size-fits-all.a: The peak of the 1973–75 band and the Zappa album most often named by prog fans; 'Inca Roads' sets a long guitar solo inside an intricate, stop-start composition.
alb.frank-zappa-1975-one-size-fits-all.o: Essential — the most prog of his records.
alb.frank-zappa-1975-one-size-fits-all.k: Zappa, George Duke, Napoleon Murphy Brock, Chester Thompson, Tom Fowler, Ruth Underwood, Johnny 'Guitar' Watson, Captain Beefheart (harmonica, as 'Bloodshot Rollin' Red')
alb.frank-zappa-1976-zoot-allures.an: A darker, guitar-centred record, largely played by Zappa himself with Terry Bozzio on drums; 'Black Napkins' became a concert staple.
alb.frank-zappa-1976-zoot-allures.kadro: Zappa (most instruments), Terry Bozzio, Roy Estrada, Dave Parlato, Ruth Underwood, Captain Beefheart (harmonica)
alb.frank-zappa-1976-zoot-allures.tr: Wind Up Workin' in a Gas Station
alb.frank-zappa-1979-sheik-yerbouti.an: Concert recordings from 1977–78, overdubbed in the studio, with Adrian Belew and Terry Bozzio; satire and some of his most complex playing side by side ('Rat Tomago', 'Yo' Mama').
alb.frank-zappa-1979-sheik-yerbouti.kadr: Zappa, Adrian Belew, Terry Bozzio, Patrick O'Hearn, Tommy Mars, Peter Wolf, Ed Mann
alb.frank-zappa-1979-joe-s-garage-acts-i: A three-act rock opera about a world where music is outlawed, first issued as two separate albums; the guitar solos were taken from concert recordings and placed into new studio tracks ('xenochrony').
Zappa, Ike Willis, Warren Cuccurullo, Vinnie Colaiuta, Arthur Barrow, Peter Wolf, Tommy Mars, Ed Mann, Dale Bozzio
alb.frank-zappa-1981-shut-up-n-play-yer-: A mail-order box of guitar solos lifted from concerts; the clearest picture of Zappa as an improviser.
Zappa (guitar) with his 1977–80 bands (incl. Terry Bozzio, Vinnie Colaiuta, Warren Cuccurullo, Patrick O'Hearn, Tommy Mars, Ike Willis)
alb.frank-zappa-1986-jazz-from-hell.an: Almost entirely realised on the Synclavier, so Zappa could hear pieces too hard for human players; it won the Grammy for Best Rock Instrumental Performance.
alb.frank-zappa-1993-the-yellow-shark.an: Recorded in Frankfurt, Berlin and Vienna in 1992 by the German new-music group Ensemble Modern; released a month before Zappa's death, his last album issued in his lifetime.
alb.frank-zappa-1993-the-yellow-shark.on: Recommended — Zappa as a composer of concert music.
alb.frank-zappa-1993-the-yellow-shark.ka: Ensemble Modern, cond. Peter Rundel; Zappa conducts some pieces
grp.captain-beefheart.name: Captain Beefheart & His Magic Band
grp.captain-beefheart.kurulus: 1965, Lancaster / Los Angeles. Don Van Vliet (1941–2010), Zappa's school friend from Lancaster, fronted a blues band that became the Magic Band.
grp.captain-beefheart.hikaye: Van Vliet and Zappa bonded as teenagers over R&B records in the Mojave Desert town of Lancaster. As Captain Beefheart he started with a raw Delta blues sound; Safe as Milk (1967) featured the 20-year-old Ry Cooder. Zappa then gave him complete freedom on his Straight label: Trout Mask Replica (1969) was rehearsed for months by a Magic Band living in a rented house under Van Vliet's control, with drummer John French transcribing his whistled and piano-tapped ideas into parts. Lick My Decals Off, Baby (1970) added the ex-Mother Art Tripp on marimba. The early-seventies albums moved toward a more accessible rock-blues (Clear Spot), and after a commercial low point he returned with a strong late trilogy (Shiny Beast, Doc at the Radar Station, Ice Cream for Crow). In 1982 he left music for painting, and exhibited widely until his death in 2010.
grp.captain-beefheart.dna: Delta blues broken into interlocking guitar lines in different meters, free-jazz saxophone, a growling multi-octave voice and surreal poetry. Nothing repeats where you expect it to; the 'mistakes' are composed.
grp.captain-beefheart.uyeler: Don Van Vliet (vocals, harmonica, saxophone). Magic Band: Ry Cooder (1967), Alex St. Clair, Jerry Handley, John French ('Drumbo'), Bill Harkleroad ('Zoot Horn Rollo'), Mark Boston ('Rockette Morton'), Jeff Cotton ('Antennae Jimmy Semens'), Victor Hayden ('The Mascara Snake'), Art Tripp ('Ed Marimba'), Gary Lucas, Jeff Moris Tepper, Eric Drew Feldman, Robert Williams.
grp.captain-beefheart.gecisler: Art Tripp came from the Mothers of Invention. Zappa produced Trout Mask Replica; Van Vliet sang on Zappa's Hot Rats and played harmonica on One Size Fits All and Zoot Allures (Bongo Fury, 1975, is a joint live album). Ry Cooder went on to a long solo career; Eric Drew Feldman later played with Pere Ubu and PJ Harvey, Gary Lucas with Jeff Buckley.
grp.captain-beefheart.etki: Trout Mask Replica became a touchstone for punk, post-punk and the avant-garde: the Residents, Pere Ubu, Devo, Tom Waits, PJ Harvey and the Rock in Opposition bands owe it something. For prog listeners it shows a completely different road to complexity — through the blues rather than the conservatory.
grp.captain-beefheart.ipucu: Start with Safe as Milk ('Electricity'), then Clear Spot — Trout Mask Replica is easier after those.
On Trout Mask Replica, listen to just one guitar at a time: every part is a fixed composition.
Compare 'Willie the Pimp' on Zappa's Hot Rats: the same voice in a very different setting.
A tough, inventive blues and R&B debut with the young Ry Cooder on guitar; 'Electricity' already points to the strangeness ahead.
Van Vliet, Ry Cooder, Alex St. Clair, Jerry Handley, John French
alb.captain-beefheart-1969-trout-mask-re: 28 pieces of fractured blues, free jazz and spoken poetry, rehearsed for months and recorded for Zappa's Straight label; one of the most influential and most divisive records in rock.
Essential — but come to it after the easier albums.
Van Vliet, Bill Harkleroad, Jeff Cotton, Mark Boston, John French, Victor Hayden
alb.captain-beefheart-1970-lick-my-decal: Tighter and even more abstract than Trout Mask, with ex-Mother Art Tripp on marimba; Van Vliet himself considered it his best.
Van Vliet, Bill Harkleroad, Mark Boston, Art Tripp, John French
I Love You, You Big Dummy
alb.captain-beefheart-1972-clear-spot.an: His most accessible album: punchy blues-rock and soul with horns, and the ballad 'Too Much Time'.
alb.captain-beefheart-1972-clear-spot.ka: Van Vliet, Bill Harkleroad, Mark Boston, Art Tripp, Roy Estrada
alb.captain-beefheart-1980-doc-at-the-ra: A late return to the angular Trout Mask style with a new young Magic Band; admired by the post-punk generation.
Van Vliet, Jeff Moris Tepper, Gary Lucas, Eric Drew Feldman, Robert Williams, John French
grp.jean-luc-ponty.name: Jean-Luc Ponty
grp.jean-luc-ponty.kurulus: Born 1942 in Avranches (France). A conservatoire-trained violinist who switched to jazz in the early sixties and pioneered the amplified violin.
grp.jean-luc-ponty.hikaye: Ponty won first prize at the Paris Conservatoire before turning to jazz, and by the late sixties was the leading violinist of European jazz. In 1969 Zappa invited him to play on Hot Rats and arranged and conducted the album King Kong, devoted to Zappa's music. He toured with Zappa's band in 1973 (he plays on Over-Nite Sensation) and then joined John McLaughlin's second Mahavishnu Orchestra (Apocalypse, Visions of the Emerald Beyond). From 1975 his own albums for Atlantic made him one of the best-selling fusion artists: melodic, sequenced and layered, with guitarists such as Daryl Stuermer and Allan Holdsworth. He later worked with Jon Anderson in the Anderson Ponty Band (Better Late Than Never, 2015).
grp.jean-luc-ponty.dna: Violin through effects pedals and synthesizers, long singing melodies over arpeggiated ostinatos, odd meters handled smoothly; fusion with the sweetness of French melody rather than the aggression of jazz-rock.
grp.jean-luc-ponty.uyeler: Jean-Luc Ponty (electric violin, keyboards). Band members included George Duke, Daryl Stuermer, Allan Holdsworth, Allan Zavod, Ralphe Armstrong, Tom Fowler, Mark Craney, Steve Smith, Joaquin Lievano, Peter Maunu.
grp.jean-luc-ponty.gecisler: Zappa (Hot Rats, King Kong, the 1973 band) → Mahavishnu Orchestra → solo. Daryl Stuermer moved from Ponty's band to Genesis's touring line-up (from 1978); Allan Holdsworth from Ponty to UK and Bruford; Steve Smith to Journey. Ponty and Jon Anderson formed the Anderson Ponty Band in 2014.
grp.jean-luc-ponty.etki: With Jerry Goodman, Eddie Jobson and Darryl Way he made the violin a lead rock instrument; his seventies albums are a bridge between fusion and symphonic prog, and a direct link from Zappa to the Yes and Genesis families.
grp.jean-luc-ponty.ipucu: Begin with Enigmatic Ocean — Holdsworth and Stuermer on the same record.
King Kong is Zappa's writing in Ponty's hands; compare its title track with the original on Uncle Meat.
If you know Eddie Jobson's violin with UK, listen to Imaginary Voyage for the source of that sound.
alb.jean-luc-ponty-1970-king-kong-jean-l: Zappa's compositions, arranged and partly conducted by Zappa himself, including the orchestral 'Music for Electric Violin and Low Budget Orchestra'.
Ponty, George Duke, Ernie Watts, Ian Underwood, Buell Neidlinger, Art Tripp, John Guerin; Zappa (guitar on one track)
Music for Electric Violin and Low Budget Orchestra
alb.jean-luc-ponty-1976-imaginary-voyage: The second Atlantic album; the side-long 'Imaginary Voyage' suite is his closest approach to symphonic prog.
Ponty, Daryl Stuermer, Allan Zavod, Tom Fowler, Mark Craney
His classic: two very different guitarists — Holdsworth's fluid legato and Stuermer's crisp rock lines — around Ponty's violin, in multi-part suites.
Ponty, Allan Holdsworth, Daryl Stuermer, Allan Zavod, Ralphe Armstrong, Steve Smith
Struggle of the Turtle to the Sea
alb.jean-luc-ponty-1978-cosmic-messenger: Shorter, brighter pieces with more synthesizer; a commercial high point.
Ponty, Joaquin Lievano, Peter Maunu, Allan Zavod, Ralphe Armstrong, Casey Scheuerell
grp.the-doors.name: The Doors
grp.the-doors.kurulus: 1965, Los Angeles. Jim Morrison (vocals) and Ray Manzarek (keyboards), who had met at the UCLA film school, with Robby Krieger (guitar) and John Densmore (drums).
grp.the-doors.hikaye: Named after Aldous Huxley's The Doors of Perception, the band had no bass player: Manzarek played bass lines on a keyboard bass with his left hand and organ with his right. After a residency at the Whisky a Go Go they signed to Elektra, and their 1967 debut, with 'Light My Fire' and the 11-minute 'The End', made them stars. Strange Days and Waiting for the Sun followed within a year; The Soft Parade added horns and strings. Morrison's drinking and the 1969 Miami concert trial overshadowed the band, but Morrison Hotel and L.A. Woman returned to a tough blues-rock. Morrison moved to Paris and died there in July 1971; the other three made two more albums before splitting in 1973.
grp.the-doors.dna: Manzarek's Vox Continental and Fender Rhodes keyboard bass, Krieger's flamenco and Indian-scale guitar, Densmore's jazz-trained drumming, and Morrison's baritone half sung, half recited. Long dramatic pieces built like theatre: build-up, breakdown, spoken poetry, explosion.
grp.the-doors.uyeler: Jim Morrison (vocals, 1965–71), Ray Manzarek (keyboards, keyboard bass), Robby Krieger (guitar), John Densmore (drums). Studio bassists included Doug Lubahn, Lonnie Mack, Ray Neapolitan and Jerry Scheff.
grp.the-doors.gecisler: Few personnel links with British prog, but a strong musical one: Manzarek and Krieger used classical (Bach on 'Light My Fire'), Weill–Brecht ('Alabama Song') and raga ideas in extended form at the same moment as The Nice and Procol Harum. Manzarek later recorded Carl Orff's Carmina Burana (1983, produced by Philip Glass).
grp.the-doors.etki: With Love and the Velvet Underground, the American band that most clearly treated rock as theatre and poetry; 'The End' and 'When the Music's Over' are models for the long dramatic rock song. Echoes in Iggy Pop, Patti Smith, Echo & the Bunnymen and the dark side of art-rock.
grp.the-doors.ipucu: Listen to 'The End' and 'When the Music's Over' as proto-prog: two long-form pieces in two consecutive albums.
Notice the missing bass guitar: everything low comes from Manzarek's left hand.
Compare the organ in 'Light My Fire' with Keith Emerson in The Nice, recorded the same year.
alb.the-doors-1967-the-doors.an: One of the great debuts: 'Break On Through', the seven-minute 'Light My Fire' with its long organ and guitar solos, and the 11-minute Oedipal drama 'The End'.
alb.the-doors-1967-the-doors.tr: Break On Through (To the Other Side)
alb.the-doors-1967-strange-days.an: Darker and more experimental, with Moog effects and studio sound collage; closes with the 11-minute 'When the Music's Over'.
alb.the-doors-1967-strange-days.kadro: Morrison, Manzarek, Krieger, Densmore; Doug Lubahn (bass)
alb.the-doors-1968-waiting-for-the-sun.a: Their only US number-one album, with shorter songs; 'Spanish Caravan' quotes Albéniz on flamenco guitar.
alb.the-doors-1969-the-soft-parade.an: Horns and strings and Krieger's increasing share of the writing; the eight-minute multi-part title track is their most prog-like structure.
alb.the-doors-1969-the-soft-parade.kadro: Morrison, Manzarek, Krieger, Densmore; horns and strings arr. Paul Harris
alb.the-doors-1970-morrison-hotel.an: A return to blues and hard rock after the orchestral detour; 'Roadhouse Blues' became their great concert opener.
alb.the-doors-1970-morrison-hotel.kadro: Morrison, Manzarek, Krieger, Densmore; Lonnie Mack, Ray Neapolitan (bass)
alb.the-doors-1971-l-a-woman.an: Recorded live in the band's rehearsal room after Rothchild withdrew; Morrison's last album, ending with the rain-soaked 'Riders on the Storm'.
alb.the-doors-1971-l-a-woman.kadro: Morrison, Manzarek, Krieger, Densmore; Jerry Scheff (bass), Marc Benno (rhythm guitar)
grp.led-zeppelin.name: Led Zeppelin
grp.led-zeppelin.kurulus: 1968, London. Jimmy Page (guitar) built the band out of the last Yardbirds line-up with Robert Plant (vocals), John Paul Jones (bass, keyboards) and John Bonham (drums).
grp.led-zeppelin.hikaye: Page and Jones were London's busiest session musicians before Page joined the Yardbirds. When Keith Relf and Jim McCarty left the Yardbirds in 1968 (to form Renaissance), Page recruited Plant and Bonham from the Birmingham band Band of Joy and Jones from the studios, toured Scandinavia as the New Yardbirds and recorded the first Led Zeppelin album in about 36 hours. Managed by Peter Grant, they became the biggest live band of the seventies. Led Zeppelin II (heavy blues), III (acoustic, written in a Welsh cottage) and the untitled fourth album with 'Stairway to Heaven' moved between hard rock, folk and Eastern modes; Houses of the Holy and the double Physical Graffiti ('Kashmir') went further into long, orchestrated forms. In 1974 they founded the Swan Song label, home of Bad Company. After Plant's car accident (Presence) and the death of his son, In Through the Out Door (1979) gave Jones's keyboards a leading role. John Bonham died in September 1980 and the band split in December; they reunited only for a few occasions, most fully at the O2 Arena in 2007 with Jason Bonham.
grp.led-zeppelin.dna: Bonham's huge, slightly behind-the-beat drums; Page's layered guitars, open tunings and studio ambience; Plant's high blues wail and Tolkien imagery; Jones's arrangements on bass, organ, mellotron and synthesizer. Blues and folk stretched into long, dynamic structures.
grp.led-zeppelin.uyeler: Jimmy Page (guitar, producer), Robert Plant (vocals), John Paul Jones (bass, keyboards, mandolin, arrangements), John Bonham (drums, 1968–80).
grp.led-zeppelin.gecisler: The Yardbirds split two ways in 1968: Page → Led Zeppelin, Keith Relf and Jim McCarty → Renaissance. Swan Song signed Bad Company (Paul Rodgers, Mick Ralphs; Boz Burrell from King Crimson). Sandy Denny of Fairport Convention sings on 'The Battle of Evermore'. Jones, a session arranger before Zeppelin (Donovan, the Rolling Stones), later produced and played with many artists and formed Them Crooked Vultures; Page worked with Paul Rodgers in The Firm and with David Coverdale (ex-Deep Purple).
grp.led-zeppelin.etki: With Deep Purple and Black Sabbath the founding triangle of hard rock and heavy metal. Their long-form pieces — 'Dazed and Confused', 'Stairway to Heaven', 'Kashmir', 'Achilles Last Stand' — gave hard rock the scale of prog, and Page's studio production became a model for both.
grp.led-zeppelin.ipucu: For the prog side, listen to 'Kashmir', 'No Quarter' and 'Carouselambra': mellotron, synthesizer and long arrangements.
III shows how much folk there is in the band — compare it with Fairport Convention and the Strawbs.
Follow the Yardbirds split: Led Zeppelin I and Renaissance's first album appeared the same year.
alb.led-zeppelin-1969-led-zeppelin.an: Recorded in about 36 hours: heavy blues reshaped with dynamic contrasts, from the acoustic 'Babe I'm Gonna Leave You' to the bowed-guitar 'Dazed and Confused'.
alb.led-zeppelin-1969-led-zeppelin-ii.an: Recorded between tour dates; 'Whole Lotta Love' with its theremin middle section, and Bonham's drum feature 'Moby Dick'.
alb.led-zeppelin-1969-led-zeppelin-ii.tr: What Is and What Should Never Be
alb.led-zeppelin-1970-led-zeppelin-iii.a: The acoustic turn, written at Bron-Yr-Aur cottage in Wales; folk and blues next to 'Immigrant Song' and the slow blues 'Since I've Been Loving You'.
alb.led-zeppelin-1971-led-zeppelin-iv.an: The untitled fourth album: 'Stairway to Heaven' grows from recorders and acoustic guitar to full band, and 'When the Levee Breaks' sets Bonham's drums in a stairwell.
alb.led-zeppelin-1971-led-zeppelin-iv.ka: Page, Plant, Jones, Bonham; Sandy Denny (vocals on 'The Battle of Evermore')
alb.led-zeppelin-1971-led-zeppelin-iv.de: The sleeve carries no title or band name — only four symbols, one chosen by each member.
alb.led-zeppelin-1973-houses-of-the-holy: Brighter and more varied, with mellotron on 'The Rain Song' and Jones's keyboard showcase 'No Quarter'.
Over the Hills and Far Away
Their first release on their own Swan Song label: a double album of new recordings and outtakes, centred on the orchestral, Eastern-scaled 'Kashmir'.
alb.led-zeppelin-1976-presence.an: Recorded in three weeks while Plant was recovering from a car accident; guitar-heavy, with the ten-minute 'Achilles Last Stand'.
alb.led-zeppelin-1979-in-through-the-out: The last studio album with Bonham; Jones's synthesizers lead, notably on the ten-minute 'Carouselambra'.
grp.jimmy-page.name: Jimmy Page (solo, The Firm, Page & Plant)
grp.jimmy-page.kurulus: Born 1944 in Heston, Middlesex. After Led Zeppelin: a soundtrack, a solo album and a series of partnerships with singers.
grp.jimmy-page.hikaye: After John Bonham's death and the end of Led Zeppelin, Page returned with the soundtrack to Michael Winner's Death Wish II (1982), played with musicians from the British prog and folk scenes. He formed The Firm with Bad Company's Paul Rodgers (1984–86), made his only solo album Outrider (1988) with Jason Bonham on drums, and worked with ex-Deep Purple and Whitesnake singer David Coverdale on Coverdale–Page (1993). In 1994 he and Robert Plant reunited for MTV's Unledded, reworking Zeppelin songs with an Egyptian ensemble and an orchestra; the studio album Walking into Clarksdale followed in 1998. Since then Page has concentrated on remastering the Zeppelin catalogue and occasional reunions.
grp.jimmy-page.dna: Layered guitar orchestration, open tunings and Eastern scales carried over from Zeppelin; in the eighties a cleaner, synth-era hard rock; in the Page & Plant years, North African and Arabic textures.
grp.jimmy-page.uyeler: Jimmy Page (guitar, producer); partners Paul Rodgers (The Firm), David Coverdale (Coverdale–Page), Robert Plant (Page & Plant); musicians include Chris Farlowe, Dave Lawson, Dave Paton, Dave Mattacks, Tony Franklin, Chris Slade, Jason Bonham, John Miles, Denny Carmassi, Charlie Jones, Michael Lee, Porl Thompson.
grp.jimmy-page.gecisler: Death Wish II brings in Dave Lawson (Greenslade), Dave Paton (Pilot, Alan Parsons Project) and Dave Mattacks (Fairport Convention). The Firm joins Page with Paul Rodgers of Bad Company, the band on Zeppelin's Swan Song label; Coverdale–Page links him to Deep Purple via David Coverdale. Unledded features Hossam Ramzy's Egyptian ensemble and arrangements by Ed Shearmur.
grp.jimmy-page.etki: Page's post-Zeppelin work never matched the band, but Unledded showed how the Zeppelin songs could live in an Arabic and orchestral setting, and it shaped later 'world music' approaches to classic rock.
grp.jimmy-page.ipucu: Start with No Quarter (Unledded): 'Kashmir' with an Egyptian orchestra.
Death Wish II is an instrumental curiosity with Greenslade's Dave Lawson on synthesizers.
Compare 'The Only One' on Outrider, with Plant as guest, to the Page & Plant reunion six years later.
alb.jimmy-page-1982-death-wish-ii.an: Page's first project after Zeppelin: a mostly instrumental film score of synthesizer moods, orchestral guitar and a few blues-rock songs.
alb.jimmy-page-1982-death-wish-ii.kadro: Page, Chris Farlowe (vocals), Dave Lawson, Dave Paton, Dave Mattacks, Gordon Edwards
alb.jimmy-page-1985-the-firm.an: The first album of Page's band with Bad Company singer Paul Rodgers; polished mid-eighties hard rock with Tony Franklin's fretless bass.
alb.jimmy-page-1985-the-firm.kadro: Page, Paul Rodgers, Tony Franklin, Chris Slade
alb.jimmy-page-1988-outrider.an: His only solo album, with Jason Bonham, son of John, on drums; Robert Plant sings 'The Only One'.
alb.jimmy-page-1988-outrider.kadro: Page, Jason Bonham, Felix Krish, Durban Laverde; vocals John Miles, Chris Farlowe, Robert Plant
alb.jimmy-page-1993-coverdale-page.an: A collaboration with the former Deep Purple and Whitesnake singer; heavy, Zeppelin-style riffs in a nineties production.
alb.jimmy-page-1993-coverdale-page.kadro: Page, David Coverdale, Denny Carmassi, Jorge Casas, Ricky Phillips
alb.jimmy-page-1993-coverdale-page.prod: Jimmy Page, David Coverdale, Mike Fraser
alb.jimmy-page-1993-coverdale-page.tr: Take Me for a Little While
The Page & Plant reunion for MTV: Zeppelin songs re-arranged with an Egyptian ensemble, Moroccan Gnawa musicians and an orchestra, plus four new pieces.
Recommended — the Zeppelin songs in an orchestral, Arabic setting.
Page, Robert Plant, Charlie Jones, Michael Lee, Porl Thompson, Nigel Eaton + Hossam Ramzy's Egyptian ensemble and the London Metropolitan Orchestra, arr. Ed Shearmur
alb.jimmy-page-1998-walking-into-clarksd: The only Page & Plant studio album, recorded by Steve Albini; 'Most High' won a Grammy.
Page, Robert Plant, Charlie Jones, Michael Lee
grp.robert-plant.name: Robert Plant (solo)
grp.robert-plant.kurulus: Born 1948 in West Bromwich, Staffordshire. Solo career since 1982.
grp.robert-plant.hikaye: Plant began his solo career in 1982 with Pictures at Eleven, recorded with guitarist Robbie Blunt and, on most tracks, Phil Collins on drums; The Principle of Moments (1983) gave him the hit 'Big Log'. Now and Zen (1988) brought Jimmy Page back as a guest, and Fate of Nations (1993) turned toward folk and acoustic colours with Nigel Kennedy and Richard Thompson. After the Page & Plant years he formed Strange Sensation (Mighty ReArranger, 2005), mixing North African and electronic sounds, and in 2007 made Raising Sand with bluegrass singer Alison Krauss and producer T Bone Burnett, which won the Grammy for Album of the Year. Later bands include Band of Joy and the Sensational Space Shifters.
grp.robert-plant.dna: The high Zeppelin wail softened into a reflective, often hushed voice; restless searching through folk, blues, North African music and Americana rather than a return to hard rock.
grp.robert-plant.uyeler: Robert Plant (vocals); collaborators include Robbie Blunt, Paul Martinez, Jezz Woodroffe, Phil Collins, Cozy Powell, Barriemore Barlow, Doug Boyle, Phil Johnstone, Chris Blackwell, Kevin Scott MacMichael, Justin Adams, Skin Tyson, John Baggott, Billy Fuller, Clive Deamer, Alison Krauss, T Bone Burnett.
grp.robert-plant.gecisler: Phil Collins (Genesis) drums on his first two albums, with Cozy Powell (Rainbow, ELP) and Barriemore Barlow (Jethro Tull) on a few tracks; Doug Boyle, later of Caravan, plays guitar on Now and Zen; Chris Hughes (Tears for Fears) produced Fate of Nations. John Baggott and Clive Deamer came from the Portishead circle.
grp.robert-plant.etki: Plant showed that a hard-rock singer could age into a curious, genre-crossing artist; Raising Sand introduced him to a whole new audience in folk and Americana.
grp.robert-plant.ipucu: The Principle of Moments shows the eighties sound with Phil Collins on drums.
Fate of Nations is the folk-flavoured bridge to his later work.
Raising Sand, with Alison Krauss, is the most praised album of his solo career.
alb.robert-plant-1982-pictures-at-eleven: His first solo album, released on Zeppelin's Swan Song label; Phil Collins plays drums on most tracks.
Plant, Robbie Blunt, Paul Martinez, Jezz Woodroffe, Phil Collins; Cozy Powell (drums on two tracks)
alb.robert-plant-1983-the-principle-of-m: Atmospheric eighties rock; 'Big Log' became his first solo hit.
Plant, Robbie Blunt, Paul Martinez, Jezz Woodroffe, Phil Collins; Barriemore Barlow (drums on two tracks)
alb.robert-plant-1988-now-and-zen.an: A bold, keyboard-heavy album; Jimmy Page plays the solos on 'Heaven Knows' and 'Tall Cool One', which samples Zeppelin riffs.
alb.robert-plant-1988-now-and-zen.kadro: Plant, Doug Boyle, Phil Johnstone, Phil Scragg, Chris Blackwell; Jimmy Page (guitar on two tracks)
alb.robert-plant-1988-now-and-zen.prod: Robert Plant, Tim Palmer, Phil Johnstone
alb.robert-plant-1993-fate-of-nations.an: Folk and acoustic colours with guests Nigel Kennedy and Richard Thompson; 'I Believe' is written for his late son.
alb.robert-plant-1993-fate-of-nations.ka: Plant, Kevin Scott MacMichael, Phil Johnstone, Charlie Jones, Chris Hughes; Nigel Kennedy (violin), Richard Thompson (guitar), Máire Brennan (vocals)
His strongest rock album since Zeppelin: North African grooves, electronics and blues with the Strange Sensation.
Plant and the Strange Sensation: Justin Adams, Skin Tyson, John Baggott, Billy Fuller, Clive Deamer
alb.robert-plant-2007-raising-sand.an: Duets with bluegrass singer Alison Krauss on songs by others; won the Grammy for Album of the Year.
alb.robert-plant-2007-raising-sand.oncel: Recommended — far from prog, but the peak of his solo career.
alb.robert-plant-2007-raising-sand.kadro: Plant, Alison Krauss, Marc Ribot, Dennis Crouch, Jay Bellerose, Norman Blake, T Bone Burnett
sec.3.intro: The late-sixties bands that stretched rock into longer forms, classical quotation, theatre and poetry before 'progressive rock' had a name: The Nice, Procol Harum, the Moody Blues, Arthur Brown, Pearls Before Swine, Aphrodite's Child and, from Los Angeles, The Doors.
sec.20.title: The Zappa Universe — Composers, Freaks and Virtuosos
sec.20.intro: Frank Zappa ran the longest-lasting school of virtuoso players in rock. Musicians who passed through his bands turn up all over the network: Adrian Belew (King Crimson), Terry Bozzio and Eddie Jobson (UK), Chester Thompson (Genesis on stage), Steve Vai and Aynsley Dunbar. Alongside Zappa in this section: his school friend Captain Beefheart and the violinist Jean-Luc Ponty (from Zappa to the Mahavishnu Orchestra).
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.name: McDonald and Giles
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.kurulus: 1970, London. Ian McDonald (reeds, keyboards, guitar) and Michael Giles (drums) left King Crimson at the end of the first US tour in December 1969 and made one album together.
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.hikaye: McDonald and Giles had written and played much of In the Court of the Crimson King, but both were exhausted by touring and uneasy with the darker direction Fripp wanted. They left within weeks of each other; Giles still played on In the Wake of Poseidon as a session musician. Their only album, McDonald and Giles (1971, Island), is the pastoral, melodic road Crimson did not take: Peter Giles on bass, Steve Winwood guesting on organ and piano, and Michael Blakesley on trombone. It sold modestly and the duo never toured. McDonald co-founded Foreigner in 1976; Michael Giles became a session drummer and, with McDonald, Mel Collins and Peter Giles, later played in the 21st Century Schizoid Band (2002–04).
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.dna: Gentle, English pastoral songwriting with jazz-tinged arrangements: flutes, saxophones and Mellotron, Giles's busy, melodic drumming, and a side-long suite ('Birdman') that recalls the long forms of the Crimson debut without its menace.
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.uyeler: Ian McDonald (saxophones, flute, keyboards, guitar, vocals), Michael Giles (drums, percussion, vocals), Peter Giles (bass); guests Steve Winwood (organ, piano), Michael Blakesley (trombone).
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.gecisler: King Crimson (1969) → McDonald and Giles (1970–71) → Ian McDonald to Foreigner (1976–79); Michael Giles to session work (Kevin Ayers, Anthony Phillips). Peter Giles had been in Giles, Giles and Fripp with Michael and Robert Fripp. All three reunite in the 21st Century Schizoid Band.
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.etki: A cult album that shows how much of the first King Crimson's melodic warmth came from McDonald; its suite form and pastoral tone sit close to early Genesis and Camel.
grp.mcdonald-and-giles.ipucu: Hear 'Flight of the Ibis' next to Crimson's 'Cadence and Cascade' — the same melody grew into two songs.
'Birdman' is the side-long suite: listen to it as the gentle twin of '21st Century Schizoid Man'.
alb.mcdonald-and-giles-1971-mcdonald-and: The only album by the two departed King Crimson founders: pastoral songs, jazzy horns and the side-long 'Birdman' suite.
Ian McDonald, Michael Giles, Peter Giles + Steve Winwood, Michael Blakesley
'Flight of the Ibis' uses the same melody as King Crimson's 'Cadence and Cascade', with different lyrics.
grp.peter-sinfield.name: Peter Sinfield
grp.peter-sinfield.kurulus: 1943–2024, London. Lyricist and lighting designer of the first King Crimson (1969–71); a band member who did not play an instrument on stage.
grp.peter-sinfield.hikaye: Sinfield met Ian McDonald in the late sixties and became King Crimson's lyricist, light-show operator and, increasingly, studio co-producer: the words of '21st Century Schizoid Man', 'Epitaph', 'In the Court of the Crimson King' and the Lizard suite are his. Fripp dismissed him at the end of 1971. He produced Roxy Music's first album (1972), wrote lyrics for Emerson, Lake & Palmer (Brain Salad Surgery, Works) and the English words for PFM's Photos of Ghosts, and recorded one solo album, Still (1973), on ELP's Manticore label. In the eighties he became a successful pop songwriter (Bucks Fizz's 'The Land of Make Believe', Celine Dion's 'Think Twice').
grp.peter-sinfield.dna: Mythic, image-heavy lyrics — jesters, courts, cardinals and seasons — set by Sinfield himself on Still to gentle folk-jazz arrangements with the Crimson horn players.
grp.peter-sinfield.uyeler: Peter Sinfield (vocals, lyrics). On Still: Greg Lake, Mel Collins, Boz Burrell, Ian Wallace and other Crimson-circle players.
grp.peter-sinfield.gecisler: King Crimson (1969–71) → Roxy Music (producer of the debut) → ELP and PFM (lyrics) → pop songwriting. Still was released on ELP's Manticore label with Greg Lake singing the title track.
grp.peter-sinfield.etki: Sinfield's words fixed the imagery of early prog — the medieval, mystical and apocalyptic register that Genesis, Yes and countless later bands echoed.
grp.peter-sinfield.ipucu: Read the lyrics of 'Epitaph' and 'Lizard' before listening to Still: it is the same poetic voice, now singing for himself.
Listen for Mel Collins and Boz Burrell: Still is the sound of the Islands-era Crimson without Fripp.
alb.peter-sinfield-1973-still.an: The lyricist's only solo album, on ELP's Manticore label: folk-jazz songs with the Islands-era Crimson players, and Greg Lake singing the title track.
alb.peter-sinfield-1973-still.kadro: Sinfield + Greg Lake, Mel Collins, Boz Burrell, Ian Wallace and others
alb.peter-sinfield-1973-still.tr: The Song of the Sea Goat
grp.adrian-belew.name: Adrian Belew (solo and Power Trio)
grp.adrian-belew.kurulus: Born 1949 in Covington, Kentucky. A drummer turned guitarist, discovered by Frank Zappa in a Nashville club in 1977.
grp.adrian-belew.hikaye: Zappa hired Belew for his 1977–78 band (Sheik Yerbouti); David Bowie took him straight from Zappa for the Stage/Lodger tour, and he then joined Talking Heads' expanded band around Remain in Light. In 1981 Robert Fripp made him singer, second guitarist and lyricist of the new King Crimson (Discipline, Beat, Three of a Perfect Pair), a role he kept through the double-trio and ProjeKct years until 2009. Alongside Crimson he ran a solo career from Lone Rhino (1982) and the pop band The Bears, and played on records by Paul Simon (Graceland) and Nine Inch Nails. Side One (2005) brought in Les Claypool and Tool's Danny Carey; the Adrian Belew Power Trio with siblings Julie and Eric Slick (later Tobias Ralph) toured from 2006 and joined Stick Men as the Crimson ProjeKCt (2011–14).
grp.adrian-belew.dna: The guitar as a sound-effects machine and as a pop voice at once: elephant trumpets, seagulls and car horns from pedals and guitar synthesizer, Beatles-inspired melodies and wordplay, and sudden Crimson-style interlocking patterns.
grp.adrian-belew.uyeler: Adrian Belew (guitar, vocals, drums, most instruments on many solo albums). Power Trio: Julie Slick (bass), Eric Slick, later Tobias Ralph (drums). Collaborators: Les Claypool, Danny Carey; The Bears: Rob Fetters, Bob Nyswonger, Chris Arduser.
grp.adrian-belew.gecisler: Frank Zappa (1977–78) → David Bowie (1978) → Talking Heads (1980–81) → King Crimson (1981–2009) → Power Trio and the Crimson ProjeKCt with Stick Men (Tony Levin, Pat Mastelotto, Markus Reuter). Guest on Porcupine Tree's Deadwing.
grp.adrian-belew.etki: Belew made noise and effects musical rather than decorative; with Fripp's patterns he defined the eighties Crimson sound that fed straight into Tool, the math-rock bands and the modern prog metal guitar.
grp.adrian-belew.ipucu: Start with Lone Rhino: 'Big Electric Cat' is the elephant guitar at its most fun.
Side One shows him with Tool's drummer — a direct line from Crimson to modern heavy prog.
On e, the Power Trio plays a five-part instrumental suite: Belew's most 'prog' solo record.
alb.adrian-belew-1982-lone-rhino.an: The first solo album, made during the Discipline era: playful songs, animal-sound guitars and short instrumental sketches.
alb.adrian-belew-1982-lone-rhino.kadro: Belew and the Illinois band GaGa
alb.adrian-belew-1983-twang-bar-king.an: A more song-based follow-up that includes a cover of the Beatles' 'I'm Down'.
alb.adrian-belew-1990-young-lions.an: His most polished pop album, with two Bowie collaborations including the duet 'Pretty Pink Rose' and a version of Crimson's 'Heartbeat'.
alb.adrian-belew-2005-side-one.an: The first of three short 'Side' records: heavy, compact pieces with Primus's Les Claypool and Tool's Danny Carey.
alb.adrian-belew-2009-e.an: An instrumental suite in five parts for the Power Trio: knotty riffs and tight interplay in the spirit of nineties Crimson.
alb.adrian-belew-2009-e.kadro: Adrian Belew Power Trio: Belew, Julie Slick, Eric Slick
grp.tony-levin.name: Tony Levin (solo and projects)
grp.tony-levin.kurulus: Born 1946 near Boston. A classically trained double bassist who became one of New York's busiest session players in the seventies.
grp.tony-levin.hikaye: Levin studied at the Eastman School of Music and moved into New York session work alongside drummer Steve Gadd: Paul Simon, Alice Cooper (Welcome to My Nightmare), John Lennon and Yoko Ono (Double Fantasy) and hundreds of others. Producer Bob Ezrin brought him to Peter Gabriel's first solo album in 1977, and he has played in Gabriel's band ever since. In 1981 he joined the new King Crimson with Fripp, Belew and Bruford, introducing the Chapman Stick to the band; he returned for the double trio and most later line-ups up to 2021. He played on ABWH (1989) and Pink Floyd's A Momentary Lapse of Reason, formed Bruford Levin Upper Extremities with Bill Bruford, David Torn and Chris Botti and Liquid Tension Experiment with Dream Theater members (both 1998), and since 2010 leads Stick Men. His solo albums began with World Diary (1995); he is also a photographer and author of tour diaries.
grp.tony-levin.dna: Bass as a melodic lead voice: Chapman Stick tapping, the NS electric upright and the 'funk fingers' (cut-down drumsticks strapped to his fingers), always in service of the groove and with a session player's economy.
grp.tony-levin.uyeler: Tony Levin (bass, Chapman Stick, NS upright, vocals). Partners on his projects: Larry Fast, Jerry Marotta, Jesse Gress, Pete Levin, David Torn, Bill Bruford, Chris Botti, Alan White, Marco Minnemann, Jordan Rudess, Pat Mastelotto, Markus Reuter.
grp.tony-levin.gecisler: Session work (Paul Simon, Lennon, Alice Cooper) → Peter Gabriel (1977–) → King Crimson (1981–84, 1994–99, 2008, 2014–21) → ABWH (1989) → Bruford Levin Upper Extremities and Liquid Tension Experiment (1998) → Stick Men and the Crimson ProjeKCt. Also on records by Pink Floyd, Steven Wilson, Steve Hackett and Yes-family musicians.
grp.tony-levin.etki: He made the Stick and the funk fingers part of the prog vocabulary and links more nodes of this atlas than any other bassist: Crimson, Gabriel's Genesis orbit, Yes (ABWH), Pink Floyd and modern prog metal.
grp.tony-levin.ipucu: Start with Bruford Levin Upper Extremities: the Crimson rhythm section of the nineties, without Fripp.
Waters of Eden shows the melodic, almost ambient side of his own writing.
Levin Minnemann Rudess is the bridge to Liquid Tension Experiment and Dream Theater.
alb.tony-levin-1998-bruford-levin-upper-: The Crimson rhythm section with David Torn's looped guitar and Chris Botti's trumpet: dark, textured and partly improvised.
Bill Bruford, Tony Levin, David Torn, Chris Botti
alb.tony-levin-2000-waters-of-eden.an: His most melodic solo album: bass-led, quietly atmospheric pieces with Gabriel colleagues Larry Fast and Jerry Marotta.
alb.tony-levin-2000-waters-of-eden.kadro: Levin + Larry Fast, Jerry Marotta, Jesse Gress and guests
alb.tony-levin-2002-pieces-of-the-sun.an: The touring Tony Levin Band in the studio: heavier, riff-driven instrumental prog with Stick and keyboards to the fore.
alb.tony-levin-2002-pieces-of-the-sun.ka: Levin, Larry Fast, Jerry Marotta, Jesse Gress, Pete Levin
alb.tony-levin-2011-levin-torn-white.an: A trio with David Torn and Yes drummer Alan White: long improvised grooves shaped afterwards in the studio.
alb.tony-levin-2011-levin-torn-white.kad: Tony Levin, David Torn, Alan White
alb.tony-levin-2011-levin-torn-white.pro: Tony Levin, David Torn, Alan White
alb.tony-levin-2013-levin-minnemann-rude: An instrumental power trio with Marco Minnemann and Dream Theater's Jordan Rudess, close to the Liquid Tension Experiment sound.
Tony Levin, Marco Minnemann, Jordan Rudess
Tony Levin, Marco Minnemann, Jordan Rudess
grp.patrick-moraz.name: Patrick Moraz (solo and Mainhorse)
grp.patrick-moraz.kurulus: Born 1948 in Morges, Switzerland. A classically trained pianist from the jazz clubs who formed Mainhorse in 1969 and moved to London.
grp.patrick-moraz.hikaye: After the single Mainhorse album (1971) Moraz formed Refugee with the Nice's Lee Jackson and Brian Davison (1974). Within months Yes chose him to replace Rick Wakeman: Relayer (1974), with its jazz-fusion edge and 'The Gates of Delirium', is his Yes album. During the 1975 solo-album year he made The Story of I, recorded with Brazilian percussionists and American fusion players, and he left Yes when Wakeman returned in 1976. After Out in the Sun (1977) he joined the Moody Blues (1978–91: Long Distance Voyager to Sur la Mer). With Bill Bruford he recorded two piano-and-drums duet albums (1983, 1985), and he has since released many solo piano and keyboard records.
grp.patrick-moraz.dna: Virtuoso, percussive keyboard playing that mixes classical technique, jazz harmony and Latin and Brazilian rhythm; bright synthesizer leads and fast, cascading piano lines.
grp.patrick-moraz.uyeler: Patrick Moraz (keyboards, piano, synthesizers). Mainhorse: Peter Lockett, Jean Ristori, Bryson Graham. Duo partner: Bill Bruford.
grp.patrick-moraz.gecisler: Mainhorse (1969–71) → Refugee (1974) → Yes (1974–76) → solo → Moody Blues (1978–91) → Moraz–Bruford duets (1983–85). Mainhorse drummer Bryson Graham later played with Spooky Tooth.
grp.patrick-moraz.etki: The bridge between Yes and the Moody Blues, and one of the few keyboardists of the era to bring Brazilian rhythm into symphonic rock.
grp.patrick-moraz.ipucu: Hear Relayer first, then The Story of I: the same restless energy, now with a samba school behind it.
Music for Piano and Drums shows Bruford and Moraz at their most playful — acoustic piano against electronic drums.
alb.patrick-moraz-1971-mainhorse.an: The Swiss-British quartet's only album: Hammond-led heavy prog in the Nice and early ELP mould.
alb.patrick-moraz-1971-mainhorse.kadro: Patrick Moraz, Peter Lockett, Jean Ristori, Bryson Graham
alb.patrick-moraz-1976-the-story-of-i.an: A continuous concept album recorded during his Yes years, mixing symphonic synthesizers with Brazilian percussion.
alb.patrick-moraz-1976-the-story-of-i.ka: Moraz + Brazilian percussionists and fusion players
alb.patrick-moraz-1977-out-in-the-sun.an: Shorter, sunnier pieces after leaving Yes; a lighter jazz-rock record.
alb.patrick-moraz-1983-music-for-piano-a: Duets for acoustic piano and Bruford's acoustic and electronic drums: composed pieces with plenty of improvisation.
alb.patrick-moraz-1985-flags.an: The second Moraz–Bruford duet album, with more synthesizer and electronic percussion.
grp.trevor-rabin.name: Trevor Rabin (solo and ARW)
grp.trevor-rabin.kurulus: Born 1954 in Johannesburg. Guitarist, singer and songwriter of the South African band Rabbitt before a solo career in London and Los Angeles.
grp.trevor-rabin.hikaye: Rabbitt were teen stars in South Africa in the mid-seventies; Rabin then moved to London, released three solo albums (1978–81) and produced others. In 1982 he formed Cinema with Chris Squire and Alan White; when Jon Anderson joined, the project became Yes again and released 90125 (1983), with Rabin's 'Owner of a Lonely Heart' as the band's only US number one. He wrote and sang much of Big Generator, Union and Talk, and released the solo Can't Look Away (1989) in between. After Yes (1994) he became a prolific film composer (Con Air, Armageddon, Remember the Titans, National Treasure). The instrumental Jacaranda (2012) marked his return to records, and from 2016 he toured with Jon Anderson and Rick Wakeman as ARW (Yes Featuring ARW).
grp.trevor-rabin.dna: Big, layered guitar arrangements with eighties studio gloss, strong pop hooks, multi-tracked vocal harmonies and a virtuoso streak that ranges from country picking to orchestral writing.
grp.trevor-rabin.uyeler: Trevor Rabin (guitar, vocals, keyboards, bass). ARW: Jon Anderson, Rick Wakeman, Lee Pomeroy, Lou Molino III.
grp.trevor-rabin.gecisler: Rabbitt → solo (1978–81) → Cinema → Yes (1983–94) → film scoring → ARW (2016–18). Cinema itself was Squire and White's project after XYZ with Jimmy Page.
grp.trevor-rabin.etki: Rabin's 90125 sound brought Yes to MTV and a new generation; his production style shaped late-eighties AOR prog and bands such as World Trade.
grp.trevor-rabin.ipucu: Can't Look Away is the 'missing' Yes album between Big Generator and Union.
Jacaranda shows the guitarist without vocals: bebop, bluegrass and rock in one record.
Live at the Apollo puts Rabin's Yes songs next to the seventies classics.
alb.trevor-rabin-1989-can-t-look-away.an: Glossy, hook-filled AOR prog in the 90125 manner, made between Big Generator and Union.
alb.trevor-rabin-2012-jacaranda.an: An instrumental guitar album after years of film work: jazz, bluegrass and rock side by side.
alb.trevor-rabin-2012-jacaranda.kadro: Rabin + Vinnie Colaiuta, Lou Molino III, Tal Wilkenfeld, Liz Constantine and others
alb.trevor-rabin-2018-live-at-the-apollo: Yes Featuring ARW live in Manchester: seventies classics and the Rabin-era hits played by three former Yes members.
Jon Anderson, Trevor Rabin, Rick Wakeman, Lee Pomeroy, Lou Molino III
Make It Easy / Owner of a Lonely Heart
alb.trevor-rabin-2023-rio.an: His first vocal solo album in 34 years: melodic rock, a touch of his South African youth and big guitar arrangements.
grp.billy-sherwood.name: Billy Sherwood (Conspiracy, Circa, solo)
grp.billy-sherwood.kurulus: Born 1965 in Las Vegas. Multi-instrumentalist and producer who co-founded World Trade (1989) and became Chris Squire's closest collaborator.
grp.billy-sherwood.hikaye: Sherwood met Yes during the Union sessions (1991) and became a co-writer and touring guitarist and keyboardist (Open Your Eyes, The Ladder, 1997–2000). With Squire he formed Conspiracy (2000), and with Tony Kaye and Alan White the band Circa (2007). He has produced and played on many tribute and progressive projects, and released solo albums such as Citizen (2015), whose guest list reads like a Yes family tree. Before his death in 2015, Squire asked him to take over as Yes's bassist; Sherwood has played bass with Yes since then (Heaven & Earth tour, Fly from Here – Return Trip, The Quest).
grp.billy-sherwood.dna: Squire-style melodic bass and stacked vocal harmonies, polished rock production and long-form songs that look back to classic Yes.
grp.billy-sherwood.uyeler: Billy Sherwood (bass, guitar, keyboards, vocals). Conspiracy: Chris Squire. Circa: Tony Kaye, Alan White (later Scott Connor), Jimmy Haun, Ricky Tierney.
grp.billy-sherwood.gecisler: Lodgic → World Trade (1989) → Yes (1997–2000, and bassist from 2015) → Conspiracy with Chris Squire → Circa with Tony Kaye and Alan White Also produced the 'Prog Collective' records with many Yes-family guests.
grp.billy-sherwood.etki: Sherwood is the thread that keeps the Yes family connected: the producer of its side projects and the heir to Squire's role.
grp.billy-sherwood.ipucu: Conspiracy (2000, with Chris Squire) is the root of the later Yes partnership.
Circa: 2007 is a mini-Yes with two original members (Kaye and White).
Citizen: count the guests — almost every Yes era is represented.
alb.billy-sherwood-2007-circa-2007.an: The first album by Circa, with Yes founder Tony Kaye on Hammond and Alan White on drums.
alb.billy-sherwood-2007-circa-2007.kadro: Billy Sherwood, Tony Kaye, Alan White, Jimmy Haun
alb.billy-sherwood-2015-citizen.an: A concept album about a soul travelling through history, with a different Yes-family guest on almost every track; one of Chris Squire's last recordings.
alb.billy-sherwood-2015-citizen.kadro: Sherwood + Chris Squire, Steve Hackett, Rick Wakeman, Tony Kaye, Patrick Moraz, Geoff Downes, Jon Davison and others
grp.keith-emerson.name: Keith Emerson (solo and film music)
grp.keith-emerson.kurulus: 1944–2016. Born in Todmorden, grew up in Worthing. Founder of The Nice (1967) and Emerson, Lake & Palmer (1970).
grp.keith-emerson.hikaye: Emerson made the Hammond organ a stage spectacle with The Nice — knives in the keys, the instrument thrown and dragged — and brought the giant Moog modular synthesizer to rock audiences with ELP. When ELP split in 1979 he turned to film music: Dario Argento's Inferno (1980), the Stallone thriller Nighthawks (1981), the Italian film Honky and several Japanese productions. He reunited with Greg Lake and Cozy Powell (Emerson, Lake & Powell, 1986), with Carl Palmer in 3 (1988), with the full ELP (1991–98, 2010) and with The Nice (2002). Later projects included the Keith Emerson Band with guitarist Marc Bonilla and the orchestral Three Fates Project (2012). He died in Santa Monica in March 2016.
grp.keith-emerson.dna: Virtuoso keyboards that fuse Bach, Bartók, Ginastera, boogie-woogie, jazz and the blues; Hammond grind and percussive Moog leads; a showman's love of fanfare and orchestral scale.
grp.keith-emerson.uyeler: Keith Emerson (keyboards). Frequent partners: Greg Lake, Carl Palmer, Cozy Powell, Marc Bonilla, Lee Jackson, Brian Davison, the Munich Radio Orchestra (Terje Mikkelsen).
grp.keith-emerson.gecisler: The V.I.P.'s and Gary Farr & the T-Bones → The Nice (1967–70) → ELP (1970–79) → film music → Emerson, Lake & Powell (1986) → 3 (1988) → ELP reunions → Keith Emerson Band / Three Fates Project.
grp.keith-emerson.etki: Every keyboard hero of prog — Wakeman, Jobson, Rudess, Moraz, Downes — measured himself against Emerson. His film scores carried the ELP language into horror and action cinema.
grp.keith-emerson.ipucu: Inferno is the best entry: a full prog album disguised as a horror soundtrack.
Compare 'Abaddon's Bolero' on ELP's Trilogy with its orchestral version on Changing States.
