Nighthawks shows how the ELP language works in an action thriller.
alb.keith-emerson-1980-inferno.an: The score for Dario Argento's horror film: dark choral passages, Verdi quotations and full ELP-style keyboard workouts.
alb.keith-emerson-1981-nighthawks.an: The thriller score for Sylvester Stallone's Nighthawks: synthesizers and big-band brass in an early-eighties style.
alb.keith-emerson-1981-honky.an: A light, holiday-mood album recorded in the Bahamas: calypso, boogie and a Bach arrangement side by side.
alb.keith-emerson-1995-changing-states.a: Material recorded around 1989–90: synthesizer pieces, an orchestral 'Abaddon's Bolero' and Prokofiev's 'Montagues and Capulets'.
alb.keith-emerson-1995-changing-states.k: Emerson + Kevin Gilbert and others, with orchestra
grp.tony-banks.name: Tony Banks (solo and orchestral works)
grp.tony-banks.kurulus: Born 1950 in East Hoathly, Sussex. Genesis's keyboardist and principal composer from the band's beginnings at Charterhouse school (1967) to its end.
grp.tony-banks.hikaye: Banks wrote or co-wrote most of Genesis's long pieces, from 'The Fountain of Salmacis' and 'Firth of Fifth' to 'One for the Vine' and 'Domino'. He was the first member of the trio-era band to make a solo album: A Curious Feeling (1979), loosely based on Daniel Keyes's Flowers for Algernon and sung by Kim Beacon of String Driven Thing. On The Fugitive (1983) he sang himself; he also scored films such as The Wicked Lady (1983) and Quicksilver (1986). Later rock albums used guest singers (Bankstatement, 1989; Still, 1991, with Nik Kershaw and Fish; Strictly Inc., 1995). From the 2000s he has concentrated on orchestral music: Seven (2004), Six Pieces for Orchestra (2012) and Five (2018).
grp.tony-banks.dna: Rich, romantic chord progressions and slowly unfolding melodies; piano, Mellotron and polysynth layers; a composer's sense of long form even in four-minute songs.
grp.tony-banks.uyeler: Tony Banks (keyboards, guitar, vocals). Guests: Kim Beacon, Chester Thompson, Daryl Stuermer, Nik Kershaw, Fish, Jayney Klimek, Jack Hues; the London Philharmonic Orchestra (Seven).
grp.tony-banks.gecisler: Garden Wall (school band with Peter Gabriel) → Genesis (1967–2000s) → solo and film music → orchestral works. Kim Beacon came from String Driven Thing, whose violinist Graham Smith later played with Van der Graaf Generator.
grp.tony-banks.etki: Banks's harmonic language is the core of the Genesis sound and of the whole neo-prog keyboard tradition (Mark Kelly, Clive Nolan, Martin Orford).
grp.tony-banks.ipucu: A Curious Feeling is the closest thing to a 'lost' trio-era Genesis album — start there.
On Seven, listen for the melodic turns you know from 'Firth of Fifth' and 'Afterglow', now for orchestra.
alb.tony-banks-1979-a-curious-feeling.an: His first solo album, a loose concept based on Flowers for Algernon: melodic, keyboard-rich songs and instrumentals in the And Then There Were Three style.
alb.tony-banks-1983-the-fugitive.an: Banks sings his own songs: shorter, synth-driven pieces in the mould of early-eighties Genesis.
alb.tony-banks-1983-the-fugitive.kadro: Banks (vocals, keyboards) + Daryl Stuermer, Mo Foster, Steve Gadd and others
alb.tony-banks-1991-still.an: Songs for guest singers, including two with Fish; polished and melancholic.
alb.tony-banks-1991-still.kadro: Banks + Nik Kershaw, Fish, Jayney Klimek and others
alb.tony-banks-2004-seven-a-suite-for-or: His first orchestral work: seven movements that carry the Genesis melodic style into a late-romantic symphonic setting.
London Philharmonic Orchestra, cond. Mike Dixon
grp.mike-rutherford.name: Mike Rutherford (solo and Mike + The Mechanics)
grp.mike-rutherford.kurulus: Born 1950 in Surrey. Genesis co-founder at Charterhouse; bassist and 12-string guitarist, then lead guitarist after Steve Hackett left.
grp.mike-rutherford.hikaye: Rutherford's first solo album, Smallcreep's Day (1980), turned Peter Currell Brown's novel about a factory worker into a side-long suite, with Anthony Phillips on keyboards, Simon Phillips on drums and Noel McCalla singing. He sang himself on Acting Very Strange (1982). In 1985 he formed Mike + The Mechanics with singers Paul Carrack and Paul Young, producer Christopher Neil and keyboardist Adrian Lee; 'Silent Running' and 'All I Need Is a Miracle' were hits, and 'The Living Years' (1988), about his late father, reached number one in the United States. The Mechanics continued with new singers (Andrew Roachford, Tim Howar) after Paul Young's death in 2000.
grp.mike-rutherford.dna: On Smallcreep's Day, twelve-string textures and long-form Genesis writing; with the Mechanics, warm, well-crafted adult pop-rock carried by two soul singers.
grp.mike-rutherford.uyeler: Mike Rutherford (guitar, bass, vocals). Mike + The Mechanics: Paul Carrack, Paul Young, Adrian Lee, Peter Van Hooke; later Andrew Roachford, Tim Howar. On Smallcreep's Day: Anthony Phillips, Simon Phillips, Morris Pert, Noel McCalla.
grp.mike-rutherford.gecisler: Anon → Genesis (1967–) → solo → Mike + The Mechanics (1985–). Paul Carrack came from Ace, Roxy Music's touring band and Squeeze; Paul Young from Sad Café.
grp.mike-rutherford.etki: The Mechanics showed how far the Genesis songwriting craft could reach in the pop market; Smallcreep's Day is a key late-seventies English concept suite.
grp.mike-rutherford.ipucu: Side one of Smallcreep's Day is the prog listener's door: a 25-minute suite in seven parts.
'The Living Years' and Genesis's 'Driving the Last Spike' show the two sides of Rutherford's storytelling.
alb.mike-rutherford-1980-smallcreep-s-da: A side-long suite based on Peter Currell Brown's novel, with Anthony Phillips on keyboards; the most 'Genesis' of the members' solo records.
Rutherford + Anthony Phillips, Simon Phillips, Morris Pert, Noel McCalla (vocals)
alb.mike-rutherford-1985-mike-the-mechan: The debut of his pop-rock band: 'Silent Running' and 'All I Need Is a Miracle' became international hits.
Rutherford, Paul Carrack, Paul Young, Adrian Lee, Peter Van Hooke
All I Need Is a Miracle
alb.mike-rutherford-1988-living-years.an: The second Mechanics album; the title song, about the death of Rutherford's father, reached number one in the US.
alb.mike-rutherford-1988-living-years.ka: Rutherford, Paul Carrack, Paul Young, Adrian Lee, Peter Van Hooke
grp.eddie-jobson.name: Eddie Jobson (solo, Zinc, UKZ)
grp.eddie-jobson.kurulus: Born 1955 in Billingham, County Durham. A teenage violin and keyboard prodigy who replaced Darryl Way in Curved Air in 1972.
grp.eddie-jobson.hikaye: After Curved Air's Air Cut (1973) Jobson replaced Brian Eno in Roxy Music (Stranded, Country Life, Siren), then toured with Frank Zappa (1976). In 1978 he co-founded UK with John Wetton, Bill Bruford and Allan Holdsworth, continuing as a trio with Terry Bozzio. He guested on Jethro Tull's A (1980) and toured with them, then released The Green Album (1983) under the band name Zinc and the Synclavier-based Theme of Secrets (1985) before spending two decades mainly writing television and library music. He returned in 2008–09 with the UKZ project (Trey Gunn, Marco Minnemann, Alex Machacek, Aaron Lippert), the Ultimate Zero tours and a UK reunion with Wetton (2011–15).
grp.eddie-jobson.dna: Electric violin — often his transparent Plexiglas instrument — against cool synthesizer textures; classical precision, odd-meter riffs and an icy, cinematic sense of space.
grp.eddie-jobson.uyeler: Eddie Jobson (violin, keyboards, vocals). Zinc: session players. UKZ: Trey Gunn, Marco Minnemann, Alex Machacek, Aaron Lippert.
grp.eddie-jobson.gecisler: Curved Air (1972–73) → Roxy Music (1973–76) → Frank Zappa (1976) → UK (1978–80) → Jethro Tull (1980) → solo, TV music → UKZ / UK reunion (2009–15).
grp.eddie-jobson.etki: Jobson is the network's great connector: nine nodes of this atlas (Curved Air, Roxy Music, Zappa, UK, Jethro Tull, Bruford, King Crimson, John Wetton) meet in his career; with Ponty and Darryl Way he made the violin a lead prog instrument.
grp.eddie-jobson.ipucu: Hear his violin on UK's 'In the Dead of Night' first.
Theme of Secrets is quiet, ambient Synclavier music — a world away from UK, and closer to Eno's Roxy than you might expect.
alb.eddie-jobson-1985-theme-of-secrets.a: An almost entirely Synclavier-made album of calm, ambient pieces for the Private Music label.
alb.eddie-jobson-2009-radiation.an: The EP of his UKZ project: dense, heavy modern prog with Crimson's Trey Gunn on Warr guitar.
alb.eddie-jobson-2009-radiation.kadro: UKZ: Jobson, Trey Gunn, Marco Minnemann, Alex Machacek, Aaron Lippert
grp.allan-holdsworth.name: Allan Holdsworth
grp.allan-holdsworth.kurulus: 1946–2017. Born in Bradford. A largely self-taught guitarist whose sound began as an attempt to make the guitar phrase like a saxophone.
grp.allan-holdsworth.hikaye: Holdsworth moved through the British jazz-rock scene of the early seventies: Igginbottom, Ian Carr's Nucleus (Belladonna), Jon Hiseman's Tempest, Soft Machine (Bundles, 1975), Tony Williams's New Lifetime, Gong (Gazeuse!) and Jean-Luc Ponty (Enigmatic Ocean). In 1978 he played on Bill Bruford's Feels Good to Me and in UK, then stayed with Bruford's band. He financed his first real solo album, I.O.U. (1982), himself; Eddie Van Halen's support led to the Road Games EP (1983). On Metal Fatigue, Atavachron and Sand he adopted the SynthAxe guitar synthesizer. He worked mostly with trios and quartets (Gary Husband, Jimmy Johnson, Chad Wackerman, Vinnie Colaiuta) and remained a musician's musician until his death in April 2017.
grp.allan-holdsworth.dna: Endless legato lines with hardly a picked note, wide intervals and unusual scales, chords voiced like a keyboard player's, and no blues clichés; in the eighties the SynthAxe gave his lines a breath-like, wind-instrument sound.
grp.allan-holdsworth.uyeler: Allan Holdsworth (guitar, SynthAxe). Bands: Paul Williams (vocals), Paul Carmichael, Jimmy Johnson, Jeff Berlin (bass), Gary Husband, Chad Wackerman, Vinnie Colaiuta (drums), Steve Hunt, Alan Pasqua (keyboards).
grp.allan-holdsworth.gecisler: Igginbottom → Nucleus → Tempest → Soft Machine (1975) → Tony Williams Lifetime → Gong (1976) → Jean-Luc Ponty (1977) → Bruford and UK (1978–79) → solo (1982–2017). Jack Bruce sang on Road Games.
grp.allan-holdsworth.etki: Eddie Van Halen, Joe Satriani, Steve Vai, John Petrucci and generations of prog-metal and fusion guitarists name him as the player who changed what the instrument could do.
grp.allan-holdsworth.ipucu: Hear him on Bruford's 'One of a Kind' and UK's 'In the Dead of Night' first.
Metal Fatigue is the most approachable solo record; Atavachron shows the SynthAxe sound.
Listen to the chords, not just the solos: his harmony is as distinctive as his speed.
alb.allan-holdsworth-1982-i-o-u.an: The self-financed first proper solo album: fusion songs with Paul Williams's vocals and long, flowing solos.
alb.allan-holdsworth-1982-i-o-u.kadro: Holdsworth, Paul Williams, Paul Carmichael, Gary Husband
alb.allan-holdsworth-1983-road-games.an: A six-track EP for Warner Bros., with Jack Bruce singing; a Grammy nominee.
alb.allan-holdsworth-1983-road-games.kad: Holdsworth, Jeff Berlin, Chad Wackerman, Jack Bruce, Paul Williams
His best-known album: the title track and 'Devil Take the Hindmost' are fusion-guitar landmarks.
Essential — the best door into his solo work.
Holdsworth, Paul Williams, Jimmy Johnson, Gary Husband, Chad Wackerman, Mark Fitzgerald
alb.allan-holdsworth-1986-atavachron.an: The first album with the SynthAxe; Tony Williams drums on one piece, closing the circle back to Lifetime.
alb.allan-holdsworth-1986-atavachron.kad: Holdsworth, Jimmy Johnson, Gary Husband, Chad Wackerman, Tony Williams, Alan Pasqua
alb.allan-holdsworth-1989-secrets.an: Warmer and more melodic, balancing guitar and SynthAxe.
alb.allan-holdsworth-1989-secrets.kadro: Holdsworth, Jimmy Johnson, Vinnie Colaiuta, Steve Hunt, Alan Pasqua and others
grp.richard-wright.name: Richard Wright (solo and Zee)
grp.richard-wright.kurulus: 1943–2008, London. Pink Floyd's founding keyboardist; he met Roger Waters and Nick Mason while studying architecture at the Regent Street Polytechnic.
grp.richard-wright.hikaye: Wright's Farfisa, Hammond and synthesizer textures and his harmonic sense shaped Pink Floyd from 'Paint Box' and 'Summer '68' to the music of 'The Great Gig in the Sky' and 'Us and Them'. His first solo album, Wet Dream (1978), was recorded in France with Snowy White and Mel Collins. During The Wall sessions Waters forced him out of the band; he played the Wall concerts as a salaried musician. In 1984 he made the synth-pop album Identity with Dave Harris of Fashion under the name Zee. He rejoined Gilmour and Mason for A Momentary Lapse of Reason (as a session player) and The Division Bell (as a member again), and released Broken China (1996), a song cycle about a loved one's depression and recovery, with Sinéad O'Connor on two songs. He toured with David Gilmour in 2006 (On an Island, Live in Gdańsk) and died in September 2008; The Endless River (2014) was built around his 1993–94 recordings.
grp.richard-wright.dna: Soft, modal harmony and slowly shifting chords; the Hammond and Farfisa sustain, string-synth pads and jazz-tinged voicings that are the 'atmosphere' of Pink Floyd.
grp.richard-wright.uyeler: Richard Wright (keyboards, vocals). On Wet Dream: Snowy White, Mel Collins, Larry Steele, Reg Isadore. Zee: Dave Harris. On Broken China: Dominic Miller, Pino Palladino, Manu Katché, Tim Renwick, Sinéad O'Connor, lyrics by Anthony Moore.
grp.richard-wright.gecisler: Sigma 6 / The Tea Set → Pink Floyd (1965–79) → solo and Zee → Pink Floyd (1987–2014) → David Gilmour's band (2006). Anthony Moore, his lyricist, came from Slapp Happy and Henry Cow.
grp.richard-wright.etki: The quiet harmonic heart of Pink Floyd — and, through them, of ambient, space rock and the Porcupine Tree generation.
grp.richard-wright.ipucu: Wet Dream sounds like Animals-era Floyd on holiday: start with 'Mediterranean C' and 'Summer Elegy'.
Broken China is a continuous cycle — listen in one sitting.
Then hear The Endless River as Gilmour and Mason's tribute to him.
alb.richard-wright-1978-wet-dream.an: A relaxed, melodic solo debut recorded in the south of France after Animals; Floyd-like textures with Mel Collins's saxophone.
alb.richard-wright-1978-wet-dream.kadro: Wright, Snowy White, Mel Collins, Larry Steele, Reg Isadore
alb.richard-wright-1984-identity.an: The one-off synth-pop duo Zee with Fashion's Dave Harris: Fairlight-driven eighties electronics that Wright later disowned.
alb.richard-wright-1996-broken-china.an: A continuous song cycle with lyrics by Anthony Moore; atmospheric, Division Bell-era sound.
alb.richard-wright-1996-broken-china.kad: Wright + Dominic Miller, Pino Palladino, Manu Katché, Tim Renwick, Sinéad O'Connor
alb.richard-wright-1996-broken-china.tr: Night of a Thousand Furry Toys
grp.jon-and-vangelis.name: Jon & Vangelis
grp.jon-and-vangelis.kurulus: 1979–1991. Yes singer Jon Anderson and the Greek composer Vangelis, friends since Vangelis's audition for Yes in 1974.
grp.jon-and-vangelis.hikaye: Vangelis nearly replaced Rick Wakeman in Yes in 1974; the friendship continued with Anderson singing on Vangelis's Heaven and Hell (1975, 'So Long Ago, So Clear'). After Anderson left Yes in 1980 the duo recorded Short Stories (1980), with the hit 'I Hear You Now', and The Friends of Mr Cairo (1981), with 'I'll Find My Way Home' and the film-noir title track. (Both albums are listed in this atlas under Jon Anderson's solo node.) Private Collection (1983) followed, including the 22-minute 'Horizon', and after a long pause Page of Life (1991). The method rarely changed: Vangelis improvised on his synthesizers and Anderson sang spontaneously over him, shaping the words later.
grp.jon-and-vangelis.dna: Warm analogue and Yamaha CS-80 synthesizer improvisation under Anderson's high, wordless and half-improvised singing; gentle pop songs next to long, drifting pieces.
grp.jon-and-vangelis.gecisler: Yes (Anderson) and Aphrodite's Child / solo career (Vangelis) → Jon & Vangelis (1979–91). Anderson also sang on Vangelis's Heaven and Hell (1975) and See You Later (1980).
grp.jon-and-vangelis.etki: A model of the synth-and-voice duo; its spontaneous working method anticipated much of the later new-age and ambient-pop sound.
grp.jon-and-vangelis.ipucu: Begin with 'I'll Find My Way Home' and 'State of Independence' (on the Anderson node), then go to 'Horizon'.
Listen for the CS-80 'brass' — the same instrument Vangelis used on Blade Runner.
alb.jon-and-vangelis-1983-private-collec: The third and most ambitious duo album, closing with the 22-minute 'Horizon'.
alb.jon-and-vangelis-1991-page-of-life.a: The last duo album, completed years after the sessions; softer and more new-age in tone.
grp.hugh-hopper.name: Hugh Hopper (solo, Soft Heap)
grp.hugh-hopper.kurulus: 1945–2009, Canterbury. Bassist and composer; with his brother Brian, Robert Wyatt and Kevin Ayers a member of the Wilde Flowers, the seed of the Canterbury scene.
grp.hugh-hopper.hikaye: Hopper was the Soft Machine's road manager before replacing Kevin Ayers on bass in 1969; his fuzz bass and his tape-loop experiments defined the Volume Two to Six albums, and pieces such as 'Facelift' and 'Kings and Queens' are his. He left in 1973 and made 1984, an album of tape loops and repetitive bass pieces named after Orwell's novel. Through the seventies and eighties he moved between Canterbury and jazz-rock groups — Isotope, Gilgamesh, Stomu Yamash'ta, Carla Bley's band, Soft Heap with Elton Dean, Alan Gowen and Pip Pyle — and released solo records such as Hopper Tunity Box. In the 2000s he returned to the old repertoire in Soft Works and Soft Machine Legacy, and kept recording until shortly before his death in 2009.
grp.hugh-hopper.dna: Distorted, melodic fuzz bass used like a lead instrument; repeating loops and riffs in odd meters; a dry humour and a taste for the raw and unfinished.
grp.hugh-hopper.uyeler: Hugh Hopper (bass, tape loops, composition). Partners: Elton Dean, Pip Pyle, Alan Gowen, Mike Travis, Dave Stewart, Gary Windo, Mark Hewins, John Etheridge, Kramer.
grp.hugh-hopper.gecisler: Wilde Flowers → Soft Machine (1969–73) → solo → Isotope → Gilgamesh → Carla Bley band → Soft Heap / Soft Head → Soft Works → Soft Machine Legacy (2004–09). Played on Robert Wyatt's, Kevin Ayers's and Syd Barrett's records.
grp.hugh-hopper.etki: Hopper's loops and fuzz bass anticipate minimalism in rock and later drone and post-rock; he is the composer behind the Soft Machine's most hypnotic music.
grp.hugh-hopper.ipucu: Hear 'Facelift' on Third first — his piece, his bass.
1984 is closer to Terry Riley than to rock: listen as you would to a tape-music piece.
alb.hugh-hopper-1973-1984.an: His first solo album after the Soft Machine: tape loops, multi-tracked bass and short jazz pieces, inspired by Orwell's novel.
alb.hugh-hopper-1973-1984.kadro: Hopper + Lol Coxhill, Gary Windo, Pye Hastings, John Marshall, Nick Evans
alb.hugh-hopper-1977-hopper-tunity-box.a: His most approachable Canterbury jazz-rock record, with Dave Stewart on keyboards and a tight horn section.
alb.hugh-hopper-1977-hopper-tunity-box.k: Hopper + Elton Dean, Gary Windo, Dave Stewart, Mike Travis, Mark Charig and others
alb.hugh-hopper-1979-soft-heap.an: The quartet of two Soft Machine alumni with Gilgamesh's Alan Gowen and Hatfield's Pip Pyle: loose, improvised Canterbury jazz.
alb.hugh-hopper-1979-soft-heap.kadro: Soft Heap: Hugh Hopper, Elton Dean, Alan Gowen, Pip Pyle
grp.daevid-allen.name: Daevid Allen (solo and Planet Gong)
grp.daevid-allen.kurulus: 1938–2015. Born in Melbourne; arrived in England in the early sixties and lodged with the Wyatt family in Kent. Co-founder of Soft Machine (1966) and founder of Gong.
grp.daevid-allen.hikaye: Allen played guitar in the first Soft Machine, but after a French tour in 1967 he was refused re-entry to Britain. In Paris, during the events of May 1968, he and Gilli Smyth began what became Gong, whose 'Radio Gnome Invisible' trilogy (Flying Teapot, Angel's Egg, You) built a whole comic mythology of pothead pixies and teapots. He left Gong in 1975, settled in Deià on Mallorca and recorded Good Morning with the local band Euterpe. In 1977 he toured as Planet Gong with the English free-festival band Here & Now, and in New York formed New York Gong with Bill Laswell. After years in Australia he returned to reunited Gong line-ups (Shapeshifter, Zero to Infinity, 2032) and many side projects (University of Errors, Acid Mothers Gong). Gong continued after his death in 2015, led by Kavus Torabi.
grp.daevid-allen.dna: Glissando guitar (a slide bowed with a metal rod through echo units), whispered and chanted poetry, humour and mysticism together, and an anarchic festival spirit.
grp.daevid-allen.uyeler: Daevid Allen (guitar, vocals). Partners: Gilli Smyth, Robert Wyatt, Didier Malherbe, Here & Now (Keith the Bass, Steffi Sharpstrings, Kif Kif Le Batteur), Bill Laswell, Euterpe.
grp.daevid-allen.gecisler: Soft Machine (1966–67) → Gong (1969–75) → solo / Planet Gong with Here & Now (1977) → New York Gong (1979–80) → Gong reunions and Mother Gong (Gilli Smyth) → University of Errors, Acid Mothers Gong. Steve Hillage, Tim Blake, Pierre Moerlen and Didier Malherbe all came through Allen's Gong.
grp.daevid-allen.etki: Allen linked the Canterbury scene to French psychedelia, the free-festival culture and later the space-rock and psytrance world; his mix of whimsy and cosmic idealism is unique in prog.
grp.daevid-allen.ipucu: Banana Moon has Robert Wyatt on drums and vocals: a Canterbury reunion just after the split.
Live Floating Anarchy 1977 shows the punk-era Gong: raw, fast and stoned.
alb.daevid-allen-1971-banana-moon.an: His first solo album, recorded in London with old friends: whimsical songs, a Wyatt vocal and the first hints of the Gong mythology.
alb.daevid-allen-1971-banana-moon.kadro: Allen + Robert Wyatt, Gary Wright, Archie Leggett, Pip Pyle, Gilli Smyth and others
alb.daevid-allen-1971-banana-moon.tr: It’s the Time of Your Life
alb.daevid-allen-1976-good-morning.an: Recorded on Mallorca after leaving Gong: gentle, acoustic, folk-psychedelic songs with the local band Euterpe.
alb.daevid-allen-1977-now-is-the-happies: The second Mallorca record: acoustic poetry, mantras and a quieter, more personal tone.
Why Do We Treat Ourselves Like We Do
alb.daevid-allen-1978-live-floating-anar: Allen and Gilli Smyth fronting the free-festival band Here & Now: a raw, punk-era version of the Gong universe.
Planet Gong: Allen, Gilli Smyth, Here & Now
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.name: Pierre Moerlen's Gong
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.kurulus: 1976–1988, Paris/London. The instrumental, percussion-led Gong that continued under drummer Pierre Moerlen (1952–2005) after Daevid Allen and Steve Hillage had left.
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.hikaye: Moerlen, a classically trained percussionist from Colmar, joined Gong for Angel's Egg (1973). After the departure of Allen (1975) and Hillage, the band became a jazz-rock ensemble built around vibraphone, marimba and drums: Shamal and Gazeuse! (both 1976) are its start. Expresso II (1978), still credited to Gong, featured Allan Holdsworth, Darryl Way and Mick Taylor as guests. From 1978 the band carried Moerlen's name: Downwind (1979) brought in Mike Oldfield and Steve Winwood, and Time Is the Key (1979) and Leave It Open (1981) refined the mallet-percussion sound. Moerlen also played with Mike Oldfield (Incantations, the Exposed tour) and Brand X. He died in 2005.
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.dna: Interlocking vibraphone, marimba and glockenspiel patterns over fast, precise drumming; fusion guitar and bass; a European, almost minimalist clarity rather than Allen's psychedelia.
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.uyeler: Pierre Moerlen (drums, vibraphone, marimba), Benoit Moerlen (vibraphone), Mireille Bauer (marimba, percussion), Hansford Rowe (bass), Bon Lozaga (guitar), François Causse (percussion), Didier Malherbe; guests Allan Holdsworth, Mick Taylor, Darryl Way, Mike Oldfield, Steve Winwood.
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.gecisler: Gong (1973–78) → Pierre Moerlen's Gong (1978–88). Moerlen also played with Mike Oldfield and Brand X; Hansford Rowe and Bon Lozaga later formed Gongzilla (1990s).
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.etki: Proof that Gong's name could stand for a completely different music; one of the finest mallet-percussion bands in jazz-rock, and a direct link from Canterbury to Oldfield's world.
grp.pierre-moerlen-s-gong.ipucu: Start with Gazeuse! on the Gong node, then Expresso II.
On Downwind, hear Mike Oldfield's guitar on the title piece and compare it with Incantations, where Moerlen plays.
alb.pierre-moerlen-s-gong-1978-expresso-: The last album still credited to Gong: virtuoso mallet-percussion jazz-rock with Holdsworth and Darryl Way as guests.
Pierre Moerlen, Benoit Moerlen, Mireille Bauer, Hansford Rowe, Bon Lozaga, François Causse + Allan Holdsworth, Mick Taylor, Darryl Way
The first album under Moerlen's name, more song-based, with Mike Oldfield and Steve Winwood as guests.
Pierre Moerlen + Mike Oldfield, Steve Winwood, Mick Taylor, Didier Lockwood and others
alb.pierre-moerlen-s-gong-1979-time-is-t: Short, crystalline instrumental pieces built on vibraphone and marimba.
Pierre Moerlen, Benoit Moerlen, Hansford Rowe, Bon Lozaga and others
alb.pierre-moerlen-s-gong-1981-leave-it-: A lighter, funk-tinged fusion record from the band's last stable period.
grp.gilgamesh.name: Gilgamesh
grp.gilgamesh.kurulus: 1972, London. Keyboardist Alan Gowen's Canterbury jazz-rock band.
grp.gilgamesh.hikaye: Gilgamesh came out of the London jazz-rock scene around Gowen (keyboards), Phil Lee (guitar), Jeff Clyne (bass) and Mike Travis (drums). In 1973 they shared concerts with Hatfield and the North as a 'double quartet', with Gowen and Dave Stewart writing for both bands — the seed of National Health, of which Gowen was a founding member. Their debut Gilgamesh (1975), produced by Dave Stewart, is one of the purest Canterbury jazz records. A second album, Another Fine Tune You've Got Me Into (1978), had Hugh Hopper on bass and Trevor Tomkins on drums. Gowen later played in Soft Heap and recorded with Hopper and Richard Sinclair; he died in 1981 at the age of 33.
grp.gilgamesh.dna: Long, through-composed pieces with Fender Rhodes and synthesizer, clean guitar and fluid electric bass; soft dynamics, complex harmony and few solos for their own sake.
grp.gilgamesh.uyeler: Alan Gowen (keyboards), Phil Lee (guitar), Jeff Clyne, later Hugh Hopper (bass), Mike Travis, later Trevor Tomkins (drums); guest Amanda Parsons (vocals).
grp.gilgamesh.gecisler: Gilgamesh + Hatfield and the North (1973 'double quartet') → National Health (Gowen, 1975–76) → Gilgamesh II (1978) → Soft Heap (Gowen, Hopper, Elton Dean, Pip Pyle). Phil Lee and Jeff Clyne also played together in Nucleus and with Ian Carr.
grp.gilgamesh.etki: The most jazz-oriented branch of Canterbury; Gowen's writing shaped National Health's sound and continues in Dave Stewart's later work.
grp.gilgamesh.ipucu: Listen right after Hatfield's The Rotters' Club — then National Health's first album to hear Gowen's role.
Pay attention to how little the pieces repeat: Gilgamesh wrote like chamber composers.
alb.gilgamesh-1975-gilgamesh.an: The debut, produced by Dave Stewart: subtle, intricate Canterbury jazz-rock and a key link between Hatfield and National Health.
alb.gilgamesh-1975-gilgamesh.kadro: Alan Gowen, Phil Lee, Jeff Clyne, Mike Travis + Amanda Parsons
alb.gilgamesh-1978-another-fine-tune-you: The second line-up with Hugh Hopper: more open and jazz-oriented, with long improvised passages.
Alan Gowen, Phil Lee, Hugh Hopper, Trevor Tomkins
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.name: Dave Stewart & Barbara Gaskin
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.kurulus: 1981, London. Keyboardist Dave Stewart (born 1950; Uriel, Egg, Hatfield and the North, National Health, Bruford) and singer Barbara Gaskin (Spirogyra, Hatfield's 'Northettes').
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.hikaye: Stewart met Gaskin in the early seventies when she sang with Spirogyra and, with Amanda Parsons and Ann Rosenthal, as the Northettes on Hatfield and the North's records. After National Health and Bruford, Stewart had a surprise hit with Colin Blunstone ('What Becomes of the Broken Hearted', 1981), and then with Gaskin a UK number one, a synthesizer version of Lesley Gore's 'It's My Party' (1981). The duo continued with intricately produced pop covers and originals (Up from the Dark, The Big Idea, Spin), and from 2009 with longer, more personal albums on their own label Broken Records (Green and Blue, Star Clocks). Stewart is also the author of well-known books on music theory for rock musicians.
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.dna: Meticulous, layered synthesizer pop with Canterbury harmony hidden inside: unusual chord changes, odd bar lengths and Gaskin's clear, unforced voice.
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.uyeler: Dave Stewart (keyboards, programming), Barbara Gaskin (vocals). Guests over the years include Pip Pyle, Gavin Harrison, Andy Reynolds, Jakko Jakszyk, Bill Bruford.
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.gecisler: Uriel / Arzachel → Egg → Khan → Hatfield and the North → National Health → Bruford (Stewart); Spirogyra → Hatfield's Northettes (Gaskin) → duo (1981–). Gavin Harrison and Jakko Jakszyk, both later in King Crimson, played on their records.
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.etki: Proof that Canterbury harmony could live inside chart pop; Stewart's arrangements and books influenced many keyboard players.
grp.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin.ipucu: Hear Gaskin's voice on Hatfield's 'Calyx' first.
Green and Blue is the most 'Canterbury' of their albums: long songs, odd meters, Pip Pyle on drums.
alb.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin-1990-the: Glossy, intricate synth-pop with covers and originals; a showcase for Stewart's production.
alb.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin-1991-spi: A more personal follow-up with longer songs and richer harmony.
alb.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin-2009-gre: The comeback after eighteen years: mature, melancholic songs with real Canterbury complexity.
Dave Stewart, Barbara Gaskin + Pip Pyle, Gavin Harrison, Andy Reynolds and others
alb.dave-stewart-barbara-gaskin-2018-sta: Wide-ranging songs about time and memory, with orchestral colours.
grp.slapp-happy.name: Slapp Happy
grp.slapp-happy.kurulus: 1972, Hamburg. Dagmar Krause (vocals), Anthony Moore (keyboards, composition) and Peter Blegvad (guitar, vocals, lyrics) — a German-English-American avant-pop trio.
grp.slapp-happy.hikaye: Moore, an English experimental composer working in Germany, formed Slapp Happy with his girlfriend Dagmar Krause and the American writer and guitarist Peter Blegvad. Their debut Sort Of (1972) was recorded with the krautrock band Faust as backing group. Virgin rejected their second album (later released as Acnalbasac Noom) but had them re-record it in London: Slapp Happy (1974), also known as Casablanca Moon. In 1974–75 they merged with Henry Cow: Desperate Straights was credited to both, and In Praise of Learning (on the Henry Cow node) followed. Moore and Blegvad soon left; Krause stayed in Henry Cow and then Art Bears. The trio has reunited occasionally (Ça Va, 1997; concerts in 2016).
grp.slapp-happy.dna: Short, crooked art songs: cabaret, Brecht–Weill, chanson and pop in odd shapes, with Krause's cool, precise voice and Blegvad's surreal lyrics.
grp.slapp-happy.uyeler: Dagmar Krause (vocals), Anthony Moore (piano, keyboards), Peter Blegvad (guitar, vocals).
grp.slapp-happy.gecisler: Slapp Happy (1972–75) → merger with Henry Cow (1974–75) → Krause to Henry Cow, Art Bears, News from Babel; Moore to solo work and lyric writing for Pink Floyd (A Momentary Lapse of Reason) and Richard Wright (Broken China); Blegvad to solo records and the Golden Palominos.
grp.slapp-happy.etki: Slapp Happy brought song and wit into Rock in Opposition, and Anthony Moore later carried something of that sensibility into Pink Floyd's lyrics.
grp.slapp-happy.ipucu: Start with Casablanca Moon (the 1974 album), then Desperate Straights.
Compare Krause's voice here with her later Art Bears recordings.
alb.slapp-happy-1972-sort-of.an: The debut, recorded in Germany with Faust as backing band: naïve, strange and charming pop songs.
alb.slapp-happy-1974-slapp-happy.an: Also known as Casablanca Moon: polished avant-pop for Virgin, with orchestral arrangements and the title song.
alb.slapp-happy-1975-desperate-straights: The first product of the merger with Henry Cow: short, angular chamber songs with Cow's instrumentalists.
grp.fred-frith.name: Fred Frith
grp.fred-frith.kurulus: Born 1949 in Heathfield, Sussex. Guitarist, violinist and composer; co-founder of Henry Cow at Cambridge University in 1968.
grp.fred-frith.hikaye: Frith and Tim Hodgkinson founded Henry Cow; Frith's compositions and his prepared and table-top guitar became central to the band. Guitar Solos (1974) was one of the first albums of entirely improvised, prepared electric guitar. After Henry Cow and Art Bears he moved to New York, where he formed Massacre with Bill Laswell, recorded Gravity (1980) and Speechless (1981) with the Rock in Opposition bands Samla Mammas Manna, the Muffins and Etron Fou Leloublan, and played in Skeleton Crew and John Zorn's Naked City. He has written for dance, film and string quartet, and taught composition at Mills College in California. The documentary Step Across the Border (1990) follows his work.
grp.fred-frith.dna: Folk-dance rhythms, odd meters and sudden noise; the guitar laid flat and played with objects; a composer's control inside apparently chaotic music.
grp.fred-frith.uyeler: Fred Frith (guitar, violin, bass, keyboards, vocals). Partners: Chris Cutler, Tim Hodgkinson, Bill Laswell, Fred Maher, John Zorn, Tom Cora, Zeena Parkins, Samla Mammas Manna, the Muffins, Etron Fou Leloublan.
grp.fred-frith.gecisler: Henry Cow (1968–78) → Art Bears (1978–81) → Massacre, Skeleton Crew, Naked City (New York) → composition and teaching. Played on Robert Wyatt's Rock Bottom and with Brian Eno (Before and After Science).
grp.fred-frith.etki: Frith turned the guitar into a sound-object for a whole generation of experimental players, and his Gravity made a dance record out of Rock in Opposition.
grp.fred-frith.ipucu: Hear him in Henry Cow's 'Ruins' first.
Gravity is surprisingly joyful: folk dances in impossible meters.
Guitar Solos is pure sound — listen as you would to electronic music.
alb.fred-frith-1974-guitar-solos.an: Improvised pieces for prepared electric guitar, recorded without overdubs; a landmark of experimental guitar.
alb.fred-frith-1980-gravity.an: A 'dance' album recorded with Sweden's Samla Mammas Manna and America's the Muffins: folk rhythms in odd meters.
alb.fred-frith-1980-gravity.kadro: Frith + Samla Mammas Manna, the Muffins
alb.fred-frith-1980-gravity.tr: The Boy Beats the Rams (Kluk Tluce Berany)
alb.fred-frith-1981-speechless.an: Rawer and noisier, with the French band Etron Fou Leloublan and his New York trio Massacre.
alb.fred-frith-1981-speechless.kadro: Frith + Etron Fou Leloublan, Massacre (Bill Laswell, Fred Maher)
grp.chris-cutler.name: Chris Cutler (Cassiber, News from Babel)
grp.chris-cutler.kurulus: Born 1947 in Washington, D.C., raised in England. Drummer, lyricist and theorist; Henry Cow's drummer from 1971 and founder of the Recommended Records label.
grp.chris-cutler.hikaye: Cutler joined Henry Cow in 1971 and wrote many of its lyrics; in 1978 he co-organised the first Rock in Opposition festival, uniting Henry Cow with Stormy Six, Samla Mammas Manna, Univers Zero and Etron Fou Leloublan. With Frith and Dagmar Krause he formed Art Bears, then Cassiber with the German musicians Heiner Goebbels, Alfred Harth and Christoph Anders, and News from Babel with Lindsay Cooper, Zeena Parkins and Krause (Robert Wyatt sang on their second album). He also drummed for Pere Ubu, the Science Group and many improvising projects, ran the ReR label and wrote the essay collection File Under Popular.
grp.chris-cutler.dna: Drumming as orchestration: unusual kits with electrified and found objects, fragmented rhythms and a political, literary approach to lyrics.
grp.chris-cutler.uyeler: Chris Cutler (drums, electrified drums, lyrics). Cassiber: Heiner Goebbels, Alfred Harth, Christoph Anders. News from Babel: Lindsay Cooper, Zeena Parkins, Dagmar Krause, guest Robert Wyatt.
grp.chris-cutler.gecisler: Henry Cow (1971–78) → Art Bears (1978–81) → Cassiber (1982–92), News from Babel (1983–86), Pere Ubu (1987–90s), duo with Fred Frith. Also played on David Bedford's Star's End.
grp.chris-cutler.etki: Through ReR and Rock in Opposition, Cutler built the network that kept European avant-rock alive; the 'RIO' label still describes a whole genre.
grp.chris-cutler.ipucu: Start with News from Babel's Work Resumed on the Tower — Henry Cow's song side, refined.
Cassiber's Man or Monkey is harsher: sampling, cut-ups and Brecht-like vocals.
alb.chris-cutler-1982-man-or-monkey.an: The debut of the German-English quartet Cassiber: collage, noise and political song.
alb.chris-cutler-1982-man-or-monkey.kadr: Cassiber: Chris Cutler, Heiner Goebbels, Alfred Harth, Christoph Anders
alb.chris-cutler-1982-man-or-monkey.tr: Sag mir wo die Blumen sind
alb.chris-cutler-1984-work-resumed-on-th: Chamber songs on the theme of the Tower of Babel, written by Lindsay Cooper with Cutler's lyrics.
News from Babel: Chris Cutler, Lindsay Cooper, Zeena Parkins, Dagmar Krause
alb.chris-cutler-1986-letters-home.an: The second and last News from Babel album, with Robert Wyatt among the singers.
alb.chris-cutler-1986-letters-home.kadro: News from Babel + Robert Wyatt, Phil Minton, Sally Potter
grp.lindsay-cooper.name: Lindsay Cooper
grp.lindsay-cooper.kurulus: 1951–2013, London. Bassoonist, oboist, flautist and composer; a member of Comus and Henry Cow.
grp.lindsay-cooper.hikaye: Cooper studied at the Royal College of Music, played in the folk-rock band Comus and joined Henry Cow in 1974, bringing bassoon and oboe to its sound (Unrest, In Praise of Learning, Western Culture, to which she contributed compositions). She also played on Mike Oldfield's Hergest Ridge and with Egg and Steve Hillage. After Henry Cow she co-founded the Feminist Improvising Group, wrote the score for Sally Potter's film The Gold Diggers, and composed the song cycles of News from Babel. Her own records — Rags (1980), The Golddiggers (1983), Music for Other Occasions (1986) and Oh Moscow (1991) — combine chamber music, song and jazz. She stopped performing in the late nineties and died in 2013.
grp.lindsay-cooper.dna: Woodwind lines with a melancholy, slightly sour colour; political song cycles; chamber writing that sits between Weill, English folk and free jazz.
grp.lindsay-cooper.uyeler: Lindsay Cooper (bassoon, oboe, flute, saxophones, piano). Partners: Chris Cutler, Fred Frith, Dagmar Krause, Sally Potter, Georgie Born, Maggie Nicols.
grp.lindsay-cooper.gecisler: Comus → Henry Cow (1974–78) → Feminist Improvising Group → News from Babel (1983–86) → solo and film music. Guest on Mike Oldfield's Hergest Ridge, Egg's The Civil Surface and Steve Hillage's records.
grp.lindsay-cooper.etki: She brought the woodwind and a feminist perspective into Rock in Opposition; her Oh Moscow is one of its most ambitious song cycles.
grp.lindsay-cooper.ipucu: Listen to her bassoon on Henry Cow's Western Culture first.
Rags tells the story of London's sweatshop seamstresses — read the notes while listening.
alb.lindsay-cooper-1980-rags.an: A song cycle about the seamstresses of nineteenth-century London, with Henry Cow colleagues.
alb.lindsay-cooper-1980-rags.kadro: Cooper + Fred Frith, Chris Cutler, Georgie Born, Sally Potter
Music for Sally Potter's feminist film, with Julie Christie: tangos, waltzes and chamber pieces.
Cooper + Georgie Born, Chris Cutler, Sally Potter and others
alb.lindsay-cooper-1991-oh-moscow.an: A song cycle about the Cold War and the divided Europe, with lyrics by Sally Potter, recorded live in Victoriaville.
alb.lindsay-cooper-1991-oh-moscow.kadro: Cooper + Sally Potter, Phil Minton and others
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.name: Darryl Way's Wolf
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.kurulus: 1972, London. Formed by violinist Darryl Way after he left Curved Air, with guitarist John Etheridge and drummer Ian Mosley.
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.hikaye: Way had co-written much of Curved Air's music ('Vivaldi', 'Back Street Luv'). With Wolf he aimed at an instrumental, virtuoso jazz-rock with classical roots. The debut Canis Lupus (1973) was produced by King Crimson's Ian McDonald and featured singer John Hodkinson; Saturation Point and Night Music (1973–74) were largely instrumental. The band split in 1974: Way returned to Curved Air, John Etheridge joined Soft Machine, and Ian Mosley went on to Trace, Steve Hackett and, from 1984, Marillion.
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.dna: Fast, classically phrased violin and guitar lines, odd-meter riffs and a powerful rhythm section; between Curved Air's art rock and Mahavishnu-style fusion.
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.uyeler: Darryl Way (violin, keyboards), John Etheridge (guitar), Dek Messecar (bass, vocals), Ian Mosley (drums), John Hodkinson (vocals on Canis Lupus).
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.gecisler: Curved Air → Wolf (1972–74) → back to Curved Air (Way); John Etheridge → Soft Machine (1975–78); Ian Mosley → Trace → Steve Hackett → Marillion (1984–).
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.etki: A short-lived band whose members connect four nodes of this atlas: Curved Air, King Crimson (through McDonald), Soft Machine and Marillion.
grp.darryl-way-s-wolf.ipucu: Hear Way's 'Vivaldi' on Curved Air's debut first.
Listen to Ian Mosley here, then on Marillion's Misplaced Childhood.
alb.darryl-way-s-wolf-1973-canis-lupus.a: The debut, produced by Ian McDonald: songs and violin-led instrumentals between Curved Air and jazz-rock.
alb.darryl-way-s-wolf-1973-canis-lupus.k: Darryl Way, John Etheridge, Dek Messecar, Ian Mosley, John Hodkinson
alb.darryl-way-s-wolf-1973-saturation-po: Mostly instrumental and more virtuoso: Way and Etheridge trading fast lines over Mosley's drumming.

alb.darryl-way-s-wolf-1974-night-music.a: The last album, mixing fusion workouts with lyrical violin pieces.

grp.woolly-wolstenholme.name: Woolly Wolstenholme (Maestoso)
grp.woolly-wolstenholme.kurulus: 1947–2010, Oldham. Stuart 'Woolly' Wolstenholme, Barclay James Harvest's keyboardist and Mellotron player from 1966 to 1979.
grp.woolly-wolstenholme.hikaye: Wolstenholme was the orchestral voice of Barclay James Harvest, playing Mellotron and writing grand, sombre songs such as 'Beyond the Grave' and 'Ra'. Uneasy with the band's softer, more commercial direction, he left in 1979 and immediately recorded Maestoso (1980) with his own band of the same name. He then largely withdrew from music, working as a farmer, before returning in the late nineties with new Maestoso albums and joining John Lees' Barclay James Harvest (Nexus, 1999), with which he toured until shortly before his death in December 2010.
grp.woolly-wolstenholme.dna: Mellotron choirs and strings, slow, solemn melodies and dramatic, almost classical song forms; the darker, symphonic side of Barclay James Harvest.
grp.woolly-wolstenholme.uyeler: Woolly Wolstenholme (keyboards, Mellotron, vocals). Maestoso: session players.
grp.woolly-wolstenholme.gecisler: The Blues Keepers → Barclay James Harvest (1966–79) → Maestoso (1980) → farming → Maestoso revival and John Lees' Barclay James Harvest (1998–2010).
grp.woolly-wolstenholme.etki: He gave Barclay James Harvest its 'Poor Man's Moody Blues' orchestral grandeur; Maestoso is a small classic of late symphonic prog.
grp.woolly-wolstenholme.ipucu: Hear 'Beyond the Grave' (Time Honoured Ghosts era) first.
Maestoso sounds like the BJH album the band chose not to make in 1980.
alb.woolly-wolstenholme-1980-maestoso.an: His first record after leaving BJH: Mellotron-heavy, symphonic songs in the band's early style.
alb.woolly-wolstenholme-1980-maestoso.tr: Mæstoso - A Hymn in the Roof of the World
grp.david-bedford.name: David Bedford
grp.david-bedford.kurulus: 1937–2011, London. A composer trained with Luigi Nono who moved between contemporary music, education and rock.
grp.david-bedford.hikaye: Bedford played keyboards and arranged for Kevin Ayers and the Whole World (1970–71), where he met the teenage Mike Oldfield. He arranged and conducted The Orchestral Tubular Bells (1975) and made a series of orchestral-rock albums for Virgin: Star's End (1974), with Oldfield and Chris Cutler and the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra, The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1975) and The Odyssey (1976). He also wrote many works for school choirs and children, string arrangements for pop records, and scores for documentaries.
grp.david-bedford.dna: Slowly building orchestral textures, choirs used as instruments, electric guitar against strings; a contemporary composer's sense of sound-masses rather than melodies.
grp.david-bedford.uyeler: David Bedford (keyboards, composition). Partners: Mike Oldfield, Kevin Ayers, Lol Coxhill, Chris Cutler, the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra.
grp.david-bedford.gecisler: Contemporary music (Nono) → Kevin Ayers and the Whole World (1970–71) → Mike Oldfield (arrangements) → orchestral-rock albums for Virgin → choral and educational works.
grp.david-bedford.etki: Bedford is the bridge between Oldfield's world and English contemporary music; his orchestral albums anticipate later ambient and post-rock orchestration.
grp.david-bedford.ipucu: Hear The Orchestral Tubular Bells on the Oldfield node first.
Star's End works best loud: listen to how the orchestra and Oldfield's guitar swap roles.
alb.david-bedford-1972-nurses-song-with-: Early experiments for voices, plastic pipes and guitars, with Ayers and the young Oldfield.
Bedford + Mike Oldfield, Kevin Ayers and others
alb.david-bedford-1974-star-s-end.an: A two-part work for orchestra, electric guitar and drums; Oldfield and Cutler as soloists.
alb.david-bedford-1974-star-s-end.kadro: Royal Philharmonic Orchestra + Mike Oldfield, Chris Cutler

grp.alan-parsons-project.name: The Alan Parsons Project
grp.alan-parsons-project.kurulus: 1975, London. Engineer and producer Alan Parsons and songwriter Eric Woolfson (1945–2009).
grp.alan-parsons-project.hikaye: Parsons engineered at Abbey Road (the Beatles' last sessions, Pink Floyd's The Dark Side of the Moon) and produced Pilot, Cockney Rebel and Al Stewart. With Woolfson, then working as a manager, he conceived a 'project' rather than a band: concept albums made in the studio with a rotating cast of singers and a core of musicians from Pilot. Tales of Mystery and Imagination (1976), after Edgar Allan Poe, was followed by I Robot (1977), Pyramid, Eve and The Turn of a Friendly Card, and by the hit album Eye in the Sky (1982). The Project never toured during its lifetime. After Gaudi (1987) Parsons and Woolfson parted; Parsons continued under his own name, Woolfson wrote musicals.
grp.alan-parsons-project.dna: Immaculate studio sound, orchestral arrangements by Andrew Powell, instrumentals between the songs, and a different lead singer for nearly every track; concept albums with a pop core.
grp.alan-parsons-project.uyeler: Alan Parsons (production, keyboards), Eric Woolfson (songwriting, keyboards, vocals). Core musicians: Ian Bairnson, David Paton, Stuart Elliott, Andrew Powell (arrangements). Singers include Lenny Zakatek, Chris Rainbow, Colin Blunstone, John Miles, Arthur Brown, Elmer Gantry.
grp.alan-parsons-project.gecisler: Abbey Road and Pink Floyd (Parsons) → production for Pilot and Cockney Rebel → The Alan Parsons Project (1975–90) → Alan Parsons solo / Alan Parsons Live Project. Arthur Brown sings on Tales; Colin Blunstone (the Zombies) on several albums; David Paton later played with Camel and Kate Bush.
grp.alan-parsons-project.etki: The Project made concept prog into a radio format; its studio craft and orchestral pop influenced the AOR era and later the film-music style of many producers.
grp.alan-parsons-project.ipucu: Start with Tales of Mystery and Imagination: Poe set to music, with Arthur Brown on 'The Tell-Tale Heart'.
Then compare the engineering with The Dark Side of the Moon — the same ears.
alb.the-alan-parsons-project-1976-tales-: Edgar Allan Poe's stories as a concept album, with the orchestral suite 'The Fall of the House of Usher'.

sec.22.title: The Jethro Tull Universe
sec.22.intro: Ian Anderson's flute, folk melodies and blues roots made Jethro Tull a world of its own within prog: from the blues of This Was to the concept albums Thick as a Brick and A Passion Play and the folk-rock trilogy of the late seventies. Anderson's solo albums continue the same line, up to the sequel Thick as a Brick 2.
sec.23.title: The Van der Graaf Universe
sec.23.intro: The darkest and most intense corner of English prog: Peter Hammill's voice and lyrics, Hugh Banton's organ, David Jackson's saxophones and Guy Evans's drums, without a lead guitar. Van der Graaf Generator and Hammill's solo work have run in parallel for fifty years; the boundary between them was never sharp.
sec.24.title: Rock in Opposition — Henry Cow and the Avant-Garde
sec.24.intro: In 1978 Henry Cow invited four bands from the continent to London under the name Rock in Opposition: a movement against the music industry, and a style of its own — composed, dissonant, politically engaged rock that borrows from contemporary classical music and free improvisation. Around the members of Henry Cow (Fred Frith, Chris Cutler, Lindsay Cooper) grew Art Bears, the song-based detour of Slapp Happy and, close by, the post-punk experiments of This Heat.
sec.25.title: The Gong Universe
sec.25.intro: Daevid Allen, an Australian who had to leave Soft Machine when he was refused re-entry into Britain, founded Gong in France: psychedelic space rock, the Radio Gnome mythology of pothead pixies and flying teapots, and Steve Hillage's glissando guitar. After Allen left, Pierre Moerlen turned the band into a percussion-led jazz-rock group, while Hillage carried the cosmic side into his solo work and later into the dance music of System 7.
sec.10.intro: Independent bands outside the big universes, fed by the same symphonic and folk sources: Gentle Giant's counterpoint, Camel's melodic instrumentals, Renaissance's classical voice, Curved Air's violin, Darryl Way's own band Wolf, Greenslade's twin keyboards, Gryphon's medieval instruments, Family's eclectic rock with Roger Chapman's voice, the flute-and-guitar duels of Focus from the Netherlands, the orchestral pastoral rock of Barclay James Harvest and the solo work of their keyboardist Woolly Wolstenholme.
sec.26.title: The Led Zeppelin Universe
sec.26.intro: From the Yardbirds, where Jimmy Page played alongside Jeff Beck, came the New Yardbirds and, in 1968, Led Zeppelin: blues, folk and Eastern modes turned into the model of hard rock. The band ended with John Bonham's death in 1980; Page went on with The Firm, with David Coverdale and, together with Plant again, with No Quarter, while Plant built a solo career that runs from synth pop to the Americana of Raising Sand.
